# S1 proofs

Final version of 2026-10-28T17:48Z (end of the run). This file collects the complete proofs behind every statement labelled THEOREM in
the report and in S1_CLOSURE.md. Each section was written and checked as a separate unit; each states its exact
hypotheses, argument, dependencies and scope, and no statement is used outside that scope. Some sections record
intermediate results that were later sharpened; where a later section supersedes an earlier constant, the later
section says so. The shipped files are those listed, with their folders, sizes and SHA-256 hashes, in
S1_NUMERICAL_CERTIFICATES.md (certificates folder) and the programs of the scripts folder; every file that the
shipped check, recomputation and recheck programs read is among them (all of them ran from a fresh restore,
S1_RESTART.md section 9). The text also names records and programs of the independent checking of single
sections that are not shipped (for example audit_serialization.py in P11.3, audit_recursive.py and its record
and log in P33, audit_bound.py and its record and log in P35, audit_extended.json and summary.json in P42), so a
file name in the text, even after the words certificate file, does not by itself mean that the file is shipped.

Convention: a strict inequality between homogeneous quantities of an argument h (norms, seminorms, or such a
quantity times a constant), for example N(h) < C E(h), is asserted for h nonzero; at h = 0 both sides vanish and
the non-strict form holds. No coefficient or conclusion depends on the strict form at zero.

Section P10.2 (tail repair) is independently checked: membership of its residual, the coefficient transfer at
R = 2^1024 and the residual lower bound 2^1028. Section P8.2 and the statement audit in P8.3 record corrections to
earlier drafts of the hypothesis list; S1_CLOSURE.md is the corrected statement. Section P8.4 gives the sharper
constants (rate 1/10 - 4800 s - 5 N_s(k)/s^(1/2)) behind version (b) of the conditional existence theorem.
Section P12 certifies whole-plane weighted residual norms by exact integration. Section P13 proves that a residual
sector r^q E with q >= -2 excludes every exact solution in the affine class reference + N_s (Theorem E of
S1_CLOSURE.md) and that the exponent cannot vary in that class; P13.1 is the characteristic version with the forced
leading correction. Section P14 constructs exact finite rational references whose residual lies in the space and
shows by certified point values that nine of the ten explicit variants violate the energy-matrix hypothesis; P14.2
certifies a whole-plane Hessian residual norm of one variant by interval polynomials. Section P15 gives sharp
weighted transform bounds for the negative-order norm with homogeneous and regularized weights and shows that the pure
homogeneous weight is not coercive; it is not used for closure. Section P16 shows that midpoint angular sampling with
too few angles can miss a residual entirely and gives a sufficient number of angles; it concerns floating-point
diagnostics only. Section P17 proves the conditional existence theorem D_w in the weighted fractional space N^w_s
(far-field weight with R = 2^35), lists the complete reference contract and bounds the residual of the checkpoint
from below in that space (P17.7: an annular duality bound N^w_s(F) > 2^89, more than 2^135 times the threshold).
Sections P6.12 to P6.16 sharpen the constants of the weighted realization X_W of P6 (radial-resolvent commutator,
derivative-energy coefficients, radial weights on higher background derivatives, the inverse norm, and a weighted
low bilinear bound); P14.3 writes one repaired reference exactly in the original stable radial coordinates.
Section P18 lowers the weight radius of Theorem D_w to R = 2^32 (decay exponent 4/9 in the low-energy bounds) and
repeats the annular bound there (N^w_s(F) > 2^82, more than 2^128 times the threshold). Section P19 keeps the
coefficients of the lower derivative components of the norm and so improves the threshold of Theorem D_w to
2^-35 in the same space (gaps more than 2^124 at R = 2^35 and 2^117 at R = 2^32). Section P20 checks exactly
that two projected refits have residuals in both spaces and shows by certified point values that they violate the
energy-matrix condition and the smallness condition. Section P21 uses the reality of the density to lower the
weighted velocity constant to 13/3 and the radial commutator coefficient to 21/2, which lowers the weight radius of
Theorem D_w to R = 2^31 with the constants of P19, and repeats the annular bound there (N^w_s(F) > 2^80, more than
2^115 times the threshold 2^-35). Section P22 shows that the frozen heat-norm bounds of P5.1 are optimal, even on
test functions with zero strain and zero origin slope. Section P23 derives what the matrix condition forces on the
vertical axis (an integrated velocity bound, concavity of a power of an exact profile, a lower bound on the size of
any correction that restores the matrix floor) and applies it to the projected refits of P20. Section P24 shows
that the matrix condition M >= (19/5) I of Theorem D_w can be replaced by M >= (5/2) I, or by the position-dependent
floor 2/5 + (11/5) c r^2/(R^2 + r^2), on the ball r <= R, with every other hypothesis and every constant unchanged.
Section P25 bounds from below, by an annular duality argument, the residuals of two exactly admissible projected
refits at the weight radius 2^31 (N^w_s(F) > 2^24, more than 2^59 times the threshold). Section P26 records
necessary point tests of the full reference contract: both refits violate the Hessian bound |D^2 rho| <= 3, and a
third admissible refit has a certified pointwise residual lower bound. Section P27 proves that no choice of
coefficients in the generator family of the projected refits, with the prescribed leading data, brings the
unweighted residual norm within a factor of 210 of the threshold of Theorem D: the first nonzero residual sector is
the same for all of them, and a distance formula for powers in a finite power space turns it into a lower bound for
the whole norm. Section P28 records point tests of the reference contract for four later refits (each violates a
fourth-derivative bound at a certified point, and certified point values bound their residuals from below).
Section P29 shows by an explicit function that the fixed sector and the power structure alone do not force a
weighted residual gap. Section P30 derives the residual scales that the threshold of Theorem D_w forces: an Hdot^-1
bound below 2^-58 for the weighted residual and a pointwise bound 2^-31 max(1, |X|^(1/5)). Section P31 sharpens the
derivative estimate of P27 (P31.1 by an integral operator bound, P31.2 by an orthonormal exponential basis that keeps
the radial factor of the cylinder derivative): the factor at the radial degree of P27 becomes more than 1308, and
the uniform bound holds for every radial degree up to 779. Section P32 computes the seventh order of the formal
stationary expansion exactly and the residual sector that becomes fixed once a seventh branch is added, with the
condition that the descendant sector (2,1) must then vanish exactly. P11.2 and P11.4 independently
check two annular lower bounds of the checkpoint residual computed in the numerical work; P11.3 audits a
floating-point summary. Sections P33 to P35 extend the uniform unweighted bound to every radial degree up to 3675,
delimit the annular obstruction and show that the seven-branch family gives
no bound exceeding the sufficient threshold; P36 and P42 treat the refits
b6 and d2; P37 bounds the strain as a velocity-gradient trace. Sections P38 to P41 and P45 to P49 prove necessary
local distances (no exact solution of any exponent near a given reference) by point, square and annular tests, with
the amplitude and negative-order embeddings of P44, P47 and P48. Section P43 is the second version of Theorem D_w
(smooth commutator, threshold 2^-30). Section P50 identifies the natural domain of the normalized linearization.
Section P51 transfers the annular witnesses to every larger weight radius, and P52 gives annular residual gaps and
distances for the refits Mpen2 and d2. Sections P53 and P55 extend and sharpen the frozen Hoelder inverse. Section
P54 certifies an off-axis violation of the fourth-derivative bound by d2. Section P56 proves that the weighted
residual norm attains a positive minimum over each finite fitting family; P57 makes it uniform in the smoothness
index and the weight radius with a finite-constant formula, P59 gives the sharp velocity constant on the angular
band of the fits, and P60 extends the floor to the seven-branch family; no value is computed. Section P58 certifies
off-axis violations of three derivative bounds by Mpen2. Section P61 shows that exact finite constraints and compact
perturbations do not make the linearization Fredholm in the critical far-field space. Section P62 evaluates a
weaker floor exactly (far below the threshold), and P63 is a consolidated audit of the second conditional
theorem (domains, normalized range, low and high inverses). Section P64 extends P61 to critical weighted Sobolev
spaces of every order m >= 3 (where the strain is continuous) and to finite parameter columns, P65 gives the
far-field spectral line Re z = c b - 1 for the growth exponent b of the space, and P66 sharpens the frozen
ordinary Hoelder constants to 97 and 96; P67 improves them to 87 for both checkpoints by a fractional heat
representation of the kernel. Section P68 extends P64 to logarithmically modified critical weights and to
closed block realizations with arbitrary Banach tail coordinates, and gives the exact membership thresholds of
polynomial-log tails. Section P69 computes the exact norm of the strain trace on H^(2+s) and its sharp
small-s asymptotics in the weighted norm of the conditional theorem, and shows that it is unbounded at s = 0.
Section P70 replaces the fractional gain by a logarithmic one: the strain is continuous exactly for beta > 1/2,
with no gradient Hoelder control. Section P71 shows that the certified low residual bounds hold in that
logarithmic space as well. Sections P72 to P87 develop the logarithmic space into a complete conditional
theorem: P72 writes the circular strain cutoff as a positive average, so the principal value is literal on the
completion, and P74 gives an explicit density with divergent strain at the endpoint beta = 1/2; P73 proves the
necessary logarithmic distances of exact profiles from the references; P75 and P77 give the fixed-background
inverse for every power 0 < beta <= 1 and the normalized range for beta > 1/2; P76 shows that the quadratic
transport term is not continuous at 0 from the space into itself; P78 to P82 prove the product and commutator
estimates; P83 and P84 introduce the native norm and its products; P85 is the conditional nonlinear theorem
(inverse 32, contraction in the low norm, threshold 2^-25 tau^beta (2 beta - 1)^(1/2)); P86 shows that the
three references remain excluded in the native norm and miss its threshold; and P87 derives four compatible
outputs (low norm, a density Hoelder norm, a projected singular moment at the center and the strain).
Section P88 is a consolidated dependency and domain audit of P85. Section P89 makes the bounds on the third
velocity derivative and the third and fourth density derivatives free parameters (with a larger hierarchy
coefficient and a smaller tau), P90 shows that the exclusions and residual gaps persist for every parameter
choice, and P91 gives exact global caps for these derivatives from the coefficients of a finite potential.
Section P92 is a second, independent certificate of the global matrix bound for the checkpoint. Section P93
audits a third one, a numerical Taylor-box covering of the plane, and recomputes its matrix numbers
independently; P94 proves that the bound is sharp: the smallest eigenvalue is at least c + 2 everywhere, with
equality only at the origin. Section P95 sets up exact compactified certificates of the global hypotheses for the
exact algebraic refits and proves the three matrix bounds M >= (19/5) I and M1, M2 >= I/2 on the whole plane for
the reference d2, and also its five fixed derivative bounds and four decay bounds; the hypotheses for Mpen2 are not
certified there. Section P96 is a second,
independent certificate on the whole plane of the auxiliary matrix bounds M_1, M_2, M_3 and of the bound on
sym DU for the checkpoint, with sharper constants.
Section P97 shows that the full absolute first-jet-subtracted moment at the center is bounded on H_beta exactly
for beta > 3/2, so it is unbounded on the logarithmic spaces of P83 to P87 (1/2 < beta <= 1), and the angular
projection in the moment of P87 cannot be omitted. Section P98 proves explicit bounds for the remainders of the
density and velocity derivatives at the center for the checkpoint on disks of radius up to 1/10 (exact
Taylor division with a rational tail and complete covers). Section P99 gives independent directed covers of the
density sign, of A >= -I/20 and of exterior matrix bounds for the checkpoint, and P101 a directed bound
|F| <= (48707/200000) r^(2 gamma - 1) for r >= 300 on its residual. Section P102 shows that the example of P97 lies in none
of the fractional weighted spaces of the earlier weighted theorem, where the full absolute moment is bounded.
Section P103 shows that polynomial growth of every density derivative and of the velocity implies polynomial
growth of every velocity derivative. Section P104 recomputes three decay bounds of the checkpoint independently.
Section P105 assembles, for the refit d2, every reference hypothesis of the parametric logarithmic theorem of P89
and proves that only the smallness of the residual fails, by a factor of more than 2^243. Section P106 shows that a smooth S1 function whose derivatives of order up
to four grow at most like <r>^(q-m) with q < 1/5 lies in every logarithmic forcing space of P83 to P89; the actual
residuals of the checkpoint, Mpen2 and d2 satisfy this, so their certified native residual floors bound finite norms.
Section P108 shows that this power is sharp: an eventual tail r^q (log r)^(-a) Theta lies in these spaces for q < 1/5,
not for q > 1/5, and at q = 1/5 exactly when a > 1/2. Section P111 compares the native norm with the norm of
the exclusions of P73 directly, E_R(h) <= (1 + 7 tau) Mstar(h), and so excludes exact profiles from the closed
native balls of radius 2^77/(2^20 + 7) around the checkpoint and 2^41/(2^20 + 7) around either exact refit.
From P33 on, part numbers equal the numbers of the checked units, so a bare two-digit number in a cross
reference (for example "by 83" or "of 72, 77") refers to the part with that number.

## P1. Source reconstruction, operator, normalization and scaling

### P1.1. Exact checkpoint recovery and an independent point evaluator

#### Inputs and scope

The source is the read-only case4 tree at repository commit 78d87a0. Its entire copied tree was checked file by file against SHA-256 hashes, with no symlinks. The checkpoint folders contain state 88, the report's handoff state, and state 131, the latest supplied accepted state. Both are treated as exact finite functions defined by stored binary64 inputs and analytic rational center elimination. These are exact interpretations of the checkpoints, not error enclosures for an unknown PDE solution.

The implementation recover_state.py uses only JSON, NPZ arrays, exact rational arithmetic and independently written differentiation. It does not import archived numerical code. Every binary64 hex string is converted to its exact dyadic rational, and the NPZ arrays and recorded NPZ SHA are checked against those strings.

#### Reconstruction

The low chart has 60 coordinates in order j=0..3, m=0..4, k=m..4. Its first stored coordinate is c_l. The 800 high coordinates have order j=0..3, m=0..9, n=0..25-max(5,m). The canonical order is j=0..3, m=0..9, k=m..25, containing 860 entries.

For a generator

    Re((x+i y)^(2m)) q^(k-m)(1+q)^(p_j-k),
    p_j=(3+1/c_l-j(1-1/c_l))/2,

the finite Taylor coefficients follow from the generalized binomial series. The center strain is four times the x^2 y^2 coefficient of the potential. The unique omitted low coefficient is obtained by solving the exact linear equation that the total strain be 1-c_l. Its coefficient is nonzero for the supplied c_l values.

The shifted Legendre polynomial used by a high coordinate has exact coefficients

    P_n(2t-1)=sum_(h=0)^n (-1)^(n-h) binom(n,h) binom(n+h,h) t^h.

Multiplication by the stored exact normalizer N_n and conversion to the canonical monomial basis therefore use only integers and rationals. The final serialization consists of the c_l rational and all 860 rationals in canonical order. Its SHA-256 agrees with the checkpoint's recorded canonical hash for both states.

The density and stream jets are computed by differentiating the potential polynomial. High modes start at potential degree ten, so they do not affect density coefficients through degree five or the residual through degree five. The recorded cubic and quintic residual coefficients are obtained by exact polynomial multiplication in (c_l X+U).grad rho-rho. Their nonzero values explain why a strict O(r^7) residual assertion is false for the exact stored functions.

#### Independent Cartesian point evaluation

The point evaluator field_eval.py groups a potential as

    chi=sum_(j,m) Re((x+i y)^(2m)) f_(j,m)(q),
    f_(j,m)(q)=sum_(k=m)^25 a_(j,m,k) q^(k-m)(1+q)^(p_j-k).

At a point with q>0, derivatives of each radial factor through order four are computed by the product rule, in Arb arithmetic. The formula q(X+H)-q(X)=2x H_x+2y H_y+H_x^2+H_y^2 converts these radial derivatives to a Cartesian jet. The harmonic-polynomial jet follows from

    partial_x^u partial_y^v Re(z^n)
      = n!/(n-u-v)! Re(i^v z^(n-u-v)).

Multiplication of the two jets gives all potential derivatives through order four. The physical fields are then exact linear combinations, including

    rho=-chi_xxy-chi_yyy,
    U=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy),
    M11=2c_l+1-2chi_xxyy-chi_yyyy,
    M22=2c_l+1+chi_xxyy,
    M12=chi_xxxy.

The last identity is a cancellation in the independently derived energy matrix. It also shows that reflection changes only the sign of M12, so the eigenvalues are invariant under reflection into a quadrant.

All coefficient conversions are outward Arb operations. Saved point values use Arb's enclosing string representation, not separate rounded midpoint and tiny radius arrays. The point files certify only their specified locations. They do not bound a region between points, and the evaluator's q>0 implementation is not an origin-box certificate.

### P1.2. Canonical operator, normalization, and scaling

#### Function class and canonical inverse

Start with a real smooth density h on R^2, even in x and odd in y, which is Schwartz. Let G=-(2 pi)^(-1)log r and define psi[h]=G*partial_x h. Set U[h]=(-partial_y psi, partial_x psi). Then, in the Fourier convention with partial_j represented by i xi_j,

    U[h]=(-R_1 R_2 h, R_1^2 h),     R_j=partial_j(-Delta)^(-1/2).

Indeed, psi=partial_x(-Delta)^(-1)h, and commuting derivatives gives the two components. Thus R_1^2 has multiplier -xi_1^2/|xi|^2. The parity of psi is odd in both x and y; U_1 is odd in x and even in y; U_2 is even in x and odd in y. At zero U=0 and

    DU[h](0)=diag(-c[h],c[h]),      c[h]=psi_xy(0).

For a growing background, require an explicitly fixed extension of the same inverse with the following properties: linearity, these parities, no harmonic velocity term, dilation covariance, and enough local differentiability for the displayed jets. A sufficient uniqueness condition for an already existing stream function is subquadratic growth of psi with the given odd/odd symmetry. The difference of two such entire harmonic stream functions is affine, by the mean-value derivative bounds applied on disks of radius tending to infinity, and parity eliminates every affine function. This is a uniqueness statement, not a construction of the inverse for every possible growing density.

For the numerical potentials, rho=-partial_y Delta chi and psi=partial_x partial_y chi imply -Delta psi=partial_x rho identically. The finite generators have chi=O(r^(3+gamma)) and psi=O(r^(1+gamma)), where 0<gamma<1. Thus their stream functions satisfy the preceding uniqueness condition when competing inverses have the same growth. The normalization does not permit adding an arbitrary harmonic strain.

#### Exact origin identity

Let rho=a y+O(r^3) at zero, with a != 0, and let F(rho,c_l)=(c_l X+U[rho]) dot grad rho-rho. Put d=c[rho]. The background field has derivative diag(c_l-d,c_l+d) at zero. Direct Taylor expansion gives

    F(rho,c_l)=(c_l+d-1)a y+O(r^3).

Therefore an exact stationary profile with nonzero a satisfies c_l+d=1. For an approximate background this is not inferred from smallness of the residual: its precise defect is

    partial_y F(0)=a(c_l+d-1).

The archived checkpoint imposes d=1-c_l through exact center elimination. Its other Taylor residual coefficients can remain nonzero.

#### Full derivative

On the normalized chart set c_l[rho]=1-c[rho]. Since c is linear, its variation is delta c_l=-c[h]. For Vbar=cbar_l X+U[rhobar], the Frechet derivative, whenever the function-space realization makes the products and c continuous, is

    L h = Vbar dot grad h-h + (U[h]-c[h]X) dot grad rhobar.                 (1)

This follows by expanding F(rhobar+h,cbar_l-c[h]); the exact remainder is

    Q(h)=(U[h]-c[h]X) dot grad h.                                        (2)

At fixed c_l the derivative instead lacks the term -c[h] X dot grad rhobar. A proof for that different operator does not prove a bound for (1).

The formulas (1)-(2) are algebraic identities on smooth functions. Calling (1) a bounded Frechet derivative on a Banach space additionally requires mapping estimates, including control of the derivative in (2). No such Banach-space conclusion is asserted here.

#### Frozen origin and the first jet

Under exact center normalization, DVbar(0)=diag(lambda,1), lambda=2cbar_l-1, and grad rhobar(0)=(0,a0). Keeping both the frozen coefficients and the normalized rank-one term gives

    L_frozen h = lambda x h_x + y h_y-h+a0 R_1^2 h-a0 c[h] y.              (3)

The translation-invariant nonlocal principal part conventionally called L0 is (3) without its last term. These are distinct operators.

For a smooth h with the stated parity, U_2[h]=c[h]y+O(r^3). Hence (U[h]-c[h]X) dot grad(a0 y)=a0(R_1^2 h-c[h]y)=O(r^3). The left side is not identically zero. Its first jet is zero. Consequently partial_y(Lh)(0)=0 for any smooth h in the normalized chart. The forcing range therefore has a center compatibility condition if the topology retains a y-derivative trace. A surjectivity assertion onto unrestricted smooth odd forcing is false.

#### Scaling and residual covariance

Let S_t rho(X)=t rho(X/t), t>0. The canonical inverse obeys U[S_t rho](X)=t U[rho](X/t) and c[S_t rho]=c[rho]. Thus c_l is unchanged and

    F(S_t rho)(X)=t F(rho)(X/t).

Differentiating at t=1 gives, with K=rho-X dot grad rho,

    L_rho K=F(rho)-X dot grad F(rho).                                    (4)

At an exact solution the right side is zero. At an approximate numerical state it must not be discarded. The same scaling leaves the coefficient a=rho_y(0) unchanged, so imposing a cannot remove this kernel direction.

If rho=r^gamma Theta(theta)+o(r^gamma), then S_t rho has leading angular profile t^(1-gamma)Theta. Suppose a Banach realization carries Theta in a normed angular space E and a bounded linear functional ell:E->R satisfies ell(Theta)!=0. The phase ell(Theta)=constant is transverse to scaling because its derivative on K is (1-gamma)ell(Theta), nonzero for gamma != 1. Merely writing this phase without proving continuity of the tail trace does not produce a normalized Banach domain.

#### Dependencies and status

The center strain formula, including its local term, is proved in section P2.1. The numerical normalization is independently checked in certificate file recover_state.py. All identities above are proved under the explicit smoothness, inverse, and growth hypotheses stated; existence or surjectivity of a global linear inverse remains open.

## P2. Center strain functional, singular moment and strain unboundedness

### P2.1. The center strain functional for the canonical full-plane inverse

#### Statement and conventions

Let h be a real Schwartz function on R^2, even in x and odd in y. Put G(X)=-(2 pi)^(-1) log|X|, so -Delta G=delta_0, psi=G*partial_x h, and c[h]=partial_x partial_y psi(0). Let b=partial_y h(0). Then

    c[h] = -b/4 + (1/pi) lim_{epsilon -> 0} integral_{|X|>epsilon} sin(3 theta) h(X)/r^3 dX.       (1)

The limit is taken with circular exclusion. The integral converges at infinity and after subtraction of the first jet at the origin. In particular, the full-plane angular-integral formula without the local term is false for this class. For any smooth radial cutoff eta which is 1 near the origin and compactly supported,

    c[h] = -b/4 + (1/pi) integral sin(3 theta) (h(X)-b y eta(r))/r^3 dX.                         (2)

The latter integral is absolutely convergent. Reflection symmetry gives factor 2/pi on a half-plane and factor 4/pi on the first quadrant, with the same local term -b/4.

#### Proof

The Hessian of G in distributions is

    partial_x^2 G = PV[cos(2 theta)/(2 pi r^2)] - delta_0/2.

Here PV uses circular exclusion. To verify the local coefficient, integrate twice by parts outside a disk against a compactly supported smooth test function. The boundary term from the normal derivative of G tends to minus one half of the test function at zero, since the circle average of cos^2(theta) is one half. The ordinary derivative away from zero is cos(2 theta)/(2 pi r^2).

As the Hessian kernel is even,

    c[h] = -b/2 + lim_{epsilon -> 0} integral_{r>epsilon} K_2(X) partial_y h(X) dX,
    K_2(X)=cos(2 theta)/(2 pi r^2).

Integrate by parts on epsilon<r<R and let R tend to infinity. The outer boundary vanishes by Schwartz decay. On the inner circle the outward normal of this domain has y-component -sin(theta). Since h(epsilon,theta)=b epsilon sin(theta)+O(epsilon^3), the inner boundary term tends to

    -b/(2 pi) integral_0^{2 pi} cos(2 theta) sin^2(theta) dtheta = b/4.

The ordinary derivative is partial_y K_2=-sin(3 theta)/(pi r^3). The result is -b/2+b/4 plus the angular integral, proving (1). Since integral sin(3 theta) sin(theta) dtheta=0, subtracting b y eta(r) leaves that integral unchanged. The subtracted function is O(r^3) near the origin by smoothness and parity, so its product with r^-3 is locally integrable. This proves (2).

#### Counterexample and independent Fourier check

Take h(x,y)=y exp(-x^2-y^2). Its angular integral is zero on every circle. The Fourier multiplier of R_1^2 is -xi_1^2/|xi|^2. Differentiating R_1^2 h at the origin weights the radial Fourier integral by xi_1^2 xi_2^2/|xi|^2, whereas h_y(0) weights it by xi_2^2. Their angular ratio is (integral cos^2 theta sin^2 theta)/(integral sin^2 theta)=1/4. Thus c[h]=-h_y(0)/4=-1/4, in agreement with (1).

The same argument applies to h=b y eta(r) for any radial smooth compactly supported eta equal to 1 near zero: c[h]=-b/4. A localized y-jet cannot be subtracted for free from c.

#### Scope

These are classical/distributional identities, with a complete informal proof. No Lean build or formal proof is claimed. Extension to the growing numerical profile needs a tail condition and the same canonical inverse. For h=O(r^beta) with beta<1 and appropriate derivative decay, the center kernel is absolutely integrable at infinity because its radial majorant is r^(beta-2). The velocity itself may need a renormalized convolution; the strain is less ambiguous. The local correction in (1) is unchanged by that extension.

### P2.2. Independent radial-integral verification of checkpoint strain

#### Statement

For each of the supplied states 88 and 131, interpret every binary input and the analytically eliminated center coefficient as exact rationals. Let chi be the resulting 860-generator potential, rho=-partial_y Delta chi and psi=partial_xy chi. With the canonical subquadratic odd-odd stream inverse, the full-plane center functional satisfies

    c[rho] = -rho_y(0)/4 + (1/pi) integral sin(3 theta) rho/r^3 dX
           = 1-c_l

exactly. The integral is understood with circular exclusion at zero. This verification computes the angular integral by exact beta integrals over all contributing radial generators. It does not substitute the normalization identity to obtain that integral.

#### Reduction to two angular modes

Write one potential generator as

    chi=Re((x+i y)^n) f(q),  q=r^2, n=2m,
    f(q)=q^(k-m)(1+q)^(p-k), p=(3+gamma-j(1-gamma))/2.

All four branches have p<2. Put

    g(q)=4[(n+1)f'(q)+q f''(q)].

Direct Cartesian differentiation gives Delta chi=Re((x+i y)^n)g(q). Differentiating once more gives density sine coefficients

    rho= -r^(n+1)g'(q) sin((n+1)theta)
          +[n r^(n-1)g(q)+r^(n+1)g'(q)]sin((n-1)theta).

This formula also treats n=0 when negative sine frequencies are folded with their sign. The sin(3 theta) projection is zero except for n=2 and n=4. Since the angular integral of sin^2(3 theta) is pi, the desired normalized angular integral is integral_0^infinity rho_3(r)r^-2 dr.

For n=2 it equals

    -8 integral_0^infinity f''(q)dq
      -2 integral_0^infinity q f'''(q)dq.                        (1)

For n=4 it equals

    40 integral_0^infinity f'(q)dq
      +20 integral_0^infinity q f''(q)dq
      +2 integral_0^infinity q^2 f'''(q)dq.                    (2)

All these integrals converge at both endpoints for the generator parameters. For instance their tail powers are p-3<-1, and the nonvanishing differentiated monomials have nonnegative powers at zero.

#### Exact integral evaluation

Leibniz' rule expresses every integral in (1) and (2) as a finite sum of terms

    coefficient times integral_0^infinity q^A (1+q)^(-A-1-B)dq
      = coefficient times Beta(A+1,B),

where A is a nonnegative integer and B>0 is rational. The beta value is exactly

    Beta(N,B)=(N-1)!/[B(B+1)...(B+N-1)], N=A+1.

This follows by substituting t=q/(1+q) and integrating by parts N-1 times. It uses only rational arithmetic here. The implementation in certificate file check_strain_beta.py uses this formula, sums the canonical generator coefficients, and then includes the local term -rho_y(0)/4. The center derivative rho_y(0) is read from the independently reconstructed density Taylor polynomial.

As a further analytical check, integration by parts reduces (1) to 6 f'(0), and (2) to -24 f(0). The code evaluates the beta sums rather than using these reduced values. Every high radial mode is included even when its total integral cancels to zero.

#### Results and scope

The resulting rational normalization defect is exactly zero for both states. The complete rational sums, contributing generators and source hashes are in certificate file state088_strain_beta.json and certificate file state131_strain_beta.json. This is a verification of the exact numerical backgrounds, not an existence proof or an uncertainty bound for a nearby exact profile. The canonical-inverse identification follows from the odd-odd stream uniqueness argument and the subquadratic growth of each generated stream, proved in the operator note.

### P2.3. A jet-subtracted singular moment and its transport estimate

#### Local class and strain bound

Fix R>0, 1<p<infinity, 0<delta<=1 and a function h even in x and odd in y. Suppose h is C^(1,delta) on the closed disk D_R and obeys |h(X)|<=H |X|^beta for |X|>R, where beta<1. Put b=h_y(0) and v=h-b y on D_R. For

    p+2 < kappa < p(1+delta)+2,
    M_(p,kappa,R)(v)=(integral_(D_R) |v|^p |X|^(-kappa)dX)^(1/p),

this moment is finite and

    |c[h]| <= |b|/4 + C_(p,kappa) R^((kappa-p-2)/p) M_(p,kappa,R)(v)
                         + 4H/[pi(1-beta)] R^(beta-1),           (1)

where, with p'=p/(p-1),

    C_(p,kappa)=pi^(-1) [A_(p') (p-1)/(kappa-p-2)]^(1/p'),
    A_(p')=integral_0^(2pi) |sin(3theta)|^(p') dtheta
           =2 sqrt(pi) Gamma((p'+1)/2)/Gamma((p'+2)/2).

The canonical functional and its local term are those proved in section P2.1. A smooth cutoff of the linear jet may be used instead of v; every full-circle angular integral of that radial-cutoff jet is zero.

Proof: C^(1,delta) regularity and parity give |v|=O(r^(1+delta)), which makes the moment finite under the strict upper bound on kappa. Holder's inequality applied to |v| r^(-kappa/p) and |sin(3theta)|r^(-3+kappa/p) gives the near contribution in (1). Its radial integral has exponent (kappa-p-2)/(p-1)>0. The far contribution uses integral_0^(2pi)|sin(3theta)|dtheta=4 and integral_R^infinity r^(beta-2)dr=R^(beta-1)/(1-beta). This proves (1), including all constants.

#### Frozen transport moment

Let lambda>1, Q=lambda+1, B=(lambda x,y), and A=B.grad-1. Assume

    p+Q < kappa < p(1+delta)+2.                                  (2)

For v in C^(1,delta)(D_R), v=O(r^(1+delta)), one has

    M_(p,kappa,R)(v) <= p/(kappa-p-Q) M_(p,kappa,R)(A v).          (3)

No zero outer-boundary condition is needed. Condition (2) is possible exactly when p delta>lambda-1.

To prove (3), integrate on an annulus epsilon<r<R with weight w=r^(-kappa). Since div B=Q and

    B.grad log r=(lambda x^2+y^2)/r^2=:b_theta >=1,

integration by parts gives the exact identity

    integral w |v|^(p-2) v A v
       = (1/p) integral_(boundary) w (B.n)|v|^p
         + integral w [kappa b_theta-Q-p]/p |v|^p.              (4)

The outer flux is nonnegative. The inner flux tends to zero by the strict upper bound in (2). The coefficient in (4) is at least (kappa-Q-p)/p>0. Applying Holder's inequality to the left side proves (3). Formula (4) also specifies the boundary terms that cannot be discarded in other realizations.

#### Nonnegative adjoint weight adapted to the characteristics

The same estimate has an explicit characteristic construction. Let tau_R(X)>0 be the first forward exit time of exp(t diag(lambda,1))X from D_R, and define

    mu(X)=integral_0^(tau_R(X)) exp((Q+p)t)
                       |exp(t diag(lambda,1))X|^(-kappa) dt.

For X != 0 in D_R, mu is nonnegative, vanishes on the outer boundary, and satisfies

    B.grad mu+(Q+p)mu=-r^(-kappa),
    0<=mu(X)<=r^(-kappa)/(kappa-Q-p).                            (5)

The first formula follows by shifting the time of integration along a characteristic and differentiating. The second uses |exp(t diag(lambda,1))X|>=exp(t)|X|. The resulting exact adjoint identity is

    integral_(D_R) mu |v|^(p-2)v A v
          =(1/p) integral_(D_R) r^(-kappa)|v|^p.                (6)

At zero the boundary term tends to zero using (5) and the same strict exponent condition; at r=R it vanishes because mu=0. Applying (5) and Holder to (6) reproduces (3). This construction uses the actual S1 field B, not the unrelated x/2 model.

#### Optimality and limitations

The coefficient (kappa-Q-p)/p is the infimum of the pointwise coefficient in (4), attained on the y-axis. It is the optimal coefficient obtained by replacing that coefficient with a uniform lower bound. No claim is made that it is the sharp operator inverse constant after angular parity restrictions.

The unrenormalized moment of h with b!=0 diverges for every kappa>p+2, so the explicit jet subtraction is essential. The estimate (3) controls the scalar transport A. The full principal frozen operator adds a R_1^2 term, and the normalized operator adds a rank term. One must estimate the jet-subtracted combination R_1^2 h-c[h]y, as well as variable coefficients and cutoff terms, in the same moment. No such absorption estimate is asserted here. In particular (3) and (1) alone do not close a bound for c[h] by the full equation.

For orientation only, with delta=1/2 and p=4, the admissible interval is lambda+5<kappa<8. It is nonempty for both checkpoints since lambda<3. Constants chosen in this interval can be evaluated exactly from the checkpoint lambda, but they are scalar-transport constants and must not be presented as full-IPM constants.

### P2.4. The center strain is unbounded on low Holder and negative-energy norms

#### Statement

Fix 0<alpha<1. There is a sequence of smooth compactly supported functions h_epsilon, even in x and odd in y, with zero center y-jet, such that

    [h_epsilon]_C^alpha is constant,
    ||h_epsilon||_Hdot^(-1) -> 0,
    |c[h_epsilon]| -> infinity.

Consequently no bound |c[h]|<=C([h]_C^alpha+||h||_Hdot^(-1)) holds even in this symmetry class with h_y(0)=0. This does not refute an estimate that additionally uses the full normalized equation, whose rank term itself contains c[h].

#### Construction and proof

Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth radial function eta supported in 1<r<2 and put phi(r,theta)=eta(r)sin(3theta). It is smooth on the plane, has the required parity and vanishes in a neighborhood of zero. The corrected kernel formula gives

    c[phi]=integral_1^2 eta(r)r^(-2)dr>0.

Set h_epsilon(X)=epsilon^alpha phi(X/epsilon). Scaling of differences yields

    [h_epsilon]_C^alpha=[phi]_C^alpha.

The Fourier definition of Hdot^(-1) in two dimensions gives

    ||h_epsilon||_Hdot^(-1)=epsilon^(alpha+2)||phi||_Hdot^(-1).

This norm is finite since phi is smooth, compactly supported and has zero integral by oddness in y. The strain kernel, of order one, gives

    c[h_epsilon]=epsilon^(alpha-1)c[phi].

This diverges because alpha<1. Every member still vanishes near zero, so adding a zero center-jet constraint does not repair the failed inequality. A fixed smooth positive radial weight near zero in the negative-energy norm also does not repair it: rescaling the compact support and using uniform smooth bounds on that weight gives the same vanishing upper bound.

#### Scope

The example proves that a local singular moment or additional regularity is an essential independent ingredient in a norm-only approach to c[h]. It does not rule out finite-rank elimination using a previously constructed inverse on compatible spaces.

## P3. Far field: tails, finite-family exclusion, stationary completion, residual lower bounds

### P3.1. Tail growth and negative-order integrability

#### Exact numerical tail representation

The archived potential generators are

    chi_(j,m,k)=r^(2k)(1+r^2)^(p_j-k) cos(2m theta),
    2p_j=3+gamma-j(1-gamma), gamma=1/c_l,
    j=0,1,2,3; m=0,...,9; k=m,...,25.

The potential determines rho=-partial_y Delta chi and psi=partial_x partial_y chi. For r>1, the binomial expansion is absolutely convergent, together with every fixed finite number of derivatives, on r>=R>1. Thus the leading potential term in branch j is

    r^(3+gamma-j(1-gamma)) sum_m C_(j,m) cos(2m theta),
    C_(j,m)=sum_(k=m)^25 a_(j,m,k).

For a potential term C r^s cos(n theta), elementary polar differentiation gives density exponent s-3 and coefficients

    sin((n+1)theta): -C(s^2-n^2)(s-2-n)/2,
    sin((n-1)theta): +C(s^2-n^2)(s-2+n)/2.

The stream function has exponent s-2 and coefficients

    sin((n+2)theta): +C(s-n)(s-n-2)/4,
    sin((n-2)theta): -C(s+n)(s+n-2)/4.

Negative sine indices are folded using sin(-k theta)=-sin(k theta). These formulas include n=0 after both contributions are combined.

If rho=r^p F(theta) and psi=r^t P(theta), the nonlinear advection is

    U dot grad rho = r^(p+t-2)[-p P'(theta)F(theta)+t P(theta)F'(theta)].

Consequently the residual has leading candidate exponent 2gamma-1. The nominal r^gamma term vanishes identically because c_l gamma=1. Its coefficient at r^(2gamma-1) is E1, containing the linear branch -1 term and the branch -0 self-advection. Since the branch -1 density has sine modes only up to 19, its linear part cannot affect sine mode 39.

#### Nonzero leading residual of the actual checkpoints

Put n=18, s=3+gamma and C=C_(0,9). The highest density and stream coefficients from branch 0 are

    A=-C(s^2-n^2)(s-2-n)/2,       B=C(s-n)(s-n-2)/4.

The sin(39 theta) coefficient of E1 is exactly

    e39=(19-gamma) A B/2.                                            (1)

For each supplied checkpoint 88 and 131 the independently reconstructed exact rational C is nonzero, 0<gamma<1, and (1) is strictly negative. The checks use exact rational arithmetic, not a floating-point threshold. Their complete inputs, coefficient tables and interval enclosures are in certificate file state088_tail.json and `state131_tail.json`; the independent program is certificate file check_tail.py.

For state 131, rounded displays are

    c_l=1.810319210199998,
    2gamma-1=0.10477753797853508,
    e39=-7.698363346447813e-7,
    ||E1||_(L2(0,pi/2))=0.0910394455355629.

The corresponding state 88 norm is 0.12112557210824139. The coefficient norms are enclosed by Arb with exact rational input. This certifies the stated finite computations subject to the arithmetic library, not the numerical profile's proximity to a true solution.

The remainder after E1 is uniformly lower order in theta because the finite family has a convergent differentiated binomial expansion. Since e39 != 0, E1 is nonzero in angular L2. Hence

    ||F(rho)(r,.)||_(L2(0,pi/2)) / r^(2gamma-1) -> ||E1|| > 0.

Both exponents are positive, so the unnormalized density residual grows. A forcing space imposing boundedness or decay on this residual cannot contain the actual background defect. Smallness of the archived normalized residual R_f=R_rho/y does not fix this incompatibility.

#### A sharp tail obstruction for ordinary homogeneous H^-1

Consider a smooth function g on R^2 which is odd in y and even in x, and equals r^beta sin(m theta) for r>=2, where m is a positive odd integer and beta is real. Then

    g belongs to homogeneous H^-1(R^2) if and only if beta<-2.           (2)

Here membership means existence of a distributional potential Phi with -Delta Phi=g and grad Phi in L2, equivalently continuity on the homogeneous H^1 test space. Smooth modifications on a bounded set with the same odd symmetry do not change the conclusion.

For necessity, choose a smooth radial cutoff chi supported in 1<r<2 with integral chi(r)r^(beta+1)dr nonzero and take test functions phi_R=chi(r/R)sin(m theta), supported on disjoint dyadic annuli. Their gradient L2 norms are independent of R, while <g,phi_R> is a nonzero constant times R^(beta+2). If beta>-2, the dual norm is therefore infinite. At beta=-2, choose N such tests on disjoint annuli and add them. Pairing grows as N while the gradient norm grows as sqrt(N), again contradicting a bounded H^-1 norm.

For sufficiency, solve the polar radial ODE for this single angular mode. Away from resonances,

    Phi_tail=-r^(beta+2)sin(m theta)/((beta+2)^2-m^2).

Its gradient is O(r^(beta+1)), square integrable at infinity precisely when beta<-2. At the possible resonant exponent beta+2=-m, replace the particular solution by a constant times r^(-m)log(r)sin(m theta); its gradient is still square integrable since m>=1. A smooth radial continuation through the inner region leaves a compactly supported odd forcing error. Such an error has zero integral; its Newtonian potential has gradient O(r^-2) at infinity and a locally square-integrable gradient. Adding that correction proves sufficiency. The case beta+2=+m is outside beta<-2.

This proof extends to any fixed nonzero smooth angular profile with odd sine modes: necessity uses a test angular profile with nonzero pairing, and sufficiency follows by angular mode estimates when the angular regularity is sufficient. The single-mode statement (2) alone already disproves any proposed space admitting arbitrary leading tails under the incompatible weights below.

#### Consequence for the weight in the prompt

Let w_s=(1+r^2/R0^2)^(-s/2), R0>0. A free leading perturbation h=r^gamma sin(m theta) at infinity gives w_s h asymptotic to R0^s r^(gamma-s)sin(m theta). The same annular proof and radial ODE show

    ||grad(-Delta)^(-1)(w_s h)||_2 < infinity  iff  s>2+gamma.

The limiting positive-matrix condition of the weighted energy in section P4.1 is s<2+gamma. There is no overlap. At equality the energy diverges logarithmically; the endpoint does not repair the problem.

For the first correction tail r^(2gamma-1)Theta_1, the lower integrability threshold is instead s>1+2gamma. Thus the heuristic window

    1+2gamma < s < 2+gamma

can apply only after the leading tail is fixed or explicitly extracted. It cannot include a freely varying leading angular profile. Exponent variation produces r^gamma log(r) terms, which also fail at or below the leading-tail threshold.

#### Subtraction order and scope

The formal nonlinear hierarchy has p_n=n gamma-(n-1)=1-n(1-gamma). If the first N orders are extracted and the remainder really has a controlled first omitted power p_(N+1), ordinary H^-1 requires p_(N+1)<-2, equivalently (N+1)(1-gamma)>3. For state 131 and state 88 the smallest possible N is 6. This is a threshold calculation, not a proof that a six-order expansion exists, that its angular equations are solvable, or that its logarithmic terms are controlled. Each of those conditions remains separate.

The leading angular profile belongs to an infinite-dimensional function space. Treating all its variations as one scalar, or changing c_l while omitting derivatives of r^(p_n(c_l)), does not define the full tangent space.

### P3.2. Audit of the finite-angular-support exclusion theorem

#### Exact statement

Let

    chi(r,theta)=sum_(m=0)^M r^(2m) cos(2m theta) v_m(r^2),

where each v_m is real and C^4 on (0,infinity). Assume chi is bounded in a punctured neighborhood of zero and chi=o(r^4) uniformly in theta at infinity. Define rho=-partial_y Delta chi, psi=partial_x partial_y chi and U=(-psi_y,psi_x). If

    (c_l X+U) dot grad rho-rho=0

at every nonzero point for a real constant c_l, then

    chi=A+B(x^2+y^2)+C(x^2-y^2),

so rho=0 and U=0. In particular no nonzero-density member of the supplied 860-generator family with c_l>1 is an exact profile.

#### Highest harmonic

Take the highest retained nonzero angular index n=2M and put q=r^2, v=v_M and w=v''. For n>0, the highest harmonics generated by r^n cos(n theta)v(q) are

    psi_top = r^(n+2) w(q) sin((n+2)theta),
    rho_top = -4r^(n+1)[(n+2)w(q)+q w'(q)] sin((n+1)theta).

These formulas follow by Cartesian differentiation, or by writing z=x+iy, partial_x=partial_z+partial_barz and partial_y=i(partial_z-partial_barz). No lower potential mode can contribute to these highest harmonics. The linear part of the residual has harmonic at most n+1, whereas the top self-advection has harmonic 2n+3. Its coefficient is

    4r^(2n+3){(n+2)w(q)[q w''(q)+2w'(q)]-(n+1)q(w'(q))^2}.

Thus the expression in braces must vanish. For n=0 both top field coefficients double, and the top residual coefficient is multiplied by four; the same ODE follows. Lower modes cannot produce harmonic 2n+3, so cancellation with them is impossible.

#### Solving the reduced equation without analyticity

On a connected interval I where w != 0, its sign is constant. Put u=|w|^(1/(n+2)). This is positive and C^2 on I. Substitution into the ODE gives

    q u''+2u'=0,

hence u=A+B/q on I. A maximal nonzero interval cannot have two finite positive endpoints: continuity of w would make u vanish at both, forcing A=B=0.

Suppose I reaches zero. If B != 0, then w has leading form C q^(-n-2) with C != 0. Integrating twice shows v has a nonzero leading multiple of q^-n for n>0, and a nonzero logarithmic term for n=0. Consequently r^n v(q) is unbounded near zero. This contradicts boundedness of chi, which implies boundedness of every Fourier coefficient. Therefore B=0 on an interval reaching zero. Then w is a nonzero constant and cannot reach a finite zero endpoint, so this interval extends to infinity.

If I instead has a finite left endpoint a>0, it must extend to infinity, and u=A(1-a/q) with A>0. Again w tends to a nonzero constant as q tends to infinity. The preceding constant case has the same property. Twice integrating w gives v(q)=Cq^2/2+o(q^2), with C != 0. Its potential Fourier coefficient r^n v(r^2) grows as a nonzero multiple of r^(n+4), contradicting chi=o(r^4). Hence no nonzero interval exists, and w is identically zero.

#### Removing the remaining modes

The top radial function is affine: v(q)=a+bq. If n>=4, the corresponding powers r^n and r^(n+2) both violate o(r^4), so a=b=0. If n=2, the quartic coefficient b is zero; the surviving a(x^2-y^2) has zero rho and U and can be removed from the equation. Repeating the argument removes each higher mode. Finally the n=0 case leaves A+Bq, also with zero rho and U. This proves the theorem.

For the 860 family, each generator is smooth at zero and has potential growth r^(3+gamma-j(1-gamma)), with 0<gamma<1. All therefore satisfy the theorem's boundedness and subquartic-growth assumptions. The conclusion is not a nonexistence theorem for an arbitrary nearby infinite-dimensional profile. A nearby exact profile must leave this finite-angular-support class.

#### Verification scope

This independently reconstructs the report's even-cosine theorem and its application to the 860 family. The report's more general claim for arbitrary complex phases and odd angular frequencies is not needed here and is not audited in this file. The highest-harmonic algebra is additionally checked in certificate file check_highest_harmonic.py when present. This is an informal proof, not a machine-checked Lean theorem.

### P3.3. Six stationary tail orders and the checkpoint's additional descendants

#### Statement and scope

Let gamma=1/c lie in (1/2,4/7), let delta=1-gamma, and set p_n=1-n delta. Let Theta_0 be a smooth angular function with the density parity: its Fourier series contains only sin(k theta) for odd positive k. The statements below hold for smooth angular functions; the exact numerical calculations use finite sine polynomials.

There are uniquely determined smooth functions Theta_1,...,Theta_5, with the same parity, and smooth odd-odd stream functions Phi_0,...,Phi_5 such that

    rho_6(r,theta)=sum_(n=1)^6 r^(p_n) Theta_(n-1)(theta),
    psi_6(r,theta)=sum_(n=1)^6 r^(p_n+1) Phi_(n-1)(theta)

solve the Poisson relation term by term and have zero stationary residual at each of the first six powers p_1,...,p_6. No logarithmic angular resonance occurs at these orders. The residual of these finite homogeneous sums is O(r^(p_7)), with p_7<-2.

If chi is a smooth radial cutoff equal to zero for r<=R and one for r>=2R, R>0, and b is any smooth compactly supported density of the correct parity, then rho=b+chi rho_6 has a canonical stream function and its stationary residual belongs to homogeneous H^-1. This is a construction of an approximate profile with an integrable residual, not an exact profile or a small-residual estimate. A compact annular density correction can impose c+c[rho]=1 without changing these tail orders or the center jet.

For the accepted checkpoints the numerical density has, in addition to its four primary powers p_1,...,p_4, two nonzero descendants above the H^-1 threshold: p_1-2=gamma-2 and p_2-2=2gamma-3. Subtracting only a sum of the six powers p_1,...,p_6 cannot remove these descendants. They must be explicitly included in the background correction or remainder definition.

Dependencies: the canonical inverse and parity convention in section P1.2; the homogeneous H^-1 tail criterion in section P3.1; the corrected strain kernel in section P2.1. All statements concern the fixed exponent c. The final section records its variation.

#### Angular Poisson inverse

For a density r^p Theta(theta),

    partial_x rho = r^(p-1) [p cos(theta) Theta - sin(theta) Theta'].

Writing its stream function as r^(p+1) Phi gives

    -[partial_theta^2+(p+1)^2] Phi
       =p cos(theta) Theta - sin(theta) Theta'.                 (1)

If Theta=sum_k a_k sin(k theta), the right side has coefficients

    (p-k)a_k/2 at sin((k+1)theta),
    (p+k)a_k/2 at sin((k-1)theta).

Negative frequencies are folded using sin(-m theta)=-sin(m theta), and sin(0)=0. Thus only positive even frequencies occur. At frequency m the inverse divides by m^2-(p+1)^2.

For n=1,...,6 and gamma in (1/2,4/7), |p_n+1|<2. All positive even m satisfy m>=2, so every denominator is strictly positive. This proves existence and uniqueness in the odd-odd angular subspace, as well as smoothness by the Fourier multiplier. The absent zero angular frequency is important: p_n+1=0 would not be a resonance in this parity either.

In polar coordinates U_r=-r^p Phi' and U_theta=(p+1)r^p Phi. Therefore the contribution of density orders i and j to U.grad rho is

    r^(p_i+p_j-1) B_(i,j),
    B_(i,j)= -p_j Phi_(i-1)' Theta_(j-1)
              +(p_i+1) Phi_(i-1) Theta_(j-1)'.                 (2)

Since p_i+p_j-1=p_(i+j), the powers close under the nonlinear operation.

#### Recursion and exact cancellation

The linear dilation term acts diagonally:

    (c r partial_r-1)r^(p_n)Theta = -(n-1)(c-1)r^(p_n)Theta.

Theta_0 is free. For n>=2 define recursively

    Theta_(n-1)=1/[(n-1)(c-1)] sum_(i+j=n, i,j>=1) B_(i,j),     (3)

where the preceding stream functions are obtained from (1). The denominator is nonzero because c>1. Formula (3) proves uniqueness and cancels the coefficient at p_n exactly. Products and derivatives preserve the density parity. For a finite initial sine polynomial all subsequent functions are finite sine polynomials.

In the finite six-order sum the remaining nonlinear pairs have i+j>=7. Since p_n decreases strictly, every remaining power is at most p_7=7gamma-6<-2. Differentiating a finite sum gives the corresponding symbol estimates. This proves the claimed residual order and requires neither convergence of an infinite series nor an existence theorem.

If the largest initial density frequency is 19, the possible largest frequency at order n is 20n-1. The exact checkpoint recursions give nonzero coefficients at that largest frequency through n=6. The sixth order thus requires frequency 119. This is consistent with, and independently illustrates, why an exact solution cannot stay in the checkpoint's fixed angular family.

#### Cutoff and the canonical velocity

Let rho=b+chi rho_6 and psi_tilde=chi psi_6. The function

    f=partial_x rho+Delta psi_tilde

is smooth and compactly supported, since (1) holds wherever chi is constant one and b vanishes. It is odd in both x and y. Set w=(-Delta)^(-1)f and psi=psi_tilde+w. Then -Delta psi=partial_x rho.

The zeroth and first moments of f vanish by parity. The expansion of the logarithmic fundamental solution against compact f therefore gives w=O(r^-2), with differentiated bounds, and its velocity is O(r^-3). This follows directly by Taylor expanding log|X-Y| in Y for r>2 sup|Y| on the support: the constant and linear terms integrate to zero, and the remainder and its derivatives have the displayed bounds. The odd-odd potential psi is o(r^2), so it is the canonical stream function under the uniqueness convention already proved.

Outside a compact disk the new velocity differs from the homogeneous velocity U_6 by O(r^-3). Its contribution to the density residual is O(r^(gamma-4)). The full residual is consequently

    F(rho)=O(r^max(p_7,gamma-4))=O(r^(p_7)),

since p_7-(gamma-4)=6gamma-2>0. All local quantities are smooth. The residual has the density parity, so the parity Hardy inequality gives

    |<F,phi>| <= ||r F||_2 ||phi/r||_2
                <= ||r F||_2 ||grad phi||_2.

Here ||rF||_2 is finite precisely because the exterior exponent is below -2. Hence F belongs to the same homogeneous H^-1 dual space used in the energy proof. This proves membership, not a useful numerical upper bound.

For the origin normalization, choose a smooth nonnegative radial eta supported in an annulus away from zero and let v=eta(r)sin(3theta). It has zero center jet and c[v]=integral eta(r)r^-2 dr>0. Adding

    t v,  t=(1-c-c[rho])/c[v],

imposes c+c[rho+t v]=1 exactly. The added density is compactly supported and its canonical velocity is O(r^-3), so the previous exterior residual conclusion persists. The coefficient t and the size of this alteration have not been certified here.

#### Exact checkpoint descendants

For a checkpoint potential term

    a_(j,m,k) r^(2k)(1+r^2)^(s_j/2-k) cos(2m theta),
    s_j=3+gamma-j delta,

the convergent expansion for r>1 is

    a_(j,m,k) r^(s_j) sum_(q>=0) binom(s_j/2-k,q) r^(-2q) cos(2m theta).

After applying -partial_y Delta, the density powers are p_(j+1)-2q. For gamma in the stated interval, the powers at least -2 are exactly

    p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4, p_1-2,p_2-2.

Their six exponents are distinct at both exact checkpoints. The two q=1 coefficients are obtained with the exact multiplier s_j/2-k before applying the polar density rule. The independent script certificate file formal_tail_completion.py does this from the verified canonical rational coefficients and also checks (1) against the independently differentiated stream series.

Quarter-plane L2 angular norms, with rigorous Arb enclosures retained in the JSON:

| State | power gamma-2 | angular norm | power 2gamma-3 | angular norm |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 88 | -1.4470673098204796 | 11.41815760429577 | -1.8941346196409594 | 25.93050345666410 |
| 131 | -1.4476112310107325 | 15.41715954657126 | -1.8952224620214648 | 40.01760144955358 |

These displayed decimals are only summaries of the enclosing values. The nonzero exact rational sine coefficients prove that neither descendant vanishes. Each term fails homogeneous H^-1 by the tail criterion. Orthogonal projection onto a nonzero sine coefficient and the annulus test proof prevent cancellation by terms at different powers. Thus a subtraction containing only p_1,...,p_6 leaves a non-H^-1 remainder for either checkpoint.

A concrete correction of the checkpoint must subtract its six actual nonintegrable sectors and add the six stationary sectors from (3), using the same cutoff. If the leading angular profile is kept fixed, the correction has seven generally nonzero angular terms: three changes at p_2,p_3,p_4, two new terms at p_5,p_6, and removal of the two q=1 descendants. The leading p_1 term cancels. The remaining original checkpoint density has order p_3-2=3gamma-4<-2. Its explicit stream expansion has the matching differentiated order; the cutoff discrepancy contributes only the harmonic O(r^-3) velocity just analyzed. The corrected residual again belongs to H^-1. No claim that this correction is small in a chosen strong norm is made.

#### Logarithms, parameters and open steps

The exact six-order construction is a finite algebraic procedure. It does not establish that every exact profile has this expansion, or that the infinite recursion converges. Additional homogeneous stream multipoles occur at faster orders after imposing a global core; they have not been discarded from the canonical construction.

The six angular Poisson inverses and scalar recursion denominators are nonresonant on the stated open c interval. Consequently there is no forced r-logarithm in these six fixed-c stationary terms. Differentiating in c is different:

    partial_c [r^(p_n(c)) Theta_(n-1)(c)]
       =r^(p_n) [partial_c Theta_(n-1)-n c^-2 log(r) Theta_(n-1)].

These logarithms, and independent variations of the leading angular function, must be coordinates of a parameter-dependent space. A norm on an ordinary decaying remainder cannot absorb them. Recursion (3) also differentiates the angular data, so its continuity on any proposed finite-regularity angular Banach space requires a separate derivative count or a scale of spaces. Neither that full mapping theorem nor a normalized global inverse is supplied by this finite-tail calculation.

### P3.4. Certified lower bounds for the checkpoint residual's Hessian norm

#### Setting and certified claim

Use the exact checkpoint 131, the fixed exponent c, and its canonical velocity. Let F=(cX+U[rho]).grad rho-rho. For sigma>2/c-1 define

    omega_2(r)=(1+4r^2)^((1-sigma)/2).

The verification script gives a rigorous lower bound on ||omega_2 D^2F||_(L2(R^2)), with the Hessian Frobenius norm and full-plane measure. It uses only r>=R0. R0 and the potential-series cutoff Q are recorded with every result. This is a residual norm statement. By itself it neither rules out an exact nearby solution nor proves that every possible existence argument fails.

#### Finite exact residual and its integrated norm

Expand each exact potential generator using the binomial series in r^-2, retaining q=0,...,Q. Sum the coefficients exactly as rational numbers before taking any absolute values. Let chi_Q be this finite potential, rho_Q=-partial_y Delta chi_Q, U_Q=(-chi_Q,xyy,chi_Q,xxy), and

    F_Q=(cX+U_Q).grad rho_Q-rho_Q.

The script constructs every angular coefficient of F_Q exactly, including all nonlinear products through q=2Q. It has the form

    F_Q=sum_a r^(p_a) sum_(m odd) e_(a,m) sin(m theta).

The leading coefficient is checked against the independently reconstructed E_1. For one term r^p e sin(m theta), the polar orthonormal Hessian components are

    e r^(p-2) [p(p-1)sin(m theta), (p-1)m cos(m theta);
               (p-1)m cos(m theta), (p-m^2)sin(m theta)].

Consequently the full-circle angular inner product of Hessians at powers p,t with the same frequency m is pi times e_p e_t r^(p+t-4) times

    J(p,t,m)=p(p-1)t(t-1)+2(p-1)(t-1)m^2+(p-m^2)(t-m^2).

Different frequencies are orthogonal. Put b=1-sigma and Rw=1/2. Since omega_2>=Rw^(-b)r^b, it suffices to bound the norm in this pure-power weight. Its squared value for F_Q outside R0 is exactly

    pi Rw^(-2b) sum_(a,d,m)
       e_(a,m)e_(d,m) J(p_a,p_d,m)
       R0^(p_a+p_d-2sigma)/(2sigma-p_a-p_d).                  (1)

All remaining powers are at most 2/c-1<sigma, so every denominator is positive. The sum includes signs and cross terms; no triangle inequality is used to estimate the finite approximation. Exact rational coefficients, Arb powers, and Arb square root enclose(1).

#### Uniform tail bound

Write gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma and q0=Q+1. At order d<=6, every omitted differentiated potential generator is bounded by its absolute input coefficient times

    binom(q+25,q)(2q+32)^d r^(gamma+3-d-j delta-2q).

Indeed |p_j-k|<26, and the angular frequency plus radial exponent in every one of the first six Cartesian differentiations is at most 2q+32. The ratio of successive positive majorants is bounded at R0 by

    ((q0+26)/(q0+1)) ((2q0+34)/(2q0+32))^d /R0^2 <1,

and decreases afterwards. A geometric tail gives component bounds T_d r^(gamma+3-d) for r>=R0. The same bound can retain the first omitted radial decay by writing T_d R0^(2q0) r^(gamma+3-d-2q0).

Exact retained angular coefficient sums give component bounds M_d r^(gamma+3-d) for chi_Q. Frobenius tensor bounds follow from the number of components:

    |D^i U_Q| <=2^((i+1)/2) M_(3+i) r^(gamma-i),
    |D^k rho_Q| <=2^(1+k/2) M_(3+k) r^(gamma-k),

and likewise with T for the errors. These deliberately overestimate correlations and signs.

The linear Hessian error is bounded by L r^(gamma-2-2q0), with

    L=R0^(2q0) [c 2^(5/2)T_6+|2c-1|4T_5].

The exact product rule gives a nonlinear error bounded by N r^(2gamma-3), where N is the sum for i=0,1,2, k=3-i, with binomial factors 1,2,1, of

    (error U_i)(retained rho_k)
       +(retained U_i)(error rho_k)+(error U_i)(error rho_k).

The pure-power weighted L2 norm of these errors is at most

    sqrt(2pi) Rw^(-b) [
       L R0^(gamma-2q0-sigma)/sqrt(2(sigma-gamma+2q0))
       +N R0^(2gamma-1-sigma)/sqrt(2(sigma-(2gamma-1)))].       (2)

Subtracting (2) from the square root of (1) is a rigorous lower bound for the original norm, by the reverse triangle inequality. This argument controls the entire exterior, not a grid or a truncated radial integral.

#### Verification and scope

The generator is certificate file residual_derivative_lower.py. It saves every exact residual-sector coefficient and the complete error budget. An independent Cartesian-jet check compares the residual Hessian with the sector evaluator at selected rational points; this checks the algebra but is not used as the exterior proof. The analytic bounds above supply the missing continuum and tail control.

The result applies to this exact checkpoint and this stated weight. Replacing the approximate background, changing the top norm, or multiplying a norm component by a small coefficient changes its use in a nonlinear closure argument. A norm lower bound must not be presented as a universal nonexistence or impossibility theorem.

| 3/10 |7.10845|1.89e-12|
| 7/20 |4.14615|1.30e-12|
| 2/5 |2.50924|9.10e-13|

Thus ||omega_2 D^2F||_2>2.50924 whenever 2gamma-1<sigma<=2/5, by monotonicity of the weight in sigma. For sigma<=2gamma-1 the norm is infinite, because the leading residual angular coefficient is nonzero and the Hessian of a nonzero r^(2gamma-1) odd angular function cannot vanish. The primary evidence is state131_residual_hessian_lower.json; the exact 157 residual sectors are saved separately. The independent Cartesian order-six potential calculation at (60,80),(100,0),(0,100),(180,240) agrees with the finite sector Hessian within the proved tail bounds. Its discrepancies are at most 1.51e-29 at radius 100 and 1.69e-41 at radius 300.

The  floating integration at sigma=0.3 gave 7.05 on a finite radial interval. This lies below the rigorous full-exterior lower bound 7.10845. At sigma=0.15 the corresponding 44.2 also omits a substantial tail. Those values remain finite-domain diagnostics and cannot be used as whole-plane residual upper bounds.

## P4. Negative-order and L2 energies, global matrix certificates, Hoelder estimate

### P4.1. Negative-order energy identities

#### Smooth compact test domain

Let rhobar and psibar be real smooth functions satisfying -Delta psibar=partial_x rhobar, Ubar=(-psibar_y,psibar_x), and V=cX+Ubar for a constant c. Let Phi be a real Schwartz function and h=-Delta Phi. Assume background derivatives have at most polynomial growth, and impose the required parities when a center functional is used. The Schwartz condition makes all integrations below legitimate. It gives

    E(h)^2 = integral |grad Phi|^2 = <h,Phi>.

These identities extend only to completions where each displayed integral has a justified limit; no automatic extension to the growing background or an arbitrary weighted space is claimed.

Write q=grad Phi. For Lh=V dot grad h-h+U[h] dot grad rhobar-c[h] X dot grad rhobar, one has

    -<Lh,Phi> = integral q^T M q + c[h] <X dot grad rhobar,Phi>,           (1)

where

    M = (2c+1)I + sym(DUbar) + [[rhobar_y,-rhobar_x/2],[-rhobar_x/2,0]]
      = [[2c+1-psibar_xy+rhobar_y, (psibar_xx-psibar_yy-rhobar_x)/2],
         [(psibar_xx-psibar_yy-rhobar_x)/2, 2c+1+psibar_xy]].              (2)

The rank-one term in (1) has no sign in this identity.

#### Derivation

Since div V=2c is constant, integration by parts gives

    <V dot grad(-Delta Phi),Phi>
      = -integral q^T DV q-c integral |q|^2.

To see every term, move V dot grad from h to Phi: the result is <h,-V dot grad Phi-2c Phi>. Pairing h=-Delta Phi with this expression gives -integral q_i (partial_i V_j)q_j -integral q_i V_j partial_j q_i-2c integral |q|^2. The middle integral is c integral |q|^2. The skew part of DV vanishes in the quadratic form. The term -h contributes -integral |q|^2.

For the coupled velocity, U[h]=(-Phi_xy,Phi_xx). Put a=rhobar_x and b=rhobar_y. Then

    integral Phi(-a Phi_xy+b Phi_xx)
      = integral (a Phi_x Phi_y-b Phi_x^2).

Indeed, after integration in x the remaining terms containing Phi itself are integral a_x Phi Phi_y-b_x Phi Phi_x. Integrating these once more gives -1/2 integral a_xy Phi^2+1/2 integral b_xx Phi^2=0 because a_xy=b_xx. Combining the terms proves (1)-(2).

#### Origin value

If c+psibar_xy(0)=1 and grad rhobar(0)=(0,a0), parity gives psibar_xx(0)=psibar_yy(0)=rhobar_x(0)=0, and

    M(0)=diag(3c+a0,c+2).

For c>1 and a0>0 the smaller eigenvalue is c+2. This is local pointwise positivity, not a global inverse bound. Exact rational values for the actual checkpoints are retained in certificate file state088_exact.json and `state131_exact.json`. The state 131 value c+2 is approximately 3.810319210199998; the other eigenvalue is approximately 15.731252522431172. Their full exact values, not these rounded displays, define any numerical claim.

#### Exact weighted identity

Let w>0 be a smooth weight, set g=wh=-Delta Phi, and now keep Phi Schwartz with h=g/w satisfying enough decay for the operators. Define

    b_w=V dot grad(log w),
    C_w g = w U[w^(-1)g]-U[g],
    D rhobar=X dot grad rhobar.

Then the exact transformed equation is

    wLh = V dot grad g-(1+b_w)g+U[g] dot grad rhobar
           +C_w g dot grad rhobar-c[h]wD rhobar.

Its energy identity is

    -<wLh,Phi> = integral q^T(M+b_w I)q
                 - (1/2) integral (Delta b_w)Phi^2
                 - integral Phi C_w g dot grad rhobar
                 + c[h] integral Phi wD rhobar.                         (3)

The sign of the Laplacian term follows from <b_w g,Phi>=integral b_w|q|^2-(1/2)integral Delta b_w Phi^2. Thus neither the weight commutator nor the Phi^2 term can simply be dropped. Formula (3) requires the actual nonlocal commutator; a pointwise matrix test alone is incomplete.

For w=(1+r^2/R0^2)^(-s/2),

    b_w = -s (V dot X)/(R0^2+r^2).

If Ubar=O(r^gamma), its first derivatives and grad rhobar are O(r^(gamma-1)), with gamma<1, then M+b_w I tends to ((2-s)c+1)I at infinity. Positivity of this limiting matrix requires s<2+1/c. This is a necessary condition for this particular positive-matrix route, not a necessary condition for every possible inverse method. The weighted H^-1 integrability of a freely varying r^(1/c) tail instead requires s>2+1/c; a proof of that obstruction is in section P3.1 when completed.

#### Scope and unresolved steps

No global positivity, commutator bound, control of the rank-one term, injectivity or surjectivity follows from these identities alone. The source checkpoint is not stationary; nothing above replaced its residual by zero. An eventual inverse theorem needs a compatible domain, the center forcing compatibility, a scaling phase, tail coordinates, and closed-range/surjectivity arguments in addition to energy coercivity.

### P4.2. A global fixed-exponent negative-energy inverse, conditional on matrix positivity

#### Exact statement

Let c>0. Let rho_bar be a smooth real function on the plane, even in x and odd in y, and let U_bar be its smooth canonical divergence-free velocity with the corresponding component parities. Assume that for some beta<1 the background and its derivatives through order three have the symbol bounds

    |D^j rho_bar(X)|+|D^j U_bar(X)| <= C_j <X>^(beta-j), 0<=j<=3.

Higher local smoothness is assumed only to make the flow preserve a smooth core. Put V=cX+U_bar, so div V=2c, V has at most linear growth, and DV is bounded. Define

    M=(2c+1)I+sym DU_bar+[[rho_bar,y,-rho_bar,x/2],[-rho_bar,x/2,0]].

Suppose there is a number m>0 such that M(X)>=m I at every point.

Let H be the completion of smooth compactly supported functions even in x and odd in y in the homogeneous H^-1 norm. On its specified generator domain, the fixed-exponent operator

    L_fix h=V.grad h-h+U[h].grad rho_bar

is one-to-one and onto H and has inverse norm at most 1/m. The domain is the transport-generator domain defined below; the bounded nonlocal perturbation leaves that domain unchanged.

This is a conditional theorem. The symbol bounds hold for the finite potential backgrounds by direct differentiation and their sublinear tails. The separate compactified polynomial certificate in section P4.3 now supplies m=19/5 for both exact checkpoint backgrounds, so this theorem applies to each with inverse norm at most 5/19. The theorem does not include -c[h]X.grad rho_bar, and no assertion about that rank term is hidden in its domain definition.

#### The parity Hardy inequality

Let P be the completion of smooth compactly supported test potentials even in x and odd in y under ||grad phi||_2. Angular Fourier series on every circle have only nonzero odd sine modes. The one-dimensional angular Poincare inequality therefore gives

    integral |phi(X)|^2/|X|^2 dX
       <= integral |partial_theta phi(X)|^2/|X|^2 dX
       <= integral |grad phi(X)|^2 dX.                          (1)

The first constant is one, since the smallest angular frequency is one. The inequality extends by completion. It also holds for any function odd under X -> -X, so it applies to the component parities used below. The space H is the dual of P, with its usual Riesz-potential norm. This can equivalently be obtained by completing the Fourier-annular core; no constant or zero-frequency mode remains in the specified parity.

#### The nonlocal coupling is a bounded operator on H

The vector multiplier U[h]=(-R1R2 h,R1^2 h) obeys

    ||U[h]||_(H vector)^2 <= ||h||_H^2,

because the sum of squared multiplier magnitudes is xi_1^2/|xi|^2<=1. Multiplication by grad rho_bar in the dual pairing is controlled as follows:

    ||grad(phi grad rho_bar)||_(L2 vector)
       <= ||grad rho_bar||_infinity ||grad phi||_2
           + ||r D^2 rho_bar||_infinity ||phi/r||_2
       <= C_B ||grad phi||_2,
    C_B=||grad rho_bar||_infinity+||r D^2 rho_bar||_infinity.       (2)

The norms of vectors and matrices in (2) are the Euclidean and Frobenius norms, which make the product estimate literal. The coefficient C_B is finite under the hypotheses. The products have the parities paired with the two velocity components. Thus

    B h=U[h].grad rho_bar

extends to a bounded operator H -> H with norm at most C_B. Inequality (1) is essential here: one cannot silently use an L2 bound for a homogeneous H1 test potential on the plane.

#### Transport semigroup and its domain

The globally Lipschitz field V has a complete smooth flow Phi_t. Its Jacobian determinant is exp(2ct). On the smooth compact core define

    T_t h(X)=exp(-t) h(Phi_t(X)), t>=0.

This is a semigroup with generator A h=V.grad h-h. If L=||DV||_infinity, duality and the change of variables Y=Phi_t(X) give

    <T_t h,phi>=exp(-(1+2c)t)<h,phi composed with Phi_(-t)>,
    ||grad(phi composed with Phi_(-t))||_2
         <= exp((L+c)t)||grad phi||_2.

Therefore ||T_t||_(H -> H)<=exp((L-c-1)t). The smooth core is invariant and its action is strongly continuous. Density extends T_t to a strongly continuous semigroup on H. Define D(A) to be its strong generator domain.

For completeness, the smooth compact core is a graph core of A. At a sufficiently large real z, the resolvent integral R_z f=integral_0^infinity exp(-zt)T_t f dt exists. For smooth compact f, finite-time Riemann sums of this integral and of the integral of T_t A f are smooth compact functions; they converge together in H, proving graph approximation of R_z f. Approximate a general f in H by smooth compact f_n and use A R_z f_n=z R_z f_n-f_n to obtain graph approximation of every element of D(A). This proves the core statement rather than assuming it.

The Dyson integral series for T_t with the bounded operator B converges uniformly in operator norm on bounded time intervals. It constructs a strongly continuous semigroup S_t whose generator is A+B on D(A). Equivalently, one can verify the integral equation S_t=T_t+integral_0^t T_(t-s) B S_s ds term by term. The generator-domain statement follows by differentiating this equation at zero and using the resolvent identity for sufficiently large z. The same compact core remains a graph core because B is bounded.

#### Energy estimate and surjectivity

For smooth compact h, let phi=(-Delta)^(-1)h. Oddness gives zero mean, so phi=O(r^-1), grad phi=O(r^-2) and the higher potential derivatives decay faster. The background symbol bounds justify all boundary terms in the energy calculation in section P4.1. It gives

    -<L_fix h,phi>=integral grad phi^T M grad phi
                        >=m ||h||_H^2.                         (3)

Graph-core approximation extends the dissipativity inequality to all h in D(A). For such h the semigroup solution is differentiable in H and satisfies

    d/dt ||S_t h||_H^2 <= -2m ||S_t h||_H^2.

Thus ||S_t||<=exp(-mt), first on the dense domain and then on H. Define

    L_fix^(-1)f=-integral_0^infinity S_t f dt.

The integral has norm at most ||f||_H/m. The same difference-quotient identity used for the frozen inverse proves that this integral belongs to D(A) and L_fix h=f. If L_fix h=0, then S_t h=h; exponential decay implies h=0. This establishes surjectivity and injectivity in the same realization. Positivity alone was not used as a substitute for generator existence.

#### Why this does not solve the normalized problem

The normalized operator is L=L_fix-c[h]g with g=X.grad rho_bar. For the checkpoint backgrounds, g has a nonzero r^gamma leading term and does not belong to unweighted H^-1. Consequently the normalized expression does not even map a trace domain containing functions with c[h]!=0 from D(A) into H. A correction space and forcing space must extract the corresponding tail response, including its logarithmic exponent variation.

If one simply restricts to c[h]=0 while retaining target H, surjectivity generally fails. Under the theorem's matrix hypothesis, take a smooth rapidly decaying h with c[h]!=0 and h in D(A). Its fixed-exponent forcing f=L_fix h lies in H. A normalized solution k in D(A) with Lk=f would need c[k]=0 because g is not in H. It would then obey L_fix k=f, forcing k=h by injectivity and contradicting c[h]!=0. Smooth examples with nonzero strain are supplied by rho=-partial_y Delta exp(-r^2).

This is the first precise compatibility obstruction when trying to turn this low-norm inverse into the requested normalized full inverse. It does not preclude a larger space with explicit tails, phase and strain coordinates.

### P4.3. Global matrix positivity by compactified polynomial certificates

#### Statement and inputs

Let rho_bar be either the state 88 or state 131 exact finite potential background reconstructed in section P1.1. The canonical coefficient hashes are respectively

    3c2195906835db3f0207302ae1ef818e284fe3d60940bd0ecff72b79d0e63c3d
    4d80cf85ea1746d41c3fcfbdc622c74465cff5b9358e68614e521531ea78fb01.

Write c for the exact stored exponent, gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma, and let

    rho_bar=-partial_y Delta chi,  psi_bar=partial_x partial_y chi,
    M=(2c+1)I+sym DU_bar+[[rho_bar,y,-rho_bar,x/2],[-rho_bar,x/2,0]].

Then, on the entire plane,

    M(X) >= (19/5) I.                                           (1)

This includes the origin, all axes and infinity. The proof uses rational polynomial identities and outward Arb enclosures at 256-bit precision. It does not use a numerical angular grid, a truncation at a finite radius, or a numerical derivative. The certificate is for the exact finite potential, not for an uncertainty neighborhood of its coefficients.

Consequently the generator-domain fixed-exponent operator in section P4.2 is bijective on the specified parity homogeneous H^-1 space and

    ||L_fix^(-1)|| <= 5/19.                                     (2)

The normalized operator, its growing rank column, and its scaling phase are not included in (2).

#### Exact compactification

The potential is the finite sum

    chi=sum_(j,m,k) a_(j,m,k) r^(2k) (1+r^2)^(p_j-k) cos(2m theta),
    p_j=(3+gamma-j delta)/2,  j=0,1,2,3,  m<=9,  m<=k<=26.

All a_(j,m,k), p_j and c are rational. Set

    t=r^2/(1+r^2),  z=cos(2theta),  w=(1-t)^(delta/2).
