## P7. Unweighted-bottom realization (Route U): low perturbation inverse, Riesz bounds, sharp coefficients, high inverse

### P7.1. The unweighted low estimate under a Lipschitz transport perturbation

#### Statement, spaces and hypotheses

Let H be the parity homogeneous H^-1 completion defined in section P4.2. Use either exact accepted checkpoint and its canonical fixed-exponent operator L_fix. Its coefficient matrix M satisfies M>=19/5 I by check 23. Let W be a C1 globally Lipschitz divergence-free vector field with the velocity parities, W(0)=0, and

    d=||sym DW||_infinity<19/5.

On the generator domain of transport by V+W, define

    A_W h=L_fix h+W.grad h.

Then A_W is one-to-one and onto H, with

    ||A_W^-1 f||_H <= ||f||_H/(19/5-d).                     (1)

The nonlocal coupling has the same bounded realization as before. No derivative of W of order two or greater is required. The field W need not decay at infinity.

If h is in H and g has globally bounded weak gradient, then the distribution U[h].grad g, defined by (5) below, obeys

    ||U[h].grad g||_H <= ||grad g||_infinity ||h||_H.         (2)

When h and g have the density parity, this distribution also has that parity. Thus the low bilinear constant is exactly bounded by one when Z(g)=||grad g||_infinity. A high space proving that Z is bounded, and uniform high solvability for W=U[k], are separate requirements.

#### Exact perturbed energy

For compact smooth h, let phi=(-Delta)^-1 h. Its decay and the at-most-linear growth of W justify integration by parts. Since div W=0,

    <W.grad h,phi>
      = integral Delta phi W.grad phi
      = -integral grad phi^T sym(DW) grad phi.              (3)

The last term from differentiating grad phi is the integral of -W.grad(|grad phi|^2)/2 and vanishes. Therefore

    -<A_W h,phi>
      = integral grad phi^T [M+sym(DW)] grad phi
      >=(19/5-d)||h||_H^2.                                  (4)

This records the sign: the perturbation adds sym(DW) to the negative-energy matrix.

#### Semigroup realization and surjectivity with only C1 coefficients

The complete C1 flow of V+W has Jacobian exp(2ct). Its derivative and inverse derivative have finite uniform bounds on any bounded time interval. The change-of-variables and duality argument in the fixed-exponent inverse proof therefore constructs a C0 transport semigroup on H. Add the same bounded operator B h=U[h].grad rhobar by its norm-convergent Duhamel series. This defines A_W on the transport generator domain.

To pass(4) to that semigroup without assuming an invariant smooth core for the C1 flow, take a nonnegative smooth radial convolution kernel of total mass one and set W_epsilon=W*eta_epsilon. The linear growth makes this convolution well-defined. Parity, divergence-free structure and W_epsilon(0)=0 are preserved, and ||sym DW_epsilon||<=d. The fields and their first derivatives converge locally uniformly to W and DW. Their first derivatives are uniformly bounded. The smooth-flow graph-core argument applies to each epsilon, and gives semigroup decay exp(-(19/5-d)t), uniformly in epsilon.

For a compact smooth initial function, the flows and inverse flows converge with their first derivatives on compact sets, uniformly on bounded time intervals. The transported functions converge locally uniformly and in L2 on a common compact set. By parity Hardy duality, a compactly supported difference f satisfies ||f||_H<=||r f||_2, so this convergence is strong in H. Uniform transport bounds extend it to every H input. The Duhamel series, using bounded B and uniform time-interval estimates, then gives strong convergence of the perturbed semigroups. Their common decay bound passes to the limiting semigroup S_t.

The Bochner integral -integral_0^infinity S_t f dt has norm at most the right side of (1). Finite-time integrals satisfy the generator identity; closedness of the generator shows that the infinite integral lies in its domain and maps to f. A kernel vector has a constant semigroup orbit and must vanish by exponential decay. This proves both assertions in (1).

#### The stream-function divergence identity

In the Fourier realization, put psi[h]=(-Delta)^-1 partial_x h. Plancherel gives ||psi[h]||_2<=||h||_H. For smooth functions, with grad_perp g=(-g_y,g_x),

    U[h].grad g=-div(psi[h] grad_perp g).                    (5)

The product on the right is in L2 whenever grad g is bounded, so its divergence is in H^-1 with norm at most ||psi[h]||_2 ||grad g||_infinity. Density defines the same distribution for general h in H and proves (2). This proof uses the stream function, which is one derivative smoother than density; it does not require the gradient to be a multiplier on homogeneous H^1.

#### Scope for the nonlinear problem

Equations(1)-(2) confirm the two low hypotheses of Route U. If a common high solution map exists on a low-closed ball, and that ball bounds ||DU[k]||_infinity and ||grad g||_infinity, they enter the abstract contraction theorem check 30. They do not establish that high solution map or smallness of any accepted residual. In particular the original checkpoint residual is outside H; an admissible improved reference must remove its nonintegrable far-field sectors.

### P7.2. Radial weighted Riesz bounds from the first-order complex derivatives

#### Statement

Let B be the Fourier multiplier exp(2i arg xi) on the plane, with the value at xi=0 irrelevant. Let U=(-R1 R2,R1^2), where Rj has multiplier i xi_j/|xi|. For R>0 and real beta write

    omega_(beta,R)(X)=(1+|X|^2/R^2)^(beta/2).

For arbitrary scalar functions take a=1 and |beta|<1. For centrally odd functions, f(-X)=-f(X), take a=2 and |beta|<2. In the respective class the canonical multiplier extends boundedly to the weighted L2 completion, and

    ||r^beta Bf||_2 <= (a+|beta|)/(a-|beta|) ||r^beta f||_2.       (1)

This pure-power bound is sharp in the indicated full angular class. For beta nonzero set

    H_a(beta)=2^(|1-|beta||/2) (a+|beta|)/(a-|beta|),
    C_a(beta)=(1+H_a(beta))/2.

Then, with the same domain restrictions,

    ||omega Bf||_2 <= H_a(beta) ||omega f||_2,
    ||omega U[f]||_(L2;R^2) <= C_a(beta) ||omega f||_2.          (2)

At beta=0 use the exact constants 1 for B and U. The bounds in (2) are not asserted sharp. They hold for every radius R with no radius-dependent factor.

Useful safely rounded consequences are

    beta=4/5, arbitrary f:       C_1(beta)<16/3;
    beta=4/5, centrally odd f:   C_2(beta)<9/5;
    beta=-1/5, arbitrary f:      C_1(beta)<3/2;
    beta=-6/5, centrally odd f:  C_2(beta)<8/3.                (3)

Thus the constants 256 and 2048 in the earlier weighted derivative proofs can be replaced by these smaller values whenever their stated input parity matches. In particular the top Hessian inputs D_ij h are centrally odd, whereas first derivatives of h are centrally even.

#### Polar derivation of the pure-power bound

Put D_+=partial_x+i partial_y and D_-=partial_x-i partial_y. Their multipliers satisfy D_+/D_-=B. For a smooth compact input f use the canonical potential

    g=D_+ Delta^-1 f,

so D_-g=f and D_+g=Bf. This identity also fixes the behavior at infinity. The derivatives of g have the ordinary singular-integral interpretation, including any local term in B.

For an angular mode g_n(r) exp(in theta),

    D_-g=exp(i(n-1)theta)(g_n'+n g_n/r),
    D_+g=exp(i(n+1)theta)(g_n'-n g_n/r).

Set t=log r and g_n(r)=r^(-beta)v_n(t). The two weighted radial squared norms, after suppressing their common angular factor 2pi, are

    int_R |v_n'+(n-beta)v_n|^2 dt,
    int_R |v_n'-(n+beta)v_n|^2 dt.                            (4)

For n nonzero the relevant boundary limits vanish. At the origin smoothness gives g_n=O(r^|n|); at infinity the canonical inverse gives the corresponding decaying modes. If f is arbitrary, the nonzero relevant n have |n|>=1, and |beta|<1 suffices. If f is centrally odd, g is centrally even, its nonzero n have |n|>=2, and |beta|<2 suffices. The far-field mean cancellation for a centrally odd compact input gives g=O(r^-2). These assertions also follow directly by expanding the kernel (X-Y)/|X-Y|^2 outside a disk containing the support. The compact-input case with support touching the origin follows by the same smooth expansion there.

For n=0 the two expressions before the substitution in (4) are identical. No integrability of v_0 itself is needed; this handles, in particular, a nonzero constant term of g at the origin. For n nonzero, one-dimensional Fourier transformation in t gives the squared ratio

    [tau^2+(n+beta)^2]/[tau^2+(n-beta)^2].                       (5)

The supremum over tau is max(1,|n+beta|^2/|n-beta|^2). Maximizing over both signs of n and over |n|>=a gives ((a+|beta|)/(a-|beta|))^2. Orthogonality of angular modes gives (1). Smooth cutoffs in t, increasingly long and slowly varying, with n having the maximizing sign and |n|=a, approach this ratio. They produce compact smooth annular inputs f=D_-g in the appropriate angular class. Hence the bound is sharp.

The argument initially applies to finite angular sums. Angular Fourier truncations converge in the radial weighted L2 norm. The uniform bound gives the extension, and agreement with the canonical Fourier multiplier follows by distributional convergence on test functions. Smooth compact functions away from the origin are dense in the weighted space. In the centrally odd case the extension is taken only on that closed parity subspace, and the zero-mean cancellation used above is preserved.

#### From pure powers to a regular radial weight

It suffices to take R=1, since B commutes with dilations. For b=|beta|>0 set a_b(r)=(1+r^2)^b and v_b(r)=1+r^(2b). Concavity for 0<b<=1 and convexity for b>=1 give

    min(a_b,v_b) <= max(a_b,v_b)
        <=2^|1-b| min(a_b,v_b).                            (6)

The pure-power estimate and the unweighted bound||B||=1 imply the same bound (a+b)/(a-b) on L2(v_b dX), because the norm squared is the sum of its unweighted and pure-power terms. Applying (6) gives the first line of (2) for beta>0.

For beta<0 use duality. The adjoint of B on unweighted L2 is B^-1. Thus the norm of B on L2(omega^(-2)dX) equals the norm of B^-1 on L2(omega^2dX). Reflection of the angular coordinate conjugates B and B^-1 and preserves both radial weights and central parity. The already established positive-beta bound therefore applies. This duality is inside the centrally odd subspace when that version is used. The radius R again follows by dilation.

#### The velocity pair and its identity term

Let C=(B+B^-1)/2 and S=(B-B^-1)/(2i). Their symbols are cos2theta and sin2theta. The velocity multipliers are

    U_1=S/2, U_2=-(I+C)/2.                                (7)

For a real input, C f and S f are real, so

    ||omega C f||^2+||omega S f||^2=||omega Bf||^2.

For a complex input the left side is half the sum of the corresponding B and B^-1 squared norms, and obeys the same upper bound. By Cauchy-Schwarz and (7),

    4||omega U[f]||^2
       =||omega f||^2+||omega C f||^2+||omega S f||^2
          +2 Re <omega f,omega C f>
       <=(1+H_a(beta))^2||omega f||^2.

This proves (2), with the local identity contribution in R1^2 retained. The arithmetic in (3) is independently checked at 384-bit precision in certificate file mellin_riesz_constants.py and its JSON output.

#### Scope

These are weighted L2 operator bounds for the actual Riesz velocity, not coefficient bounds or inverse estimates. They are valid on the full weighted completions and do not require support on one annulus. The sharpness assertion concerns(1) on the full centrally odd class or unrestricted class; no sharpness is asserted on the narrower even-x, odd-y class or for the velocity pair. Replacing a constant in a subsequent energy theorem still requires recomputing that theorem's scalar inequalities.

### P7.3. Compactified derivative bounds for the accepted checkpoint

#### Objects and algebraic reduction

Use exact checkpoint 131 and the canonical potential chi of the source audit, with rho=-partial_y Delta chi. Set t=r^2/(1+r^2), z=cos2theta, delta=1-1/c and w=(1-t)^(delta/2). All polynomials below have exact rational coefficients obtained directly from the recovered generator list.

After d Cartesian derivatives, one canonical potential term has the form

    coefficient * r^(2k-d+2l) (1+r^2)^(p_j-k-l) trig(n theta).

This follows inductively from the polar derivative rule already proved in the compact matrix certificate. For d=5, collecting equal angular modes leaves nonnegative integer powers k-3+l. Consequently

    D^5 chi = sqrt(t(1-t)) sum_(j=0)^3 w^(j+1) P_j(t,z) A(theta),

where A is sin theta for an odd number of y derivatives and cos theta otherwise. The angular quotients sin((2m+1)theta)/sin theta and cos((2m+1)theta)/cos theta are polynomials in z. They satisfy the recurrence R_m=2z R_(m-1)-R_(m-2), with initial pairs(1,2z+1) and (1,2z-1), respectively. This proves the conversion without angular sampling.

For d=6 the corresponding formula is

    D^6 chi=(1-t) sum_(j=0)^3 w^(j+1) P_j(t,z) A(theta),

where A=sin2theta when the y derivative count is odd and A=1 otherwise. The angular polynomials are the ordinary Chebyshev T and U polynomials. All potentially negative radial powers are checked to cancel exactly before any interval evaluation. The existing d=4 polynomials give grad rho.

The coefficient functions relevant to the second-derivative energy are

    D^2rho, <r>D^2rho, <r>^2D^3rho, <r>D^2U,
    omega D^2rho, omega D^3rho, omega D^2U,
    Db/sqrt(v), S=(v_xy rho_x-v_xx rho_y-v_x rho_xy+v_y rho_xx)/2,

with omega=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), v=omega^2 and b=v grad rho. Every tensor norm is its full Frobenius norm, counting mixed derivatives with their binomial multiplicities.

#### The differentiated weighted coefficient

Write rho_x=w-sum P_x sin2theta, rho_y=w-sum P_y, and use P_xx,P_xy,P_yy for the d=5 polynomials of D^2rho, whose angular factors are sin theta, cos theta, sin theta. Factoring

    sqrt(t) (1-t)^(1/10)(1+3t)^(-3/5)

from Db/sqrt(v), its four polynomial entries are

    xx: (1+3t)P_xx+(32/5)(1+z)P_x,
    yx: (1+3t)P_xy+(32/5)(1-z)P_x,
    xy: (1+3t)P_xy+(32/5)P_y,
    yy: (1+3t)P_yy+(32/5)P_y.

Their angular factors are sin theta, cos theta, cos theta, sin theta. The sums over w^(j+1) are implicit. These formulas are direct differentiation of v, since grad v=(32/5)X(1+4r^2)^(-1/5).

The scalar S has common radial factor

    (1/2)(1-t)^(1/5)(1+3t)^(-6/5)

and branch polynomial

    -(128/25)t(1-z^2)P_x
    +[-32/5(1+3t)+(128/25)t(1+z)]P_y
    -(16/5)t(1+z)(1+3t)P_xy
    +(16/5)t(1-z)(1+3t)P_xx.

This retains all terms from the exact gradient identity, including the mixed derivatives of the weight. A direct Cartesian jet comparison is required in the certificate audit.

#### Interval proof method and status rule

Convert each polynomial on [0,1]x[-1,1] to a tensor Bernstein basis. On a binary subrectangle, the polynomial range lies in the convex hull of its Bernstein coefficients. Treat w on its exact monotone interval and take a further degree-four Bernstein hull in w. The positive radial and angular factors are bounded on the same rectangle. Summing the squared component bounds with their tensor multiplicities bounds each stated Frobenius norm. For S use its absolute value.

Subdivision only improves the cover and does not decide truth through floating-point samples. Every accepted leaf must pass all desired inequalities with Arb intervals. The retained leaves must form a complete binary partition, including the compactified endpoint t=1. An independent audit must reconstruct every leaf at greater precision from the exact polynomials, verify coverage and hashes, and compare the polynomial formulas with finite Cartesian jet values. Only after this audit does a numerical target become a certified bound. The current status and targets are recorded in the certificate JSON and chronological independent check ledger, not inferred from this derivation alone.

    |D^2rho|_F <=3, <r>|D^2rho|_F <=8, <r>^2|D^3rho|_F <=32,
    <r>|D^2U|_F <=3, omega|D^2rho|_F <=8,

    |D(v grad rho)|_F/sqrt(v) <=28, |S|<=40.

All input functions extend smoothly to r=0; the compactified inequalities include that endpoint and the limit at infinity. Quadrant parity makes the tensor and matrix bounds global.

where A is sin theta for an odd number of y derivatives and cos theta otherwise. The collected radial power is k-4+l; all negative powers cancel exactly. Thus multiplying D^3U and D^4rho by omega gives the additional factors

### P7.4. A common high-regularity fixed-exponent inverse with an unweighted bottom

#### Statement and exact norms

Use the exact accepted checkpoint 131, its canonical velocity, fixed exponent c, and operator L_fix. Let H denote the parity homogeneous H^-1 space. Define the already certified norms

    E0(h)^2=||h||_2^2+(2000/21)||h||_H^2,
    E1(h)^2=||grad h||_2^2+12000 E0(h)^2.

Their semigroups decay at rates 11/4 and 1/20, respectively. Put omega=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), and define

    P2(h)=||omega D^2h||_2,
    E2(h)^2=P2(h)^2+2^53 E1(h)^2.                              (1)

Then the fixed-exponent generator-domain inverse on the completion of compact smooth parity functions under E2 is bijective and has norm at most 40. This is an unconditional linear theorem, using the completed M2>=1/2 certificate in section P6.9. It admits forcing with sufficiently repaired tails; the original checkpoint residual is not in E2 because its unweighted H^-1 component diverges.

The subsequent higher-regularity extension is stated below with its own explicit estimates. None of these linear theorems asserts uniform high solvability for the rough nonlinear transport perturbation U[k].

#### Weighted second derivative energy

Use identity(6) of section P6.10 with v=omega^2, f=partial_j h, and sum over j. The completed continuum certificate gives the principal matrix M2>=1/2 I. Denote the verified coefficient bounds by

    B1=16, B2=8192, B3=1048576, BV2=4096,
    D=B2+4B1=8256, Z=8B1+2B2=16512.

Here B2 bounds <r>D^2rho, B3 bounds <r>^2D^3rho, and BV2 bounds <r>D^2U. Since omega<=2<r> and omega<=2<r>^2, every lower term can be controlled by E1 and P2:

    gradient-identity term:       2D*256 ||grad h||_2 P2,
    lower transport:             2BV2 ||grad h||_2 P2,
    two differentiated couplings:4B2 ||grad h||_2 P2,
    undifferentiated velocity:   2B3 ||h||_2 P2,
    scalar identity error:       4Z ||grad h||_2^2.             (2)

The factor 256 in the first line is the weighted Riesz bound for omega. The other velocity factors have unweighted L2 norm at most one; using 256 in those lines would also be safe but unnecessary. The bounds are for ordered derivative tensors with their Frobenius norms, so summing components adds no unrecorded dimension factor.

The cross coefficients in (2) sum to less than 2^23 and 4Z<2^17. Consequently

    -<D^2L_fix h,omega^2D^2h>
      >=(1/2)P2^2-2^23 E1 P2-2^17 E1^2
      >=(1/4)P2^2-2^47 E1^2.                                 (3)

Add 2^53 times the E1 inequality with decay 1/20. Since 2^53/40>2^47, the result is

    -<L_fix h,h>_E2 >=(1/40)E2(h)^2.                         (4)

All coefficient derivatives and all nonlocal lower terms have been included. In particular the U[h]D^3rho term is present in (2).

#### Auxiliary weighted third derivatives

This auxiliary norm uses exactly the same omega on third derivatives. Its purpose is a finite semigroup growth bound; it is not asserted to be a dissipative third-order energy. Put Q3=||omega D^3h||_2.

The principal matrix is

    M3_aux=(1+c+V.grad log omega)I-3 sym(DV)+A.

The completed exact compactified certificate gives

    M3_aux>=-5/4 I.                                         (5)

It uses k=3 and sigma=6/5 in the general matrix formula, since k-1-sigma=4/5 gives exactly the same omega. Its 282-leaf binary partition covers the entire compactified quadrant and every leaf was recomputed at 384-bit precision. Independent Cartesian evaluations verify the matrix formula. This is a lower bound on an auxiliary growth matrix, not a third-order coercivity assertion.

Apply the same exact gradient identity to each ordered second derivative f=partial_i partial_j h. Its lower terms are bounded by D*256 P2 Q3+Z P2^2. The remaining differentiated transport terms are bounded by

    3||D^2U||_infinity P2 Q3
        +2||<r>D^3U||_infinity ||grad h||_2 Q3.

The remaining nonlocal terms are bounded by

    3||D^2rho||_infinity*256 P2 Q3
        +6||<r>D^3rho||_infinity ||grad h||_2 Q3
        +2||<r>^2D4rho||_infinity ||h||_2 Q3.                (6)

The verified constants are 35,77,2^14,2^14 and 2^84 in the indicated positions. The last deliberately coarse constant is proved in the next section. Their total cross coefficient, including the identity error, is less than 2^86. Equations(5)-(6) and Young's inequality therefore give

    -<D^3L_fix h,omega^2D^3h>
      >=-(3/2) Q3^2-2^173 E2^2.                                 (7)

Set

    E3(h)^2=Q3(h)^2+2^173 E2(h)^2.                            (8)

Adding 2^173 times (4) proves -<L_fix h,h>_E3>=-(3/2) E3^2. Thus its semigroup grows by at most exp(3t/2).

#### An exact global fourth-density-derivative bound

Each potential generator is a P(X)(1+r^2)^t, where P=Re(z^(k+m) conjugate(z)^(k-m)) has degree 2k, t=p_j-k, and 2p_j=3+gamma-j delta. For every ordered Cartesian derivative of order ell,

    |D^ell P| <=(2k)!/(2k-ell)! r^(2k-ell),

with zero when ell>2k. This follows directly from the product rule, |D_x z|=|D_y z|=1, and the binomial falling-factorial identity. No assertion about arbitrary bounded homogeneous polynomials is needed.

For n derivatives of (1+r^2)^t, partition the derivative slots into a singletons and b pairs, a+2b=n. Since derivatives of the quadratic vanish above order two, the resulting upper bound is

    sum_(a+2b=n) [n! 2^a/(a! b!)] |(t)_(a+b)|
                         r^a (1+r^2)^(t-a-b).               (9)

Here (t)_j is the falling factorial. Combining(9) with the product rule and r<=<r> gives a rational coefficient C(k,t,d) such that

    <r>^(d-3-gamma)|D^d(a P(1+r^2)^t)|<=|a| C(k,t,d).

The extra factor <r>^(-j delta) is at most one. Sum these exact rational coefficients over the recovered checkpoint. For d=7, each D4rho component is the sum of two potential derivatives, and there are 16 ordered components. Therefore

    ||<r>^2D4rho||_infinity
      <=8 sum_generators |a|C(k,t,7)<2^84.                 (10)

The weaker displayed weight is valid because 7-3-gamma>3>2. The exact sum and upward power-of-two bound are in certificate file higher_coefficient_bounds.json. Its large size is a quantitative weakness, not an unproved remainder.

#### Domains, consistency and interpolation

Transport by V has a complete smooth flow. Its derivatives through order three, multiplied by the weights needed in (1),(8), remain bounded on finite time intervals. This follows by differentiating the flow ODE, using <Phi_t(X)> comparable to<r>, bounded DV, and the bounds on <r>D^2V and <r>D^3V. Thus transport acts as a C0 semigroup on the completions E2 and E3. The product rule, the weighted Riesz estimate 256, and (2),(6),(10) make B h=U[h].grad rho a bounded operator on each space.

The compact smooth parity core is invariant under transport, dense, and a graph core by the resolvent-integral argument in section P4.2. Bounded perturbation preserves this domain property. Consequently the energy inequalities extend to the generator domains. The semigroups agree on common inputs by their Duhamel series. They also agree with the earlier H^-1 realization.

Let theta=1/122, and define X_theta=[E2,E3]_theta by complex interpolation of these Hilbert completions. The common semigroup obeys

    ||S_t||_(X_theta to X_theta)
       <=exp[-((1-theta)/40-(3/2)theta)t]=exp(-t/80).            (11)

The compact core is dense in X_theta. Strong continuity follows there by interpolation and density. The integral -integral_0^infinity S_t f dt lies in the X_theta generator domain and provides a bijective inverse with norm at most 80, exactly as in the previous onto proofs. No inference of surjectivity from an energy inequality alone is used.

#### Density, velocity and strain regularity

Use Bessel Sobolev norms with Fourier multiplier <xi>^s and Plancherel normalization(2pi)^-2. The coefficient sizes in (1),(8) imply the norm-one inclusions E2 into H^2 and E3 into H^3. Exact Hilbert interpolation therefore gives

    ||h||_(H^(2+theta))<=||h||_(X_theta).                   (12)

The vector Riesz multiplier U has Euclidean norm at most one at each frequency, so the same bound holds for U[h]. Let alpha=theta/2. Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz gives explicit constants

    ||grad h||_infinity, ||DU[h]||_infinity
       <=[2 sqrt(pi theta(1+theta))]^-1 ||h||_(X_theta),

    [grad h]_(C^alpha), [DU[h]]_(C^alpha)
       <=[2^(-alpha)/sqrt(pi)]
          sqrt(Gamma(2+alpha)Gamma(theta-alpha)/Gamma(2+theta))
          ||h||_(X_theta).                                (13)

Their independently evaluated 384-bit bounds are 3.10314695566 and 8.76992283409, so the safe integer bounds are 4 and 9. Thus the inverse gives ||grad h||inf,||DU[h]||inf<=320||f||_Xtheta, and the two Holder seminorms are at most 720||f||_Xtheta. In particular c[h]=partial_y U_2[h](0) and b=h_y(0) are continuous on this same space. The functions and their first derivatives tend to zero at spatial infinity by the Fourier L1 representation and the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma. Thus the leading angular profile and exponent remain fixed in the affine correction class rhobar+X_theta; the scaling direction is outside this space.

For f in X_theta and h=L_fix^-1 f, use the first-order Taylor expansions of h and U[h] at the center in the equation. Since V(0)=0, no second derivative of h is needed. This gives the exact range identity

    f_y(0)=a0 c[h].                                        (14)

Hence the inverse restricts to a bijection from the continuous hyperplane f_y(0)=0 onto the generator-domain hyperplane c[h]=0, with the same bound 80. This is the compatible fixed-tail normalization realization. It is not a full inverse allowing arbitrary variations of c or of the leading angular profile.

#### A compatible singular local moment

Put alpha=1/244, b=h_y(0), p=512 and kappa=516. The parity gives grad h(0)=(0,b). Define the jet-subtracted moment

    M(h)=[integral_(r<1) r^(-516)|h(X)-by|^512 dX]^(1/512).

The first-order Taylor formula and (13) give |h(X)-by|<=9||h||_Xtheta r^(1+alpha)/(1+alpha). The radial integral has positive exponent gap p(1+alpha)+2-kappa=6/61. Consequently M(h)<=10||h||_Xtheta, with the exact gamma-function bound evaluated in route_u_constants.json. The same parameters satisfy the transport-moment inequality kappa>p+lambda+1 because lambda<3. This controls the same moment by the common high inverse, rather than by an unproved low-norm nonlocal absorption.

Since ||h||_infinity<=||h||_Xtheta and ||grad h||_infinity<=4||h||_Xtheta, splitting increments at distance one gives ||h||_(C^alpha)<=5||h||_Xtheta. The continuous low embedding has norm at most one. Thus the fully explicit common estimate is

    ||h||_H+||h||_(C^alpha)+M(h)+|c[h]|
       <=1600 ||L_fix h||_Xtheta.                           (15)

It also holds on the normalized hyperplanes in (14). This is a complete linear estimate on its stated forcing space. Its high forcing norm and the huge coefficients in the chosen energy are essential qualifications.

Closed X_theta balls are closed in the H metric: every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence in this Hilbert space; continuous injection into H identifies its weak limit with a given strong H limit, and weak lower semicontinuity bounds the norm. Adding the continuous X_theta condition c[h]=0 preserves this argument. Thus this high space also supplies the low-closedness hypothesis of the two-norm theorem.

#### Remaining nonlinear and numerical conditions

For W=U[k],(13) bounds the low perturbation in check 35 and the gradient multiplier in its constant-one bilinear estimate. It does not by itself prove a high energy inequality for A_W on X_theta: differentiating three times would require derivatives of k unavailable from H^(2+theta). Interpolating smooth-W estimates with a constant involving D^3W would leave this gap unresolved. A direct fractional or tame estimate and a compatible generator construction remain necessary.

The original residual is excluded by its H^-1 tail. Any improved reference and residual must have all nonintegrable stationary and descendant sectors removed, and the coefficient certificates must then be checked for that reference or transferred by a proved perturbation bound. No numerical closure follows from this linear high inverse alone.

### P7.6. Three explicit fractional estimates used in the high-norm audit

#### Statement and conventions

Use Fourier transform fhat(xi)=integral exp(-iX.xi)f(X)dX, and Bessel norms ||f||_(H^s)^2=(2pi)^-2 integral <xi>^(2s)|fhat(xi)|^2 dxi. Let 0<s<1. The following formulas verify the corresponding tools in a draft argument. They are not a completed weighted high inverse theorem.

#### Fractional transport identity

Put

    C_s=4^s s Gamma(1+s)/(pi Gamma(1-s)),
    E_s(f)=||Lambda^s f||_2^2
          =(C_s/2) integral integral |f(x)-f(y)|^2/|x-y|^(2+2s) dx dy.

For smooth compact f and a C1 Lipschitz vector field b with at most linear growth,

    -<Lambda^s(b.grad f),Lambda^s f>
      =(C_s/4) integral integral |f(x)-f(y)|^2/|x-y|^(2+2s)
         [div b(x)+div b(y)
          -(2+2s)(b(x)-b(y)).(x-y)/|x-y|^2] dx dy.           (1)

To prove it, apply b(x).grad_x+b(y).grad_y to |f(x)-f(y)|^2 and integrate by parts in both variables. First remove |x-y|<epsilon and put an outer cutoff; the boundary errors converge to zero because f is smooth and s<1, and because the kernel decays at infinity. Equivalently use a smooth radial regularization before taking the limit. Along the line segment from y to x,

    |(b(x)-b(y)).(x-y)|<=||sym Db||_infinity |x-y|^2.

Consequently the absolute value of (1) is bounded by

    [||div b||_infinity+(1+s)||sym Db||_infinity] E_s(f).     (2)

The constants and sign in the draft's identity are correct. For an affine field the exact bracket should be retained instead of using (2).

#### A bounded-Lipschitz coefficient commutator

The kernel constant of Lambda^s is

    kappa_s=2^s(s/2)Gamma(1+s/2)/(pi Gamma(1-s/2)).

For bounded Lipschitz scalar a, the commutator has kernel

    kappa_s (a(x)-a(y)) / |x-y|^(2+s),

up to the irrelevant overall sign. The pointwise difference bound is the minimum of ||grad a||_infinity |x-y| and 2||a||_infinity. For any ell>0, radial integration below and above ell gives both Schur integrals bounded by

    B_s(a;ell)=2pi kappa_s
       [||grad a||_infinity ell^(1-s)/(1-s)
        +2||a||_infinity ell^-s/s].                         (3)

Thus ||[Lambda^s,a]f||_2<=B_s(a;ell)||f||_2. This is a lower-order coefficient error. Since the component velocity multipliers have norms 1/2 and 1, respectively, the draft's bound B=(1/2)B_s(rho_x;ell)+B_s(rho_y;ell) for the coupled commutator follows directly.

#### An explicit product estimate

For f in H^s and g in H^(1+s),

    ||fg||_(H^s)<=P_s ||f||_(H^s)||g||_(H^(1+s)),
    P_s=2^(s-1)/sqrt(pi)*sqrt(1/s+4/(1-s)).                 (4)

Also ||g||_infinity<=[2sqrt(pi s)]^-1 ||g||_(H^(1+s)). The latter is direct Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz and the exact integral of <xi>^(-2-2s), equal to pi/s.

For (4), Fourier convolution and Cauchy-Schwarz reduce the square of the constant to (2pi)^-2 times

    sup_xi I(xi),
    I(xi)=integral <xi>^(2s)/[<eta>^(2s)<xi-eta>^(2+2s)] deta.

Set R=|xi|. On |eta|>=R/2, <xi><=2<eta>, giving a contribution at most 2^(2s)pi/s. On |eta|<R/2, one has <xi><=2<xi-eta> and <xi-eta>^2>=1+R^2/4. This contribution is at most

    2^(2s)pi [(1+R^2/4)^(1-s)-1]/[(1-s)(1+R^2/4)]
      <=2^(2s)pi/(1-s).

This is already stronger than the draft's stated 4/(1-s) term, so (4) holds. The convolution proof first applies to Schwartz functions and extends by density. In particular the differentiated products (D^2W)grad h and (DW)D^2h admit H^s bounds when W,h are in H^(2+s), without assuming D^3W.

#### What remains before using these estimates

The displayed estimates are unweighted. A weighted global high inverse still needs compatible localization, weight ratios in nonlocal interactions, the exact principal matrices, all coefficient and cutoff errors, and a semigroup realization for the rough perturbed field. The product bound alone does not prove the common high solvability required by nonlinear closure.

#### Verification of the kernel normalization

For 0<s<1, the Gaussian integral and the identity r^(-2-2s)=Gamma(1+s)^-1 integral_0^infinity t^s exp(-tr^2)dt give

    integral_R^2 (1-cos(x.xi))/|x|^(2+2s) dx
      =pi/Gamma(1+s) integral_0^infinity
             t^(s-1)(1-exp(-|xi|^2/(4t)))dt
      =pi Gamma(1-s)|xi|^(2s)/(4^s s Gamma(1+s)).

The last equality follows from u=|xi|^2/(4t) and one integration by parts. Tonelli applies to the nonnegative integrand. This proves the stated C_s and, by replacing s with s/2, the stated kappa_s. The energy normalization follows from Plancherel and the factor 2 in |exp(ix.xi)-exp(iy.xi)|^2.

### P7.7. A decaying weighted residual is not an unweighted negative-norm bound

#### Claim being audited

The numerical  N12 plan at 02:30Z describes ||r w F||_2, w=(1+r^2)^-1, as a Hardy bound for the unweighted H^-1 component in Route U. This claim is false. The valid parity Hardy inequalities are

    ||F||_(H^-1)<=||rF||_2,
    ||wF||_(H^-1)<=||rwF||_2.

They follow by pairing against phi and using ||phi/r||_2<=||grad phi||_2. These are different forcing norms.

#### A counterexample to a uniform replacement

Choose a nonzero smooth density-parity f supported in 1<r<2. Set f_R(X)=R^-2 f(X/R), R>=1. Fourier scaling gives

    ||f_R||_(H^-1)=||f||_(H^-1)>0.

After X=RY,

    ||rw f_R||_2^2
      =integral |Y|^2/(1+R^2|Y|^2)^2 |f(Y)|^2 dY
      <=R^-4 integral |Y|^-2 |f(Y)|^2 dY.

Thus the proposed right side tends to zero, even though the unweighted negative norm stays fixed. No universal constant repairs that replacement. The true quantity ||r f_R||_2 is independent of R.

#### Scope

The weighted quantity may be useful in an optimization objective, but it must be labeled as such. It is not a certificate, surrogate upper bound, or smallness test for the unweighted Route U forcing norm. An actual modewise H^-1 computation or the genuine ||rF||_2 bound is required there.

## P8. Rough-velocity inverse, conditional existence, reference independence

### P8.1. A uniform inverse for rough perturbing velocities and a conditional existence theorem

#### Exact statement and scope

All functions on R^2 are real, even in x and odd in y. The canonical velocity is U[h]=(-R1 R2 h,R1^2 h), with Rj=partial_j(-Delta)^(-1/2). Let H be the homogeneous H^-1 completion of smooth compactly supported functions with this parity. Its norm is ||(-Delta)^(-1/2)h||_2. Use all ordered derivatives in tensor norms and set

    omega=(1+4|X|^2)^(2/5), b0=20/21, B=2^14,
    E2(h)^2=||omega D^2h||_2^2
             +B||Dh||_2^2+16B||h||_2^2+16Bb0||h||_H^2.

For use below define also E3(h)^2=||omega D^3h||_2^2+2^173 E2(h)^2 on the same compact core, and take its completion. The singular functional is c[h]=partial_y U_2[h](0)=psi_xy[h](0), with psi=partial_x(-Delta)^-1 h; its local and principal-value representation is proved in section P2.1. For N_s inputs it is defined by the bounded C1 velocity representative. Write lambda=2c-1.

The space E2 is the completion of that smooth compact core. Set J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), and let N_s be its core completion for the norm

    N_s(h)=E2(J^s h),                 0<s<=1/2.

Let a smooth reference density rho_bar have the prescribed parity, canonical velocity u, exponent c, sublinear growth and bounded first derivatives. Assume c+c[rho_bar]=1, a0=partial_y rho_bar(0) !=0, and the following two explicit hypotheses.

1. The fixed-exponent operator

       Lh=(cX+u).Dh-h+U[h].D rho_bar

   has its consistent transport-plus-bounded-coupling realization on E2, with energy decay 1/10. The coefficient conditions sufficient for this hypothesis are listed in section P7.5: M>=19I/5, A>=-I/20, N<=I, M1>=9I/10, M2>=I/2 and its five derivative bounds. Its low realization on H has energy decay 19/5.

2. Writing ||T||_(Sigma,infinity)=sum_I ||T_I||_infinity, where I ranges over all ordered tensor indices, the finite quantity

       Mstar=|c|+||Du||_(Sigma,infinity)
          +||omega D^2u||_(Sigma,infinity)+||omega D^3u||_(Sigma,infinity)
          +||D rho_bar||_(Sigma,infinity)
          +sum_(j=2)^4 ||omega D^j rho_bar||_(Sigma,infinity)

   is at most 4096.

These hypotheses hold for exact accepted state 131. The additional D^3u and D^4rho certificates are audited in section P7.3. They do not automatically hold for a numerical refit.

For k in N_s define A_k=L+U[k].D. Its maximal distributional domain in N_s is the generator domain of a strongly continuous semigroup, and

    ||exp(t A_k)||_(N_s->N_s)
       <=exp[-t(1/10-1024 s Mstar-128 N_s(k)/sqrt(s))].          (1)

Whenever the rate beta in (1) is positive, A_k is bijective from its domain to N_s, with inverse norm at most 1/beta. If c[k]=0, its inverse takes precisely the forcing hyperplane f_y(0)=0 to the solution hyperplane c[h]=0.

In particular choose

    s=2^-28, r=2^-27, eta=2^-27/20.                           (2)

For every k with N_s(k)<=r the rate is at least 11/160>1/20, and the inverse norm is at most 20. If the actual reference residual R=F(rho_bar) belongs to N_s and N_s(R)<=eta, then there is a unique h in

    {h in N_s: N_s(h)<=r, c[h]=0}

such that F(rho_bar+h)=0 with the same exponent c. This is a conditional a posteriori theorem. The original accepted residual fails the H component and does not satisfy its hypotheses. No existence near that original state is asserted.

#### 1. Fractional kernels and weights

Use the unitary Fourier convention in dimension 2, so multiplication gives a convolution factor 1/(2pi). The weight obeys

    omega(x)/omega(y)<=m(x-y),  m(z)=(1+2|z|)^(4/5)<=1+2|z|,
    ||D omega||_infinity<=2, ||D log omega||_infinity<=4/5,
    |X| |D log omega(X)|<=4/5.                                (3)

The first inequality follows by applying the triangle inequality to (1,2x). The other inequalities follow by differentiating. In particular |W.D log omega|<=(4/5)||DW||_infinity if W(0)=0.

For 0<s<1,

    J^s f=f+int kappa_s(z)(f(x)-f(x-z)) dz,
    kappa_s(z)=s/[2 Gamma(1-s/2)]
       int_0^infinity exp(-t) p_t(z) t^(-1-s/2) dt,
    p_t(z)=(4pi t)^(-1) exp(-|z|^2/(4t)).                    (4)

This follows by applying the scalar Laplace integral for a positive fractional power to 1+|xi|^2 and separating its value at xi=0. Direct Gaussian moments yield

    int |z| kappa_s = (s sqrt(pi)/2) Gamma((1-s)/2)/Gamma(1-s/2),
    int |z|^2 kappa_s=2s.                                   (5)

The second identity is 2s, not 4s. With A=Gamma((1-s)/2)/Gamma(1-s/2), the weighted bounds are

    int |z| m(z) kappa_s <=s(sqrt(pi) A/2+4)<=17s,
    int |z|^2 m(z)|D kappa_s| <=s(3sqrt(pi) A/2+16)<=54s.     (6)

Indeed Gamma((1-s)/2)<5, from splitting its integral at 1, and Gamma(1-s/2)>exp(-1). Thus A<5e for 0<s<=1/2, which proves the rounded constants.

The Bessel kernels of J^-s and J^-2 are positive probability kernels with second moments 2s and 4. Equations(3) and Cauchy-Schwarz imply

    ||omega J^-s f||_2<=3||omega f||_2,
    ||omega J^-2 f||_2<=5||omega f||_2.                      (7)

Also

    ||omega partial_i partial_j J^-2 f||_2<=28||omega f||_2. (8)

Here is an independent check including the singular local term. Away from zero the kernel is q_ij=int exp(-t) partial_ij p_t dt. Its unweighted operator norm is at most 1. The bound |partial_ij p_t| <= (|z|^2/(4t^2)+1/(2t))p_t gives int |z||q_ij|<=2pi. Since |omega(x)/omega(y)-1|<=2|x-y|, the weight commutator has norm at most 4pi. The local term of this particular second-derivative Bessel kernel is -(delta_ij/2)delta_0, which is multiplication by a scalar and commutes with the weight. This statement does not apply to derivatives of delta_0. Thus 1+4pi<14 already suffices, and 28 is safe. Alternatively int |z|m(z)|q_ij|<=2pi+20<27.

From (4), the mean-value theorem and (6),

    ||omega[J^s,d]f||_2<=17s ||omega Dd||_(Sigma,infinity)||f||_2,
    ||omega[J^s,d]f||_2<=17s ||Dd||_(Sigma,infinity)||omega f||_2,
    ||[J^s,omega]f||_2<=34s||f||_2.                          (9)

For the first bound insert the weight at each point on the segment from x-z to x and use (3). These arguments allow unbounded d with the displayed derivative bounds.

#### 2. Smooth background commutator with full bookkeeping

For a smooth vector field d, Taylor-expand

    d_j(x)-d_j(x-z)=sum_l partial_l d_j(x) z_l+R_j(x,z).

The remainder satisfies |R_j|<=|z|^2||D^2d_j||_(Sigma,infinity)/2 and |D_z R_j|<=|z|||D^2d_j||_(Sigma,infinity). The linear term in [J^s,d.D]J^-s is exactly

    -s sum_(j,l) (partial_l d_j) partial_l partial_j J^-2.

For the remainder integrate the derivative off J^-s h(x-z). Equations(6)-(8) give

    ||omega[J^s,d.D]J^-s h||_2
       <=s(28||Dd||_(Sigma,infinity)+132||D^2d||_(Sigma,infinity))
          ||omega h||_2.                                  (10)

The 132 is 3(54/2+17). The small-circle boundary is O(epsilon^(1-s)), hence vanishes. The unweighted estimate is no larger. No derivative is lost.

Let h=J^s g, T=[J^s,u.D], and Qg=U[g].D rho_bar. Differentiation, with all ordered contractions, gives

    D^2Tg=T D^2g+2[J^s,Du]D^2g+[J^s,D^2u]Dg,
    D^2[J^s,Q]g=[J^s,D rho_bar]U[D^2g]
                 +2[J^s,D^2rho_bar]U[Dg]+[J^s,D^3rho_bar]U[g]. (11)

Both velocities are divergence free. Therefore

    Tg=div([J^s,u]g),
    [J^s,Q]g=div([J^s,rho_bar]U[g]).                       (12)

This last identity does not require bounded multiplication by rho_bar. It gives an H bound 17s Mstar ||h||_2 for each commutator.

Write P=||omega D^2h||_2, a=||Dh||_2, b=||h||_2, and E=E2(h). The four square-root weights in E are 1,128,512,512sqrt(b0). The following bounds use (9)-(12), ||U||_(L2->L2-vector)<=1, and the unweighted contraction J^-s. Each entry bounds the indicated output norm divided by s Mstar:

| output | T g | [J^s,Q]g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| weighted second derivative | 194P+17a | 17P+34a+17b |
| first derivative | 177a | 17a+17b |
| L2 | 160b | 17b |
| H | 17b | 17b |

For example 194=28+132+2(17); no third derivative of u is used in the top transport term, only in its final multiplication commutator. After inserting the four norm weights and using P<=E, a<=E/128, b<=E/512, the first column has E2 norm at most 565s Mstar E by the triangle inequality. The second has E2 norm at most (493/4)s Mstar E. These deliberately loose sums retain every ordered contraction.

Finally Fourier differentiation gives

    [J^s,X.D]J^-s=s(I-J^-2).

Its E2 norm is at most 6s. Since 565+493/4+6=2777/4<1024, we have proved

    ||[J^s,L]J^-s h||_E2<=1024 s Mstar E2(h).             (13)

#### 3. Rough transport without third derivatives of k

For 0<s<=1 and all xi,eta,

    |eta| |<xi>^s-<eta>^s|<=|xi-eta|<eta>^s.             (14)

Divide by <eta>^s and use |t^s-1|<=|t-1| and the 1-Lipschitz property of <xi>. Fourier convolution and Cauchy-Schwarz now give

    ||[J^s,W.D]F||_2<=c_s||W||_(H^(2+s))||J^s F||_2,
    c_s=1/[2sqrt(pi s(1+s))].                            (15)

The integral used here is int |xi|^2<xi>^(-4-2s) dxi=pi/[s(1+s)]. The same calculation gives ||DW||_infinity<=c_s||W||_(H^(2+s)). Euclidean tensor norms require no extra dimension factor.

Set T_W=[J^s,W.D]. For divergence-free W, integration by parts in (4) gives the exact, absolutely integrable commutator

    [omega,T_W]F(x)=int D kappa_s(z).(W(x)-W(x-z))
                             (omega(x)-omega(x-z))F(x-z) dz. (16)

Its norm is at most 108s||DW||_infinity||F||_2. Combining(9),(15),(16) gives

    ||omega T_W F||_2
       <=c_s(1+142s)||W||_(H^(2+s))||omega J^s F||_2.    (17)

The required product estimate, including its weight, is

    ||vf||_(H^s)<=s^-1/2||v||_(H^(1+s))||f||_(H^s),
    ||omega J^s(vf)||_2
       <=(1+44s)s^-1/2||v||_(H^(1+s))||omega J^s f||_2. (18)

For completeness, the first bound follows by Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz: split the integral of <xi>^(2s)/(<eta>^(2+2s)<xi-eta>^(2s)) according to |xi-eta|>=|xi|/2. The two contributions are at most 2pi/s and 16pi, so their sum is at most 10pi/s for s<=1/2. The convolution normalization is 1/(2pi), and sqrt(10pi)/(2pi)<1. The weighted bound follows by commuting J^s past omega twice using (9), together with ||v||_infinity<=||v||_(H^(1+s))/(2sqrt(pi s)); its numerator is at most 1+34s+17s/sqrt(pi)<1+44s. The proof also applies to Euclidean tensor contractions.

Take W=U[k]. Since E2 dominates H^2,

    ||W||_(H^(2+s))<=N_s(k), ||DW||_infinity<=c_s N_s(k).

For h=J^s g,

    D^2J^s(W.Dg)=W.D D^2h+T_W D^2g
                   +2J^s(DW D^2g)+J^s(D^2W Dg).         (19)

The first term has energy cost at most (4/5)c_s N_s(k)P(h)^2. Apply(17) to the second and (18) to the last two. For the last term use v=Dg and f=D^2W. Every second derivative of k is centrally odd, so the independently proved Mellin estimate gives

    ||omega J^s D^2W||_2<= (9/5)||omega D^2 J^s k||_2
                         <=(9/5)N_s(k).                (20)

Thus the full top energy cost, in units N_s(k)N_s(g)^2/sqrt(s), is at most

    (4/5)(3/10)+(3/10)(1+142s)+(19/5)(1+44s)
       <=109.24.                                       (21)

Here c_s sqrt(s)<3/10, and s<=1/2. The lower gradient and L2 components cost at most 1.3 and 0.3 in the same units. The H component is handled separately by

    J^s(W.Dg)=div J^s(Wg).

Equation(18) and Cauchy-Schwarz give cost at mostsqrt(b0)/2<1/2 after its norm weight is included. The total is less than 111.34<128. Therefore

    |Re (J^s(W.Dg),J^s g)_E2|
       <=128 N_s(k)N_s(g)^2/sqrt(s).                    (22)

Equation(22) is initially an energy-form inequality on the smooth graph core. It does not assert that W.D is a bounded map from N_s to N_s, or that its displayed inner product is separately defined for every N_s input. The realization below passes this core inequality to semigroup bounds. This proof uses only N_s(k), not D^3W. Combining(13),(22) with the assumed E2 energy inequality proves (1) on smooth functions.

#### 4. Realization, surjectivity and injectivity

First J^s extends to an isometric bijection N_s->E2. To check that its range is dense, apply J^-s to a smooth compact core function. The result is Schwartz and has the same parity. Its smooth cutoff approximations converge in Schwartz topology; applying J^s preserves that topology. Schwartz convergence implies E2 convergence, including H convergence by the parity Hardy inequality ||f||_H<=|| |X|f||_2. This proves density and then the assertion by completion. Equation(7) also yields E2(g)<=3N_s(g).

Choose k_n in the smooth compact parity core converging to k in N_s. Then W_n=U[k_n] converges to W in W^(1,infinity), by (15) and the corresponding zero-derivative embedding. Each W_n is smooth, divergence free, vanishes at zero, and has bounded derivatives with sufficient decay. Its complete transport flow acts strongly continuously on E2: the field grows at most linearly, its derivative is bounded, and its higher derivatives satisfy the weighted bounds needed by the chain rule. This is the same direct flow construction as in the E2 base theorem. The coupling Q is bounded there.

For each fixed n, conjugation by J^s gives a bounded perturbation on E2, by the smooth version of (13) applied to u+W_n. The required smooth coefficient constants are finite, although no uniform higher-derivative bounds in n are claimed. The fixed Q commutator is already covered by (11)-(13). Hence A_(k_n) generates a strongly continuous semigroup S_n on N_s. Smooth cutoff approximation justifies the integrations above on a graph core, so (1) bounds S_n with its stated rate.

On any finite time interval and for fixed initial f in N_s, S_n(t)f is Cauchy in C_t L2. Indeed the difference equation has forcing (W_n-W_m).D S_m(t)f. Its L2 norm tends uniformly to zero: the velocity difference converges uniformly and the gradient is bounded by the uniform N_s estimate. The ordinary L2 transport estimate has constants independent of n,m, since div W_n=0 and Q is a fixed bounded L2 operator. Gronwall proves the assertion.

The N_s bounds give weak compactness. Every weak subsequential limit equals this L2 limit, so it defines S(t)f in N_s with the same decay, by lower semicontinuity. Uniqueness of the L2 equation gives the semigroup law. At zero, L2 continuity plus the N_s bound imply weak N_s convergence to f. The bound in (1) gives limsup N_s(S(t)f)<=N_s(f), hence the Hilbert norm identity gives strong N_s continuity.

For clarity about the domain, the complete globally Lipschitz field cX+u+W defines the usual strongly continuous L2 transport group. Its generator is the maximal distributional transport operator: this follows by mollification and radial cutoff, since the field has at most linear growth and bounded first derivative. Adding the fixed bounded Q preserves that characterization. The N_s semigroup is its restriction, by the L2 uniqueness just used. Thus its generator is the part of that L2 generator with both h and A_k h in N_s, exactly the maximal distributional domain asserted above. Equivalently, apply the L2 Duhamel identity to any h with A_k h in N_s; the integral of S(t)A_k h then converges in N_s and identifies its N_s derivative.

For positive rate beta, -int_0^infinity S(t)f dt converges in N_s and solves A_k h=f on the generator domain, with norm at most beta^-1. Conversely A_k h=0 makes S(t)h constant, and exponential decay forces h=0. This proves onto and injectivity, not just an a priori inequality.

#### 5. Normalization, complete ball and nonlinear contraction

The Fourier estimates give N_s subset H^(2+s) subset C^1. Write mu=partial_y(cY+u_2)(0). First-order Taylor expansion of A_k h=f at zero, using the parity and U[h](0)=0, gives

    f_y(0)=(mu-1+c[k])h_y(0)+a0 c[h].                   (23)

Only C^1 regularity is needed: the field vanishes at zero, so its product with Dh has its linear term determined by Dh(0). The background normalization makes mu=1. Therefore c[k]=0 implies f_y(0)=0 if and only if c[h]=0.

For (2), the background loss is at most 2^22 s=1/64 and the rough loss is 128r/sqrt(s)=1/64. This gives beta>=11/160>1/20. Also d=||DU[k]||_infinity<=c_s r<2^-13. The low H inverse has norm at most

    K_L=(19/5-d)^-1<1.

Here is a construction and consistency proof; no H solution is assumed to lie in L2. For each smooth k_n used in section 4, let d_n=||DU[k_n]||_infinity. On the common smooth graph core the exact negative-order identity is

    Re <U[k_n].Dg,g>_H
       = -int D_i Phi D_i U_j[k_n] D_j Phi,
    Phi=(-Delta)^-1 g.

Thus its absolute value is at most d_n||g||_H^2. Add the background H decay 19/5. The resulting low energy inequality extends to the high generator domain by graph approximation, since the inclusions N_s -> H and A_(k_n)N_s -> H are continuous in the graph norm. Differentiate the H norm of a semigroup orbit starting in that domain and integrate. Approximation of arbitrary high initial data then gives

    ||S_n(t)f||_H <= exp[-(19/5-d_n)t]||f||_H,
    f in N_s.

The uniform N_s bounds and the C_t L2 convergence from section 4 identify all weak H limits. Weak lower semicontinuity and d_n -> d give this bound for S(t)f. The space N_s is dense in H, since it contains its defining compact smooth parity core. Therefore S(t) extends uniquely to a bounded semigroup S_H(t) on H with the same decay. Strong continuity at zero follows first on N_s from its strong high continuity and then on all of H by density and the uniform finite-time bound. The integral -int_0^infinity S_H(t)f dt gives a surjective inverse on its generator domain with bound K_L; an invariant orbit and decay prove injectivity.

This low semigroup agrees with the L2 semigroup on H cap L2. To justify the needed simultaneous density, first approximate the Fourier transform on annuli away from zero by smooth compact functions, preserving parity, in both weighted L2(|xi|^-2 dxi) and ordinary L2. Their inverse transforms are Schwartz. Smooth parity-preserving spatial cutoffs approximate each of them in L2 and H, the latter by ||g||_H<=||r g||_2. Hence a common core is dense in the intersection with the sum norm. The two semigroups agree on that core by their high construction, and their bounds pass this agreement to the intersection. Limits in H and L2 represent the same distribution because pairing with a compact smooth test function is continuous in either topology.

In particular, suppose w in N_s and A_k w=f in H cap L2 distributionally. The maximal L2 realization places w in its generator domain. Its integrated orbit identity reads

    S_2(t)w-w=int_0^t S_2(tau)f dtau.

By the intersection consistency, both sides equal the corresponding H expressions as distributions; the H integral exists by strong continuity. Thus this identity holds in H. Dividing by t and taking t down to zero shows w belongs to the low generator domain with A_(k,H)w=f. This is exactly the domain statement needed for the contraction difference below.

Let B_r={k:N_s(k)<=r,c[k]=0} with the H metric. This metric space is complete. A Cauchy sequence converges in H; weak compactness of its bounded N_s ball identifies the same limit in N_s, lower semicontinuity retains its radius, and continuity of c on N_s retains c=0. Define T(k)=-A_k^-1 R. The exact reference normalization gives R_y(0)=0, so (23) puts T(k) in c=0. The high inverse and N_s(R)<=r/20 put T(k) in B_r.

For k,l in B_r,

    A_k(T(k)-T(l))=-U[k-l].D T(l).

The streamfunction identity U[z].Dv=-div(psi[z] D^perp v), and ||psi[z]||_2<=||z||_H, imply

    ||U[z].Dv||_H<=||z||_H ||Dv||_infinity.

The difference w=T(k)-T(l) belongs to N_s. Its forcing belongs to H by this bilinear estimate and to L2 since U[k-l] is bounded and D T(l) is in L2. The low-domain argument above therefore applies to w. Consequently T is a contraction with constant at mostK_L c_s r<2^-13. Its fixed point h satisfies Lh+U[h].Dh=-R and c[h]=0. Since c remains fixed, this is precisely F(rho_bar+h)=0. Conversely any solution in B_r is a fixed point, which proves the stated uniqueness.

#### 6. One compatible estimate for density, moment and strain

The same space, without an extra regularity assumption, controls the requested quantities. For the explicit s in (2), put delta=s/2=2^-29, p=2^31 and kappa=p+4, and define

    Mloc(h)=[int_(|X|<1) |X|^-kappa |h(X)-h_y(0)y|^p dX]^(1/p).

Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz gives ||h||_(C^(1/2))<=N_s(h), where the norm is supremum plus seminorm. Indeed the supremum constant is at most 1/(2sqrt(pi)), and the half-Holder constant is at most 1/2. Similarly

    [Dh]_(C^delta)<=2^-delta sqrt(Beta(2+delta,s-delta)/pi) N_s(h)
                   <=s^-1/2 N_s(h).

The last inequality uses Beta(2+delta,s-delta)<=1/(s-delta)=2/s and 2/pi<1. Taylor's integral remainder is at most [Dh]_(C^delta)|X|^(1+delta)/(1+delta). Since p delta=4, the moment integral is 2pi/(p delta-2)=pi, and pi^(1/p)<2. Thus Mloc(h)<=2s^-1/2 N_s(h). Also |c[h]|<=c_s N_s(h)<s^-1/2 N_s(h), and ||h||_H<=N_s(h). Hence

    ||h||_H+||h||_(C^(1/2))+Mloc(h)+|c[h]|
       <=2^16 N_s(h)<=20*2^16 N_s(A_k h).               (24)

The first inequality in (24) holds for every h in N_s. The second is asserted for N_s(k)<=r and h in the maximal N_s generator domain D(A_k), with parameters (2). This controls h itself in a direct Holder norm. The very large p records the small fractional regularity used by this conservative closure argument. It is a finite, explicit exponent. It is compatible with the local transport moment window: kappa-p-lambda-1=3-lambda>0 for the certified state, and p(1+delta)+2-kappa=2>0.

#### 7. Scaling and tail scope

If the reference has the nonzero uniform leading profile r^gamma Theta0(theta), gamma=1/c<1, corrections in N_s tend uniformly to zero at infinity, by uniform continuity and L2 integrability. They preserve c and the entire Theta0. The scaling transformation t rho(X/t) changes Theta0 to t^(1-gamma)Theta0. Hence no nontrivial scaling stays in the same affine correction class. This also excludes the infinitesimal direction without differentiating an unproved tail remainder: if K=rho-r partial_r rho belonged to N_s, then K would tend uniformly to zero. Sublinear growth and integration of partial_r(rho/r)=-K/r^2 give rho(r,theta)=r int_r^infinity K(t,theta)/t^2 dt, which would tend uniformly to zero, contrary to the nonzero growing leading profile.

For a precise optional augmented phase, fix a radial smooth cutoff chi_inf, zero on r<=1 and one on r>=2, and a number 0<gamma<1. The leading-tail coordinate space is L2 of the parity angular functions on the circle. Form the direct sum Z_gamma={chi_inf r^gamma theta(theta_angle)+h: theta in L2(S1), h in N_s} with norm ||theta||_L2+N_s(h). The decomposition is unique because a nonzero growing homogeneous angular term is not in L2(R2). The coordinate functional P(theta)=<theta-Theta0,Theta0>_L2 is bounded on this space, and its derivative along the explicit scaled leading coordinate is (1-gamma)||Theta0||_2^2>0. This establishes only the phase-coordinate transversality; no nonlinear inverse or differentiable scaling action on every rough Z_gamma element is asserted. The nonlinear theorem above uses the fixed coordinate Theta0, not this enlarged space.

This theorem freezes the exponent and leading angular function. It does not claim to allow their logarithmic or functional variations inside N_s. A tail-completed reference can be treated if its actual residual belongs to N_s and all the explicit background hypotheses are independently reverified. The finite-family nonexistence theorem and the original growing residual remain fully consistent with this conditional result.

#### 8. A certified route from ordinary derivative residual norms to N_s

No uniform replacement of N_s(f) by E2(f) is asserted merely because s is small. The following quantitative bound is sufficient. If E=E2(f) and Q=||omega D^3f||_2 are finite, then

    N_s(f)<=E^(1-s)(2Q^2+16410E^2)^(s/2)+34sE.            (25)

For E=0 the assertion means f=0. To prove it for E>0, introduce the Hilbert-valued function

    T f=(omega D^2f,128Df,512f,512sqrt(b0) Lambda^-1 f).

Its L2 norm is E. Its H1 norm squared is E^2 plus the squared L2 norms of the derivatives of these four entries. Since ||D omega||_infinity<=2,

    ||D(omega D^2f)||_2^2<=2Q^2+8||D^2f||_2^2.

The other three derivative contributions are B||D^2f||_2^2,16B||Df||_2^2 and 16Bb0||f||_2^2. Hence

    ||Tf||_H1^2<=2Q^2+(B+25+b0)E^2<2Q^2+16410E^2.

Fourier Holder interpolation gives ||J^s Tf||_2<=||Tf||_2^(1-s)||Tf||_H1^s. The only commutator between T and J^s is its first entry, bounded by 34s||D^2f||_2<=34sE. This proves (25), first on the core and then by completion. It also proves that E3 membership implies N_s membership for every 0<s<=1/2.

In terms of the earlier E3, the weaker convenient bound is

    N_s(f)<=2^(s/2) E2(f)^(1-s) E3(f)^s+34sE2(f).         (26)

If Q<=2^(173/2)E2(f), then E3(f)<=2^87E2(f), so the multiplier in (26) is at most 2^(175s/2)+34s. Any numerical use must certify the stated Q bound or use (25) with actual certified E,Q; finite-point comparisons of an evaluator do not certify these norms.

For 0<s<1/34, the same commutator also gives the useful reverse comparison

    N_s(f)>=(1-34s)E2(f).                                  (27)

Indeed unweighted Bessel expansion gives ||Tf||_2<=||J^s Tf||_2. The sole commutator between T and J^s is again its weighted Hessian entry, so

    E2(f)<=||J^s Tf||_2<=N_s(f)+34s||D^2f||_2
            <=N_s(f)+34s E2(f).

This proves (27) on the smooth core, and it extends by completion using the already established E2<=3N_s inclusion. It also applies directly to every smooth residual with finite E,Q. In particular, certified lower bounds for any square sum of ordinary E2 components give a rigorous N_s lower bound after multiplication by 1-34s. Equality of E2 and N_s is not asserted.

### P8.2. Reference independence of the energy hierarchy

This audit concerns section 3, Theorem A, and Proposition C of the S1_CLOSURE.md as read at 2026-10-28T03:43Z. It separates sufficient structural hypotheses from numerical coefficient bounds. It is not a transfer of checkpoint certificates to a refit.

Let a smooth parity reference rho, its canonical velocity u, and c satisfy the(B0)-(B8), with all derivative bounds interpreted as full Frobenius tensor supremums. Add the exact center identity c+c[rho]=1 when claiming the normalized range identity. Then the E0,E1,E2,E3 and interpolation inverse theorems of check 46 hold with exactly the stated constants. No finite-potential representation is required. The representation is needed only by the particular coefficient-certification algorithms.

For the rough N_s theorem, use Mstar with Du, rather than DV, as in section P8.1. If Mstar<=4096, its explicit inverse and conditional existence statements follow. A general reference need not satisfy the checkpoint's numerical value of Mstar; that is a new coefficient hypothesis or a new certificate.

If the reference has a nonzero uniform leading profile r^(1/c)Theta0, the correction class fixes that profile and is transverse to scaling. The (B0)-(B8) inequalities alone do not assert that such a leading profile exists. Claims about its value and the scaling phase require this additional asymptotic hypothesis.

### P8.3. Audit of the conditional-existence statements

Audited versions: S1_CLOSURE.md, checkpoint 2026-10-28T03:50Z, and the report, checkpoint 2026-10-28T03:52Z. The timestamp of the completed audit is recorded by the independent verifier. This audit concerns the written statements, not a new assumption about the numerical residual.

#### 1. Confirmed nonlinear theorem and exact hypotheses

Theorem D is valid with (B0), (B0n), (B1)-(B5), (B7), (B9) and (B10), using the maximal distributional realizations and the common parity core specified in the proof. Neither (B6) nor (B8) is needed for its fractional-norm proof. The additional leading-profile condition (B11) is needed only for its assertions about the particular asymptotic profile and scaling. The completeness argument for the ball is valid: an H-Cauchy sequence in a bounded N_s ball has a weak N_s subsequence, the continuous embedding identifies its H limit, and weak lower semicontinuity retains the norm bound. The continuous linear functional c retains its value under this weak convergence. This proves completeness without incorrectly asserting that an arbitrary N_s-bounded sequence converges strongly in N_s.

The embeddings, maximal-domain solvability, forcing/solution hyperplane correspondence, and low-norm contraction are proved in section P8.1. In particular the ordinary C^(1/2) norm, defined as the supremum norm plus the seminorm, is at most N_s(h). The first derivatives of h tend to zero at infinity because they are in L2 and uniformly continuous; their uniform continuity follows from H^(2+s) with s>0. The pointwise equation follows from this regularity and the corresponding regularity of U[h].

The theorem's positive-slope conclusion follows from the given hypotheses, but the numerical lower bound should be written explicitly. Parity and (B0n) give

    DUbar(0) = diag(c-1, 1-c),
    A(0) = diag(a0, 0),
    M1(0) = diag(2-c+a0, c).

Consequently (B4) implies

    a0 >= c - 11/10 > 7/10.

Thus |h_y(0)| <= c_s r < 2^-13 is enough for a positive slope for every allowed reference. The conclusion does not require importing the checkpoint's particular a0 approximately 10.3 into the general-reference theorem.

#### 2. Required domain qualifications

1. The pure-power Beurling formula in Theorem A6 is valid only for |beta|<a, where a=1 in the general class and a=2 in the centrally odd class. The displayed formula without this restriction is false, for example it gives a negative alleged norm at beta>a. Include the restriction in every summary of this formula. The particular regular-weight estimates at beta=4/5 are unaffected.

2. Theorem A4 must explicitly be stated on X, or on N_s with s>0, and its generator domain. A point value f_y(0) is not a continuous trace on E2, and is not even generally defined on E0 or E1. A general statement over every space in Theorem A1 is therefore not established. The X or N_s statement is exactly the one used in the nonlinear theorem and is confirmed.

3. In the abstract Theorem B, an arbitrary closed affine constraint need not contain zero. The asserted iteration starting at h0=0 requires 0 in B. Without that extra hypothesis start from any h0 in B and replace the error numerator by ||h1-h0||_L. The application c[h]=0 has 0 in B, so its stated iteration is valid.

4. The sentence that every correction class listed tends to zero at infinity is too broad: H is a negative-order completion and does not even consist only of continuous functions. State this conclusion for E2, X and N_s, and for first derivatives only in the stronger X or N_s spaces. The nonlinear theorem uses N_s and is unaffected.

5. Theorem C should retain the structural assumptions on the reference, rather than state only two abstract decay conclusions and finite Mstar. The proved version assumes a smooth sublinear parity reference, canonical velocity, bounded first derivatives, a0 nonzero, center normalization, and the consistent transport realizations. These may be imposed directly, or by retaining (B0), (B0n) together with the two decay hypotheses. This prevents an unintended application to unrelated abstract semigroups with the same decay constants.

#### 3. Qualifications in the overview

The assertion that an N_s residual must decay faster than r^-2 is a power-asymptotic criterion, not a pointwise characterization of N_s. For example a suitably cut off odd angular function r^-2 (log r)^-1 at r>e has r times the function in L2 and therefore lies in H by the parity Hardy inequality, despite not being O(r^(-2-epsilon)) for any epsilon>0. Its derivatives satisfy the required weighted bounds. State the r^-2 rule for nonzero pure-power sectors, with borderline logarithms treated separately.

The phrase that no phase condition is needed should say that no additional scalar phase equation is imposed: the fixed leading profile and decaying correction class already remove scaling. Automatic normalization alone does not remove it.

The leading-profile conclusion in the report's general-reference summaries requires (B11). It is true for the original checkpoint and for the explicit potential splice, for which that hypothesis was checked. It is not part of (B0)-(B9) by definition.

Finally, check 51-check 52 now give an explicit reference with an admissible residual and all coefficient conditions. Its residual is much too large, N_s(R)>=2^1028. The earlier statement that no reference with all coefficient hypotheses has an admissible residual is therefore obsolete. The remaining obstruction is smallness for a reference with the requisite coefficient certificates.

#### 4. Numerical wording not supported by the experiments

The m10 and m12 experiments do not prove that the near-origin residual loss is forced by the leading moment constraints within their finite family. Such a statement needs a lower bound over every feasible coefficient vector, not two optimization outputs. The observation that two fits have comparable loss is valid. Their reported norm tables remain floating-point observations, with no quadrature error certificate.
