To see it, differentiate the original commutator and commute J with derivatives. Moving partial_j outside B adds sum_j B_(partial_ji u_j), which vanishes by div u=0. Applying T to (14), then multiplying by w, yields divergences of wTv and wB_Du v, products of these vectors with a, and the final term -wT(a.v). Divergence maps vector L2 to Hdot^-1 with norm at most 1. The non-divergence terms are centrally odd, so Hardy applies. Equation (14) and the v1 estimate for the last term yield

    L(T_u h) <=s[(27/5)(9D1+8D2)+(16/5)(5D2)]L(h). (16)

Each coefficient tensor is contracted in Frobenius norm before integration. For example B_Du v contracts the input index of Du; its derivative is D2u, whose pointwise norm is bounded by D2. The estimate does not replace D2 by a sum of component suprema.

For B_d the identity [partial_i,B_d]=B_(partial_i d) similarly gives one divergence, the weight-gradient products, and B_Dd v. The last term uses Hardy and (13). Thus

    L(B_d h)<=5s[(27/5)A1+A2]L(h),
    A2=||<r>D2d||_(F,infinity).                    (17)

The formulas hold for tensor inputs and contracted tensor coefficients as well as scalar ones. In every non-divergence remainder the final density parity is central oddness. In particular Qh=U[h].D rho has

    L([J^s,Q]J^-s h)
       <=5s[(27/5)*3+32]*(13/3)L(h).              (18)

Here J commutes with the canonical U, and U is applied on the low space before (17); no L2(w^2) Riesz bound is asserted.

The same factorization for the radial operator J^-2 has no derivative commutator, so (11)'s scalar positive-kernel bound gives

    L(J^-2 h)<=(27/5)*3 L(h)=(81/5)L(h).          (19)

For all these arguments v need not be unweighted L2. It belongs to L2(w^2), and every operator just used is bounded in that weighted space and in L2(<r>^2w^2) where needed. Polynomially weighted cutoffs and smoothing justify the identities. Density then defines the bounded low operators and identifies their distributional action.

#### 6. Assemble every component

Write H=J^s h. The exact product identities are

    D2[J^s,u.D]h=[J^s,u.D]D2h
                   +2[J^s,Du]D2h+[J^s,D2u]Dh,
    D[J^s,u.D]h=[J^s,u.D]Dh+[J^s,Du]Dh,
    D2[J^s,Q]h=[J^s,D rho]U[D2h]
                   +2[J^s,D2rho]U[Dh]+[J^s,D3rho]U[h],
    D[J^s,Q]h=[J^s,D rho]U[Dh]+[J^s,D2rho]U[h].

The factor 2 denotes the sum of the two ordered first-derivative terms and is estimated by the triangle inequality. The exact weight ratios are

    omega2/omega1<=2<r>, omega2/omega0<=2<r>^2,
    omega1/omega0=<r>.

Consequently the coefficient gradients in the three cross terms are at most 32 for D2u, 64 for D2rho with output omega2, 1024 for D3rho, and 32 for D2rho with output omega1. Using (5), (7), the J^-s bound 2 and the stated Riesz bounds gives

    P2([J^s,u.D+Q]h)
      <=s[(C_T+2*6*3*2+6*3*(9/5)*2)P2(H)
           +(34*32*2+2*34*64*(3/2)*2)P1(H)
           +34*1024*(8/3)*2 P0(H)].               (20)

Similarly

    P1([J^s,u.D+Q]h)
      <=s[(C_T+6*3*2+6*3*(3/2)*2)P1(H)
           +34*32*(8/3)*2 P0(H)].                (21)

Using P0,P1<=E/2048, the top component coefficient is 83641/240. Multiplying (21) by 2048 gives 90094/15. Equations (16),(18) give the low coefficient

    (27/5)[9*(14/5)+8*3]+(16/5)(5*3)
       +5[(27/5)*3+32]*(13/3)=101851/75.          (22)

Multiplication by the low component weight 2^(53/2) cancels L(H)<=2^(-53/2)E(H).

Finally [J^s,cX.D]J^-s=sc(I-J^-2). On either derivative weight, the positive J^-2 kernel has norm at most 1+pi<5, so each derivative component costs at most 12s. The low component costs at most 2(1+81/5)s=172s/5 by (19). The scalar term -h commutes. Adding the component norms gives

    83641/240+90094/15+101851/75+24+172/5
       =9325421/1200 <8192,

proving (1). Addition of component norms is an upper bound for the Hilbert norm and needs no orthogonality claim.

#### 7. Consequence for the conditional existence theorem

For completeness, the reference contract used for this corollary is as follows. Set R=2^31 and d=4/9. Require rho and its canonical velocity to be smooth, sublinear and of the prescribed parity, with

    9/5<c<37/20, a0=rho_y(0)>=1, c+c[rho]=1.

Writing V=cX+u, A=[[rho_y,-rho_x/2],[-rho_x/2,0]], and

    M=(2c+1)I+sym Du+A,
    Mk=(1+c+V.D log omegak)I-k sym DV+A, k=1,2,

require the pointwise inequalities

    M >= [2/5+(11/5)c r^2/(R^2+r^2)]I on r<=R,
    M1>=I/2, M2>=I/2 on the whole plane.

Require the global decay bounds

    sup r^d(|D rho|+r|D2rho|)<=186,
    sup r^(-1+d)|u|<=22, sup r^d|Du|<=22,
    sup r^(1+d)|D2u|<=56,

and all of the global derivative bounds

    |Du|<=14/5, |D rho|<=16,
    <r>|D2u|<=3, <r>|D3u|<=16,
    |D2rho|<=3, <r>|D2rho|<=8,
    <r>^2|D3rho|<=32, <r>^2|D4rho|<=512.

Every tensor is measured as in section 1. These hypotheses include (H) and are the position-dependent contract proved in part P24. Require also the actual residual F=(cX+u).D rho-rho to belong to N. For the leading-profile conclusion require a nonzero continuous angular function Theta such that r^(-gamma)rho(r,theta) converges uniformly to Theta, with gamma=1/c. The full leading angular function is fixed in the affine space. By the stated c range, 1/5<gamma<1.

The existing consistent base generators then have low decay at least 1/5 and E decay at least 1/20. Combining (1) with the independently proved rough loss 400 N(k)/sqrt(s) from part P19 gives, for A_k=L0+U[k].D,

    ||exp(t A_k)||_(N->N)
      <=exp[-t(1/20-2^13 s-400N(k)/sqrt(s))].      (23)

Its domain is the maximal distributional domain in N. A positive displayed rate gives a bijective inverse with the reciprocal-rate bound. The justification is the existing common-P0 realization: approximate k by smooth core functions, use uniform convergence of their velocity gradients, and pass to the unique P0 transport-plus-bounded-coupling evolution. Weak high compactness and the norm bound give strong continuity. The P0 radial-cutoff and local Friedrichs argument identifies its maximal domain; the high Duhamel identity gives the maximal N domain. The new input needed for this construction is precisely the bounded commutator (1). Strict decay gives injectivity, and the convergent inverse integral gives surjectivity.

Set

    s=3*2^-21, r0=5*2^-27, eta=2^-30.             (24)

The ratios 2^13s=3/256 and r0/sqrt(s)=5/(65536sqrt(6)) are identical to the corresponding ratios in part P19. Therefore on N(k)<=r0 the high rate is greater than 6283/245760>1/40. The native low rate 1/5-12||DU[k]||_infinity is greater than 1/6. Low and high inverse integrals agree by the common P0 realization and the unchanged inclusion L(h)<=6*2^(-53/2)N(h). For a nonlinear difference the extra source U[k1-k2].Dh belongs to P0 and L by the established derivative and bilinear bounds. Thus the low inverse estimate applies on its actual domain, rather than by an arbitrary maximal-domain assertion on negative-order distributions.

If the actual residual satisfies N(F)<=eta, the map T(k)=-A_k^-1 F preserves the radius r0 ball, since 40eta=r0. The low bilinear bound 2048 N(h)L(g)/sqrt(s) gives contraction factor at most 15/(16sqrt(6))<2/5. The high ball is complete in the low metric: a low Cauchy sequence has a weak high subsequential limit in the closed ball, identified distributionally with its low limit; this also preserves the closed normalization hyperplane by weak high continuity of the trace. The contraction therefore has a fixed point h. It solves the full nonlinear profile equation.

For normalized k, the origin identity is (A_k h)_y(0)=a0 c[h]. The residual has F_y(0)=0, so T preserves c[h]=0. The slope variation is at most 4r0/sqrt(s)<2^-12, and the positive center slope is retained. Growth |h(X)|<=16max(1,r)^(1/5)N(h) preserves the full leading angular data and excludes both exponent and logarithmic variations from this space. With alpha=s/2, p=8/s and kappa=p+4, define

    C_ad(h)=||h||_(C^alpha(B2))
      +sup_(j>=0) 2^(-j/4)
          (||h||_(Linf(Aj))+2^(j alpha)[h]_(C^alpha(Aj))),
    Aj={2^j<=r<=2^(j+1)},
    M(h)=(integral_(r<1) r^(-kappa)|h-h_y(0)y|^p dX)^(1/p),
    c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0).

Part P37 proves L(h)+C_ad(h)+M(h)+|c[h]|<=146N(h)/sqrt(s). Thus at (24), for every h in the maximal domain,

    L(h)+C_ad(h)+M(h)+|c[h]|<=2^23 N(A_kh).

This conditional theorem raises the sufficient residual threshold by a factor 32 in a different fractional norm, with the same spatial weights. A value measured at the old s is not silently substituted. The compact weak exclusions of parts P39 and P41 apply uniformly at this new s and already exclude the entire proposed ball around the original 131, Mpen2 and d2 references: r0=5*2^-27<2^-23. Thus this improvement does not establish existence near those references.

## P44. Smaller amplitude constants in the weighted space

### P44.1. Small amplitude from the retained lower-order energy

Status: independent proof written before numerical use. Exact constant checks and draft review are pending. The theorem concerns the correction space, with no hypothesis on a numerical reference.

#### 1. Exact statement

Let R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12. Put

    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    omega0=<r>^(-6/5), omega1=<r>^(-1/5),
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    Pj(f)=||omegaj D^j f||_2,
    L_R(f)=||w_R f||_(Hdot^-1),
    E_R(f)^2=P2(f)^2+2^22 P1(f)^2+2^53 L_R(f)^2,
    N_(s,R)(h)=E_R(J^s h), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2).

Take the completion of real compact smooth S1 parity densities, even in x and odd in y, in N_(s,R). The canonical velocity is

    U[h]=(-R1R2 h,R1^2 h), Rj=partial_j(-Delta)^(-1/2).

No harmonic or polynomial velocity is added. Every tensor norm below is the Euclidean norm of the ordered Cartesian derivative tensor; vector estimates use the Hilbert sum. Every h in this space has continuous representatives satisfying

    |h(X)| <= (1/12) max(1,|X|)^(1/5) N_(s,R)(h),
    |U[h](X)| <= (3/16) max(1,|X|)^(1/5) N_(s,R)(h).       (1)

Both inequalities are uniform in the stated R and s ranges. They improve the constants 16 and 104 previously used in the necessary-distance estimates. They do not assert a gradient bound independent of s.

#### 2. The planar Fourier interpolation inequality

For a scalar or finite-dimensional Hilbert-valued f in H2(R2), write A=||f||_2 and D=||D2 f||_2. The Fourier transform is unitary, with inverse factor 1/(2pi). For every lambda>0, Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    |f(X)|^2 <= (1/(4pi^2))
         [D^2+lambda^4 A^2]
         integral_R2 (lambda^4+|xi|^4)^(-1) dxi.

The integral is exactly pi^2/(2lambda^2): in polar coordinates set u=r^2 and integrate (lambda^4+u^2)^(-1). Therefore

    ||f||_infinity^2 <= D^2/(8lambda^2)+lambda^2 A^2/8.

If A,D are positive, choose lambda^2=D/A. The zero cases follow by Plancherel. This proves

    ||f||_infinity <= (1/2) sqrt(||f||_2 ||D2 f||_2).      (2)

For a vector f, apply the scalar estimate to its inner product with every unit vector. The corresponding two scalar L2 norms are bounded by the Hilbert-valued norms, so the same constant works. Equivalently, one can use the Hilbert-valued Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz inequality directly. The argument first applies to Schwartz functions and extends to H2 by the proved uniform estimate and density.

#### 3. Small lower-order norms after Bessel smoothing

Write H=J^s h and n=E_R(H). The weighted interpolation proof in part P6 and P7 gives, uniformly for R>=1,

    P0(H)^2 <= P1(H)^2+26L_R(H)^2,
    P0(H),P1(H) <= n/2048, P2(H)<=n.                    (3)

Let b_s be the positive probability kernel of J^-s. The gamma-density calculation in part P43, section 2, proves

    integral |z| b_s(z) dz <=2s,
    integral |z|^2 b_s(z) dz =2s.

Only these radius-independent kernel identities are used from part P43; no smooth-reference or R>=2^31 assumption is imported. The weight ratios at separation z have the bounds

    omega0(X)/omega0(X-z) <=(1+|z|)^2,
    omegaj(X)/omegaj(X-z) <=1+2|z|, j=1,2.

Minkowski's inequality and the moment bounds imply

    P0(h) <=(1+6s)P0(H),
    P1(h) <=(1+4s)P1(H), P2(h)<=(1+4s)P2(H).

Thus throughout the stated s range,

    P0(h)<=a0 n, P1(h)<=a1 n, P2(h)<=a2 n,
    a0=2051/4194304, a1=1025/2097152, a2=1025/1024.     (4)

There is no unweighted L2 assumption on h in this argument.

#### 4. Localize only the two norms used by (2)

Use the explicit radial partition from part P17. For completeness, let

    P(t)=35t^4-84t^5+70t^6-20t^7, 0<=t<=1,

extended by 0 for t<0 and 1 for t>1, and let chi(X)=1-P(|X|-1). Put chi0=chi and, for j>=1,

    chi_j(X)=chi(2^-j X)-chi(2^(-j+1)X), t_j=2^j,
    F_j(Y)=chi_j(t_jY)h(t_jY).

The nonnegative chi_j sum to 1. The rescaled cutoffs have supremum at most 1, gradient at most 9, and ordered Hessian norm at most 150. Their supports for j>=1 lie in t_j/2<=r<=2t_j. The j=0 support lies in B2. The explicit cutoff derivative bounds and their endpoint regularity are proved in part P17.

The changes of variables and weights give

    ||h(t_j .)||_(L2,support) <=3t_j^(1/5)P0(h),
    ||D_Y h(t_j .)||_(L2,support) <=2t_j^(1/5)P1(h),
    ||D_Y^2 h(t_j .)||_(L2,support) <=t_j^(1/5)P2(h).

For example, the first two use 5^(3/5)<3 and 5^(1/10)<2. The last uses omega2>=t_j^(4/5) on the annular support; for j=0 it uses omega2>=1. Keeping the two separate norms rather than their H2 sum, the product rule gives

    ||F_j||_2 <=3t_j^(1/5)P0(h),
    ||D2 F_j||_2 <=t_j^(1/5)
           [450P0(h)+36P1(h)+P2(h)].                    (5)

The coefficient 36 is 2*9*2, including both first-derivative product terms. The coefficient 450 is 150*3. Equations(2) and (5) imply

    ||F_j||_infinity <=(1/2)t_j^(1/5)
           sqrt(3P0(h)[450P0(h)+36P1(h)+P2(h)]).

At any point at most three partition functions are nonzero. For r>=1 their scales satisfy t_j<=2r; for r<1 only j=0 contributes. Since 2^(1/5)<5/4, reconstruction and (4) yield

    |h(X)| <= C_h max(1,r)^(1/5)n,
    C_h=(15/8)sqrt(3a0[450a0+36a1+a2]).                 (6)

The exact rational comparison C_h^2<1/144 proves the first assertion of (1). No Sobolev norm or large weight coefficient has been discarded before the interpolation step.

#### 5. Apply the same calculation to the canonical velocity

The proved weighted Riesz estimates, including their central-parity improvement, give

    P0(U[h]) <=(8/3)P0(h),
    P1(U[h]) <=(3/2)P1(h),
    P2(U[h]) <=(9/5)P2(h).                              (7)

For the first and third inequalities the scalar inputs are centrally odd. For the first derivative the inputs are centrally even, and the unrestricted omega1 estimate 3/2 applies. Sum all derivative components in Hilbert norm after applying the scalar-to-vector bounds. In particular (7) uses no bound of a Riesz transform on L2(w_R^2).

Apply the vector-valued version of (2) and the identical cutoff calculation to U[h]. Equations(4),(6),(7) give

    |U[h](X)| <= C_U max(1,r)^(1/5)n,
    C_U=(15/8)sqrt(8a0[1200a0+54a1+(9/5)a2]).           (8)

The exact comparison C_U^2<9/256 proves the second assertion of (1).

#### 6. Completion, canonical representative and scope

For the compact core, h and the canonical velocity satisfy the bounds just proved. A Cauchy sequence in N is consequently uniformly Cauchy for h and U[h] on every compact set. Its limits agree with the established distributional realization by continuous weighted Sobolev injection. Parity fixes their origin values and excludes an additive constant. The canonical velocity distribution is fixed by the Fourier multiplier and the earlier sublinear construction; the pointwise estimate cannot introduce another harmonic velocity. Thus (1) extends to the entire completed space.

For any actual forcing f in N, the first bound immediately implies the necessary pointwise test

    N(f) >=12 |f(X)|/max(1,|X|)^(1/5).                   (9)

For the compact weak-distance theorem of part P41 one may replace its constants H=16g and B=104g by H=g/12 and B=3g/16. The proof uses exactly the two estimates (1), so every sign, exponent-rigidity and compact integration argument is unchanged. The numerical strict inequalities must be recomputed with these constants before a stronger candidate radius is reported.

These smaller amplitudes arise from the large positive coefficients of the first-derivative and low terms in the chosen norm. They are not statements about unweighted H2 alone, do not remove the s dependence of gradient or strain traces, and do not establish existence near a numerical reference.

#### Dependencies

Section P6.14 gives the R-uniform interpolation (3). Section P17.1 supplies the explicit partition and weighted localization. Section P43.1 section 2 gives the positive Bessel moment estimates. Section P7.2 gives (7). The completed canonical space and uniform gradient representatives were established in parts P17 and P19. The exact algebra accompanying(6),(8) is checked separately under verification.

## P45. Improved necessary distances and residual point bounds

### P45.1. Stronger necessary distances from the same certified residual data

Status: standalone argument established before numerical evaluation. Numerical results are recorded separately after two arithmetic checks. This theorem gives necessary distances, not an existence theorem.

#### 1. Space, references and exact statement

For R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12 let

    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2),
    N_(s,R)(h)^2=||(1+4r^2)^(2/5)D2 J^s h||_2^2
                 +2^22||<r>^(-1/5)D J^s h||_2^2
                 +2^53||w_R J^s h||_(Hdot^-1)^2.

The space is the completion of real smooth compact densities even in x and odd in y, using the canonical velocity U[h]=(-R1R2 h,R1^2 h), with Rj=partial_j(-Delta)^(-1/2). All tensor norms are ordered Cartesian Euclidean norms. Put g(X)=max(1,|X|)^(1/5). Part P44 proves the uniform estimates

    |h(X)|<=(g(X)/12)N(h), |U[h](X)|<=(3g(X)/16)N(h).     (1)

A reference is a smooth canonical pair (bar_rho,U[bar_rho]) with

    bar_rho(r,theta)=r^gamma Theta(theta)+o(r^gamma),
    U[bar_rho]=O(r^gamma), 1/5<gamma<1, Theta nonzero,
    c=1/gamma, bar_V=cX+U[bar_rho], F=bar_V.D bar_rho-bar_rho.

The error in the density expansion is uniform in angle. The exact references below are the recovered state 131 and the canonical generator handoffs nb_Mpen2_exact and nb_d2_exact. Their source, normalization, and common nonzero leading density were checked in parts P1.2, P3, P20, P40 and P42. A numerical handoff is used only through those exact rational coefficients.

Let S be a closed square of half side delta, on which F has one strict sign and

    |F|>=f>0, |bar_V|<=V, |D bar_rho|<=D, g(X)<=g_S.

Define

    H=g_S/12, B=3g_S/16, d=15/(4delta),
    A=H[Vd+|2c+1|]+BD, Q=HBd.                         (2)

Every exact canonical profile bar_rho+h of any real prospective exponent, with n=N(h), satisfies f<=An+Qn^2. Hence f>Aq+Qq^2 excludes the entire closed N ball of radius q. This conclusion is uniform in the stated R,s ranges.

For the original state 131 there is also the annular version. Let zeta be a real C1 test supported in T<=r<=2T, T>=1, with |zeta|<=Z and |D zeta|<=C/T. Define

    H_T=(2T)^(1/5)/12, B_T=3(2T)^(1/5)/16,
    V_T=2cT+22(2T)^(5/9), D_T=186T^(-4/9),
    A_T=3pi T^2 {H_T[V_T C/T+(2c+1)Z]+B_T D_T Z},
    Q_T=3pi T H_T B_T C.                              (3)

If |integral F zeta|>=P_T>0 and P_T>A_Tq+Q_Tq^2, the same closed ball exclusion follows.

Finally, for any reference whose residual F belongs to N, every point X gives

    N(F)>=12|F(X)|/g(X).                              (4)

If membership has not been proved, (4) is a necessary lower bound conditional on membership; failure of membership already prevents applying a theorem that requires F in N. A lower residual bound alone is not a distance theorem.

#### 2. Exponent rigidity and the compact identity

The bounds (1) imply that h and U[h] grow at most r^(1/5). Thus T^-gamma(bar_rho+h)(TX) converges uniformly on every compact annulus to G(X)=|X|^gamma Theta(arg X), while T^-gamma U[bar_rho+h](TX) stays uniformly bounded. In the rescaled weak stationary equation with exponent c', the nonlinear term is T^(gamma-1) times the divergence of the product of these two rescaled fields. It tends to zero against every compact smooth test because gamma<1. The limit gives c'X.DG-G=0. Exact homogeneity gives X.DG=gamma G, and G is nonzero. Hence c'=c. No derivative decay of h or positivity of the corrected center slope is needed.

Subtracting the reference residual from the exact equation gives

    0=F+bar_V.Dh-h+U[h].D bar_rho+U[h].Dh.

Local C1 representatives are supplied by the completed-space embeddings of parts P17 and P19. Since div bar_V=2c and div U[h]=0, compact integration by parts yields

    integral F zeta=integral h[bar_V.D zeta+(2c+1)zeta]
                    -integral U[h].D bar_rho zeta
                    +integral h U[h].D zeta.           (5)

The same identity extends to compact C1 tests by approximation. It contains no derivative of the correction.

#### 3. Square and annular estimates

On the square centered at X0 use

    phi(t)=(1-t^2)^2 for |t|<=1, zero outside,
    zeta(X)=phi((x-x0)/delta)phi((y-y0)/delta).

The exact one-dimensional integrals are integral phi=16/15 and integral |phi'|=2. Thus its mass is M=delta^2(16/15)^2 and integral |D zeta|<=15M/(4delta). The sign hypothesis gives |integral F zeta|>=fM. Applying (1) to each term of (5) gives at most (An+Qn^2)M, proving(2).

For the annular test the support has area 3pi T^2. The original state 131 satisfies the independently certified pointwise bounds |U[bar_rho](X)|<=22r^(5/9) and |D bar_rho(X)|<=186r^(-4/9). These, (1), and (5) give (3).

The specific test is the audited C9 test from part P39:

    zeta_T(X)=(1+r^2/T^2)^(-11/10)chi(r/T)sum_m a_m sin(m theta),
    chi(t)=(t-1)^2(2-t)^2 on [1,2], zero outside,
    a_m=630 e_m/(18+m^2), S0=sum|a_m|, S1=sum m|a_m|,
    Z=S0/16, C=91S0/160+S1/16.

Here e_m are the exact leading residual sine coefficients of the original state. The bounds follow from |chi|<=1/16, |chi'|<=1/2, the weight derivative bound 11/(10T), and the angular derivative bound S1/T. The previously audited C9 pairing minus its absolute analytic remainder is a lower bound P_T. This step reuses the actual signed integral, not a residual norm.

Applying the first inequality (1) to F proves (4) whenever F is in N.

#### 4. Exact data reuse and independent arithmetic

Part P41 already enclosed F, bar_V, and D bar_rho on each tested square by directed interval Taylor expansions through potential derivative order 7. Its independent audit reconstructed every generator, checked the polar derivative recurrence against Cartesian polynomial differentiation, checked every center residual derivative by a second Cartesian method, and recomputed every strict inequality with rational endpoints. The present calculation uses those unchanged raw center jets and highest-derivative boxes. It recomputes the Taylor bounds with the constants (2). It does not substitute a point sample for a square enclosure.

Explicitly, d0=sqrt(2)delta and the raw derivative tensor bounds give

    f=|F(X0)|-d0|DF(X0)|-d0^2|D2F(X0)|/2-d0^3 sup_S|D3F|/6,
    V=|bar_V(X0)|+d0|D bar_V(X0)|+d0^2|D2 bar_V(X0)|/2
                                      +d0^3 sup_S|D3 bar_V|/6,
    D=|D bar_rho(X0)|+d0|D2 bar_rho(X0)|+d0^2|D3 bar_rho(X0)|/2
                                      +d0^3 sup_S|D4 bar_rho|/6.

Frobenius norms are sums of squares with binomial multiplicities. For an upper bound, each interval component is replaced by its largest absolute endpoint before taking the norm. For f the first term uses its smallest absolute endpoint. Only positive f is used. The square growth factor is bounded using |X|^2<=(|x0|+delta)^2+(|y0|+delta)^2.

The first new implementation uses Arb directed intervals. A separately written rational implementation parses every decimal interval as rational endpoints, encloses positive roots by checked integer powers, and verifies the strict dyadic comparisons independently. For the annular calculation it uses the rigorous rational bound pi<22/7, proved by the positive integral integral_0^1 x^4(1-x)^4/(1+x^2)dx=22/7-pi. Thus the second calculation has deliberately different rounding and constants. Each implementation records hashes of its inputs, its own code, this proof, and the amplitude proof. Every upstream dependency hash is checked before reuse. The old certificates remain unchanged.

#### 5. Scope and dependencies

All exclusions concern exact canonical profiles inside the stated weighted affine balls. The correction can lie outside every finite-dimensional ansatz. No global nonexistence is implied. The annular estimate is specific to the original reference's verified decay constants; no such constants are silently assigned to a refitted reference. The square estimate needs only certified local field bounds and the exact leading tail.

Dependencies: part P44 gives (1); parts P17 and P19 give local representatives; parts P39 and P40 give the common leading-tail facts and weak limit; part P41 gives the raw Taylor boxes; part P42 gives the exact d2 handoff; section P11.4 and audit_c9_Q4.json give the original signed annular pairing and analytic remainder. All numerical claims in the accompanying records are strictly separated from the conditional existence theorem of part P43.

## P46. Centered weak tests

### P46.1. Centered weak tests and the small weighted L2 norm

Status: analytical argument written before the numerical calculation. This strengthens a necessary-distance test and makes no existence assertion.

#### 1. Exact setting

Use the real canonical S1 space N_(s,R) from part P45, with every R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12:

    N(h)^2=||(1+4r^2)^(2/5)D2 J^s h||_2^2
            +2^22||<r>^(-1/5)D J^s h||_2^2
            +2^53||w_R J^s h||_(Hdot^-1)^2,
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2).

Densities are even in x and odd in y; U=(-R1R2,R1^2) is the canonical velocity. The space is the completion of compact smooth parity densities. Put omega0=<r>^(-6/5) and a=2051/4194304. The proved embeddings of part P44 give, with n=N(h),

    ||omega0 h||_2<=a n,
    ||omega0 U[h]||_2<=(8/3)a n,
    |h(X)|<=(2/25)g(X)n, |U[h](X)|<=(11/60)g(X)n,
    g(X)=max(1,|X|)^(1/5).                            (1)

The first estimate retains the lower-order energy coefficient. The second is the centrally odd weighted Riesz bound. No hypothesis on a numerical reference is needed for (1). The slightly sharper rounded amplitude constants follow from the raw squared constants already proved in part P44: 3596147769375/562949953421312<4/625 and 1168572376125/35184372088832<121/3600. These two comparisons are exact rational inequalities; no new localization argument is needed.

Let the smooth canonical reference bar_rho have the exact nonzero leading tail r^gamma Theta(theta), with 1/5<gamma<1, uniform angular remainder o(r^gamma), U[bar_rho]=O(r^gamma), and exponent c=1/gamma. Put bar_V=cX+U[bar_rho] and F=bar_V.D bar_rho-bar_rho. Let S be the square centered at X0 with halfside delta>0, and suppose throughout S

    |bar_V|<=V, |D bar_rho|<=D, |D3F|<=K,
    g(X)<=g_S, omega0(X)^(-1)<=W.

D3F has its full ordered Cartesian Frobenius norm. The following quantities are all explicit:

    H=2g_S/25, B=11g_S/60,
    d1=15/(4delta), d2=5sqrt(6)/(7delta^2), e2=5/(7delta),
    d_infty=25sqrt(6)/(32delta^3),
    A=V min(H d1,a W d2)
      +|2c+1| min(H,a W e2)
      +D min(B,(8/3)a W e2),
    Q=min(HB d1,a W B d2,(8/3)a W H d2,
                           (8/3)a^2 W^2 d_infty).       (2)

Define the centered Taylor average and its error bound

    T=F(X0)+(delta^2/14)[F_xx(X0)+F_yy(X0)],
    e=(sqrt(2)/21)delta^3 K.

If a certified f>0 satisfies |T|-e>=f, then every exact canonical profile bar_rho+h in the affine class, of any prospective real exponent, obeys

    f<=A N(h)+Q N(h)^2.                               (3)

Thus f>Aq+Qq^2 excludes every exact profile in the closed N ball of radius q. No pointwise sign condition on F over S is required. The conclusion is uniform in R,s in the stated ranges.

#### 2. The centered residual pairing

Let phi(t)=(1-t^2)^2 on [-1,1], zero outside, and zeta(X)=phi((x-x0)/delta)phi((y-y0)/delta). Normalize zeta to the probability measure dmu=zeta dX/M, where M=delta^2(16/15)^2. If Z=X-X0, evenness and the exact one-dimensional integrals imply

    E_mu Z=0, E_mu(Z_x Z_y)=0,
    E_mu Z_x^2=E_mu Z_y^2=delta^2/7.

Indeed integral t^2 phi(t)dt=16/105 and integral phi=16/15. Taylor's theorem along the segment inside the convex square gives

    F(X0+Z)=F(X0)+DF(X0).Z+(1/2)D2F(X0)[Z,Z]+R(Z),
    |R(Z)|<=K|Z|^3/6.

Since |Z|<=sqrt(2)delta,

    E_mu |Z|^3<=sqrt(2)delta E_mu |Z|^2
                  =(2sqrt(2)/7)delta^3.

Averaging the Taylor formula therefore gives

    |integral F dmu-T|<=(sqrt(2)/21)delta^3 K=e.

Consequently |integral F zeta|>=fM. This estimate uses the signed Laplacian term, not an absolute Hessian estimate, and it remains valid when F changes sign in the square.

#### 3. Exact test norms

Elementary integration gives

    integral phi=16/15, integral |phi'|=2,
    integral phi^2=256/315, integral (phi')^2=256/105.

The resulting two-dimensional norms, divided by M, satisfy

    ||D zeta||_1/M<=d1,
    ||D zeta||_2/M=d2,
    ||zeta||_2/M=e2,
    ||D zeta||_infinity/M<=d_infty.                    (4)

For the first inequality use |D zeta|<=|zeta_x|+|zeta_y|. For the L2 gradient use orthogonal Euclidean components, giving ||D zeta||_2^2=2(256/315)(256/105). The supremum follows from ||phi||_infinity=1 and ||phi'||_infinity=8/(3sqrt(3)); hence ||D zeta||_infinity<=8sqrt(2)/(3sqrt(3)delta). Division by M gives 25sqrt(6)/(32delta^3). These are full-plane norms of the zero extension. The test is C1 and compactly supported.

#### 4. Pairing the correction equation

The fixed leading tail and (1) force the exponent of any exact profile in the affine class to equal c. The proof is the rescaling argument in part P45: T^-gamma rho(TX) converges to the nonzero leading homogeneous density, the nonlinear weak term vanishes as T^(gamma-1), and the limit forces c'gamma=1.

For this fixed exponent, the exact compact identity is

    integral F zeta=integral h bar_V.D zeta
                    +(2c+1)integral h zeta
                    -integral U[h].D bar_rho zeta
                    +integral h U[h].D zeta.            (5)

It follows from the difference equation using div bar_V=2c and div U[h]=0. The completed space has the local C1 representatives needed for this identity; alternatively, approximate the compact C1 test by smooth tests.

For each linear term there are two independent bounds. The pointwise bound in (1) gives, after division by M, respectively HVd1 n, H|2c+1|n, and BDn. Weighted Cauchy-Schwarz and (4) give respectively aWVd2 n, aW|2c+1|e2 n, and (8/3)aWD e2 n. Each term may use the smaller of its two bounds. Their sum is An.

For the quadratic term, pointwise bounds on both factors give HBd1 n^2. Use weighted Cauchy-Schwarz on h and the pointwise bound on U[h] to obtain aWBd2 n^2. Reverse their roles to obtain (8/3)aWHd2 n^2. Finally use Cauchy-Schwarz on both weighted L2 factors and the supremum norm of omega0^-2 D zeta:

    |integral h U[h].D zeta|/M
      <=||(omega0 h)||_2 ||omega0 U[h]||_2
                               ||omega0^-2 D zeta||_infinity/M
      <=(8/3)a^2 W^2 d_infty n^2.

The minimum of these four valid bounds is Qn^2. Combining(5) with the lower bound in section 2 proves (3).

#### 5. Computation and scope

The raw center derivatives and full-square highest derivative bounds are exactly the unchanged part P41 Taylor records, already independently reconstructed and checked against the original generator handoffs. Unlike the earlier sign test, every recorded square may be considered here; only positivity of the centered pairing lower bound matters. The V,D bounds are the same full-square Taylor bounds. Take

    r_max^2=(|x0|+delta)^2+(|y0|+delta)^2,
    g_S=max(1,r_max^2)^(1/10), W=(1+r_max^2)^(3/5).

An interval calculation evaluates the signed center Laplacian, the error bound, and (2). An independent rational calculation must reconstruct the same bounds from decimal interval endpoints, verify roots by exact powers, and check the strict dyadic comparisons. No sampling replaces the uniform remainder bound. All dependencies and code are hashed.

These are necessary local distances, not upper bounds on an inverse. The result applies to arbitrary corrections in the completed space and does not assume that the exact profile belongs to a finite ansatz. Neither positivity of a global energy matrix nor a global residual norm is used. Larger corrections remain open.

#### 6. Independently checked consequences

The complete interval and rational calculations confirm all 48 positive centered-pairing tests, including 3 squares where the previous pointwise-sign test was inconclusive. They give, uniformly for allR>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12 and any prospective exponent,

| Exact reference | Excluded closed radius | Center | Halfside |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| nb_Mpen2_exact | 2^-14 | (0,4/5) | 2^-10 |
| nb_d2_exact | 2^-15 | (0,2/5) | 2^-10 |

At the selected Mpen2 square the normalized pairing lower bound exceeds 0.0196177, and the strict comparison margin exceeds 0.0030107. At the selected d2 square those values exceed 0.0040851 and 0.0001233. The quadratic coefficient is exactly 56.32 at both selected squares.

The original state retains its separate annular exclusion 2^-14 from part P45. The best two square tests use the pointwise alternatives in (2). The weighted L2 alternatives are valid but do not improve these particular best radii with the currently available highest-derivative boxes. The obstacle to using wider squares is the interval third-derivative remainder, not a proved failure of the true centered pairing.

## P47. Weighted Bessel bound and negative-order weak tests

### P47.1. Weighted Bessel cancellation and negative-order weak tests

Status: analytical argument written before numerical implementation. Independent arithmetic checks and draft review are pending. No existence assertion is made.

#### 1. Weighted negative-order Bessel bound

Let R>=1, sigma=11/5, w_R(X)=(1+|X|^2/R^2)^(-sigma/2), and let L_R(h)=||w_R h||_(Hdot^-1(R^2)). The density space is the completion of real centrally odd compact smooth functions in this norm, with the canonical Fourier realization. Vector norms are Hilbert sums. Put J=(1-Delta)^(1/2). For 0<s<=2^-12 define

    C_R=41/(5R)+17/R^2+327/(5R^3)+1309/(10R^4)+924/(5R^5).

Then J^-s extends to this space and

    L_R(J^-s h)<=(1+s C_R)L_R(h)<=(11/10)L_R(h).       (1)

The same estimate holds for each centrally odd component of a vector. It uses no reference profile. In particular, for the S1 norm

    N_(s,R)(h)^2=||(1+4r^2)^(2/5)D2 J^s h||_2^2
                   +2^22||<r>^(-1/5)D J^s h||_2^2
                   +2^53 L_R(J^s h)^2,

we have

    L_R(h)<=ell N_(s,R)(h),
    L_R(U[h])<=(13/3)ell N_(s,R)(h),
    ell=(11/10)2^(-53/2), U=(-R1R2,R1^2).             (2)

The second bound uses the real centrally odd velocity theorem in part P21. The narrower S1 parity (even in x, odd in y) is included. The constant ell may be replaced by (1+s C_R)2^(-53/2) whenever a particular R,s is fixed.

##### Proof of (1)

Let B=J^-s, with its positive radial Bessel kernel b_s, normalized by integral b_s=1. For M_j=integral |z|^j b_s(z)dz the heat-mixture calculation from part P43 gives, throughout the larger range 0<s<=1/16,

    M1<=2s, M2=2s, M3<=6s, M4<=17s, M5<=84s.         (3)

Only the last inequality is new here. Put b=1+s/2<=33/32. Jensen's inequality for the square root under a gamma density gives Gamma(b+1/2)/Gamma(b)<=sqrt(b), so

    M5/s=30sqrt(pi) Gamma(b+3/2)/Gamma(b)
          <=54(b+1/2)sqrt(b)
          <=54(49/32)sqrt(33/32)<84.

The last strict comparison is checked after squaring positive rational quantities. The preceding four bounds have their complete proofs in part P43 section 2.

For a core density h, let q=D(-Delta)^-1(w_R h). Thus -div q=w_R h, ||q||_2=L_R(h), and q is centrally even. Put a=Dlog w_R=-sigma X/(R^2+r^2), and T=w_R B w_R^-1 on vector fields. In distributions,

    w_R B h=-div(Tq)+a.Tq-T(a.q),
    B(w_R h)=-div(Bq).

Consequently the exact cancellation identity is

    w_R B h=B(w_R h)-div((T-B)q)+[a,T]q,             (4)

where [a,T]q=a.Tq-T(a.q). The first term has Hdot^-1 norm at most L_R(h), because the Fourier multiplier of B is bounded by 1. The second has Hdot^-1 norm at most ||(T-B)q||_2.

Write z=X-Y and t=|z|. The radial weight is moderate:

    w_R(X)/w_R(Y), w_R(Y)/w_R(X)<=(1+t/R)^sigma
                                             <=(1+t/R)^3.

Hence the absolute difference of its ratio from 1 is at most (1+t/R)^3-1. Young's inequality yields

    ||(T-B)q||_2 <=(3M1/R+3M2/R^2+M3/R^3)||q||_2.    (5)

The remaining term in (4) is centrally odd. The parity Hardy inequality says ||f||_(Hdot^-1)<=||r f||_2 for every centrally odd f for which the right side is finite. To apply it, differentiate a. Its tangential eigenvalue is -sigma/(R^2+r^2), and its radial eigenvalue is -sigma(R^2-r^2)/(R^2+r^2)^2. Therefore

    |Da(Z)|_op<=sigma/(R^2+|Z|^2).

For each Z on the segment from Y to X, |X|<=|Z|+t and

    |X| |Da(Z)|_op<=sigma(1/(2R)+t/R^2).

The segment formula and the moderation estimate now give

    r(X)|a(X)-a(Y)| w_R(X)/w_R(Y)
       <=sigma t(1/(2R)+t/R^2)(1+t/R)^3.

Young's inequality and parity Hardy imply

    ||[a,T]q||_(Hdot^-1)
      <=sigma[M1/(2R)+5M2/(2R^2)+9M3/(2R^3)
                             +7M4/(2R^4)+M5/R^5]||q||_2.  (6)

Combining (3)--(6) gives C_R exactly as stated. For R>=1, C_R<=4063/10. Since s<=1/4096, 1+s C_R<=1+4063/40960<11/10. This proves (1).

All three terms in (4) have now been bounded in the target space. The identity first follows with smooth annular approximations of q and then in distributions, since T and T-B are bounded on L2 and the last term converges in Hdot^-1 by (6). This justifies the computation even when w_R^-1 q is not in unweighted L2. Extension from the compact density core is unique by continuity. On that core it agrees with the canonical Bessel operator; hence the extended operator is the one used in the N completion. Equation (2) follows by applying (1) to J^s h and then part P21 to h.

#### 2. Additional weak test bounds

Let bar_rho be a smooth canonical S1 reference with the fixed nonzero leading tail r^gamma Theta(theta), 1/5<gamma<1, and bar_U=O(r^gamma), with c=1/gamma and bar_V=cX+bar_U. The exponent-rigidity argument of part P45 applies to every exact profile bar_rho+h with h in N. It fixes its prospective exponent to c.

On a square S with center X0 and halfside delta, assume pointwise bounds

    |bar_V|<=V, |D bar_V|_F<=V1,
    |D bar_rho|<=D, |D2 bar_rho|_F<=D1,
    w_R^-1<=W, |Dlog w_R|<=k.

Let zeta(X)=phi((x-x0)/delta)phi((y-y0)/delta), where phi(t)=(1-t^2)^2 on [-1,1] and zero outside, and M=integral zeta=delta^2(16/15)^2. Define

    e2=5/(7delta), d2=5sqrt(6)/(7delta^2),
    d3=45/(7delta^3), m=|2c+1|.

Then, writing n=N(h), the two linear groups in the exact weak identity satisfy

    |integral h[bar_V.Dzeta+(2c+1)zeta]|/M <= A_h n,
    |integral U[h].Dbar_rho zeta|/M <= A_u n,

where

    A_h=ell W[V d3+(V1+m+kV)d2+km e2],
    A_u=(13/3)ell W[(D1+kD)e2+D d2].                (7)

The exact identity and all the alternative L2 and amplitude bounds of part P46 remain available. In particular, A_h can be replaced by the minimum of (7) and the sum of the first two linear terms of part P46, and A_u by the minimum of (7) and its third term. The same Q from part P46 controls the quadratic term. If f is a certified lower bound on |integral F zeta|/M, every exact profile satisfies

    f<= [min(A_h,A_h_old)+min(A_u,A_u_old)] n+Q n^2. (8)

##### Proof

Negative Sobolev duality gives |integral h f|<=L_R(h)||D(w_R^-1 f)||_2. The product rule for f=bar_V.Dzeta+(2c+1)zeta gives

    |Df| <= V |D2zeta|_F+(V1+m)|Dzeta|,
    |f|<=V|Dzeta|+m zeta.

Multiplication by w_R^-1 and differentiation of this weight give the first bound in (7). For the vector test f=Dbar_rho zeta, the product rule gives |Df|_F<=D1 zeta+D|Dzeta| and |f|<=D zeta. Apply the vector Hilbert form of negative Sobolev duality and (2) to obtain A_u. These arguments require only compact H1 tests; the chosen zeta is C1 with square-integrable weak second derivatives, so all tests are admissible.

The norms e2,d2 were proved in part P46. For d3, the one-dimensional integrals are

    I0=integral phi^2=256/315,
    I1=integral (phi')^2=256/105,
    I2=integral (phi'')^2=128/5.

The zero extension has no boundary delta in its second weak derivative, because phi and phi' vanish at both endpoints. Thus

    ||D2zeta||_2^2/M^2
        =delta^-6 (2I2 I0+2I1^2)/(16/15)^4
        =2025/(49delta^6).

This proves the stated d3 and (7)--(8).

#### 3. Nested-square certificates

The centered pairing bound from part P46 is valid for every delta with

    f<=|F(X0)+delta^2 Delta F(X0)/14|
                    -(sqrt(2)/21)delta^3 sup_S |D3F|.

A certified derivative bound on a larger concentric square is also valid on S. Therefore the unchanged part P41 highest-derivative records at halfside delta_parent may be used for every 0<delta<=delta_parent. Taylor expansion from the certified center jets gives

    V <= |V0|+d0|DV0|+d0^2|D2V0|/2+d0^3 sup|D3V|/6,
    V1<=|DV0|+d0|D2V0|+d0^2 sup|D3V|/2,
    D <= |Drho0|+d0|D2rho0|+d0^2|D3rho0|/2+d0^3 sup|D4rho|/6,
    D1<=|D2rho0|+d0|D3rho0|+d0^2 sup|D4rho|/2,
    d0=sqrt(2)delta.

All norms are ordered Cartesian Frobenius norms. Uniformly for all R>=1 one may take W=(1+r_max^2)^(11/10) and k=11/10, where r_max^2=(|x0|+delta)^2+(|y0|+delta)^2. The derivative of log w has norm sigma r/(R^2+r^2)<=sigma/(2R)<=11/10.

Only strict interval or rational comparisons certify (8). A failure of the comparison is inconclusive, not evidence for existence or a sharp distance. The argument excludes corrections in the full completed function space and makes no finite-ansatz assumption.

#### 4. Independently checked numerical consequences

The unchanged part P41 derivative boxes, with the nested-square rule above, give 294 positive centered pairings. A512-bit interval implementation and a separate rational endpoint implementation both verify every reported strict comparison. They exclude, uniformly for all R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12 and every prospective exponent,

| Exact reference | Excluded closed N radius | Center | Halfside |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| nb_Mpen2_exact | 2^-11 | (0,2/5) | 5/2048 |

## P48. Negative-energy amplitude embeddings and larger necessary distances

### P48.1. Pointwise amplitudes from the retained negative energy

Status: analytical proof written before numerical implementation. Exact constant checks and draft review are pending. These are embeddings and necessary-distance estimates, not existence assertions.

#### 1. Statement and spaces

Use the real S1 space N_(s,R), its canonical velocity U, and the weights of part P47, for every R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12. Explicitly,

    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    omega0=<r>^(-6/5), omega1=<r>^(-1/5),
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2),
    N(h)^2=||omega2 D2 J^s h||_2^2
                  +2^22||omega1 D J^s h||_2^2
                  +2^53||w_R J^s h||_(Hdot^-1)^2.

This is the completion of compact smooth functions even in x and odd in y. Derivative norms are ordered Cartesian Frobenius norms. The canonical velocity is U[h]=(-R1R2 h,R1^2 h), with no added harmonic field. Then the continuous representatives satisfy

    |w_R(X)h(X)| <= N(h)/1000,
    |w_R(X)U[h](X)| <= N(h)/400.                   (1)

The vector inequality uses the Euclidean norm. The bounds are uniform in R,s. They may be combined with the growth bounds of part P46, giving

    |h(X)|<=min(w_R(X)^-1/1000, (2/25)max(1,r)^(1/5))N(h),
    |U[h](X)|<=min(w_R(X)^-1/400, (11/60)max(1,r)^(1/5))N(h).

No reference-profile hypothesis is used. These bounds retain the coefficient 2^53 of the negative component and remain finite as s tends to zero.

#### 2. A Fourier interpolation inequality

Let f be scalar or take values in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, with f in Hdot^-1 and D2 f in L2 on R^2, in the canonical Fourier realization. Then f has a bounded continuous representative and

    ||f||_infinity <= C ||f||_(Hdot^-1)^(1/3)
                              ||D2 f||_2^(2/3),
    C=2^(-5/6)3^(-1/4).                           (2)

Use the unitary two-dimensional Fourier convention, so the inverse has factor (2pi)^-1. For a,b>0, Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    ||f||_infinity^2 <=(2pi)^-2
       [integral dxi/(a|xi|^-2+b|xi|^4)]
       [a||f||_(Hdot^-1)^2+b||D2f||_2^2].

The radial integral is

    2pi integral_0^infinity r^3/(a+b r^6)dr
       =2pi^2/(3sqrt(3)) a^(-1/3)b^(-2/3).

For completeness, after scaling and then putting u=r^2, the only scalar integral is one half of integral_0^infinity u/(1+u^3)du. Its partial fraction decomposition is

    u/(1+u^3)= -1/[3(u+1)]+(u+1)/[3(u^2-u+1)].

The logarithmic terms cancel at infinity; completing the square in the second denominator gives integral u/(1+u^3)=2pi/(3sqrt(3)). This proves the radial formula without a special-function estimate.

Put b=1 and a=||D2f||_2^2/(2||f||_(Hdot^-1)^2). Simplification gives

    ||f||_infinity^2 <=2^(-5/3)3^(-1/2)
                  ||f||_(Hdot^-1)^(2/3)||D2f||_2^(4/3),

which is (2). If either norm vanishes, f vanishes in the canonical realization and the assertion follows by a limit. The Cauchy-Schwarz calculation proves integrability of the Fourier transform, hence continuity and the pointwise representative. It extends by completion from Fourier cutoffs. The vector case uses the Hilbert norm inside the Fourier integral and has the same constant.

#### 3. Differentiating the density weight

Put sigma=11/5 and t=r/R. For R>=1,

For the Hessian the tangential and radial eigenvalues are

Since |(sigma+1)t^2-1|<=(sigma+1)(1+t^2), its Frobenius norm is at most

Multiplication by <r>^(6/5)<=R^(6/5)(1+t^2)^(3/5) leaves an additional factor R^(-4/5)(1+t^2)^(-3/2)<=1. Finally sigma^2[1+(sigma+1)^2]=34001/625<225/4, proving the Hessian bound in (3).

For U[h], the first three right sides can respectively be multiplied by 8/3,3/2,9/5, by the central-parity weighted Riesz estimates. Its last right side is multiplied by 13/3, by part P21. ## P49. A negative-order annular exclusion around the checkpoint

### P49.1. A negative-order annular distance for the original profile

Status: analytical proof and all three strict comparisons are independently CONFIRMED. The conclusion is a necessary distance, independent of the sufficient inverse theorem.

#### 1. Exact statement and dependencies

Let R>=2^31 and 0<s<=2^-12. Use the real canonical S1 completion N_(s,R) defined in part P48, with w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), high derivative weight (1+4r^2)^(2/5), first derivative weight<r>^(-1/5), and squared coefficients 2^22 and 2^53. Densities are even in x and odd in y, and U=(-R1R2,R1^2) has no extra harmonic velocity.

Let bar_rho be the exact rational original state 131, reconstructed from the read-only accepted checkpoint, and set

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, d=4/9,
    bar_V=cX+U[bar_rho], F=bar_V.Dbar_rho-bar_rho.

The independently proved global coefficient bounds are

    |U[bar_rho]|<=22r^(1-d), |DU[bar_rho]|_F<=22r^-d,
    |Dbar_rho|<=186r^-d, |D2bar_rho|_F<=186r^(-d-1).

The exact leading density tail is nonzero, with degree gamma=1/c in (1/5,1). All these source-specific facts are proved and certified in parts P3, P18 and P21. Therefore the exponent-rigidity argument of part P39 applies to every exact canonical profile bar_rho+h, h in N, regardless of the size of N(h) or the corrected origin slope. Any prospective exponent is c.

The present theorem gives a necessary inequality P_T<=A_T N(h)+Q_T N(h)^2 for the audited signed C9 pairings. Its coefficients are specified below. A strict comparison P_T>A_T q+Q_T q^2 excludes the entire closed radius q. Larger distances and corrections outside this weighted space are not covered.

#### 2. Small global weighted L2 norms

For every scalar or finite-dimensional Hilbert-valued g in the canonical Hdot^-1 realization with D2g in L2,

    ||g||_2 <= ||g||_(Hdot^-1)^(2/3)||D2g||_2^(1/3).   (1)

Indeed the integrand |g_hat|^2 is the product of (|xi|^-2|g_hat|^2)^(2/3) and (|xi|^4|g_hat|^2)^(1/3). Holder's inequality with exponents 3/2 and 3 proves (1), first on Fourier cutoffs and then by monotone convergence.

The proved bounds of parts P47 and P48 are, with n=N(h),

    ||w_Rh||_(Hdot^-1)<=ell n,
    ||w_RU[h]||_(Hdot^-1)<=(13/3)ell n,
    ||D2(w_Rh)||_2<=d_h n,
    ||D2(w_RU[h])||_2<=d_u n,
    ell=(11/10)2^(-53/2),
    d_h=8436585/8388608, d_u=7604905/4194304.

Consequently

    ||w_Rh||_2<=b_h n, ||w_RU[h]||_2<=b_u n,

The two rounded constants are checked exactly after cubing:

    ell^2 d_h<190000^-3,
    (13/3)^2 ell^2 d_u<60000^-3,
    ell^2=121/(100*2^53).

No regularity of h beyond the completed N norm is assumed here.

#### 3. The annular test and its derivatives

Let e_m be the exact coefficients of the original leading residual angular vector, and put

    a_m=630e_m/(18+m^2),
    S_j=sum_(m positive odd) m^j |a_m|, j=0,1,2,
    chi(t)=(t-1)^2(2-t)^2 on [1,2], zero outside,
    b(t)=(1+t^2)^(-11/10), B(t)=b(t)chi(t),
    zeta_T(X)=B(r/T) sum_m a_m sin(m theta).

This is precisely the test whose signed residual pairing was independently audited in C9Q4, at T=2^31,2^32,2^35. The test is compactly supported in the annulus T<=r<=2T. It is C1, with square-integrable weak second derivatives. Define

    Z=S0/16,
    C1=91S0/160+S1/16,
    C2=6101S0/1600+303S1/320+S2/16.

Then

    |zeta_T|<=Z, |Dzeta_T|<=C1/T,
    |D2zeta_T|_F<=C2/T^2.                         (3)

Here is a direct proof of the new Hessian bound. For x=t-1 in [0,1], chi=x^2(1-x)^2, so |chi|<=1/16, |chi'|<=1/2 and|chi''|<=2. If l=log b, then |l'|<=11/10, |l''|<=11/10 on [1,2]. Thus |b'|<=11/10 and|b''|<=231/100. The product rule gives

    |B|<=1/16, |B'|<=91/160, |B''|<=5191/1600.

For A(theta)=sum a_m sin(m theta), the Hessian in the orthonormal polar frame has entries

    T^2 H_rr=B''A,
    T^2 H_rtheta=(B'/t-B/t^2)A',
    T^2 H_thetatheta=(B'/t)A+(B/t^2)A''.

Using t>=1 and|H|_F<=|H_rr|+sqrt(2)|H_rtheta|+|H_thetatheta|, with sqrt(2)<3/2, proves C2 in (3). The gradient estimate gives C1 and the amplitude gives Z. At the two annular boundaries, B=B'=0. Hence the zero extension has no surface delta in its second weak derivative, as required by the following duality calculation.

#### 4. Negative-order linear pairing and L2 quadratic pairing

Fix R_min=2^31 and any of the three T above. Every R>=R_min satisfies, on the test annulus,

    w_R^-1<=W=(1+4T^2/R_min^2)^(11/10),
    |Dlog w_R|<=k=(11/5)T/(R_min^2+T^2).            (4)

To verify k, first minimize the denominator by R=R_min. The function r/(R_min^2+r^2) decreases for r>=R_min, and T>=R_min. Its maximum on the annulus is therefore at r=T. No assumption R=T is made.

Use the following upper bounds for the reference:

    V=2cT+22(2T)^(5/9), V1=sqrt(2)c+22T^(-4/9),
    D=186T^(-4/9), D1=186T^(-13/9), m=2c+1.

The annulus has area 3pi T^2. Define

    A_h=ell W sqrt(3pi)[(V/T)C2+(V1+m+kV)C1+kmTZ],
    A_u=(13/3)ell W sqrt(3pi)[(D1+kD)TZ+DC1],
    A_T=A_h+A_u,
    Q_T=b_h b_u W^2 C1/T.                         (5)

Then every exact profile in the affine class obeys

    |integral F zeta_T|<=A_T n+Q_T n^2.            (6)

To prove this, exponent rigidity and the exact difference equation give

    integral F zeta_T
       =integral h[bar_V.Dzeta_T+(2c+1)zeta_T]
        -integral U[h].Dbar_rho zeta_T
        +integral h U[h].Dzeta_T.

For the first term, negative Sobolev duality bounds it by L_R(h) times

    ||D{w_R^-1[bar_V.Dzeta_T+(2c+1)zeta_T]}||_2.

The product rule bounds this derivative pointwise by

    W[V|D2zeta_T|_F+(V1+m+kV)|Dzeta_T|+km|zeta_T|].

Its L2 norm is at most sqrt(3pi)T times the supremum, yielding A_h. Applying vector negative Sobolev duality to the second term gives L_R(U[h]) times the norm of D(w_R^-1 Dbar_rho zeta_T), bounded by

    W[(D1+kD)|zeta_T|+D|Dzeta_T|].

This yields A_u. The tests are compact H1 functions by section 3, so both duality pairings are legitimate in the completed spaces.

For the quadratic term, use both global weighted L2 bounds in (2):

    |integral h U[h].Dzeta_T|
       <=||w_Rh||_2 ||w_RU[h]||_2
                            ||w_R^-2 Dzeta_T||_infinity
       <=b_h b_u n^2 W^2 C1/T.

There is no area factor in this Cauchy-Schwarz bound. This is the reason to retain the weighted L2 norms rather than pointwise amplitudes. No derivative of h is estimated here; the derivative was transferred to the test in the exact weak identity. This proves (6).

#### 5. Certified comparison and scope

The input P_T is the lower endpoint of the already audited signed C9Q4 pairing minus its full analytic remainder upper endpoint. It is positive at each T. Since the right side of (6) increases with n>=0, any verified P_T>A_Tq+Q_Tq^2 excludes the closed radius q, uniformly for every R>=2^31 and 0<s<=2^-12, and for any prospective exponent.

The original generator vector and every e_m are exact rational inputs bound to their read-only source by hashes. A large numerical value for q is not accepted without both checks. The result is independent of coefficient coercivity, surjectivity of a linearized operator, and any residual upper bound.

    rho=bar_rho+h, N_(s,R)(h)<=2^57.

## P50. The natural normalized maximal domain and forcing compatibility

### P50.1. The maximal domain of the full normalized operator

Status: independent analytical derivation complete.  No new numerical hypothesis is introduced.

#### 1. Exact space and reference assumptions

Fix R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12. Let N=N_(s,R) be the real Hilbert completion of smooth compact densities even in x and odd in y in the norm

    N(h)^2=||(1+4r^2)^(2/5) D2 J^s h||2^2
           +2^22 ||<r>^(-1/5) D J^s h||2^2
           +2^53 ||w_R J^s h||_(Hdot^-1)^2,
    J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10).

All derivatives are ordered Cartesian tensors with Euclidean norms. Use the canonical velocity U=(-R1R2,R1^2), with no harmonic addition. The established embeddings in parts P19 and P37 give locally C1 representatives, a continuous strain functional c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0), and

    |h(X)|+|U[h](X)| <= C_s N(h) max(1,r)^(1/5).       (1)

The finite constant in (1) need not be small; for example C_s=120 is valid from part P19. Only the exponent 1/5 is used below.

Assume a smooth real reference bar_rho of the same parity has canonical velocity bar_u, and

    T^(-gamma) bar_rho(TX) -> G(X)=|X|^gamma Theta(arg X)

uniformly on every compact annulus as T tends to infinity. Here 1/5<gamma<1, Theta is continuous and not identically zero, and |bar_u(X)|<=C(1+|X|). For the nonlinear statement in section 4, assume additionally bar_u(X)=o(|X|) uniformly at infinity. Set c0=1/gamma and

    g=X.Dbar_rho,
    L_fix h=(c0 X+bar_u).Dh-h+U[h].Dbar_rho,
    A_k h=L_fix h+U[k].Dh,
    B_k h=A_k h-c[h]g,                                  (2)

Here B_0 is the derivative at bar_rho of the normalized residual with exponent c0-c[h]. For nonzero k, B_k is the frozen transport operator used in the inverse iteration; it is not asserted to be the full derivative at bar_rho+k. The latter has further terms. In (2), k is any fixed element of N. Products are first defined as distributions by their locally C1 representatives; no bounded map N->N is asserted.

Let D(A_k)={h in N:A_kh belongs to N distributionally}. This is the maximal distributional high domain proved in the inverse theorem when its coefficient and smallness hypotheses hold. Define independently

    D(B_k)={h in N:B_kh belongs to N distributionally}.    (3)

The main assertion, requiring no invertibility or smallness assumption, is

    D(B_k)={h in D(A_k):c[h]=0},
    B_kh=A_kh on this domain.                            (4)

Thus there is no cancellation between a nonzero exponent column and an inadmissible transport term hidden in the larger maximal-domain definition (3).

#### 2. A rescaling lemma for the linearized expression

For a function q define q_T(X)=T^(-gamma)q(TX). If q belongs to N, (1) shows q_T->0 uniformly on every compact annulus. It also shows U[q](TX)/T->0 uniformly there. The same applies to a forcing f in N.

Let h,k belong to N. We claim

    T^(-gamma)(A_kh)(T .) -> 0

in distributions on each compact annulus. The dilation and scalar terms equal c0 X.Dh_T-h_T and tend to zero distributionally. For the background transport term, let phi be a compact smooth test on the annulus. Since bar_u is divergence free,

    <T^(-gamma) bar_u(T .).Dh(T .),phi>
        =-integral h_T(X) [bar_u(TX)/T].Dphi(X) dX.        (5)

The bracketed vector is uniformly bounded on the support by the at-most-linear growth assumption. Since h_T tends uniformly to zero, (5) tends to zero. The perturbing transport has the identical formula with bar_u replaced by U[k], whose quotient by T even tends to zero.

For the coupling term, divergence freedom gives

    <T^(-gamma) U[h](T .).Dbar_rho(T .),phi>
        =-integral bar_rho_T(X) [U[h](TX)/T].Dphi(X) dX.   (6)

The first factor is uniformly bounded and the second tends uniformly to zero. Hence (6) tends to zero. These arguments use no asymptotic estimate on Dh or Dbar_rho and no derivative of k beyond its established local regularity.

Meanwhile

    T^(-gamma) g(TX)=X.Dbar_rho_T(X) -> X.DG=gamma G       (7)

in distributions. The first convergence follows by integration by parts and local uniform convergence of bar_rho_T. The last identity follows from the exact homogeneity G(tX)=t^gamma G(X): differentiating the scaling identity under a compact test proves Euler's relation distributionally. No angular derivative of Theta is required.

If h belongs to D(B_k), write B_kh=f in N and rescale the equality. Equations (5)-(7) and f_T->0 imply

    0=-c[h] gamma G.

Since gamma>0 and G is nonzero, c[h]=0. Then A_kh=f belongs to N, proving the nontrivial inclusion in (4). The reverse inclusion follows directly from (2). This proves (4).

The identical proof permits an independent scalar b in place of c[h]:

    h in N and A_kh-b g in N  imply b=0 and h in D(A_k).  (8)

Thus a free exponent coordinate cannot be appended to this fixed-tail forcing space without also changing its tail coordinates.

#### 3. Range, inverse, and the center compatibility

Assume in addition the exact reference normalization

    c0+c[bar_rho]=1, a0=partial_y bar_rho(0)>0,

and suppose A_k is bijective from D(A_k) onto N with inverse norm at most K. These assumptions are fulfilled under the explicit conditional coefficient contract and positive semigroup rate of part P43. Suppose c[k]=0.

Define the closed forcing hyperplane

    N_0={f in N:partial_y f(0)=0}.

For h in D(A_k), local C1 regularity suffices to compute the first jet:

    partial_y(A_kh)(0)=c[k]partial_y h(0)+a0 c[h]
                      =a0 c[h].                         (9)

To justify this without assuming D2h continuous, write Dh(X)=Dh(0)+o(1), use that the transport field vanishes at zero, and expand that field to first order. Its derivative at zero is diag(2c0-1-c[k],1+c[k]). The term U[h].Dbar_rho contributes a0 c[h] to the y derivative. The scalar -h cancels the unperturbed transport contribution. This proves (9) using only first-order expansions.

By (4) and (9), B_k maps D(B_k) into N_0. For any f in N_0, h=A_k^(-1)f satisfies c[h]=0 by (9), hence lies in D(B_k) and solves B_kh=f. Injectivity follows from that of A_k. Consequently

    B_k:D(B_k) -> N_0 is bijective,
    N(B_k^(-1)f)<=K N(f).                                (10)

The operator is closed: convergence in its graph norm is convergence in the graph of the closed operator A_k, and the additional condition c[h]=0 is closed in N. This also proves that the natural maximal realization has exactly the constrained realization previously used in the fixed-point theorem.

At the parameters and under all the conditional hypotheses of part P43,

    R=2^31, s=3*2^-21, N(k)<=5*2^-27, c[k]=0,

one may take K=40. With the same adapted Holder norm and jet-subtracted moment as parts P37 and P43, the compatible estimate is

    L_R(h)+C_ad(h)+M(h)+|c[h]| <=2^23 N(B_kh),
    h in D(B_k).                                        (11)

The strain term vanishes on this particular domain, but its continuity in the ambient space was necessary to define the domain and prove its closure. The estimate does not create a bounded exponent column on N and does not assert surjectivity onto forcing with nonzero y-jet.

#### 4. Nonlinear forcing membership also fixes the exponent

Under the additional sublinear velocity assumption in section 1, let h belong to N, let rho=bar_rho+h, and let c1 be any real scalar. If

    F(rho,c1)=(c1 X+U[rho]).Drho-rho

belongs to N distributionally, then c1=c0. To prove this, rho_T tends uniformly to G, U[rho](TX)/T tends uniformly to zero on compact annuli, and the rescaled forcing tends uniformly to zero by (1). In the weak equation the nonlinear transport becomes

    -integral rho_T [U[rho](TX)/T].Dphi,

which tends to zero. The limit of the remaining equation is c1 X.DG-G=0, hence (c1 gamma-1)G=0. Nonzero G proves the assertion.

In particular, if the normalized exponent is c1=c0-c[h] and the normalized residual belongs to N, then c[h]=0. This is stronger than the stationary version of exponent rigidity, since the forcing need not vanish. It also shows why the fully normalized nonlinear residual is not a map from an open N ball into N: every h with c[h]!=0 has residual outside N. On the hyperplane c[h]=0, derivative loss may still prevent the residual from belonging to N for arbitrary h; the quasilinear inverse iteration addresses that separate issue.

The assertion that this hyperplane is proper follows, for example, by taking a Schwartz parity density with Fourier transform -i xi_y exp(-|xi|^2). Its strain is a nonzero constant times the integral of -xi_x^2 xi_y^2 exp(-|xi|^2)/|xi|^2. Thus arbitrarily small nonzero-strain elements exist in N.

#### 5. Scope and dependencies

This theorem identifies the domain and range of the full normalized expression within the fixed leading angular class. It does not allow variations of Theta, a leading exponent logarithm, or an added harmonic velocity. Such coordinates need a larger realization and separate estimates. The affine tail constraint also removes scaling, since scaling changes the nonzero leading function to t^(1-gamma)Theta.

parts P19 and P37 supply the actual embeddings and continuous strain. Part P39 supplies the stationary rescaling argument, extended here to an inhomogeneous equation and to the linearized maximal domain. parts P17, P21, P24 and P43 supply A_k only under their complete explicit hypotheses; (4) itself needs none of their coercivity assumptions. All existence and inverse claims remain conditional on those hypotheses. The original and currently audited refit residuals fail the required smallness conditions.

## P51. Exterior weight transfer of the annular witnesses

### P51.1. Exterior transfer of annular negative-norm witnesses

Status: independent analytical proof and three exact integer bounds are CONFIRMED. 

#### 1. Statement and exact spaces

For q>=1 and a radius R>0 let w_R(X)=(1+|X|^2/R^2)^(-q). Suppose T>0, R>=T, and phi is a real compact H1 function supported in {|X|>=T}. Then

    ||D[(w_T/w_R)phi]||2 <= ||Dphi||2.                 (1)

Consequently, whenever w_R f belongs to the canonical homogeneous negative space Hdot^-1(R2),

    ||w_R f||_(Hdot^-1) >= |<w_T f,phi>|/||Dphi||2.   (2)

The pairing on the right is interpreted distributionally whenever multiplication by the smooth weights is defined. A zero test is omitted. In the application phi is compact C1, f is a smooth S1 residual, and the density and test have the even-x, odd-y parity. The homogeneous negative space is the Fourier realization or, equivalently, the dual of the homogeneous Dirichlet completion with that parity. No monotonicity of weighted negative norms on arbitrary functions is claimed.

#### 2. Proof of the multiplier contraction

Set a=w_T/w_R and z=|X|^2, D0=R^2-T^2>=0. Then 0<a<=1 and

    partial_z log a = -q D0/[(T^2+z)(R^2+z)].

For a radial function of z in two dimensions, Delta a=4(z partial_z^2 a+partial_z a). Direct differentiation gives

    Delta a/a = 4q D0 [z^2+q D0 z-T^2 R^2]
                       /[(T^2+z)^2(R^2+z)^2].        (3)

The numerator bracket equals (z-T^2)(z+T^2+qD0)+(q-1)T^2D0. Both terms are nonnegative for z>=T^2 and q>=1. Thus Delta a>=0 on {|X|>=T}. For a smooth compact test supported there, integration by parts gives the exact identity

    integral |D(a phi)|^2
       =integral a^2 |Dphi|^2-integral a Delta a phi^2
       <=integral |Dphi|^2.                           (4)

The same identity holds for compact H1 tests by approximation, or by the weak product rule and integration of D(phi^2). Their traces at the boundary of their support cause no boundary term. This proves (1). Finally

    <w_T f,phi>=<w_R f,a phi>,

and homogeneous duality followed by (1) proves (2). The proof also works for Hilbert-valued tests and forcings, though only the scalar version is needed here.

#### 3. Application to the original state 131

Fix q=11/10 and the exact original state 131 and canonical residual F recovered from the read-only case4 checkpoint. Its exponent is

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248.

Use the norm N_(s,R) and completed density space of part P47, for every R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12:

    N_(s,R)(h)^2=||(1+4r^2)^(2/5)D2 J^s h||2^2
                  +2^22||<r>^(-1/5)D J^s h||2^2
                  +2^53||w_R J^s h||_(Hdot^-1)^2.

The original growing residual belongs to this space, as proved in section P21.2. The inverse Bessel estimate of part P47 gives

    N_(s,R)(F) >= 2^(53/2) L_R(F)/(1+s C_R),
    C_R=41/(5R)+17/R^2+327/(5R^3)+1309/(10R^4)+924/(5R^5).

Each positive term of C_R decreases with R. The independently audited C9 tests at T in {2^31,2^32,2^35} are supported on T<=r<=2T. Their positive pairing divided by their exact Dirichlet norm exceeds the integer l_T listed below:

    l_(2^31)=372474829674258475,
    l_(2^32)=1602697408584840334,
    l_(2^35)=127617579877087467912.

Thus (2) and the Bessel estimate prove, uniformly in R>=T and 0<s<=2^-12,

    N_(s,R)(F)>2^(53/2) l_T/[1+2^-12 C_T].           (5)

These integers are lower bounds for particular dual witnesses, not floating point approximations to the full negative norm. All source hashes and the previously independently checked endpoints must be verified in the numerical refresh. Exact integer squaring suffices to turn (5) into a lower integer bound and a gap over eta=2^-30. No numerical integration is needed for that refresh.

#### 4. Scope

This strengthens a necessary residual lower bound for one exact reference. It neither supplies a norm upper bound nor establishes a uniform lower bound over the nonlinear finite potential family. Part P29 already constructs a residual-shaped function in the larger finite linear power space with the same tail and norm below the threshold; a useful weighted family obstruction must use nonlinear realizability. This result also does not alter the independent exact-profile distance theorem of part P49.

Dependencies: part P47 for the Bessel estimate, part P21 for membership and the canonical low norm, and section P11.4 with audit_c9_Q4.json for the original-source annular witnesses. All constants in (5) are exact rational numbers apart from sqrt(2^53).

| Weight radius | Strict integer lower bound for N_(s,R)(F) | Gap over eta=2^-30 |
|---|---|---|

## P52. Annular residual gaps and necessary distances for the refits Mpen2 and d2

### P52.1. Annular residual and distance bounds for the later exact refits

Status: analytical argument written before computation. The particular numerical comparisons below remain OPEN until both arithmetic audits finish. The scope is the two named exact references, not their entire generator family.

#### 1. Statement and spaces

Fix R_min=2^31, R>=R_min and 0<s<=2^-12. Set J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), omega_1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10) and omega_2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5). Use the real S1 completion of compact smooth densities, even in x and odd in y, in the norm

    N_(s,R)(h)^2 = ||omega_2 D2 J^s h||_2^2
          +2^22 ||omega_1 D J^s h||_2^2
          +2^53 ||w_R J^s h||_(Hdot^-1)^2.

The homogeneous negative norm is its canonical Fourier realization, and derivatives have Euclidean or Frobenius norms. The canonical velocity is U[h]=(-R1 R2 h,R1^2 h), without an added harmonic field.

The two references are nb_Mpen2_exact and nb_d2_exact from the numerical  exact JSON data. Each determines a rational potential

    bar_chi=sum a_(j,m,k) r^(2k)(1+r^2)^((3+gamma-j delta)/2-k) cos(2m theta),
    bar_rho=-partial_y Delta bar_chi,
    bar_u=(-partial_x partial_y^2 bar_chi, partial_x^2 partial_y bar_chi),
    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma.

Its indices satisfy 0<=j<=5, 0<=m<=59 and m<=k<=75. Exact reconstruction, the fixed nonzero leading tail r^gamma Theta, origin normalization and cancellation of every residual sector above p_star=gamma-6delta<-2 were already proved in parts P20 and P42. They are checked afresh here. In particular F=(cX+bar_u).Dbar_rho-bar_rho belongs to N_(s,R), by its smooth symbol decay of order p_star and the Bessel mapping argument of part P21. This membership assertion is separate from a bound for its size.

For either reference and any T>=1 passing the tests below, there are explicit positive P_T, A_T, Q_T and L_T such that

    ||w_R F||_(Hdot^-1)>=L_T,  N_(s,R)(F)>=L_T/ell,
    P_T<=A_T N_(s,R)(h)+Q_T N_(s,R)(h)^2                 (1)

for every exact canonical profile bar_rho+h with h in N_(s,R), of any prospective exponent. Here ell=(11/10)2^(-53/2). Thus P_T>A_T q+Q_T q^2 excludes the whole closed ball N_(s,R)(h)<=q. No invertibility or energy positivity hypothesis is used.

#### 2. Exact residual expansion and its full remainder

Expand each radial factor in r^-2 through q=3. Perform Cartesian differentiation and multiplication in exact angular Laurent polynomials, preserving all cancellations. Write the resulting finite residual as

    F_t=sum_(h,q) r^(gamma-h delta-2q) E_(h,q)(theta),
    E_star=E_(6,0)=sum_m e_m sin(m theta).

Verify exactly that E_star is nonzero, every other nonzero exponent is less than p_star, and the leading potential moments equal the original checkpoint. For d=3,4,5, let B_(d,j,q) be the largest, over all order-d Cartesian derivatives, of the sum of absolute complex Fourier coefficients of the differentiated potential sector. Put A_j=sum_(m,k)|a_(j,m,k)| and q0=4. Define

    M_d(T)=sum_(j,q<=3) B_(d,j,q) T^(-j delta-2q),
    tau_d=((q0+76)/(q0+1))*((2q0+132)/(2q0+130))^d/T^2,
    T_d(T)=binom(q0+75,q0)(2q0+130)^d T^(-2q0)
                       *sum_j A_j T^(-j delta)/(1-tau_d).

Require tau_d<1. The exact index bounds give |(3+gamma-j delta)/2-k|<76 and

    |3+gamma-j delta|+2m+2(d-1)<130, d<=5.

The binomial coefficient is bounded by binom(q+75,q); an order-d Cartesian derivative costs at most (2q+130)^d in angular coefficient sum. The majorant ratio decreases in q and is at most tau_d at q=q0. Consequently, for r>=T, each Cartesian component satisfies

    |D^d bar_chi_t|<=M_d(T) r^(gamma+3-d),
    |D^d(bar_chi-bar_chi_t)|<=T_d(T)(T/r)^8 r^(gamma+3-d).  (2)

Both the finite coefficient sum and the omitted tail decrease after division by r^(gamma+3-d), so C_d=M_d+T_d bounds the full derivative on r>=T. The harmless increase from 128 to 130 in part P25's majorant accommodates the fifth derivative.

By the product rule and Cauchy-Schwarz, part P25's residual remainder argument gives

    |F-F_t|<=Ctail r^p_star, r>=T,
    Ctail=(2sqrt(2)c T_4+2T_3)T^(gamma-p_star)
                +4(T_3 M_4+M_3 T_4+T_3 T_4)T^(2gamma-1-p_star). (3)

Indeed density is a sum of two third derivatives, its gradient is a vector of two such fourth-derivative sums, and velocity comprises two third derivatives. The linear error is bounded by 2sqrt(2)c r T_4 r^(gamma-1)+2T_3 r^gamma; the three quadratic errors have coefficient 4. The factors (T/r)^8 absorb the powers because 8>6delta and 8>5delta. In the product of two tails one may discard one of these factors.

#### 3. A positive annular pairing

Define

    d_m=1/35+m^2/630, a_m=e_m/d_m,
    S=sum_m e_m^2/d_m, S_j=sum_m m^j |a_m| (j=0,1,2),
    chi(t)=(t-1)^2(2-t)^2 for 1<=t<=2, and 0 elsewhere,
    phi_T(r,theta)=chi(r/T)sum_m a_m sin(m theta).

This is a compact C1 function with square-integrable second weak derivatives; both chi and chi' vanish at the two boundaries. Orthogonality and the exact integrals int chi=1/30, int chi^2=1/630, int t(chi')^2=1/35 imply

    ||Dphi_T||_2^2<=pi S.

For each nonleading residual sector set C_(h,q)=sum_m a_m E_(h,q,m). Let

    B_T=sum_(p<p_star) max(0,-C_(h,q))T^(p-p_star),
    b_T=S-B_T-2Ctail S_0.

Require b_T>0. Each sine coefficient of an error bounded by Ctail r^p_star has absolute value at most (4/pi)Ctail r^p_star<2Ctail r^p_star. Therefore the signed angular pairing is at least pi b_T r^p_star at every r>=T. Positive subleading cross coefficients are discarded and negative ones decrease relative to r^p_star. Since p_star+1<0,

    int F phi_T >= P_T:=pi b_T T^(p_star+2)2^(p_star+1)/30. (4)

Let W=(1+4T^2/R_min^2)^(11/10). For every R>=R_min, w_R>=1/W on this annulus, so the same positive angular pairing proves

    int w_R F phi_T>=P_T/W,
    L_T:=P_T/(W sqrt(pi S))<=||w_R F||_(Hdot^-1).       (5)

The Bessel duality theorem of part P47 yields L_R(F)<=ell N_(s,R)(F), proving the first inequality in (1). The use of the radial weight is valid because the angular integral has a fixed positive sign at each radius; no pointwise sign of F phi_T is assumed.

#### 4. Derivative bounds for the weak test

Put

    Z=S_0/16, C1=S_0/2+S_1/16,
    C2=5S_0/2+27S_1/32+S_2/16.

Then |phi_T|<=Z, |Dphi_T|<=C1/T and |D2phi_T|_F<=C2/T^2. To check the last constant, the orthonormal polar Hessian has components

    T^2 H_rr=chi'' A,
    T^2 H_rtheta=(chi'/t-chi/t^2) A',
    T^2 H_thetatheta=(chi'/t)A+(chi/t^2)A'',

where A=sum_m a_m sin(m theta). The bounds |chi|<=1/16, |chi'|<=1/2, |chi''|<=2 and t>=1 give |H|_F<=|H_rr|+(3/2)|H_rtheta|+|H_thetatheta|, which is exactly C2. The zero extension introduces no boundary distribution in D2phi_T.

On the annulus, (2) gives the following bounds for the full reference:

    |bar_u|<=sqrt(2)C_3(2T)^gamma,
    |Dbar_u|_F<=2C_4 T^(gamma-1),
    |Dbar_rho|<=2sqrt(2)C_4 T^(gamma-1),
    |D2bar_rho|_F<=4C_5 T^(gamma-2).

The signs of gamma, gamma-1 and gamma-2 specify which endpoint maximizes each power. Accordingly set

    V=2cT+sqrt(2)C_3(2T)^gamma,
    V1=sqrt(2)c+2C_4 T^(gamma-1),
    D=2sqrt(2)C_4 T^(gamma-1), D1=4C_5 T^(gamma-2),
    k=(11/10)/R_min, m=2c+1.

For every R>=R_min, |Dlog w_R|<=(11/10)/R<=k on the whole plane. This uniform k is valid whether T is smaller or larger than R_min.

#### 5. Necessary distance from every exact profile

The embedding proved in part P19 gives h,U[h]=O(r^(1/5)). Since each reference has nonzero leading degree gamma>1/5 and sublinear velocity, the weak rescaling argument of part P39 fixes the exponent of every exact bar_rho+h to c=1/gamma. It requires neither a small norm nor an assumption on the corrected center slope. Thus the exact weak difference equation is

    int F phi_T = int h[(cX+bar_u).Dphi_T+m phi_T]
             -int U[h].Dbar_rho phi_T+int h U[h].Dphi_T.  (6)

Part P49 supplies, for n=N_(s,R)(h),

    ||w_R h||_(Hdot^-1)<=ell n,
    ||w_R U[h]||_(Hdot^-1)<=(13/3)ell n,
    ||w_R h||_2<=n/190000, ||w_R U[h]||_2<=n/60000.

The latter two follow from Fourier interpolation between the negative norm and the controlled weighted second derivatives. Their constants are proved uniformly in the present parameter range. No bound for a derivative of h is needed in (6).

Differentiate the two compact test factors in (6) and use the annular area 3pi T^2. Negative-order duality and the product rule give

    A_h=ell W sqrt(3pi)[(V/T)C2+(V1+m+kV)C1+kmTZ],
    A_u=(13/3)ell W sqrt(3pi)[(D1+kD)TZ+D C1],
    A_T=A_h+A_u,
    Q_T=W^2 C1/(190000*60000*T).                     (7)

For the quadratic term use Cauchy-Schwarz on the two global weighted L2 norms and the supremum W^2 C1/T. This yields (1) from (4). The compact test factors belong to H1 because bar_rho is smooth and phi_T is compact H2. Thus the duality argument is valid for completed-space corrections, by distributional approximation. The nonlinearity is locally integrable by the same embeddings; derivative loss is not hidden in a forcing norm.

#### 6. Verification contract and scope

The first computation reconstructs both exact references from JSON, independently recovers the original checkpoint exponent and leading moments, verifies all sector cancellations with rational arithmetic, and evaluates(2)-(7) with directed Arb intervals. At the best successful annulus it compares the full Cartesian potential evaluator with the independently constructed Laurent expansion. The second program uses fixed-point integer intervals, rounded outwards after every operation.
