## P53. The frozen heat inverse for the full parameter range

### P53.1. The full parameter range of the frozen heat inverse

Status: complete analytical argument; independent review and elementary verification are pending. This is a theorem for the complete coupled fixed-coefficient frozen operator, not for the variable-coefficient profile operator.

#### 1. The exact operator and realization

Let lambda>1, a>0, sigma=a/(lambda-1), and 0<alpha<min(1,sigma). Put b=sigma-alpha>0 and

    D=lambda x partial_x+y partial_y,
    L0=D-1+a R1^2, Lambda=(-Delta)^(1/2),
    H_t=exp(t Delta), t>0.

The Fourier multiplier of R1^2 is -xi_1^2/|xi|^2. Let S_ann be the real Schwartz functions with smooth Fourier transform compactly supported away from zero. Restrict to even-x, odd-y functions. On this core define

    ||h||_X = sup_(t>0) t^(b/2) ||H_t Lambda^sigma h||_infinity. (1)

Let X be its completion. This norm is equivalent to the ordinary homogeneous C^alpha seminorm on the core and hence defines the same little homogeneous Hoelder completion, with the additive constant fixed by parity. The equivalence constants depend only on alpha, sigma and a fixed Fourier cutoff. No value 1 for those constants is asserted.

Let L0 be the generator realization on X specified below. Then it is bijective from its generator domain onto X, and

    ||L0^-1 f||_X <= (1-alpha)^-1 ||f||_X.             (2)

The operator domain is exactly the set of h in X for which the strong limit (S_t h-h)/t as t decreases to 0 exists in X, where S_t is given in section 3. On S_ann this generator equals the displayed differential and Riesz expression. Formula (2) is a same-order estimate for h itself; no derivative of h is an independent unknown. Its constant is 2 at alpha=1/2 whenever sigma>1/2. It is not claimed that the standard C^alpha seminorm inverse constant is 2.

#### 2. Norm equivalence, including both directions

Use the radial cutoff eta and dyadic partition phi(xi)=eta(|xi|)-eta(2|xi|) of part P5, with eta=1 on [0,1], eta=0 on [2,infinity), and the explicitly given C4 polynomial transition. Let Delta_j have multiplier phi(2^-j xi). Let tilde_phi be a C4 compact annular multiplier equal to 1 on the support of phi and supported in 1/4<=|xi|<=4. For a core function g, put

    ||g||_B = sup_j 2^(-bj)||Delta_j g||_infinity,
    ||g||_H = sup_(t>0) t^(b/2)||H_t g||_infinity.

First B<=C H. The multiplier K(xi)=phi(xi)exp(|xi|^2) is compactly supported away from zero and has finite convolution L1 norm C_K. At t=2^(-2j), the identity

    Delta_j g = K(2^-j D) H_t g

gives 2^(-bj)||Delta_j g||_infinity<=C_K||g||_H.

Conversely, choose a constant C_phi for which the inverse Fourier transform of exp(-v|xi|^2)tilde_phi(xi) has L1 norm at most

    C_phi(1+v)^2 exp(-v/16), v>=0.                    (3)

Here C_phi is finite and depends only on the chosen cutoff. To prove(3), write k for that inverse transform and use

    ||k||_1 <= sqrt(pi)|| (1+|X|^2)k ||_2
             =sqrt(pi)/(2pi)|| (1-Delta_xi)[exp(-v|xi|^2)tilde_phi] ||_2.

On the fixed annulus, all derivatives of order at most 2 of the exponential are bounded by a fixed constant times (1+v)^2 exp(-v/16). The cutoff and its first two derivatives are bounded and have support of finite area. This proves (3), without a multiplier assertion at xi=0.

Since tilde_phi=1 on the support of each rescaled Delta_j, the finite reconstruction of a core function yields

    t^(b/2)||H_t g||_infinity
       <=C_phi ||g||_B sum_j v_j^(b/2)(1+v_j)^2 exp(-v_j/16),
    v_j=t 2^(2j).

This sum is bounded uniformly in t. Choose J so that 1<=v_J<4. For j<=J, the sum is bounded by 25*2^b/(1-2^-b). For j=J+k, k>=1, use 4^k<=v_j<4^(k+1), 1+v_j<=2v_j, and obtain the summable bound

    4 sum_(k>=1) 4^((k+1)(b/2+2)) exp(-4^k/16).

Thus H<=C B. Both estimates extend to completions. Taking g=Lambda^sigma h identifies(1) with part P5's dyadic norm of order alpha, up to these explicit finite constants.

For completeness, the last equivalence with the C^alpha seminorm has the following direct proof. The compact annular kernel of |xi|^sigma phi(xi) has zero integral and a finite alpha-weighted L1 moment. The latter follows from its four square-integrable derivatives, using Cauchy-Schwarz with polynomial spatial weights; alpha<1 suffices. Its cancellation bounds 2^(-bj)||Delta_j Lambda^sigma h||_infinity by a fixed constant times [h]_C^alpha. In the other direction the compact annular multiplier |xi|^-sigma tilde_phi(xi) and its gradient have integrable kernels. They give

    ||Delta_j h||_infinity<=C0 2^(-alpha j)||Lambda^sigma h||_B,
    ||D Delta_j h||_infinity<=C1 2^((1-alpha)j)||Lambda^sigma h||_B.

For points at distance d, sum the second bound over 2^j d<=1 and twice the first over 2^j d>1. Both sums are geometric because 0<alpha<1, giving [h]_C^alpha<=C||Lambda^sigma h||_B. Core reconstruction and uniform difference bounds justify the limit. The completion is the closure of this core, not the whole nonseparable Hoelder space.

#### 3. Exact coupled flow and heat contraction

Let A_t=diag(exp(lambda t),exp(t)), and T_t g(X)=g(A_t X). Fourier differentiation gives on S_ann

    Lambda^sigma L0=(D+sigma-1)Lambda^sigma.

Indeed [Lambda^sigma,D]=sigma Lambda^sigma-sigma(lambda-1)Lambda^sigma R1^2, and a=sigma(lambda-1). Thus the exact core flow is

    S_t h=exp((sigma-1)t)Lambda^-sigma T_t Lambda^sigma h. (4)

Its derivative at 0 is L0; S_(t+u)=S_t S_u. All these identities hold without a low-frequency convention issue on the Fourier-annular core.

For any positive definite diagonal matrix A with smallest diagonal entry m>0, the chain rule for the heat equation gives

    H_u(g(A .)) = [exp(u AA^T:D2)g](A .).

The covariance AA^T-m^2 I is nonnegative. Therefore exp(u(AA^T-m^2 I):D2) is convolution by a probability Gaussian, possibly a point mass in one coordinate, and contracts L-infinity. Factoring the two commuting heat operators gives

    ||H_u(g(A .))||_infinity <= ||H_(um^2) g||_infinity,
    ||g(A .)||_H <= m^-b ||g||_H.                    (5)

The exponent m^-b follows by changing variable v=um^2 in the supremum defining H. This is a direct Gaussian estimate and retains the anisotropic cancellation in L0.

For A=A_t, m=exp(t). Equations(1), (4), and (5) give

    ||S_t h||_X <= exp((sigma-1-b)t)||h||_X
                 =exp(-(1-alpha)t)||h||_X, t>=0.     (6)

The estimate is a contraction with decay, without a dyadic convolution constant. It is valid on the core and extends to X. Continuity in t on the core follows from continuity in its Schwartz topology with Fourier supports remaining in a compact annulus on bounded time intervals, together with the norm equivalence above. Density and (6) then give a strongly continuous semigroup on the entire completion.

#### 4. Onto solvability and uniqueness in the specified domain

For f in X the Bochner integral

    h=-integral_0^infinity S_t f dt

converges by (6) and has norm at most (1-alpha)^-1||f||_X. The semigroup law gives

    (S_u h-h)/u = (1/u)integral_0^u S_t f dt -> f

strongly in X. Hence h belongs to the generator domain and L0 h=f. This proves surjectivity and (2). If L0 h=0 in the generator domain, the differentiable orbit S_t h is constant, while (6) forces it to converge to 0. Thus h=0, proving injectivity. A generator is closed by its semigroup realization; no passage from a coercive estimate to surjectivity is being assumed.

The S1 parity subspace is closed and all operators used preserve it, so the same argument proves the asserted inverse there. For the exact state 131 data, sigma=6.355702...>1/2, and alpha=1/2 is permitted. The only numerical verification needed for the constant 2 is that strict rational inequality.

#### 5. Scope and remaining issues

The contraction bound already appears in section P5.1 under the sufficient restriction sigma>4, and its sharpness for the checkpoint parameters is proved in part P22. The new content here is the norm equivalence and inverse realization for every 0<alpha<min(1,sigma), without sigma>4. There is no improvement of the checkpoint inverse constant. However, the full normalized frozen linearization also has the term -a c[h]y, and c[h] is unbounded on low-order C^alpha alone. The theorem here concerns L0, not that full operator. It also supplies no estimate for variable coefficients, localization commutators, freely changing leading tails, a center jet, or the nonlinear derivative loss. Those require the compatible weighted Sobolev theory developed separately. The Gaussian contraction can improve the frozen building block without claiming that it closes the full nonlinear problem.

## P54. Off-axis violation of the fourth-derivative bound by the refit d2

### P54.1. Off-axis fourth-derivative test for the exact d2 reference

Status: the verification method is complete. A particular failed inequality remains OPEN until both computations described below pass.

#### Statement and scope

Let bar_chi be the exact rational potential specified by nb_d2_exact.json in the numerical work, reconstructed and independently checked in parts P20, P42 and P52. Its density is bar_rho=-partial_y Delta bar_chi. Its canonical coefficients are those with serialization hash f1e761a9849e7c0af0fba2cc5ba2a9aa83c3f3230727737fe3196ef1b03e07fc; the JSON source hash is f3339f85eff0ac81033a2a1f0fd07e12298ef9bd74da501a4e874c3cef6057e3. The exponent is c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma. There are 1322 nonzero canonical terms, all of the form

    a_(j,m,k) r^(2k)(1+r^2)^((3+gamma-j delta)/2-k) cos(2m theta),
    0<=j<=5, m<=k<=75.

These terms are smooth everywhere because r^(2m)cos(2m theta)=Re(x+iy)^(2m) is a polynomial. The noninteger radial power has a strictly positive argument. Define the Frobenius norm of the symmetric fourth derivative tensor by

    |D4 bar_rho(X)|_F^2=sum_(i=0)^4 binom(4,i)|partial_x^i partial_y^(4-i)bar_rho(X)|^2.

The reference hypothesis W3 in the conditional weighted existence theorem requires

    (1+|X|^2)|D4 bar_rho(X)|_F<=512 for every X in R2.       (1)

A single rational point X at which the squared left side is strictly greater than 512^2 disproves(1). This does not disprove the other W3 requirements or the other sufficient hypotheses. It does not imply nonexistence of an exact profile. The prior eight selected-point tests remain valid at their specified points.

#### Exact test identity

Write chi_(a,b)=partial_x^a partial_y^b bar_chi(X). Commuting smooth derivatives gives

    d_i:=partial_x^i partial_y^(4-i)bar_rho(X)
        =-chi_(i+2,5-i)-chi_(i,7-i),  i=0,...,4.

Consequently the quantity to be compared with 512^2 is exactly

    (1+x^2+y^2)^2 sum_(i=0)^4 binom(4,i) d_i^2.             (2)

There is no tensor-normalization or angular-quadrature approximation in (2). All weights and multiplicities at a rational point are rational.

#### Two differentiation methods and a rational final audit

The first method expands each canonical potential summand in a bivariate Cartesian Taylor algebra around the rational point, through total order 7. The coefficient of the degree (a,b) monomial is multiplied by a!b! to recover chi_(a,b). The polynomial harmonic is evaluated through Re(x+iy)^(2m); the smooth radial factor uses the finite binomial expansion through the requested order, with its point value enclosed by directed Arb arithmetic. Because a seventh-order derivative depends only on the seventh Taylor jet, no remainder estimate is required for these point derivatives.

The second method differentiates in polar variables using the chain-rule operators partial_x=cos(theta)partial_r-sin(theta)partial_theta/r and partial_y=sin(theta)partial_r+cos(theta)partial_theta/r. It collects radial polynomials in t=r^2/(1+r^2) for each branch and angular Fourier mode. At the rational point, sine and cosine values are computed recursively from x/r and y/r. These derivatives are enclosed separately with directed Arb arithmetic. This uses a different derivative recurrence and a different basis from the Cartesian method. Every required seventh derivative must overlap between the two methods.

The first certificate records all required raw seventh derivatives, the density components d_i, the value of (2), and the square root. The second arithmetic audit parses its printed outward decimal intervals as exact rational endpoints, rechecks every input and code hash, rederives d_i and (2) with rational interval operations, and checks a displayed integer lower bound by squaring. A claim that (1) fails is recorded only if the exact rational lower endpoint exceeds 512^2. Checking just the printed approximate norm or agreement between two numerical values would not suffice.

The source JSON, canonical reconstruction, original checkpoint exponent and both differentiation implementations are bound by hashes in the evidence folder. The proof concerns this named exact reference only. The numerical  floating scan supplies the point to try, not the proof.

## P55. A smaller ordinary Hoelder constant for the frozen inverse

### P55.1. Scale-adjusted conversion to the ordinary Hoelder seminorm

Status: the analytical argument is complete and precedes the computations. Numerical sufficient constants remain OPEN until a separate audit passes.

#### Statement and dependencies

Let lambda>1, a>0, sigma=a/(lambda-1), and 0<alpha<1. Let p be a positive integer such that sigma>2p-1, and let mu>0. Use the Fourier transform hhat(xi)=int exp(-i X.xi)h(X)dX with inverse factor (2pi)^-2. Define

    L0=lambda x partial_x+y partial_y-1+a R1^2,
    [h]_alpha=sup_(X!=Y)|h(X)-h(Y)|/|X-Y|^alpha,
    H(h)=sup_(t>0)t^((sigma-alpha)/2)||exp(t Delta)Lambda^sigma h||_infinity.

Since sigma>2p-1>=1, one has sigma>alpha. On the real Fourier-annular Schwartz core, completed in these equivalent norms, take the generator realization of L0 from part P53. One may restrict throughout to even-x, odd-y functions; parity fixes the additive constant. The existing theorem gives

    H(L0^-1 f)<=(1-alpha)^-1 H(f).

This is a theorem for the complete coupled frozen operator, without the normalized rank term or the variable reference coefficients. Define the radial multiplier m_sigma(r)=r^sigma exp(-r^2) and

    I_p(mu)=int_0^infinity r |(1-mu Delta_rad)^p m_sigma(r)|^2 dr,
    A_p(mu)^2=mu^(-alpha-1) Gamma(alpha+1) Gamma(2p-alpha-1)
                 *I_p(mu)/(2 Gamma(2p)),
    b=sigma-alpha,
    C_b=((b+1)^(b+1)/(pi b^b))^(1/2),
    B_opt=4(C_b/2)^alpha/[Gamma(sigma/2) alpha(1-alpha)].

Then

    H(h)<=A_p(mu)[h]_alpha,
    [h]_alpha<=B_opt H(h),
    [L0^-1 f]_alpha<=A_p(mu)B_opt(1-alpha)^-1[f]_alpha.  (1)

Every positive mu supplies a valid bound. Selecting the smallest bound among finitely many rational choices needs no optimization theorem. No claim of the sharp ordinary-seminorm inverse constant is made. The previously proved sharp heat-norm inverse constant remains unchanged.

#### Forward kernel estimate with a free spatial scale

Let k_sigma be the inverse Fourier transform of m_sigma. Its weak derivatives in frequency through order 2p are square-integrable when sigma>2p-1. Indeed the worst local power is r^(sigma-2p), whose squared radial integral converges exactly under this strict inequality; derivatives at infinity have Gaussian decay. Thus (1+mu|X|^2)^p k_sigma is in L2. Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    int |X|^alpha |k_sigma(X)|dX
       <=[int |X|^(2alpha)(1+mu|X|^2)^(-2p)dX]^(1/2)
                        ||(1+mu|X|^2)^p k_sigma||_2.

The first squared factor is, by v=mu r^2 and the beta integral,

    pi mu^(-alpha-1) Gamma(alpha+1)Gamma(2p-alpha-1)/Gamma(2p).

The parameter 2p-alpha-1 is positive because p>=1 andalpha<1. Plancherel makes the second squared factor I_p(mu)/(2pi), proving the stated A_p(mu). The same estimates without |X|^alpha imply k_sigma in L1. Its integral is m_sigma(0)=0. Cancellation and scaling therefore imply

    |exp(t Delta)Lambda^sigma h(X)|
       <=[h]_alpha t^((alpha-sigma)/2)int |Y|^alpha|k_sigma(Y)|dY,

which proves the first inequality in (1).

#### Reverse heat integral with an optimized split

On the annular core, Fourier integration gives

    h=Gamma(sigma/2)^-1 int_0^infinity t^(sigma/2-1)
                                      exp(t Delta)Lambda^sigma h dt.

For d=|X-Y| and a free tau>0, split the difference of this integral at t=tau^2 d^2. The small-time part is at most

    H(h)d^alpha Gamma(sigma/2)^-1 (4/alpha)tau^alpha.

For any unit vector v, the heat kernel has derivative L1 norm 1/sqrt(pi t). Splitting a time t into t/(b+1) andbt/(b+1), using the semigroup property, gives

    ||partial_v exp(t Delta)Lambda^sigma h||_infinity
                      <=C_b H(h)t^(-(b+1)/2).

The large-time part of the difference is at most

    H(h)d^alpha Gamma(sigma/2)^-1 [2C_b/(1-alpha)]tau^(alpha-1).

Both integrals converge since 0<alpha<1. Differentiating the positive sum in tau shows its unique minimum at tau=C_b/2: the derivative is

    4 tau^(alpha-1)-2C_b tau^(alpha-2).

At this value the sum is 4(C_b/2)^alpha/[alpha(1-alpha)]. This proves the second inequality in (1), and then the inverse estimate follows by composition with the existing heat inverse. All estimates extend to the little completion by density. Surjectivity and injectivity are those of the already specified semigroup domain, not consequences inferred just from (1).

#### Exact evaluation of the radial integral

For a Laurent polynomial Q(r)=sum_j q_j r^(2j), write a radial function as r^sigma exp(-r^2)Q(r). The radial Laplacian replaces each coefficient q_j by contributions

    j-1: (sigma+2j)^2 q_j,
    j:   -4(sigma+2j+1)q_j,
    j+1: 4q_j.

Starting with q_0=1 and applying 1-mu Delta_rad exactlyp times produces coefficients q_j(sigma,mu) supported on-p<=j<=p. Then

    I_p(mu)=sum_(j,k) q_j q_k
                  Gamma(sigma+j+k+1)/(2*2^(sigma+j+k+1)).       (2)

All gamma arguments are positive under the stated hypothesis. This is a finite exact formula; no radial quadrature is used. One implementation checks the recurrence by symbolic differentiation and evaluates(2) with directed Arb arithmetic. A second implementation will use direct symbolic radial derivatives to form the polynomial and independent directed interval special-function arithmetic, checking the source hashes and every final sufficient integer. Both retain the tested mu values; choosing a good mu is not represented as proving a global minimum.

#### Scope

The improvement concerns ordinary C^alpha bounds for the principal frozen operator only. It gives no center derivative trace, no normalized rank-column estimate and no full variable-coefficient inverse. The actual accepted state's a andlambda are recovered from the original checkpoint, not fitted. Failure of residual smallness and the separately proved distance obstructions remain unchanged.

## P56. A positive weighted residual minimum over each finite fitting family

### P56.1. A positive weighted residual minimum from nonlinear properness

Status: complete analytical argument written before the elementary verification. Independent  This is a qualitative positive-minimum theorem. It gives no certified numerical lower bound and does not yet exclude the sufficient threshold 2^-30 or 2^-35 uniformly over the family.

#### 1. The abstract finite-dimensional theorem

Let V be a nonzero finite-dimensional real linear subspace of L2(R2), with the norm ||v||_V=||v||_L2. Its canonical velocity and bilinear transport distribution are

    U[v]=(-R1 R2 v,R1^2 v),
    B(v,z)=div(z U[v]),   Q(v)=B(v,v).                 (1)

The Fourier multiplier of R1^2 is -xi_1^2/|xi|^2. The velocity is divergence-free andbelongs toL2. Since z U[v] belongs toL1, B(v,z) is a well-defined distribution. For smooth functions it equals U[v].Dz. Let Y be a real Banach space continuously andinjectively embedded in distributions. Suppose B(v,z) belongs toY for everyv,z inV. Let f inY and A:V->Y be linear. Define

    F(v)=f+A v+Q(v),
    nu=min_(||v||_V=1)||Q(v)||_Y,
    C_A=max_(||v||_V=1)||A v||_Y,   M=||f||_Y.          (2)

Then nu>0 and C_A is finite. Moreover

    ||F(v)||_Y>=nu||v||_V^2-C_A||v||_V-M.              (3)

Thus F:V->Y is proper: the preimage of each compact set in Y is compact in V. The real function v->||F(v)||_Y attains its global minimum. If F(v) is never zero, this minimum is strictly positive.

For precision, if F has no zero, define

    B=1+[C_A+sqrt(C_A^2+8nu M)]/(2nu),
    delta_Y=min_(||v||_V<=B)||F(v)||_Y.                 (4)

Then delta_Y>0 and ||F(v)||_Y>=delta_Y for all v in V. These are exact variational definitions of constants, not numerical certificates. If V is the zero space, the same conclusion is simply delta_Y=||f||_Y>0 when f is nonzero.

#### 2. Why the quadratic term has no nonzero zero

The canonical velocity is divergence-free and bounded on L2. Suppose Q(v)=0 as a distribution. Choose a smooth radial cutoff chi, with 0<=chi<=1, chi=1 on r<=1 andchi=0 on r>=2. Let chi_L(X)=chi(X/L). The compact test y chi_L is legitimate, and integration by parts gives

    0=int Q(v)y chi_L
       =-int v U_2[v]chi_L-int v y U[v].Dchi_L.        (5)

Since v andU[v] are in L2, their product is integrable. The first term tends to-int v U_2[v] by dominated convergence. On L<=r<=2L, one has |y Dchi_L|<=2||Dchi||_infinity. Its absolute value is at most 2||Dchi||_infinity ||v||_(L2(r>=L))||U[v]||_(L2(r>=L)), and therefore tends to 0. No pointwise decay or finite first moment is required. Equation(5) is the distributional definition of Q, so no derivative of v is being assumed. Therefore

    0=-int v R1^2 v=||R1 v||_2^2.                     (6)

Plancherel identifies the last expression with (2pi)^-2 int (xi_1^2/|xi|^2)|vhat(xi)|^2 dxi. Thus vhat vanishes almost everywhere off the line xi_1=0. That line has Lebesgue measure zero; an L2 Fourier function supported there is zero. Hence v=0. No assertion about a point-supported Fourier distribution is needed or permitted here.

This proof uses the canonical velocity and square integrability. A nondecaying shear depending only on y has zero self-advection but is not an L2 counterexample to this statement. An added harmonic velocity is also outside the hypotheses.

#### 3. Compactness and attainment

Choose a basis v_1,...,v_d for the density space V. By the hypotheses, A v_i andall B(v_i,v_j) belong to Y. Therefore A is continuous andQ is a continuous quadratic map into Y: its expansion has only finitely many fixed vectors in Y. The L2 unit sphere of V is compact. By section 2, Q does not vanish on this sphere. The Y norm is continuous and vanishes only at the zero distribution. Its minimum nu on the sphere is consequently positive. The same compactness gives finite C_A.

Writing v=r z with ||z||_V=1 andusing Q(rz)=r^2Q(z), the reverse triangle inequality proves (3). Since the right side tends to infinity withr, a sequence whose image under F is bounded must itself be bounded in V. Continuity then makes the preimage of a compact set closed and bounded in V, hence compact. To prove attainment of the residual norm, take a minimizing sequence. Its norms are bounded by (3), so it has a convergent subsequence in V; continuity gives a minimizer.

At v=0 the residual norm is M. Whenever r>B, equation(3) is strictly greater than M by the definition ofB. Thus every minimizer belongs to the closed radiusB ball, proving(4). If F has no zero, a zero minimum on that compact ball would give an actual zero by attainment, which is impossible. This establishes strict positivity without invoking a closed-image property in an infinite-dimensional space.

#### 4. The exact six-branch IPM family

Take

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248,
    gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma.

For a fixed finite integerK>=59, consider real potentials

    chi=sum_(0<=j<=5,0<=m<=59,m<=k<=K) a_(j,m,k)
              r^(2k)(1+r^2)^((3+gamma-j delta)/2-k)cos(2m theta).

Impose the six exact leading angular moment constraints from part P27:

    sum_(m,k)a_(j,m,k)cos(2m theta)=C_(j+1)(theta), j=0,...,5,

where C_1,...,C_6 are the stationary homogeneous potential coefficients uniquely determined from original state 131. Their complete exact rational data are in certificate file state131_splice.json. Also impose the two first-descendant constraints of part P27, forj=0,1. Assume this affine family is nonempty. It is nonempty atK=75 because the separately reconstructed exact references belong to it.

Set rho=-partial_y Delta chi andu=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy). Choose any one referencebar_rho in the affine density family. Let V_K be the vector space of all density differencesrho-bar_rho arising from coefficient differences satisfying the homogeneous versions of the constraints. This is the image in functions, not the coefficient parameter space: any redundant potential representation is quotiented out automatically. Distinct points of V_K are distinct L2 densities. Since the coefficient support is finite, V_K is finite-dimensional andclosed in its L2 norm.

For each potential difference all six leading angular moments vanish. The expansion(1+r^-2)^a=1+O(r^-2), together with its differentiated expansions, gives

    D^d(chi-bar_chi)=O(r^(1+gamma-d)),
    v=rho-bar_rho=O(r^(gamma-2)),
    U[v]=O(r^(gamma-2)),   Dv=O(r^(gamma-3)).            (7)

These estimates hold with all further differentiated symbol bounds. Smoothness at the origin follows from k>=m andthe polynomial r^(2m)cos(2m theta)=Re(x+iy)^(2m). Since epsilon=1-gamma>0, bothv andU[v] are square-integrable. The additional descendant constraints only improve decay in some branches; they are not needed for the nonzero-quadratic argument.

The potential expression for U[v] is indeed the canonical velocity. It is divergence-free, it satisfies the Poisson relation -Delta(chi_xy difference)=partial_x v, andboth v andU[v] are inL2 by (7). Fourier transformation away from zero gives precisely the multipliers in section 1. Any remaining distribution supported atzero would be a polynomial field andcannot belong to L2. Hence no harmonic ambiguity enters(6).

#### 5. Membership in the specified weighted forcing space

Fix any R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12. Put J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), omega_1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10) andomega_2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5). Let Y=Y_(s,R) be the real even-x, odd-y completion of compact smooth functions in

    ||g||_Y^2=||omega_2 D2 J^s g||_2^2
               +2^22||omega_1 D J^s g||_2^2
               +2^53||w_R J^s g||_(Hdot^-1)^2.        (8)

Use the same canonical homogeneous negative realization as in parts P17, P19, P21 and P47. This space has an injective realization in distributions, fixed by parity, as proved there.

Here is a direct sufficient membership criterion. If a smooth functiong of the required parity satisfies |D^a g(X)|<=C_a(1+r)^(p-|a|) for every multi-indexa and somep<1/5, then g belongs toY. Indeed the parity Hardy inequality gives

    ||w_R h||_(Hdot^-1)<=||r w_R h||_2.

For h=g-Delta g, all three components of the unfractional energyE_R(h) are integrable. At infinity their worst radial powers after the weight are p-6/5: for omega_1 Dg, omega_2 D2g, andr w_R g alike. Their squares with planar radial measure are integrable precisely whenp<1/5. Terms with further derivatives decay more strongly. At the origin all functions are smooth andthe weights are bounded.

The positive Bessel-kernel estimate of part P29, section 4, gives

    E_R(J^(-tau)h)<=821 E_R(h), 0<tau<=2, R>=1.

Its proof uses weight-ratio bounds by (1+|z|)^4, radial kernel momentbound<152 andthe parity divergence decomposition; those estimates hold for everyR>=1. Set tau=2-s to obtain ||g||_Y<=821 E_R(g-Delta g). For smooth radial cutoffs g_n supported onr<=2n andequal tog onr<=n, the same derivative andHardy estimates give E_R((g-g_n)-Delta(g-g_n))->0. The derivative terms of the cutoff have the matching powers n^-k on their annuli. Hence ||g-g_n||_Y->0, so this is membership in the specified completion andnot merely formal finiteness of (8).

The reference has bar_rho,bar_u=O(r^gamma) with full symbol bounds. Its stationary six leading moments andtwo descendants cancel all residual powers above p_star=gamma-6delta<-2, as proved in part P27. Thus f=F(bar_rho) belongs to the above membership class. Let

    A v=(cX+bar_u).Dv-v+U[v].Dbar_rho,
    Q(v)=U[v].Dv.

By (7), A v has symbol order at mostgamma-2<1/5; the two mixed products have order 2gamma-3<gamma-2. Every bilinear termU[v].Dz has order 2gamma-5<1/5. All have the required parity. The criterion proves every membership assumption of the abstract theorem. It also applies to finite linear combinations, so there is no hidden continuity or derivative-loss assertion outside the finite-dimensional family.

#### 6. Why the residual has no zero in this family

The exact residual expansion has powers

    gamma-h delta-2q, 0<=h<=11, q=0,1,2,... .

The coefficient atp_star=gamma-6delta is the fixed nonzero sine polynomial e(theta) of part P27. It is determined solely by the six fixed leading moments; exact original-source arithmetic gives its full-circle L2 norm greater than 3081.27. Its nonzero status alone is used here.

No other radial descendant can alter this coefficient. Equality of powers requires(6-h)delta=2q. With q>0 one must haveh<6. Since 0<delta<1/2, this forcesq=1, andthe exact rationaldelta is not 2/(6-h) for anyh=0,...,5. With q=0 one hash=6. The q=0 contribution at that index contains only products of the prescribed leading branches because there is no seventh potential branch. This proves invariance for every finiteK, independently of coefficient sizes andof the lower radial moments.

The radial factors are analytic inr^-2 near infinity. Their generalized power expansions are differentiable there andhave the stated nonresonance atp_star. An identically zero residual would have every coefficient zero, includinge, which is impossible. Thus F(bar_rho+v) never vanishes forv inV_K. This argument does not infer exact nonexistence from a finite grid or from a small but nonzero computed residual.

#### 7. The resulting positive minimum and its limits

Apply sections 1-3 with V=V_K, Y=Y_(s,R), andthe exact f,A,Q above. For every fixed finiteK for which the family is nonempty, every fixedR>=1 andevery fixed 0<s<=2^-12, there is a strictly positive number

    delta_(K,s,R)=min_(v inV_K)||F(bar_rho+v)||_(Y_(s,R))>0.       (9)

It is attained. Its value is independent of the choice ofbar_rho used to parametrize the same affine family. Additional closed affine normalization or center-jet constraints produce a subfamily andcannot lower this positive bound. The exponentc is fixed throughout. The statement does not require orassert that the normalized residual maps an open neighborhood in the full function space intoY; part P50 shows why that broader assertion would fail.

Equation(9) is a qualitative uniform statement over all real coefficients of this fixed family. It does not supply a numerical value ofdelta_(K,s,R), andthe present proof does not show that it exceeds either sufficient residual threshold. No lower bound uniform inK, s orR is asserted. No claim is made for freely changing leading moments, adding a branch, or an infinite-dimensional correction space.

The linear relaxation in part P29 can contain arbitrarily different finite-power coefficient vectors with tiny weighted norm andthe same invariant. Those vectors have not been realized as nonlinear IPM residuals. The nonzero self-advection lemma andthe properness argument are exactly the additional nonlinear facts used here. The two results are therefore compatible. Establishing a certified quantitative bound large enough to exclude the sufficient threshold over the entire family remains OPEN.

#### 8. Why no infinite-dimensional quadratic floor follows

The finite-dimensional assumption is essential even within smooth compactly supported parity functions. Fix a nonzero real smooth even-x, odd-y functionv supported in 1<r<2, normalized by ||v||_2=1. Define

    v_L(X)=L^-1 v(X/L),  L>=max(1,R).

Then ||v_L||_2=1 andthe degree-zero Riesz multipliers give

    U[v_L](X)=L^-1 U[v](X/L),
    Q(v_L)(X)=L^-3 Q(v)(X/L).

The functionq=Q(v) is smooth andsupported in the same annulus because Dv vanishes outside it. It is nonzero by section 2. If q_L=L^-3 q(X/L), then ||D^k q_L||_2=L^(-2-k)||D^k q||_2. On its support, omega_1<=L^(-1/5), omega_2<=17^(2/5)L^(4/5), andw_R<=R^(11/5)L^(-11/5). Consequently

    ||omega_1 Dq_L||_2<=C L^(-16/5),
    ||omega_2 D2q_L||_2<=C L^(-16/5),
    ||r w_R q_L||_2<=C_R L^(-16/5).

The corresponding terms forDelta q_L gain a further factorL^-2. Parity Hardy andthe Bessel estimate from section 5 therefore imply

    ||Q(v_L)||_(Y_(s,R))<=C_R' L^(-16/5) ->0.

HereC_R' is finite anddepends on the fixed testv andR; the same bound holds uniformly for 0<s<=2^-12. Thus no positive inequality ||Q(v)||_Y>=nu||v||_2^2 can hold over this whole infinite-dimensional class. EveryindividualQ(v_L) is nonzero, andthere is no contradiction with the compact unit-sphere argument on a fixed finite-dimensionalV. This example is not a family of small full IPM residuals anddoes not change the absence of a certified quantitative value in (9).

## P57. A constructive positive floor, uniform in the smoothness index and the weight radius

### P57.1. Constructive constants for the finite-family weighted obstruction

Status: analytical proof written before the elementary audit.  No Gram spectrum or family-wide numerical remainder constant has been evaluated. The theorem below gives an explicit finite-constant certificate and a positive lower bound uniform in the weight parameters. It does not certify that the minimum exceeds either sufficient residual threshold.

#### 1. Statement and spaces

Fix a finite radial degree K for which the affine six-branch family of part P56 is nonempty. Its exponent is

    c = 4076476460239181/2251799813685248,
    gamma = 1/c,  delta = 1-gamma,
    p = gamma-6 delta,  beta = 2-4 delta.

The potentials have branches j=0,...,5, angular modes cos(2m theta) with 0<=m<=59, and radial generators

    r^(2k) (1+r^2)^((3+gamma-j delta)/2-k),  m<=k<=K.

Their six leading potential moments are the exact stationary C_1,...,C_6 determined from original checkpoint 131. The first descendants of branches j=0,1 are zero, as in part P27. All coefficients are real. Densities and canonical velocities are

    rho = -partial_y Delta chi,
    U[rho] = (-chi_xyy,chi_xxy) = (-R1 R2 rho,R1^2 rho),
    F_c(rho) = (c X+U[rho]).D rho-rho.

Let bar_rho be any member and let V be the finite-dimensional space of density differences. Remove any redundant coefficient directions before choosing a basis v_1,...,v_d of V. The case d=0 is treated in section 8. Define

    f = F_c(bar_rho),
    A v = (c X+U[bar_rho]).D v-v+U[v].D bar_rho,
    B(v,z) = U[v].D z,  Q(v)=B(v,v).

Thus F_c(bar_rho+v)=f+A v+Q(v). Fix any R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12. With J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), set

    w_R = (1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    omega_1 = (1+r^2)^(-1/10),  omega_2 = (1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    N_(s,R)(g)^2 = ||omega_2 D2 J^s g||_2^2
                    +2^22 ||omega_1 D J^s g||_2^2
                    +2^53 ||w_R J^s g||_(Hdot^-1)^2.

The forcing space is the real even-x, odd-y completion of compact smooth functions in this norm, in the canonical distributional realization of parts P17 and P19. Every residual and mixed term above belongs to this space, by part P56 and the stronger tails proved below.

For this fixed K there exists delta_K>0 such that

    N_(s,R)(F_c(rho)) >= delta_K

for every rho in the entire affine family, every R>=1 and every 0<s<=2^-12. Sections 2-7 give a formula for such a delta_K in terms of finitely many Gram matrices, integrals and symbol bounds. These quantities depend on K and the chosen basis. No positive bound uniform in K is asserted. The exponent and six leading moments are fixed throughout.

#### 2. A uniform norm majorant

For a smooth parity function g define h=g-Delta g and

    Mcal(g)^2 = ||omega_2 D2 h||_2^2
                 +2^22 ||omega_1 D h||_2^2
                 +2^53 ||r h||_2^2.                         (1)

If Mcal(g) is finite and g has the symbol bounds used here, then

    N_(s,R)(g) <= 821 Mcal(g)                                (2)

uniformly in R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12. Indeed parity Hardy gives

    ||w_R h||_(Hdot^-1) <= ||r w_R h||_2 <= ||r h||_2.

The Bessel-kernel estimate of part P29 gives E_R(J^(-tau)h)<=821 E_R(h) for 0<tau<=2, uniformly in R>=1. Take tau=2-s. Smooth radial cutoffs converge in (1), by the derivative and tail estimates, so this proves membership in the completion as well as (2).

In this particular family, the two descendant constraints improve each tangent density to

    D^a v(X) = O(r^(p-beta-|a|)),  r>=2.                     (3)

To check (3), the leading moments cancel in every branch. In branches 0 and 1 the first descendants also cancel. The largest remaining density power is therefore gamma-2 delta-2=p-beta, from the first descendant of branch 2. The second descendant of branch 0 has smaller power gamma-4, and all later branches and descendants are smaller. The same bounds hold for the canonical velocity. Directly from the exact rational exponent,

    p < -2,  0 < beta < delta,  p-beta < -2.

The reference residual has leading power p, with the fixed nonzero angular sine polynomial e of part P27. All later residual powers are at most p-beta. Consequently f has symbol order p, A v_i has symbol order p-beta, and B(v_i,v_j) has symbol order at most 2(p-beta)-1. All these orders are strictly below -2. Thus every Mcal value needed in (2) is finite. This stronger integrability is the reason a uniform result in R is available here.

#### 3. A finite Gram certificate for the quadratic term

Define the real symmetric matrices

    G_ij = int v_i v_j,
    H_ij = int U[v_i].U[v_j],
    (G_L)_ij = int_(r>=L) v_i v_j,
    (H_L)_ij = int_(r>=L) U[v_i].U[v_j],  L>=1.

The canonical multipliers give

    H_ij = int (R1 v_i)(R1 v_j) = -int v_i R1^2 v_j.         (4)

Both G and H are positive definite. For H, if the quadratic form vanishes, R1 v=0 for a vector v in V; the L2 Fourier function vhat would be supported on xi_1=0 and hence zero. Also H<=G. Suppose the following finite matrix inequalities have been certified:

    G >= g I,  H >= mu G,
    G_L <= tau_v G,  H_L <= tau_u G,
    g>0,  mu>0,  tau_v>=0,  tau_u>=0,
    kappa := mu-(19/4)sqrt(tau_v tau_u) > 0.                 (5)

Such numbers exist: G,H are positive definite, and both tail matrices tend to zero entrywise and in matrix norm as L tends to infinity. In particular one can always use tau_u=1, since H_L<=H<=G, and then make tau_v sufficiently small. The inequalities are in the Loewner sense, not entrywise.

Let chi(t)=1 for 0<=t<=1, chi(t)=P(t-1) for 1<=t<=2, and chi(t)=0 for t>=2, where

    P(z)=1-10z^3+15z^4-6z^5.

This cutoff is C2, lies in [0,1], and satisfies |chi'|<=15/8. It can be approximated in C1 by compact smooth cutoffs, so it is legitimate in the weak divergence identity even for L2 densities. Test Q(v) against phi_L(X)=y chi(r/L). As in part P56,

    int Q(v) phi_L = -int v U_2[v] chi(r/L)
                     -int v y U[v].D(chi(r/L)).             (6)

The full first term without its cutoff equals ||R1 v||_2^2. Its omitted part has absolute value at most ||v||_(r>=L)||U[v]||_(r>=L). On the annulus of the cutoff derivative, |y D(chi(r/L))|<=15/4. Equations(4)-(5) therefore imply

    int Q(v) phi_L >= kappa ||v||_2^2.                      (7)

Part P48 proves the amplitude bound 1000 w_R |g|<=N_(s,R)(g). Because w_R>=w_1 for R>=1, this yields

    |int g phi_L| <= N_(s,R)(g) D_L,
    D_L := (33/7000) L^3 (1+4L^2)^(11/10).                  (8)

For completeness, the angular integral of |sin theta| is 4, and

    int_0^2 t^2 chi(t) dt = 33/28.

Bounding w_1^-1 by (1+4L^2)^(11/10) on the support gives (8) exactly. Combining(7)-(8) proves the parameter-uniform quadratic estimate

    N_(s,R)(Q(v)) >= nu ||v||_2^2,
    nu := kappa/D_L > 0.                                  (9)

No compactness minimum of a nonlinear map appears in this formula.

#### 4. A uniform bound on every small-residual coefficient vector

Choose certified finite numbers m_0,m_1,...,m_d satisfying

    Mcal(f)<=m_0,  Mcal(A v_i)<=m_i.

Define

    M=821 m_0,
    C=821 sqrt(sum_i m_i^2/g),
    B_*=[C+sqrt(C^2+4nu(M+1))]/(2nu).                       (10)

For v=sum_i a_i v_i, (5) gives |a|<=||v||_2/sqrt(g). Cauchy-Schwarz and (2) give N_(s,R)(A v)<=C||v||_2 and N_(s,R)(f)<=M. Equation(9) and the reverse triangle inequality now show

    N_(s,R)(F_c(bar_rho+v))
       >=nu||v||_2^2-C||v||_2-M.

Hence every residual with norm at most 1, for any of the allowed R,s, satisfies ||v||_2<=B_*. This is a uniform coefficient bound; it does not assume any smallness of the reference or of the affine coefficient vector.

#### 5. Finite tail data

Let E_0=||e||_(L2(S1))>0 and E_1=||partial_theta e||_(L2(S1)), with full-circle measure. Fix r_*>=2. Suppose constants d_0,d_i,d_ij>=0 have been certified for r>=r_*:

    |f(r,theta)-r^p e(theta)| <= d_0 r^(p-beta),
    |A v_i(r,theta)| <= d_i r^(p-beta),
    |B(v_i,v_j)(r,theta)| <= d_ij r^(p-beta).                (11)

They exist by section 2. Set

    C_0=d_0,
    C_1=sqrt(sum_i d_i^2/g),
    C_2=sqrt(sum_(i,j) d_ij^2)/g,
    C_*=C_0+C_1 B_*+C_2 B_*^2.                             (12)

Cauchy-Schwarz in the coefficient vector and in its tensor square gives, for every ||v||_2<=B_*,

    |F_c(bar_rho+v)(r,theta)-r^p e(theta)|
       <=C_* r^(p-beta),  r>=r_*.                          (13)

The constants in (11) need not be sharp. These are ordinary absolute bounds on specified functions. They do not require interval optimization over all coefficients.

There is a direct way to obtain finite bounds from the exact generator list. After differentiating, each field is a finite sum of angular trigonometric polynomials times r^a(1+r^-2)^b. Group terms with the same exponent modulo even integers and impose the exact known cancellations. For t=r^-2<=1/4, the elementary binomial estimate

    sum_(n>=d) |binom(b,n)| t^n
       <= (|b|)_d t^d/d! * (1-t)^(-|b|-d), d>=0,           (14)

bounds every remaining radial tail; (|b|)_d is the rising factorial, with its usual value 1 at d=0. To prove(14), use |b(b-1)...(b-n+1)|<=(|b|)_n and (d+k)!>=d!k!, then sum the positive binomial series. Multiplying the absolute angular coefficient sums gives explicit constants in (11). Terms with extra decay can be bounded at r_*. Integrals in (1) and the Gram entries likewise have a compact part and explicit integrable tails. This describes finite certificate tasks; no numerical result for those tasks is asserted here.

#### 6. A uniform annular lower bound

Choose any T>=r_* such that

    C_* sqrt(2pi) T^(-beta) <= 2^(p+1) E_0/2.               (15)

Since beta>0, such a finite T exists. A dyadic T can be chosen by exact comparisons. Let b(t)=(t-1)^2(2-t)^2 for 1<=t<=2, zero elsewhere, and put zeta_T(X)=b(r/T)e(theta). This compact C1 test belongs to H1 and is supported away from the origin.

For a residual satisfying the norm bound at most 1, equation(13) and the facts b>=0, p<-2 give

    int F_c(bar_rho+v) zeta_T
       >= T^(p+2) [E_0^2 int_1^2 t^(p+1)b(t)dt
              -C_* T^(-beta) ||e||_1 int_1^2 t^(p-beta+1)b(t)dt]
       >= T^(p+2) 2^(p+1) E_0^2/60 =: P_T > 0.             (16)

Indeed int b=1/30, t^(p+1)>=2^(p+1), t^(p-beta+1)<=1, and ||e||_1<=sqrt(2pi)E_0; (15) then leaves at least half the first term.

Part P47 gives, for every allowed R,s,

    ||w_R g||_(Hdot^-1) <= ell N_(s,R)(g),
    ell=(11/10)2^(-53/2).

Its uniform Bessel factor 1.1 is valid even at R=1 and s=2^-12. Pair with zeta_T/w_R to obtain

    |int g zeta_T| <= ell N_(s,R)(g) ||D(zeta_T/w_R)||_2.   (17)

On the annulus, w_R^-1<=(1+4T^2)^(11/10) and

    |D log(w_R^-1)| = (11/5)r/(R^2+r^2) <=11/(5T).

Polar differentiation and the three radial bounds

    int_1^2 t b'(t)^2 dt=1/35,
    int_1^2 b(t)^2/t dt<=1/630,
    int_1^2 t b(t)^2 dt=1/420

give

    ||D(zeta_T/w_R)||_2 <= D_T,
    D_T=(1+4T^2)^(11/10)
          [sqrt(E_0^2/35+E_1^2/630)+(11/5)E_0/sqrt(420)].  (18)

Every factor is independent of R,s. Combining(16)-(18), a residual of norm at most 1 must have norm at least P_T/(ell D_T).

#### 7. The certificate and its scope

Define

    delta_K = min(1, P_T/(ell D_T)),                        (19)

where (5), (10)-(12), (15), (16) and (18) specify all constants. It is strictly positive. If a residual has norm greater than 1, it is at least delta_K. If it has norm at most 1, sections 4-6 give the same conclusion. This proves the theorem simultaneously for every R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12.

The finite numerical tasks required to evaluate(19) are explicit: a basis with certified Gram inequalities(5), upper bounds for the finitely many majorants in (10), tail constants (11), and a scalar comparison (15). The exact moment constraints, exponents and nonzero polynomial e are already certified in parts P27, P52 and P56. The remaining tasks have not been completed for the whole K=75 family. In particular, neither delta_K>2^-30 nor delta_K>2^-35 is claimed. The known point and annular certificates for specific references remain much stronger evaluated statements than this unevaluated formula.

The proof does not accommodate arbitrary leading angular perturbations, a variable exponent, or extra branches. Closed affine center or normalization constraints only restrict the family and preserve the lower bound. There is no contradiction with the linear residual relaxation in part P29: (9) and the coefficient bound (10) use the actual nonlinear self-advection map.

#### 8. Degenerate tangent space

If V={0}, there is one density and no matrices are needed. Set B_*=0 and C_*=d_0 from a certified tail bound for its residual. Equations(15)-(19) give the same uniform positive lower bound. The invariant e is still nonzero. This covers every nonempty fixed finite affine family, including a singleton.

## P58. Off-axis violations of three derivative bounds by the refit Mpen2

### P58.1. Three global derivative tests for the exact Mpen2 reference

The method below is proved before evaluating the chosen points. The numerical claims remain OPEN until both directed differentiation and the independent rational audit pass. Read RESULTS.md for the completed status.

#### Statement, exact reference and scope

Let chi be the smooth real potential reconstructed from nb_Mpen2_exact.json in the numerical work. The source SHA256 is 07bb884b96121b22ca099c3b9d3451d19a65d6af684422b595b305e48d918e05 and the canonical serialization SHA256 is 0083c8377b84714b3ae29d2122eef35d66648a57c204410614d04c1309b7fed6. Part P20 reconstructs its coefficients exactly from the numerical file and part P52 checks that reconstruction independently. The exponent is c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c and delta=1-gamma. The canonical potential is a finite sum

    chi(r,theta)=sum a_(j,m,k) r^(2k) (1+r^2)^((3+gamma-j delta)/2-k) cos(2m theta),

with rational coefficients, j in {0,...,5} and nonnegative integers k>=m. It is smooth at the origin because r^(2m)cos(2m theta)=Re(x+iy)^(2m), and its noninteger radial powers have a positive argument. Define

    rho=-chi_xxy-chi_yyy,       U=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy).

For a scalar g, the Frobenius norm of its ordered derivative tensor is

    |D^n g|_F^2=sum_(i=0)^n binom(n,i) (partial_x^i partial_y^(n-i) g)^2.

For a vector field the squared norms of its two components are added. Three of the global reference hypotheses W3 of the conditional weighted theorem are

    sqrt(1+r^2)|D^3 U|_F <=16,
    (1+r^2)|D^3 rho|_F <=32,
    (1+r^2)|D^4 rho|_F <=512.                         (1)

Each inequality is required at every point of the full plane. To refute one, it suffices to exhibit one rational point with a strictly larger value. The counterexamples are to these sufficient reference hypotheses for this named potential. They do not contradict the earlier selected-point tests, and they do not imply nonexistence of an exact IPM profile.

#### Exact derivative identities

Write chi_(a,b)=partial_x^a partial_y^b chi(X). Since the potential is smooth, its mixed derivatives commute. For i=0,...,3,

    u_(1,i)=-chi_(i+1,5-i),
    u_(2,i)= chi_(i+2,4-i),
    d_(3,i)=-chi_(i+2,4-i)-chi_(i,6-i).

These are the components of D^3 U and D^3 rho. For i=0,...,4,

    d_(4,i)=-chi_(i+2,5-i)-chi_(i,7-i).

Consequently the three squared quantities in (1) are exactly

    S_U=(1+x^2+y^2) sum_(i=0)^3 binom(3,i)(u_(1,i)^2+u_(2,i)^2),
    S_3=(1+x^2+y^2)^2 sum_(i=0)^3 binom(3,i)d_(3,i)^2,
    S_4=(1+x^2+y^2)^2 sum_(i=0)^4 binom(4,i)d_(4,i)^2.     (2)

All weights and multiplicities in (2) are rational at a rational point. No angular quadrature or tensor normalization is implicit.

#### Verification method and dependencies

Compute all sixth derivatives chi_(i,6-i), i=0,...,6, and all needed seventh derivatives chi_(i,7-i), i=0,...,6, by two different recurrences. The first evaluates the finite seventh Cartesian Taylor jet of each potential summand. Its coefficients are multiplied by factorials to give derivatives. Only that finite jet is needed for the point derivatives, so no Taylor remainder is involved. The second uses the exact polar chain rule, collects radial polynomials in r^2/(1+r^2), and evaluates its angular factors recursively from x/r and y/r. These implementations are described fully in parts P12, P14, P28 and P54. At nonzero rational points both enclose their nonalgebraic powers with 768-bit directed Arb arithmetic.

The primary record must contain all raw sixth and seventh derivative intervals for both methods, their overlap checks, the three squared quantities and their square roots. An independent audit then parses the displayed intervals as exact rational endpoints and rederives(2) with rational interval operations. The audit checks source, reconstruction, proof, implementation and evidence hashes. For a displayed strict rational lower bound b, it proves S>b^2 separately from both sets of raw derivative intervals. Each claimed failure additionally requires the rational lower endpoint of S to exceed the corresponding number 16^2, 32^2 or 512^2.

Agreement of approximate values by itself is not a certificate. The floating scan in the numerical work only suggests where to test. A final CONFIRMED value or REFUTED inequality is recorded only after the directed calculations and the rational endpoint audit have both passed. This proof uses no claim that any other global reference inequality holds.

## P59. Sharp Riesz coercivity on a finite angular band

### P59.1. Sharp Riesz energy on a finite S1 angular band

Status: analytical proof complete before the arithmetic audit. Numerical rational comparisons are OPEN until their verification records pass. This result supplies a constant for the finite-family argument; it does not evaluate a whole-family residual floor.

#### 1. Space and theorem

Let N be a positive integer. Define V_N as the closed real subspace of L2(R2) with polar representation

    v(r,theta)=sum_(j=0)^(N-1) v_j(r) sin((2j+1)theta),
    v_j in L2((0,infinity),r dr).

Every such density is even in x and odd in y. Use the unitary Fourier transform and the canonical multipliers R_i=partial_i(-Delta)^(-1/2) and U[v]=(-R1R2 v,R1^2 v). Then

    ||U[v]||_2^2=||R1 v||_2^2 >= mu_N ||v||_2^2,
    mu_N=sin^2(pi/(4N+2)).                              (1)

The constant mu_N is optimal on V_N, even if the test functions are required to be real Schwartz functions with Fourier support in a compact annulus. Also ||U[v]||_2<=||v||_2.

For a potential with finitely many angular factors cos(2m theta), 0<=m<=M, the density -partial_y Delta chi has only sine modes of odd order at most 2M+1. Thus every L2 density difference in that potential family belongs to V_(M+1), independently of its radial functions or radial degree. In particular the six-branch family with M=59 belongs to V_60. The seven-branch family with M=69 belongs to V_70.

#### 2. Angular matrix and its exact spectrum

Fourier transformation preserves each fixed angular harmonic subspace. For smooth functions this follows by changing variables under rotations in the Fourier integral, or by the elementary angular Fourier expansion of exp(-i r q cos(theta-phi)); the claim for L2 follows by density and unitarity. The transform multiplies each mode by a constant phase, which does not change its span. Real even-x, odd-y densities have imaginary odd Fourier transforms, and these have the same sine angular band.

At a fixed Fourier radius write a(theta)=sum_j a_j sin((2j+1)theta), allowing complex coefficients. The sine functions are mutually orthogonal with squared norm pi. The multiplier of the squared Riesz norm is cos^2(theta). The identity

    cos^2(theta)=(1+cos(2theta))/2

and the product-to-sum formula show that

    pi^(-1) int cos^2(theta)|a(theta)|^2 dtheta = a* C_N a,

where C_N has diagonal (1/4,1/2,...,1/2), adjacent off-diagonal entries 1/4 and every other entry zero. The exceptional first diagonal is essential: sin(theta)cos(2theta)=(sin(3theta)-sin(theta))/2. Put T_N=4C_N.

For k=1,...,N, let theta_k=2k pi/(2N+1) and define

    z_j=sin((j+1/2)theta_k), j=0,...,N-1.

Extend this sequence by z_-1=-z_0 and z_N=0. The latter identity is sin(k pi)=0. The tridiagonal recurrence then gives, including its first and last rows,

    T_N z=(2+2cos(theta_k))z.

These N eigenvalues are distinct, and each vector is nonzero. They exhaust the spectrum of the real symmetric matrix. Its smallest eigenvalue is at k=N and equals 4sin^2(pi/(4N+2)). Dividing by 4 proves the angular inequality. Integrating in Fourier radius proves the lower bound in (1).

Pointwise in Fourier space, the squared vector multiplier of U is

    (xi_1 xi_2)^2/|xi|^4 + xi_1^4/|xi|^4 = xi_1^2/|xi|^2.

Plancherel proves the equality and the upper bound in (1). Sharpness follows by taking the minimizing angular eigenvector, multiplying it by i times any nonzero real smooth radial function supported in 1<|xi|<2, and using that as vhat. It satisfies vhat(-xi)=conjugate(vhat(xi)) and the S1 parity, so its inverse transform is a real admissible Schwartz density. The angular quotient equals mu_N at every Fourier radius.

The potential-to-density band assertion follows from the polar Laplacian, which preserves cos(2m theta), followed by partial_y=sin(theta)partial_r+cos(theta)partial_theta/r, which produces only sin((2m+1)theta) and sin((2m-1)theta). The two spatial derivatives in Delta do not create angular modes of order 2m+2.

#### 3. Consequence for the weak quadratic transport test

For any real v in V_N, Q(v)=div(v U[v]) is a distribution because both factors are in L2. Let chi be the C2 quintic cutoff of part P57, equal to 1 on [0,1], zero on [2,infinity), and satisfying |chi'|<=15/8. With phi_L(X)=y chi(r/L), distributional integration by parts gives

    <Q(v),phi_L>=-int v U_2[v] chi(r/L)
                    -int v y U[v].D(chi(r/L)).

The full first integral with chi replaced by 1 is ||R1 v||_2^2. The omitted part has absolute value at most ||v||_(r>=L)||U[v]||_(r>=L). The second term is bounded by (15/4) times the same product. Therefore

    <Q(v),phi_L> >= mu_N||v||_2^2
                   -(19/4)||v||_(r>=L)||U[v]||_(r>=L).    (2)

This is valid by C1 approximation of the compact test. If a subspace V of V_N has a uniform density tail estimate

    ||v||_(r>=L)^2 <= tau ||v||_2^2, v in V,

then the last factor in (2) is at most sqrt(tau)||v||_2^2, since ||U[v]||_2<=||v||_2. Thus the lower constant is mu_N-(19/4)sqrt(tau). The tail condition, unlike the angular constant, depends on the radial space.

For the six-branch M=59 class, the scalar comparison mu_60>1/6000 is to be checked independently. If also tau<=1/57000^2, then

    <Q(v),phi_L> >=(1/12000)||v||_2^2.                   (3)

For the weighted forcing norms of part P57, every R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12, its already proved dual bound is

    |<g,phi_L>| <= D_L N_(s,R)(g),
    D_L=(33/7000)L^3(1+4L^2)^(11/10).

Consequently, whenever Q(v) belongs to that forcing space,

    N_(s,R)(Q(v)) >= 7||v||_2^2/[396 L^3(1+4L^2)^(11/10)]. (4)

This removes the separate velocity Gram matrix inequality H>=mu G from part P57. The remaining requirements are a density Gram lower bound, a density tail matrix bound G_L<=G/57000^2, and the norm and remainder majorants in that part. No such whole-family density tail radius L or numerical residual floor is evaluated here.

For M=69 the analogous scalar comparison is mu_70>1/8100. A density tail fraction at most 1/76950^2 then gives the weak quadratic constant 1/16200. The finite seven-branch residual problem requires its own treatment of the earlier free descendant sector; the present angular estimate does not by itself supply that treatment.

#### 4. Verification contract

The primary audit checks the tridiagonal characteristic polynomials for small N by two exact constructions, the eigenvector residual for N=60 and 70 with directed arithmetic, the two rational lower bounds, the multiplier identity and the cutoff scalar arithmetic. A separate rational audit bounds pi from the Machin identity using alternating arctangent series, uses sin(x)>=x-x^3/6 for 0<x<1, and rechecks both lower bounds and the cutoff constants. Exact candidate records are inspected only to confirm their angular limits. No radial quadrature, spectral grid or floating matrix eigensolver is used.

Verified 2026-10-28T10:49:10.528659+00:00, independent check 154.

For the real L2 S1 angular band spanned by sin(theta),sin(3theta),...,sin((2N-1)theta), the exact sharp inequality is ||U[v]||_2^2=||R1 v||_2^2 >= sin^2(pi/(4N+2)) ||v||_2^2. ## P60. A positive weighted floor for the seven-branch family

### P60.1. A uniform positive weighted residual floor for seven stationary branches

Status: analytical proof written before numerical scalar verification.  The family-wide Gram and tail constants are not evaluated; no comparison with a sufficient existence threshold is claimed.

#### 1. Family, norm and statement

Fix c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c and delta=1-gamma. For an integer K>=69, consider the nonempty affine family of real potentials

    chi = sum_(j=0)^6 sum_(m=0)^69 sum_(k=m)^K
              a_(j,m,k) r^(2k)(1+r^2)^((3+gamma-j delta)/2-k) cos(2m theta).

Fix its seven leading homogeneous potentials to the stationary orders C_1,...,C_7 reconstructed from the original state 131 in part P32. Set the first descendants of branches 0 and 1 to zero. The first descendant of branch 2 may vary freely. Any additional closed affine center or normalization constraints are permitted. Define the canonical density, velocity and residual by

    rho=-partial_y Delta chi,
    U[rho]=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy)=(-R1R2 rho,R1^2 rho),
    F_c(rho)=(cX+U[rho]).D rho-rho.

For R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12 let N_(s,R) be the forcing norm and its compact smooth parity completion defined in part P57:

    N_(s,R)(g)^2=||omega_2 D2 J^s g||_2^2
                 +2^22 ||omega_1 D J^s g||_2^2
                 +2^53 ||w_R J^s g||_(Hdot^-1)^2,
    omega_2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), omega_1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10),
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2).

There is a number d_K>0, independent of R and s, such that

    N_(s,R)(F_c(rho)) >= d_K                              (1)

for every member of this affine family. Sections 3-6 give a finite-constant formula. This is a positive lower bound for each fixed radial cap K, not a positive bound uniform in K. It concerns the fixed exponent and fixed seven stationary leading moments. It does not extend to freely varying leading angular data.

#### 2. The two leading residual powers

Put

    q=gamma-2delta-2= -1-3delta,
    p=gamma-7delta=1-8delta,
    beta=2-4delta.

The exact rational exponent gives

    q>p, q<-2, p<-2, 0<beta<delta,
    p-beta=gamma-3delta-2,
    gamma-4 < p-beta.

Part P32 proves that the residual coefficient at radial power p is the same nonzero full-circle sine polynomial e=E_7 for every member. Its norm E_0=||e||_L2(S1) lies between 9679.9655 and 9679.9656. Define E_1=||partial_theta e||_L2(S1).

For every member there is a sine polynomial a_rho(theta) such that, with symbol bounds under every fixed number of derivatives,

    F_c(rho)(r,theta)=r^q a_rho(theta)+r^p e(theta)
                         +O(r^(p-beta)).                 (2)

Here a_rho is the possibly nonzero residual sector(2,1). This is why a nonnegative test against the fixed sector alone is insufficient without a further argument.

To check (2), each finite generator has a convergent binomial expansion in r^-2 for r>1. The density and residual powers are gamma-h delta-2n, with 0<=h<=13 in the residual and integer n>=0. The seven stationary moments remove(h,0), h=0,...,6. The two descendant constraints remove(0,1),(1,1). Among the remaining powers, (2,1) is q and (7,0) is p. The next possible power is (3,1)=p-beta: (8,0)=p-delta is smaller, and every n>=2 power is at most gamma-4<p-beta. There are no collisions between sectors: writing delta=A/B in lowest terms, B=4076476460239181>13, equality would force B to divide h-h'. Thus the fixed coefficient e cannot change when radial coefficients vary. This argument is independent of K.

#### 3. Uniform control of coefficient vectors with residual norm at most one

Choose a reference bar_rho and a density basis v_1,...,v_d for its finite-dimensional tangent space V, removing redundant potential directions. Put

    f=F_c(bar_rho),
    A v=(cX+U[bar_rho]).D v-v+U[v].D bar_rho,
    B(v,z)=U[v].D z, Q(v)=B(v,v).

Then F_c(bar_rho+v)=f+A v+Q(v). Because every leading moment is fixed and the first descendants of branches 0,1 are fixed, every v and U[v] has symbol order at most q<-2. The reference residual and A v_i have order at most q, and B(v_i,v_j) has order at most 2q-1. They all belong to every forcing completion in section 1. Their Mcal majorants from part P57 are finite, and the same proof gives

    N_(s,R)(g)<=821 Mcal(g)                              (3)

uniformly in R,s. The potential derivative velocity is canonical here because both it and the multiplier velocity are L2, solve the same Poisson relation, and have a harmonic L2 difference, necessarily zero.

Let G be the L2 density Gram matrix in the chosen basis. Select g>0 and L>=1 for which

    G>=g I,
    int_(r>=L) |v|^2 <= ||v||_2^2/76950^2 for every v in V. (4)

Such choices exist: G is positive definite and the density tail matrices tend to zero in the finite-dimensional matrix norm. Every tangent density has sine modes of odd order at most 139, so part P59 supplies mu_70>1/8100. Its cutoff argument gives

    N_(s,R)(Q(v))>=nu ||v||_2^2,
    nu=7000/[33*16200*L^3(1+4L^2)^(11/10)]>0.            (5)

This only requires the density tail matrix in (4), not a velocity Gram lower bound.

Choose finite m_0,m_i with Mcal(f)<=m_0 and Mcal(A v_i)<=m_i. Define

    M=821m_0, C=821 sqrt(sum_i m_i^2/g),
    B_*=[C+sqrt(C^2+4nu(M+1))]/(2nu).                    (6)

The reverse triangle inequality and (3)-(5) show that any residual with norm at most 1 has ||v||_2<=B_*. In particular its coefficient vector a obeys |a|<=B_*/sqrt(g). This is uniform in R,s.

#### 4. Finite tail constants

Let a_f(theta) and alpha_i(theta) be the coefficients at power q of f and A v_i. The power-p coefficient of f is e; those of A v_i and B(v_i,v_j) vanish, by the invariance of e under every real coefficient vector and the polynomial dependence on that vector. The quadratic terms have order 2q-1<p-beta, so they also have no q coefficient.

Choose r_*>=2 and finite nonnegative constants d_0,d_i,d_ij such that for r>=r_*, uniformly in theta,

    |f-r^q a_f-r^p e| <= d_0 r^(p-beta),
    |A v_i-r^q alpha_i| <= d_i r^(p-beta),
    |B(v_i,v_j)| <= d_ij r^(p-beta).                     (7)

They exist by the finite binomial expansions just proved. They can be certified by the elementary absolute binomial-tail bound in part P57, section 5, or any sharper rigorous bounds. Define

    C_*=d_0+sqrt(sum_i d_i^2/g) B_*
                  +sqrt(sum_(i,j) d_ij^2) B_*^2/g.      (8)

Cauchy-Schwarz gives, on the entire residual sublevel set of norm at most 1,

    |F_c(bar_rho+v)-r^q a_v(theta)-r^p e(theta)|
                   <=C_* r^(p-beta),                  (9)
    a_v=a_f+sum_i a_i alpha_i(theta),

where a_i are the real coordinates of v. No bound on this angular polynomial is required below.

#### 5. A compact radial test that annihilates the earlier free sector

Let b_0(t)=(t-1)^2(2-t)^2 on 1<=t<=2, zero elsewhere, and for real z put

    I(z)=int_1^2 t^z b_0(t)dt,
    c_*=I(q+2)/I(q+1),
    b(t)=b_0(t)(c_*-t),
    J_*=int_1^2 t^(p+1)b(t)dt.

Then 1<c_*<2 and

    int_1^2 t^(q+1)b(t)dt=0,
    J_*>0.                                               (10)

The first identity is exact. For strict positivity, M(z)=I(z+1)/I(z) is the mean of t under the positive probability density t^z b_0(t)/I(z). Differentiating on this compact interval gives

    M'(z)=Cov_z(t,log t)
          =(1/2) int int (t-u)(log t-log u) dP_z(t)dP_z(u)>0.

Strict inequality follows because the integrand is positive for t!=u and b_0 is positive on the interval interior. Since q>p,

    J_*=I(p+1)[M(q+1)-M(p+1)]>0.

There is also the explicit rational lower bound

    J_*>1/67200.                                         (10a)

To prove it, set d=q-p. The exact exponent comparisons give 0<d<1, d>1/5 and p+q+1>-4. A symmetrized product of moments gives

    J_* I(q+1)=(1/2) int int b_0(t)b_0(u)t^(p+1)u^(p+1)
                           (u-t)(u^d-t^d)dtdu.

For 1<=t,u<=2, the mean-value theorem gives (u-t)(u^d-t^d)>=d 2^(d-1)(u-t)^2. Also t^(p+1)u^(p+1)>=2^(2p+2), and I(q+1)<=I(0)=1/30. The exact moments I(1)=1/20 and I(2)=8/105 yield

    (1/2) int int b_0(t)b_0(u)(u-t)^2dtdu
               =I(0)I(2)-I(1)^2=1/25200.

Consequently J_*>=d 2^(p+q+1)/840>1/67200, as asserted.

Also |b|<=b_0 and b'=b_0'(c_*-t)-b_0, so

    int |b|dt<=1/30,
    (int t|b'|^2dt)^(1/2)<=1/sqrt(35)+1/sqrt(420),
    int b^2/t dt<=1/630,
    int t b^2dt<=1/420.                                  (11)

These follow from the b_0 integrals in part P57 and the triangle inequality; the possible sign change of b does not affect them.

Choose T>=r_* sufficiently large that

    C_* sqrt(2pi) T^-beta <=15 J_* E_0.                   (12)

The compact C1 test zeta_T(X)=b(r/T)e(theta) annihilates the entire q-sector in (9), independently of its angular polynomial:

    int r^q a_v(theta) zeta_T(X)dX
        =T^(q+2) [int a_v e dtheta][int t^(q+1)b(t)dt]=0.

Using p-beta+1<0, ||e||_1<=sqrt(2pi)E_0, (9), (11), and (12), one gets

    int F_c(bar_rho+v) zeta_T
       >=T^(p+2)[E_0^2 J_*-C_* T^-beta sqrt(2pi)E_0/30]
       >=T^(p+2)E_0^2 J_*/2=:P_T>0.                    (13)

Thus the earlier free sector cannot cancel this tested fixed coefficient, even if its amplitude is large.

#### 6. Dual norm and positive floor

The part P47 low-norm comparison holds uniformly for all allowed R,s:

    ||w_R g||_(Hdot^-1)<=ell N_(s,R)(g),
    ell=(11/10)2^(-53/2).

On the annulus T<=r<=2T one has w_R^-1<=(1+4T^2)^(11/10) and |D log w_R^-1|<=11/(5T). Using (11) as in part P57 gives

    ||D(zeta_T/w_R)||_2<=D_T,
    D_T=(1+4T^2)^(11/10)
       [sqrt(E_0^2(1/sqrt(35)+1/sqrt(420))^2+E_1^2/630)
                          +(11/5)E_0/sqrt(420)].         (14)

The radial/angular terms are orthogonal in the gradient and the angular L2 factors are E_0,E_1. The weight derivative term uses ||zeta_T||_2<=T E_0/sqrt(420). Negative-order duality now gives

    |int g zeta_T|<=ell N_(s,R)(g) D_T.

Combining with (13) proves (1), with

    d_K=min(1,P_T/(ell D_T))>0.                          (15)

If the residual norm is above 1 the bound is immediate; otherwise the uniform coefficient and tail estimates apply. If V={0}, omit the Gram calculation and take B_*=0, C_*=d_0; the same annular argument proves the result for the single density.

All constants in (4), (6), (7), (12)-(15) refer to finitely many integrals or symbol bounds. Their existence is proved, but the full family values are not evaluated here. In particular d_K>2^-30 and d_K>2^-35 remain OPEN. For a version involving no numerical evaluation of J_*, use (10a): choose T with C_* sqrt(2pi)T^-beta<=E_0/4480 and replace P_T by T^(p+2)E_0^2/134400. These rational constants and the exponent comparisons can be checked without performing any whole-family optimization.

#### 7. Dependencies and limits

Part P32 gives the exact original-source stationary coefficients and fixed nonzero E_7. Part P35 checks the seven-branch sector indexing and nonresonance for arbitrary finite K. parts P47, P48 and P57 give the uniform low dual estimate, pointwise amplitude estimate, norm majorant and cutoff constants. Part P59 supplies the angular coercivity independent of K. The proof above supplies the extra signed radial test needed when sector(2,1) is not constrained to vanish.

There is no claim about an infinite radial span, varying exponent, varying leading profile, or an eighth potential branch. Such changes require new arguments. This is an obstruction for the actual quadratic residual map on each fixed finite affine family, not for an independently relaxed linear residual span.

### P60.2. Verified seven-branch obstruction

Verified 2026-10-28T10:51:49.394952+00:00, independent check 155.

For each fixed nonempty finite seven-branch family of part P35, with exponent c and seven stationary leading moments fixed and descendants 0,1 zero, there is a strictly positive weighted residual floor uniform in all R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12. Descendant 2 remains free. The proof supplies a finite-constant formula; it does not evaluate that formula for the entire numerical family or compare it with 2^-30.

The residual has an earlier free sector r^q a(theta), q=gamma-2delta-2, followed by the fixed nonzero r^p E7(theta), p=gamma-7delta. A signed annular test b(t)=b0(t)(cstar-t), b0=(t-1)^2(2-t)^2, cstar=I(q+2)/I(q+1), I(z)=integral_1^2 t^z b0(t)dt, exactly annihilates the entire earlier sector.
