The canonical angular constant of part P59 bounds the small-residual coefficient set uniformly in R,s. Symbol bounds then control the next remainder at exponent p-(2-4delta), and negative-order duality gives the positive floor. All arguments retain the free earlier sector; exact cancellation of (2,1) is not required for this finite-family result.

The remaining whole-family numerical tasks are a density Gram lower bound, a density tail radius, finitely many norm majorants and uniform tail coefficients. No bound uniform in radial cap K, no infinite-family obstruction and no existence claim is made.

The numerical scalar contract in section P60.1 is satisfied. The directed calculation gives Jstar in the displayed interval around 0.00010641916338990461785715; only the independently proved rational lower bound 1/67200 is used in the simplified theorem.

## P61. Exact finite constraints do not repair the critical far-field space

### P61.1. Exact finite constraints do not repair the critical far-field space

Status: independent analytical derivation. The proof strengthens the endpoint result of part P6 and P7 by imposing every finite constraint exactly, including constraints not continuous in the endpoint norm. No statement is made about the strict subcritical space used by the conditional existence theorem.

#### 1. Precise statement

Fix 0<gamma<1, c=1/gamma, and a smooth real S1 background bar_rho with canonical divergence-free velocity bar_u. Assume for some finite C_0

    |bar_u(X)|<=C_0 <r>^gamma,
    |Dbar_rho(X)|<=C_0 <r>^(gamma-1).

The background has the parity even in x, odd in y. Define the real Hilbert space

    Z_gamma = completion of C_c^infinity densities with this parity,
    ||h||_Z = ||<r>^(-1-gamma) h||_L2(R2),
    <r>=(1+r^2)^(1/2).

Use the canonical velocity U[h]=(-R1R2 h,R1^2 h). On compact smooth parity densities put

    A h=(cX+bar_u).Dh-h+U[h].Dbar_rho,
    B h=A h-c[h]X.Dbar_rho,
    c[h]=partial_y U_2[h](0).

When c+c[bar_rho]=1, B is the full normalized linearization at the reference. The counterexample itself needs only the displayed growth assumptions.

Let C_0^flat be the real vector space of compact smooth parity densities supported away from the origin and having c[h]=0. Every h in this space has all center derivatives zero, B h=A h, and A h belongs to Z_gamma.

Let m>=0, and let ell_1,...,ell_m be arbitrary real linear functionals defined on C_0^flat. They need not be continuous in Z_gamma. Let K:Z_gamma->Z_gamma be any compact linear operator. Then there are h_n in C_0^flat satisfying

    ||h_n||_Z=1,
    ell_i(h_n)=0 for every i,
    h_n converges weakly to zero in Z_gamma,
    ||(B+K)h_n||_Z -> 0.                                (1)

Thus no positive lower bound holds for B+K on this exactly constrained core. No bounded inverse estimate can be repaired there by finitely many linear phase equations or a compact bounded perturbation. In particular bounded finite-rank perturbations do not remove this obstruction.

If a closed operator T on Z_gamma contains this constrained core in its domain and agrees with B+K there, then T is not Fredholm. This last assertion concerns a closed operator with its graph norm; it does not assume that the unrestricted normalized expression defines a bounded map on Z_gamma.

#### 2. The canonical weighted velocity bound

We use the following elementary parity estimate, and recall its proof to specify the realization:

    ||U[h]||_Z <= C_gamma ||h||_Z, 0<gamma<1.             (2)

Here C_gamma is some finite constant depending on gamma; no numerical value is needed in this counterexample. Decompose a centrally odd compact smooth h by radial cutoffs into a central ball and dyadic annuli of radii r_j>=1. The unweighted scalar-to-vector multiplier norm of U is at most 1. Therefore on nearby input and output annuli its block norm is uniformly bounded after weighting.

For separated annuli the nonlocal kernel has finite bounds |K_U(Z)|<=C|Z|^-2 and |DK_U(Z)|<=C|Z|^-3. The local identity part in U_2 is absent between disjoint annuli. Each radial source piece is odd and has integral zero. For an inner source r_j much smaller than the output radius r_i, subtract K_U(X) before integration. Cauchy-Schwarz and the kernel derivative bound give

    ||1_(A_i) U[h_j]||_2 <= C (r_j/r_i)^2 ||h_j||_2.

For an outer source r_j much larger than r_i, the integral of K_U(-Y)h_j(Y) vanishes because the kernel is even and the source is odd. Subtracting this term gives

    ||1_(A_i) U[h_j]||_2 <= C (r_i/r_j)^2 ||h_j||_2.

The central ball is treated as radius 1. Multiplication by the weight, comparable to r_i^(-1-gamma) on an annulus, changes the inner-source block bound to C(r_j/r_i)^(3+gamma) and the outer-source block bound to C(r_i/r_j)^(1-gamma). Both sequences are geometrically summable. Applying the elementary l2 convolution bound to this block matrix and using finite overlap proves (2). The same argument works for each output parity component. Density then defines the canonical bounded velocity on Z_gamma, with no harmonic addition.

For compact h, U[h] is smooth near the origin. At infinity its zero integral and the kernel subtraction give U[h]=O(r^-3). The background assumptions therefore imply A h in Z_gamma. This justifies the operator expressions on the stated core.

#### 3. One packet with zero strain exactly

Choose a nonzero real chi in C_c^infinity((0,1)). For L>=2 define

    f_L(r,theta)=L^(-1/2) r^gamma sin(5theta)
                           chi((log r-L)/L).

It is compactly supported in e^L<r<e^(2L), smooth on the plane and has the S1 parity. Its center derivatives vanish. The exact canonical strain formula for a compact density is

    c[h]=-h_y(0)/4+(1/pi)PV int sin(3theta)h/r^3 dX.

Angular orthogonality gives c[f_L]=0 exactly, since the only density harmonic is sin(5theta). Thus B f_L=A f_L; there is no unbounded exponent column to estimate.

Substituting t=log r and u=(t-L)/L gives

    ||f_L||_Z^2
      =pi int_0^1 (1+exp(-2L(1+u)))^(-1-gamma)chi(u)^2du
      ->pi||chi||_2^2>0.                                 (3)

The same calculation, with the radial and angular derivatives, gives a uniform bound on ||r Df_L||_Z. The pure dilation term is

    (c r partial_r-1)f_L
         =c L^(-3/2)r^gamma sin(5theta)chi'((log r-L)/L),

so its norm is O(L^-1). On the support, |bar_u|/r=O(exp(-(1-gamma)L)), proving

    ||bar_u.Df_L||_Z=O(exp(-(1-gamma)L)).                  (4)

For the remaining coupling put delta=1-gamma and T=exp(L/2). On r>=T, the background gradient bound and (2) give

    ||1_(r>=T) U[f_L].Dbar_rho||_Z
              <=C exp(-delta L/2)||f_L||_Z ->0.          (5)

On r<T the source and observation point are separated. The even-kernel cancellation used in section 2 gives

    |U[f_L](X)|
      <=C |X| L^(-1/2) int_(e^L)^infinity R^(gamma-2)dR
      <=(C/delta) r L^(-1/2)exp(-delta L).                (6)

The background gradient is globally bounded, and direct polar integration gives

    ||1_(r<T)<r>^(-1-gamma)r||_2<=C_gamma T^(1-gamma).

Thus the inner coupling norm is O(L^-1/2 exp(-delta L/2)), also tending to zero. Equations(3)-(6) prove

    ||A f_L||_Z ->0,
    inf_(L sufficiently large) ||f_L||_Z>0.              (7)

All implicit constants are finite and independent of L. They depend only on gamma,C_0 and the fixed chi. This is enough to construct the sequence below; no asymptotic equality is used as a numerical bound.

#### 4. Enforcing every finite constraint exactly

For each integer n>=2, take m+1 normalized packets

    g_(n,j)=f_(3^j n)/||f_(3^j n)||_Z, j=0,...,m.

Their supports are pairwise disjoint, because each lies between e^(3^j n) and e^(2*3^j n), while the next support starts after e^(3*3^j n). They are therefore orthonormal in the real weighted L2 inner product. They all belong to C_0^flat, their supports lie outside r=e^n, and

    max_(0<=j<=m) ||A g_(n,j)||_Z ->0.                   (8)

Form the real m by (m+1) matrix M_n with entries ell_i(g_(n,j)). Its nullspace has a nonzero vector regardless of the rank or the sizes of its entries. Choose a real vector a_n in that nullspace with Euclidean norm 1, and set

    h_n=sum_(j=0)^m a_(n,j)g_(n,j).

Orthonormality gives ||h_n||_Z=1. Linearity gives all ell_i(h_n)=0 exactly; c[h_n]=0 and every center derivative also vanish exactly. The triangle and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities imply

    ||A h_n||_Z<=sqrt(m+1) max_j ||A g_(n,j)||_Z ->0.

For any fixed z in Z_gamma, its norm outside r=e^n tends to zero. Since h_n is supported there and normalized, its inner product with z tends to zero. Hence h_n converges weakly to zero. Compactness of K implies ||K h_n||_Z->0: otherwise a subsequence of its images would have a nonzero strong limit, while bounded linearity sends weak convergence to weak convergence and forces that limit to be zero. This proves (1).

The construction does not infer exact constraints from merely small functional values. The linear algebra imposes them exactly at each n, and their continuity is unnecessary. Functions of the form h_n also have zero leading far-field coefficient individually, since each is compactly supported. Thus adding finitely many ordinary asymptotic phase conditions to the core does not remove these tests.

#### 5. Closed-operator consequence

Suppose T is closed, includes the constructed sequence in its domain and agrees with B+K on it. Give D(T) the Hilbert graph norm

    ||h||_D^2=||h||_Z^2+||Th||_Z^2.

Then ||h_n||_D->1, and h_n converges weakly to zero in D(T): for any z in D(T), both <h_n,z>_Z and <Th_n,Tz>_Z tend to zero. If T were Fredholm, its kernel would be finite dimensional and its range closed. Let P be the graph-orthogonal projection onto ker T. Finite dimensionality and weak convergence imply ||P h_n||_D->0. Closed range and the bounded inverse theorem on the graph-orthogonal complement give

    ||h-P h||_D<=C||Th||_Z for all h in D(T).

For h=h_n, the right side tends to zero while the left side tends to 1, a contradiction. Thus T is not Fredholm.

This conclusion is limited to realizations containing the specified compact constrained core. A different radiation domain that removes such annular packets requires its own analysis and is not ruled out by this statement.

#### 6. Application and scope

The exact original S1 states satisfy c=1/gamma and 0<gamma<1. Their finite regularized-power potentials give the sublinear background and derivative bounds in section 1. The same applies to the finite tail repairs and admissible refits with this leading exponent. Therefore the theorem applies to their critical weighted L2 realization Z_gamma, including the full normalized expression on c[h]=0.

It does not contradict the successful conditional inverse on N_(s,R), whose high derivative weight enforces a strictly smaller growth exponent. It does not assert that the full normalized expression maps an open Z_gamma set into Z_gamma; only its values on the zero-strain core are used. No actual profile is proved or excluded in a neighborhood of the numerical state by this endpoint result alone.

Dependencies: the canonical strain formula in part P2; the endpoint packet and parity block argument in section P6.6; elementary weighted L2 duality, finite-dimensional nullspaces and closed-operator graph norms. The original-source exponent check and exact packet linear-algebra tests are in verification. No floating spectral evidence is used.

## P62. An evaluated weighted floor from the finite power representation

### P62.1. Explicit weighted residual floors from the finite power representation

Status: analytical derivation written before numerical evaluation. This gives a completely evaluated formula for a lower bound, independent of coefficient size. It does not claim that the bound exceeds the sufficient existence threshold.

#### 1. Exact family, norm and statement

Set c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c and delta=1-gamma. Let J be6 or 7, K>=10J-1 an integer, and epsilon either 0 or 1. Consider the real potentials

    chi=sum_(0<=j<J, 0<=m<=10J-1, m<=k<=K)
        a_(j,m,k) r^(2k)(1+r^2)^((3+gamma-j delta)/2-k)cos(2m theta).

Set rho=-partial_y Delta chi, U=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy) and F=(cX+U).D rho-rho, with the canonical S1 full-plane realization. Fix the J leading potential branches to the exact stationary homogeneous branches determined from the original state 131. Require the first descendants of branches 0 and 1 to vanish. If epsilon=1, require the first descendant of branch 2 to vanish as well. These are exact linear conditions on the potential coefficients. The center normalization may also be imposed, but is not used in this theorem. Coefficients are unrestricted in magnitude.

The exact source of the six stationary branches is part P10.2; part P32 independently constructs the seventh. Let

    e_J(theta)=sum_(m odd, m>0) e_(J,m) sin(m theta)

be the fixed residual coefficient at radial degree 1-(J+1)delta. For J=6 it is the six-branch invariant from parts P25 and P27; for J=7 it is order 8_fixed_defect in part P32. Both vectors are nonzero. Put E_J=||e_J||_L2(0,2pi), so E_J^2=pi sum_m e_(J,m)^2.

For R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12 use the actual weighted norm

    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), omega0=<r>^(-6/5),
    omega1=<r>^(-1/5), omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    L_R(h)=||w_R h||_(Hdot^-1), Pj(h)=||omegaj D^j h||_2,
    E_R(h)^2=P2(h)^2+2^22 P1(h)^2+2^53 L_R(h)^2,
    N_(s,R)(h)=E_R(J_b^s h), J_b=(1-Delta)^(1/2).

Here J counts the potential branches; J_b denotes the Bessel operator. All scalar spaces are the real even-x, odd-y compact smooth completions. Cartesian derivative tensors use their ordered Euclidean norm.

Let M=2K+4 and a_star=(J+1)delta/2-2. Form the following finite set of indexed exponents:

    A={ell delta/2+k-2 : 1<=ell<=2J, 0<=k<=M},

with the indices (ell,0),1<=ell<=J, and (1,1),(2,1) removed. If epsilon=1 also remove(3,1). All retained exponents are distinct and greater than -1/2; a_star is retained. Define

    D_(J,K,epsilon)
      =(2a_star+16/5)^(-1/2)
         product_(a in A, a!=a_star)
                  |a-a_star|/(a+a_star+16/5).                (1)

Then every residual in the stated family satisfies, uniformly in R,s,

    N_(s,R)(F) >= [2048/(1+6s)] E_J D_(J,K,epsilon)/sqrt(2)
                > 2045 E_J D_(J,K,epsilon)/sqrt(2) >0.       (2)

The strict second inequality uses nonzero E_J and D. For each fixed J and epsilon, the last expression strictly decreases as K increases. Every quantity in (1)-(2) is obtained from exact source coefficients and a finite product. No Gram matrix, coefficient norm bound or nonlinear compactness constant remains to be estimated. The result is a sufficient lower bound; its value below 2^-30 is inconclusive about the actual infimum.

#### 2. From the actual fractional norm to a weighted density norm

First prove the universal inequality

    P0(h) <= (1+6s)N_(s,R)(h)/2048.                         (3)

For a compact smooth parity function H set a=omega0^2/w_R. Since R>=1,

    a <= omega1, |Da| <=5 omega0.

Indeed a=(1+r^2)^(-6/5)(1+r^2/R^2)^(11/10)<=omega1. Logarithmic differentiation bounds |Da| by (23/5)a/<r><5omega0. Homogeneous negative-order duality applied to w_R H and aH gives

    P0(H)^2 <= L_R(H)[P1(H)+5P0(H)].

The dual test is compact smooth and has the required parity. Twice using Young's inequality gives

    P0(H)^2 <= P1(H)^2+26L_R(H)^2 <=2^-22 E_R(H)^2,       (4)

because 26*2^22<2^53. Density extends(4) to E_R.

Let b_s be the positive radial kernel of J_b^-s, of total mass1. Its heat-mixture formula is

    b_s(X)=Gamma(s/2)^(-1) int_0^infinity
                  exp(-t)(4pi t)^(-1)exp(-r^2/(4t))t^(s/2-1)dt.

It gives integral r^2 b_s=2s and integral r b_s<=2s for 0<s<=1/16. For the latter, put q=s/2. The exact first moment is sqrt(pi)Gamma(q+1/2)/Gamma(q). Jensen's inequality for the square root under a gamma probability law gives

    Gamma(q+3/2)/Gamma(q+1)<=sqrt(q+1),

so the first moment is at most sqrt(pi)s sqrt(1+s/2)/(1+s)<2s. Squaring the positive last comparison, pi<22/7 and s<=1/16 suffice.

The elementary triangle inequality for <X> gives

    omega0(X)/omega0(Y) <=(1+|X-Y|)^(6/5)
                         <=(1+|X-Y|)^2.

Minkowski and Young therefore give

    P0(J_b^-s H) <=[int(1+r)^2b_s]P0(H)
                  <=(1+6s)P0(H).

Use H=J_b^s h and (4). The canonical Bessel realization on the compact parity completion makes J_b^-s J_b^s h=h distributionally; no polynomial representative is inserted. This proves (3). Finally

    2048/(1+6*2^-12)>2045

is the exact integer inequality 2048*4096-2045*4102=18>0.

#### 3. Exact radial representation and measure factors

Put u=(1+r^2)^(-1), t=1-u. The finite generator differentiation in parts P27 and P35 gives every angular coefficient of F the exact form

    F_m(r)=sqrt(t)u^(-1/2)H_m(u),
    H_m(u)=sum_(ell=1)^(2J)u^(ell delta/2)P_(ell,m)(t),
    deg P_(ell,m)<=2K+3.

For clarity, the degree bound comes from three and four Cartesian derivatives of a generator, whose compactified integer degrees after removal of the common radial factors are at most K+1 and K+2. Their product has degree at most 2K+3. Smoothness of each generator at the origin removes the apparent negative integer powers before distinct fractional branches are combined. The linear terms have no larger degree. Quadratic multiplication adds the branch indices, explaining the range 1,...,2J.

Set v_m=t u^-2 H_m. It belongs to span{u^a:a in A}; multiplication by t increases the degree by at most 1. The exact stationary leading conditions and descendant conditions remove exactly the indices listed in section 1. The conversion from the expansion at infinity to u is triangular within each fractional exponent class. Its u^a_star coefficient is e_(J,m), because no potential branch j=J is present and no different fractional branch can contribute to that exponent. For J=7 and epsilon=0, the earlier free descendant (3,1) remains in A. The argument below does not discard it or require its coefficient to be small.

The reduced denominator of delta is 4076476460239181, and differences of ell are at most 13. Therefore there is no collision between distinct indexed exponents for any finite K. Checking the smallest remaining exponents directly gives a>-1/2. The identities above, together with smoothness at the origin, also show that every F belongs to N_(s,R): its first possible radial degree is strictly below -2 and its differentiated decay has the corresponding symbol bounds. Cutoffs converge in the weighted norm. This is the finite-ladder membership argument of part P13.

Angular orthogonality and r dr=-du/(2u^2) give the exact identity

    P0(F)^2=(pi/2)sum_m int_0^1 u^(11/5)|v_m(u)|^2/(1-u)du
            >=(pi/2)sum_m ||u^(11/10)v_m||_L2(0,1)^2.     (5)

The factor 1/(1-u) is at least 1. Dropping it is a one-sided lower bound; no origin approximation or cancellation across angular modes is made.

#### 4. Shifted monomial distance

For any distinct real b_i>-1/2 and a distinguished b_star, the Gram matrix of u^b_i in L2(0,1) has entries 1/(b_i+b_j+1). Its Cauchy determinant and the Schur complement, or the rational Mellin-transform calculation in part P27, give

    dist(u^b_star, span{u^b_i:i!=star})
       =(2b_star+1)^(-1/2)
                  product_(i!=star)|b_i-b_star|/(b_i+b_star+1).

This formula does not require b_star to be the smallest exponent. One direct derivation is to let q be the orthogonal residual of u^b_star. Its Mellin transform has simple poles at -b_i-1, zeros at b_i for i!=star, and residue 1 at -b_star-1. Those conditions determine the rational function, whose value at b_star equals ||q||_2^2. This yields the displayed product with a positive square root.

Apply it to b_i=a_i+11/10. The denominators become a_i+a_star+16/5 and the distinguished norm factor becomes 2a_star+16/5. Since the coefficient of u^(a_star+11/10) in u^(11/10)v_m is e_(J,m),

    ||u^(11/10)v_m||_2 >= |e_(J,m)|D_(J,K,epsilon).

Combining this inequality with (5), E_J^2=pi sum_m e_(J,m)^2, and (3) proves (2).

Increasing K adds exponents greater than a_star. Every added product factor lies strictly between 0 and 1, because its denominator minus numerator is 2a_star+16/5>0. The source vector E_J is fixed. This proves strict monotonicity for fixed J,epsilon.

#### 5. Scope and numerical audit

This is a theorem for the actual weighted fractional norm, uniform in all R>=1 and 0<s<=2^-12, on the displayed fixed finite families. It is a lower bound over a linear enlargement of their nonlinear residual sets. It can consequently be much smaller than the true nonlinear minimum from parts P56 to P60. A tiny value does not exhibit a reference attaining it, prove feasibility or weaken any independently certified point or annular obstruction for a particular reference.

The argument fixes the exponent and full leading angular function. It supplies no result for an infinite union over K, additional potential branches or freely changing leading data. The original source coefficients and each finite product will be evaluated twice, once with gamma-product balls and once with individual factors, before any decimal threshold is called certified. Dependencies are the source reconstruction and stationary invariants in parts P10.2, P25, P27 and P32, the exact finite radial representation in 26/35, and the explicit universal norm argument in section 2 above. No reference matrix positivity or W3 condition is used.

#### 1. Exact statement

Write \(\langle r\rangle=(1+r^2)^{1/2}\), let \(R=2^{31}\), and set

#### 2. Previously proved analytic inputs and their scope

The weighted low proof in part P24 and the derivative hierarchy in part P6 and P7 give consistent smooth-reference generators on \(L\) and \(E\), decaying at rates at least \(1/5\) and \(1/20\). #### 3. Construction in a common lower topology

Choose compact smooth \(k_m\to k\) in \(N\). Then \(DU[k_m]\to DU[k]\) uniformly. Parity gives \(U[k_m](0)=0\), hence

\[
 |U[k_m](X)-U[k_n](X)|\le d_{mn}|X|,

\]

For each smooth approximant the transported compact core, followed by the bounded smooth-reference coupling, constructs an \(E\) generator. Conjugation by \(J^s\) uses the proved bounded commutator. Its \(N\) semigroup has the energy bound

\[
 \|S_m(t)\|_{N\to N}\le
 \exp\left[-t\left(\frac1{20}-2^{13}s-\frac{400N(k_m)}{\sqrt{s}}\right)\right].
\]

The finite-time bounds are uniform in sufficiently large \(m\).

Use \(P_0=\|\omega_0h\|_2\) as the common topology. The Lipschitz field \(cX+\bar u+U[k]\) has at most linear growth, so its characteristics exist in both time directions. The divergence and the logarithmic derivative of the weight bound its transport group on \(P_0\) for finite times. The coupling \(Qh=U[h]\cdot D\bar\rho\) is bounded there, since \(|D\bar\rho|\le16\) and the centrally odd weighted velocity bound is \(8/3\). Therefore the transport-plus-coupling equation has a unique strongly continuous \(P_0\) evolution by its convergent finite-time Duhamel series.

For high solutions with common initial data the difference forcing obeys

\[
 P_0\big((U[k_m]-U[k_n])\cdot Dh_n\big)
 \le d_{mn}P_1(h_n)\le2d_{mn}N(h_n).
\]

The \(P_0\) variation formula and Gronwall's inequality make the approximating solutions Cauchy in \(C([0,T];P_0)\). Weak compactness in the Hilbert space \(N\) identifies their weak high limits with this unique lower limit. Lower semicontinuity passes the energy bound to it. At time zero, weak convergence to the initial datum and the limiting upper norm bound imply strong \(N\) convergence. Uniqueness in \(P_0\) proves the semigroup law. This constructs a strongly continuous high semigroup with the same rate.

#### 4. The maximal domain and both inverse directions

For a Lipschitz field of at most linear growth, the \(P_0\) transport domain is its maximal distributional domain. To check the assertion, suppose \(h\) and \(b\cdot Dh\) belong to \(P_0\). Multiply by radial cutoffs at radius \(T\). The commutator \((b\cdot D\chi_T)h\) tends to zero in \(P_0\): its coefficient is bounded uniformly and its support escapes to infinity. On each fixed compact set, mollification converges in the graph norm by the Friedrichs commutator identity. The identity follows by subtracting \(b(X)-b(Y)\) in the differentiated convolution; the Lipschitz bound gives a uniform local \(L^2\) operator bound, and convergence follows first for smooth functions, then by density. Adding bounded \(Q-1\) preserves this domain description.

Passing the characteristic integral identity along these approximants proves

\[
 S(t)h-h=\int_0^tS(v)A_kh\,dv
\]

in \(P_0\). If \(h,A_kh\in N\), the same integral is a high-space Bochner integral and agrees under the continuous embedding. Its high difference quotient tends to \(A_kh\). Thus every maximal distributional high-domain element is in the high generator domain. The reverse inclusion follows by testing strong high difference quotients against compact smooth functions. This proves the equality of domains, rather than assuming it from an energy inequality.

Let \(\beta=1/20-2^{13}s-400N(k)/\sqrt{s}>0\). The integral

\[
 h=-\int_0^\infty S(t)f\,dt
\]

converges in \(N\). On finite intervals the generator identity gives \(A_k(-\int_0^TS(t)f\,dt)=f-S(T)f\). Closedness and the exponential bound give \(A_kh=f\). This proves surjectivity. A kernel element has a constant orbit, which the strict decay forces to vanish. This proves injectivity and the bound \(1/\beta\).

#### 5. Why the low inverse applies to nonlinear differences

The native low transport estimate has rate \(1/5-12\|DU[k]\|_\infty\). The low and \(P_0\) evolutions agree on their intersection. A simultaneous dense core is obtained using inner and outer radial cutoffs and then mollification. The cutoff operators are uniformly bounded on the parity-restricted negative space: test the multiplier against \(\dot H^1\), bound its derivative by \(C/r\), and use the angular Hardy inequality. Density gives strong convergence. Compactly supported \(P_0\) functions are locally \(L^2\), so mollification works in both norms. For smooth velocities the two constructions have the same characteristics and coupling series. Uniform convergence of velocity gradients gives local \(C^1\) convergence of their flows, preserving this agreement in the limit. No unrelated extension on negative-order distributions is selected.

Since \(N\) embeds in both lower spaces, the convergent low and high inverse integrals agree on common forcing data when their rates are positive. A further domain check is needed. If \(h\in N\) and \(A_kh\in L\cap P_0\), the maximal \(P_0\) identity of section 4 holds. Consistency makes its right side a low-space Bochner integral. Dividing by time proves that \(h\) belongs to the actual low generator domain with value \(A_kh\). Thus the low inverse estimate is available for such \(h\).

For the difference equation in the iteration, the extra source is \(U[k_1-k_2]\cdot Dh\). Its \(P_0\) norm is bounded by \(\|DU[k_1-k_2]\|_\infty P_1(h)\), since the velocity vanishes at zero. Its low norm is bounded by the bilinear inequality in section 2. That inequality is obtained by dual multiplication: one derivative falls on the test function and is controlled by \(\|Dh\|_\infty\); the other falls on \(Dh\) and is controlled by \(D^2h\in L^{2/(1-s/2)}\) with weight and the complementary \(\dot H^1\to L^{4/s}\) estimate on dyadic annuli. It does not treat quadratic transport as an ordinary \(C^\alpha\) forcing.

#### 6. Normalization, range, and the fixed point

The continuous first derivatives of \(h\) and \(U[h]\), parity, and the reference normalization give the first-order expansion

\[
 (A_kh)_y(0)=c[k]h_y(0)+a_0c[h].
\]

No continuous second derivative of \(h\) is needed: the transport field vanishes at the origin, so its linear term multiplies \(Dh(0)+o(1)\). Also \(F_y(0)=a_0(c+c[\bar\rho]-1)=0\). If \(c[k]=0\), the inverse therefore takes \(N_0\) exactly to \(D(A_k)\cap\ker c\).

To identify the maximal normalized domain, rescale on a compact annulus by \(T^{-\gamma}\). Every high function is \(O(T^{1/5})\), so its rescaling tends uniformly to zero. The dilation term of \(A_kh\) tends to zero distributionally. For the background transport term, integrate by parts to put the derivative on the test function; the remaining factor is \(h_T\bar u(TX)/T\), which tends to zero. For the coupling use \(\bar\rho_TU[h](TX)/T\), which also tends to zero. The same argument handles the rough transport. On the other hand

\[
 T^{-\gamma}(X\cdot D\bar\rho)(TX)\longrightarrow X\cdot DG=\gamma G
\]

distributionally. Thus \(B_kh\in N\) forces \(c[h]\gamma G=0\), hence \(c[h]=0\). This proves the domain identity and then the exact range assertion.

At the stated parameters,

\[
 \beta>\frac{6283}{245760}>\frac1{40},\quad
 \frac15-12\|DU[k]\|_\infty>\frac16,\quad40\eta=r_0.
\]

Consequently \(T(k)=-A_k^{-1}F\) maps the closed normalized high ball into itself. For two inputs its difference solves

\[
 A_{k_1}(T(k_1)-T(k_2))=-U[k_1-k_2]\cdot DT(k_2).
\]

Section 5 gives

\[
 L(T(k_1)-T(k_2))\le\frac{6\cdot2048r_0}{\sqrt{s}}L(k_1-k_2)
 =\frac{15}{16\sqrt6}L(k_1-k_2)<\frac25L(k_1-k_2).
\]

The normalized high ball is complete in this low metric. A low Cauchy sequence has a low limit. A weakly convergent high subsequence exists by its uniform Hilbert bound, and both limits agree as distributions. Weak lower semicontinuity retains the high ball, and the continuous linear high functional \(c\) retains its zero value. The contraction theorem now applies on an explicitly complete space.

The fixed point satisfies the exact nonlinear equation and normalization. Conversely any normalized high-ball solution is such a fixed point by the high inverse uniqueness, so it is unique there. The slope variation is at most \(4r_0/\sqrt{s}<2^{-12}\). The four-output estimate follows from \(146N(h)/\sqrt{s}\) and \(40\cdot146/\sqrt{s}<2^{23}\).

Finally \(1/5<\gamma<1\) and the growth bound preserve the entire leading angular function. Scaling multiplies that function by the nontrivial factor \(t^{1-\gamma}\); therefore the affine class excludes every different scale. It also excludes exponent derivatives \(r^\gamma\log r\) and nonzero leading angular variations. Their exclusion is a restriction of the theorem, not an estimate for those directions.

## P64. Critical weighted Sobolev spaces and finite augmentations

### P64.1. Critical Sobolev weights and finite augmentations

#### 1. Statement and notation

The critical weight makes a slowly varying copy of the leading homogeneous density nearly stationary under dilation. Adding local derivatives makes the origin strain well-defined, but does not remove this far-field obstruction. We prove that fact on one compatible Hilbert space and retain arbitrary finite constraints exactly.

Fix an integer m>=3 and a real number 0<gamma<1. Put c=1/gamma, delta=1-gamma, r=|X| and <r>=(1+r^2)^(1/2). For a scalar or vector field define

    ||h||_(X_gamma,m)^2
       = sum_(j=0)^m ||<r>^(j-1-gamma) D^j h||_2^2.       (1)

D^j is the full ordered Cartesian derivative tensor with its Euclidean norm; D^0 h=h. Let X_gamma,m be the real Hilbert completion in (1) of smooth compactly supported scalar fields with S1 parity, even in x and odd in y. The vector version only requires central oddness. Both spaces embed in local H^m. Set C_flat equal to the scalar smooth compactly supported S1 fields that vanish on some neighborhood of the origin.

Use the canonical full-plane velocity

    U[h]=(-R1 R2 h, R1^2 h),
    Rj=partial_j (-Delta)^(-1/2),

with no harmonic addition. On compact smooth densities its kernel away from zero is even and homogeneous of degree -2; R1^2 also has its usual local identity term. Define

    c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0).

Suppose a real smooth S1 background bar_rho and its canonical velocity bar_u satisfy, for j=0,...,m,

    |D^j bar_u(X)| <= C_j <r>^(gamma-j),
    |D^(j+1) bar_rho(X)| <= C'_j <r>^(gamma-1-j),         (2)

with finite constants C_j,C'_j. The exact normalization c+c[bar_rho]=1 may additionally be imposed, but is not needed for the obstruction. Write

    A h=(c X+bar_u).D h-h+U[h].D bar_rho,
    B h=A h-c[h] X.D bar_rho.                           (3)

The value B h is used below only for c[h]=0. We do not assume that X.D bar_rho belongs to X_gamma,m.

**Theorem.** Under these hypotheses:

1. U extends to a bounded operator from X_gamma,m to its vector version. For every fixed 0<alpha<1, h and U[h] have local C^(1,alpha) representatives. In particular, c is a bounded real linear functional on X_gamma,m.
2. Given any finite list of real linear functionals ell_1,...,ell_d on C_flat and any bounded compact operator K on X_gamma,m, there are h_n in C_flat such that

       ||h_n||_X=1,      h_n weakly ->0 in X,
       c[h_n]=0,        ell_i(h_n)=0 for every i,
       ||B h_n||_X ->0, ||K h_n||_X ->0.                (4)

   Every center derivative of h_n is zero. The ell_i need not be continuous in X.
3. Let p,q be finite nonnegative integers. Let T be any closed linear operator from X_gamma,m direct-sum R^p to X_gamma,m direct-sum R^q whose domain contains the pairs (h,0) for h in C_flat satisfying c[h]=0 and any specified finite list of real linear domain constraints. Suppose, on those pairs,

       T(h,0)=(B h+K h, zeta_1(h),...,zeta_q(h)),        (5)

   where the zeta_i are real linear functionals on that core and K is as above. Then T is not upper semi-Fredholm: it cannot have both closed range and finite-dimensional kernel. Consequently it has no bounded inverse estimate on the graph-orthogonal complement of a finite-dimensional kernel.

The values of T on nonzero finite coordinates are unrestricted by the theorem. Thus the conclusion applies to finite parameter columns, phase equations and finite additional output coordinates whenever their closed realization contains the stated core and obeys(5). No automatic closedness of such an augmented expression is asserted.

All constants in the estimates below are finite and depend only on gamma,m, the chosen fixed cutoffs and the finite constants in (2). There is no numerical constant to certify and no estimate uniform as gamma approaches 0 or 1, or as m tends to infinity.

#### 2. The canonical velocity in the weighted Sobolev space

Choose a smooth radial partition of unity {eta_j}_{j>=0}, with eta_0 supported in r<4 and eta_j supported where r is comparable to R_j=2^j for j>=1. Set R_0=1. The derivatives satisfy |D^a eta_j|<=C_a R_j^(-a). Each eta_j is centrally even, so h_j=eta_j h is centrally odd and has zero integral. The usual finite-overlap estimates and the product rule give

    sum_j sum_(a=0)^m R_j^(2a-2-2gamma)||D^a h_j||_2^2
        <= C ||h||_X^2.                                (6)

Conversely, weights are comparable to their R_j powers on each annulus. We bound every target derivative of U[h_j] in the corresponding target annulus of radius R_i. Put

    a_j^2=sum_(a=0)^m R_j^(2a-2-2gamma)||D^a h_j||_2^2.

When R_i and R_j are comparable, the unweighted L2 multiplier norm of the vector U is at most 1. Commutation with Cartesian derivatives and (6) bound the weighted target norm of each derivative order l<=m by C a_j. The local identity term causes no separated-annulus contribution.

For R_j much smaller than R_i, subtract the kernel at X and use the zero integral of h_j. A derivative of order l of the kernel has size O(r^(-2-l)), and its first difference has size O(|Y| r^(-3-l)). Hence

    ||D^l U[h_j]||_(L2(target i))
          <= C R_i^(-2-l) R_j^2 ||h_j||_2.

Here the factor R_i is the square root of target area, while
int |Y||h_j(Y)|dY<=C R_j^2||h_j||_2. After inserting the target weight and the source order-zero weight, the block bound is

    R_i^(l-1-gamma) ||D^l U[h_j]||_(L2(target i))
          <= C (R_j/R_i)^(3+gamma) a_j.                 (7)

For R_j much larger than R_i, evenness of the kernel and oddness of h_j give U[h_j](0)=0. At derivative order l=0, subtract the kernel at -Y. The resulting factor |X| yields

    ||U[h_j]||_(L2(target i))
          <= C R_i^2 R_j^(-2)||h_j||_2,

and therefore a weighted block bound C(R_i/R_j)^(1-gamma) a_j. At orders 1<=l<=m the direct differentiated kernel estimate suffices:

    ||D^l U[h_j]||_(L2(target i))
          <= C R_i R_j^(-1-l)||h_j||_2,

with weighted block bound

    C(R_i/R_j)^(l-gamma) a_j
       <= C(R_i/R_j)^(1-gamma) a_j.                    (8)

The same estimates hold for the target core ball with R_i=1. The sequences 2^(-k(3+gamma)) and 2^(-k(1-gamma)), k>=1, are summable. Applying the discrete convolution inequality to (7),(8) and the finitely many comparable blocks, then summing the finitely many derivative orders, proves

    ||U[h]||_X <= C_(gamma,m) ||h||_X.                 (9)

For compact h, each derivative D^l U[h] is O(r^(-3-l)) at infinity. Its truncations by smooth radial cutoffs converge in the vector version of (1), including the cutoff derivatives. Thus U[h] lies in the stated completion, not merely in a larger distributional weighted space. Density now extends U uniquely and boundedly. The construction uses precisely the canonical compact-source inverse and cannot introduce an unspecified harmonic field.

On each fixed ball, the weights in (1) are bounded above and below, so the completion embeds continuously into H^m there. For completeness, the needed local C^(1,alpha) embedding follows by multiplying by a compact cutoff and using Fourier inversion and Cauchy-Schwarz. The bound |exp(i xi.X)-exp(i xi.Y)|<=C_alpha |xi|^alpha |X-Y|^alpha reduces the gradient seminorm to the integral of |xi|^(2+2alpha)(1+|xi|^2)^(-m) in two dimensions. It is finite at infinity for m>2+alpha, which holds for m>=3 and 0<alpha<1. Evaluation of the first derivative at the origin is therefore bounded. Apply this argument to U[h] and (9) to obtain continuity of c[h].

For a compact h, the transport part of A h is compactly supported. At infinity, every derivative of U[h].D bar_rho of order j<=m is O(r^(gamma-4-j)), by (2). Multiplication by the order-j weight leaves O(r^-5), which is square-integrable. Locally all factors are smooth. Cutoff and local mollification show A h lies in X. This verifies the operator values used on the compact core.

#### 3. A smooth annular approximate nullvector

Fix a nonzero real chi in C_c^infinity((0,1)). For L>=2 put

    f_L(r,theta)=L^(-1/2) r^gamma sin(5theta)
                             chi((log r-L)/L).          (10)

This belongs to C_flat, is supported between e^L and e^(2L), and has S1 parity. The exact compact-source strain formula is

    c[h]=-h_y(0)/4+(1/pi)PV int sin(3theta)h/r^3 dX.

The origin term vanishes for f_L. Angular orthogonality gives c[f_L]=0 exactly. Thus B f_L=A f_L, with no contribution from an exponent column.

Set t=log r and F_L(t)=L^(-1/2)chi((t-L)/L). For every fixed derivative order j, Cartesian differentiation has the form

    D^j(r^gamma sin(5theta)F_L(log r))
        =r^(gamma-j) sum_(a=0)^j P_(j,a)(theta) F_L^(a)(t),

where the tensors P_(j,a) are smooth and depend only on gamma,j. Since
||F_L^(a)||_(L2(dt))=L^(-a)||chi^(a)||_2, the critical weights and polar area measure give a uniform bound on the order-j norm for every fixed j. The order-zero part has the exact formula

    ||<r>^(-1-gamma) f_L||_2^2
       =pi int_0^1 (1+exp(-2L(1+u)))^(-1-gamma)chi(u)^2du
       -> pi||chi||_2^2>0.                             (11)

In particular, the full X norm is bounded above and bounded away from zero as L tends to infinity. We also have uniform control of the analogous weighted derivative of order m+1, which is used only to estimate the transport of this smooth packet.

Because c gamma=1, the dilation term is exactly

    (c r partial_r-1) f_L
       =c L^(-3/2) r^gamma sin(5theta)
                               chi'((log r-L)/L).

The same derivative formulas yield

    ||(c X.D-1)f_L||_X <= C/L.                         (12)

A product-rule term of order j in bar_u.D f_L contains D^a bar_u times D^(j+1-a) f_L. The ratio of its weighted factor to the critical weight of that packet derivative is bounded by C<r>^(gamma-1). On the support r>=e^L, this gives

    ||bar_u.D f_L||_X <= C exp(-delta L).              (13)

This uses (2) through order m and the just-proved packet estimates through order m+1. There is no assertion that A is bounded on all of X.

#### 4. The nonlocal coupling tends to zero in the same norm

Set T=exp(L/2). On r>=T, each term of derivative order j in U[f_L].D bar_rho is bounded after weighting by

    C <r>^(-delta) <r>^(l-1-gamma)|D^l U[f_L]|,
       0<=l<=j.

Consequently(9) gives

    ||1_(r>=T) D^j(U[f_L].D bar_rho)
                                      <r>^(j-1-gamma)||_2
       <= C exp(-delta L/2)||f_L||_X.                 (14)

No derivative of the indicator occurs: this is a split of the norm of an already differentiated smooth function.

For r<T, the source support r>=e^L is separated from X, with |X| at most e^L/2 for L>=2 log2. The kernel cancellation at the origin gives

    |U[f_L](X)| <= C r L^(-1/2) exp(-delta L).

At each order 1<=l<=m, a direct derivative of the kernel gives

    |D^l U[f_L](X)|
       <= C L^(-1/2) int_(e^L)^infinity R^(gamma-l-1)dR
       <= C L^(-1/2) exp(-(l-gamma)L).                (15)

The constants absorb 1/(l-gamma). Since <r><=e^L in this inner region for L>=2, these inequalities imply, for all 0<=l<=m,

    |D^l U[f_L](X)|
       <= C L^(-1/2) exp(-delta L) <r>^(1-l).         (16)

Using (2) in the product rule now gives

    <r>^(j-1-gamma)|D^j(U[f_L].D bar_rho)|
       <= C L^(-1/2) exp(-delta L) <r>^-1.

Its squared integral over r<T is bounded by
C L^-1 exp(-2delta L) log(1+T^2). Since log(1+T^2)<=L+log2, the inner X norm is at most C exp(-delta L). Combining this with (12)-(14) proves

    ||B f_L||_X=||A f_L||_X
       <= C (L^-1+exp(-delta L/2)),                   (17)

while (11) bounds ||f_L||_X away from zero. This is an analytical bound with finite constants for each specified background, not a numerical approximation.

#### 5. Exact finite constraints and finite block coordinates

Given d functionals ell_i, use the d+1 packets

    g_(n,j)=f_(3^j n)/||f_(3^j n)||_X, 0<=j<=d.

Their supports, and the supports of every derivative, are disjoint. They are therefore orthonormal in the real Hilbert inner product (1). Form the d by (d+1) matrix with entries ell_i(g_(n,j)). Choose a unit Euclidean vector a_n in its nullspace and set

    h_n=sum_(j=0)^d a_(n,j)g_(n,j).

Then all finite constraints hold exactly, ||h_n||_X=1 and c[h_n]=0. Every center derivative vanishes. The triangle and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities and (17) imply ||B h_n||_X->0. The support of each derivative of h_n lies outside r=e^n. Pairing with any fixed element of X and using its weighted derivative tails proves h_n converges weakly to zero. Bounded compactness of K gives ||K h_n||_X->0. This proves (4).

For (5), include every domain constraint and every zeta_i in the same finite list before forming h_n. Then v_n=(h_n,0) belongs to D(T), has norm 1 in X direct-sum R^p, converges weakly to zero there and satisfies T v_n->0 in X direct-sum R^q. Its graph norm tends to 1. It converges weakly to zero in the graph Hilbert space as well, because for every v in D(T),

    <v_n,v>_graph=<v_n,v>_ambient+<T v_n,T v>_target ->0.

If ker T were finite dimensional, its graph-orthogonal projection P would satisfy P v_n->0 in graph norm. If ran T were also closed, the restriction of T from (ker T)^perp in the graph space onto ran T would be a bounded bijection of Banach spaces. Its inverse would be bounded, yielding

    ||v-Pv||_graph <= C ||T v||_target.

At v=v_n, the left side tends to 1 and the right side to zero. This contradiction proves that T is not upper semi-Fredholm. No assumption about finite codimension of its range is used.

#### 6. Application and limits

Every fixed original case4 reference and every finite regularized-power refit with this leading exponent satisfies (2) for each finite m: differentiate its finite smooth potential representation, and use that its fastest density and velocity growth is r^gamma. The exact source exponent has 0<gamma<1 and c gamma=1. Thus the theorem applies to their critical weighted Sobolev realizations and any closed finite augmentation satisfying(5).

A pure nonzero leading term r^gamma Theta(theta) is still outside (1), because its order-zero squared norm diverges logarithmically. The packets in (10) are compact and have zero individual leading trace, yet approach that critical behavior on longer logarithmic annuli. They therefore survive finite leading phase conditions as well as finite center conditions. Local C^(1,alpha) regularity and a continuous c[h] do not correct the endpoint transport obstruction.

The theorem does not rule out the strict subcritical N_(s,R) conditional inverse, an infinite-dimensional tail realization, or a domain that excludes the stated compact annular core. It does not prove existence or nonexistence of a nonlinear profile near a numerical reference. Its conclusion is confined to the closed operators, norms and finite augmentations explicitly stated above.

Dependencies: the canonical compact-source velocity and strain formula of part P2; elementary L2 Fourier multiplier bounds, weighted annular estimates, finite-dimensional nullspaces and the bounded inverse theorem on a graph Hilbert space. ## P65. A far-field spectral line in weighted Sobolev spaces

### P65.1. A far-field spectral line

#### 1. Statement

The endpoint obstruction has a quantitative version away from the endpoint. A weighted space selects a growth exponent b. Dilation acts on r^(b+i tau) by the scalar cb-1+i c tau. Slowly cutting off this power on logarithmic annuli turns that scalar into approximate spectrum of the full coupled operator. The background terms decay in the same norm.

Fix an integer m>=3, an exponent 0<gamma<1 and c=1/gamma. For every -3<b<1 let X_(b,m) be the complex Hilbert completion of smooth compactly supported complex S1 scalar fields in

    ||h||_X^2=sum_(j=0)^m ||<r>^(j-1-b)D^j h||_2^2.    (1)

The complexification is only for the spectral statement; the tau=0 packet can be real. Define the canonical U, strain c[h], core C_flat and operators A,B as in part P64, and assume its smooth-background symbol bounds

    |D^j bar_u|<=C_j <r>^(gamma-j),
    |D^(j+1) bar_rho|<=C'_j <r>^(gamma-1-j),
               0<=j<=m.                              (2)

Let p be finite. Let T be a closed complex linear operator on
H=X_(b,m) direct-sum C^p. Suppose its domain contains (h,0) for each h in C_flat satisfying c[h]=0 and a specified finite list of complex linear domain constraints. Suppose on that core

    T(h,0)=(B h+K h, zeta_1(h),...,zeta_p(h)),          (3)

where K is bounded compact on X_(b,m), and the zeta_i are complex linear functionals on the core. Their continuity is not required. Real finite constraints and real closed operators can be complexified. As in part P64, no condition is imposed on T at nonzero finite coordinates, and no automatic closedness is inferred from its formula.

**Theorem.** For each real tau, put

    lambda_tau=cb-1+i c tau.                          (4)

There are v_n=(h_n,0) in D(T) with ||v_n||_H=1, v_n weakly converging to zero, and

    ||(T-lambda_tau)v_n||_H ->0.                      (5)

Every h_n has zero strain, all center jets zero and every prescribed finite constraint exactly zero. It follows that:

- For every tau, T-lambda_tau is not upper semi-Fredholm. In particular the complete vertical line Re z=cb-1 lies in the spectrum and in the set where T-z is not Fredholm.
- If z belongs to the resolvent set, then Re z differs from cb-1 and

      ||(T-z)^(-1)|| >= 1/|Re z-(cb-1)|.              (6)

  In particular a bounded inverse at zero, when it exists and b differs from gamma, has norm at least 1/|1-cb|. At b=gamma no such inverse exists.
- If T generates a strongly continuous semigroup S(t), t>=0, then

      ||S(t)|| >= exp((cb-1)t), every t>=0.            (7)

  A bound ||S(t)||<=M exp(-omega t), with finite M independent of t, therefore requires omega<=1-cb.

Only the stated spectral line is asserted. We do not identify the entire spectrum, infer invertibility for b different from gamma, or transfer(6) to a different norm or space without proving that transfer.

#### 2. Canonical velocity and strain on X_(b,m)

The proof of part P64, section 2, works with b in place of gamma in every weight. The inner-source block exponent is 3+b; the outer-source order-zero exponent is 1-b; the higher-order outer-source exponent is l-b>=1-b for l>=1. These are positive exactly in the range needed here, -3<b<1. For clarity, after source and target weights are inserted the respective factors are

    (R_source/R_target)^(3+b),  R_source<<R_target,
    (R_target/R_source)^(1-b),  R_source>>R_target.

The nearby blocks use the unweighted Fourier multiplier bound and all derivatives through order m. Both geometric sums converge. A compact centrally odd source has D^j U[h]=O(r^(-3-j)); the weighted tail of its order-j squared norm has radial power -7-2b, integrable precisely when b>-3. The same cutoff argument places U[h] in the vector completion. Thus U is bounded on X_(b,m) for this whole interval.

The local H^m embedding and Fourier proof of C^(1,alpha) regularity for 0<alpha<1 are unchanged. Consequently c[h] is bounded. A compact source has coupled derivative D^j(U[h].D bar_rho)=O(r^(gamma-4-j)); after weighting this is O(r^(gamma-b-5)). It is square-integrable since b>-3 and gamma<1 imply gamma-b<4. This proves A h belongs to X for compact h. The zero-strain B values in (3) are therefore defined in the claimed target.

#### 3. Oscillatory logarithmic packets

Fix nonzero real chi in C_c^infinity((0,1)). For L>=2 define

    f_(L,tau)=L^(-1/2) r^(b+i tau) sin(5theta)
                                    chi((log r-L)/L).  (8)

This is a complex smooth compact S1 function vanishing near the origin. The contact term in c[f] is zero, and the integral kernel angular factor sin(3theta) is orthogonal to sin(5theta). Hence c[f_(L,tau)]=0 exactly.

The derivative recursion in part P64 with b+i tau in place of gamma gives uniform critical weighted bounds at every fixed order through m+1. The constants may depend on tau. The order-zero norm obeys

    ||<r>^(-1-b) f_(L,tau)||_2^2
       =pi int_0^1(1+exp(-2L(1+u)))^(-1-b)chi(u)^2du
       ->pi||chi||_2^2>0.                             (9)

This formula is valid also when 1+b is negative; its factor remains uniformly bounded above and below for L>=2. Therefore ||f_(L,tau)||_X is bounded above and bounded away from zero. The exact dilation defect is

    (c X.D-1-lambda_tau) f_(L,tau)
       =c L^(-3/2) r^(b+i tau) sin(5theta)
                                    chi'((log r-L)/L).

Its X norm is O(L^-1). The perturbing transport bar_u.D f has X norm O(exp(-(1-gamma)L)), by the product-rule weight comparison from part P64. This comparison depends on the background exponent gamma and does not replace it by b.

It remains to control U[f].D bar_rho. On r>=T=exp(L/2), boundedness of U and the symbol bounds (2) give an X norm of at most C exp(-(1-gamma)L/2).

On r<T, the kernel estimates for the separated source give

    |U[f](X)|<=C r L^(-1/2)exp(-(1-b)L),
    |D^l U[f](X)|<=C L^(-1/2)exp(-(l-b)L), 1<=l<=m.

All integrals converge because b<1. Since <r><=e^L for L>=2, these imply

    |D^l U[f](X)|<=C L^(-1/2)exp(-(1-b)L)<r>^(1-l).

After multiplying by the background derivative and the target weight, every order j<=m is at most

    C L^(-1/2)exp(-(1-b)L)<r>^(gamma-b-1).             (10)

Put d=gamma-b. The L2 norm over r<T of the last spatial factor is bounded by C T^d if d>0, by C sqrt(1+log T) if d=0, and by a finite constant if d<0. Thus the inner coupling tends to zero. Indeed its exponential decay rates can be chosen as

    1-(gamma+b)/2 >0, if b<gamma;
    1-b >0,                  if b>=gamma,             (11)

with only a harmless factor L^-1/2, or its cancellation at equality. These are strictly positive since gamma<1 and b<1. Consequently

    ||(B-lambda_tau) f_(L,tau)||_X ->0.                (12)

The full nonlocal coupling has been estimated in the same derivative norm, including its effect inside the annulus hole.

#### 4. Constraints, spectrum and resolvent

Take d+1 normalized packets with L=3^j n for the total number d of domain and output functionals in (3). They are orthonormal because their supports and all derivative supports are disjoint. A unit vector in the nullspace of the resulting d by (d+1) complex constraint matrix gives h_n of norm 1 satisfying all those constraints exactly. Each packet has zero strain, so does h_n. Their supports leave every compact set, implying weak convergence to zero in X. The finite sum, (12), and compactness of K give (5).

The graph-norm proof in part P64 applies to T-lambda_tau verbatim. Its kernel cannot be finite dimensional with closed range. Thus lambda_tau is not a resolvent point, and T-lambda_tau is not Fredholm. This proves the first conclusion without a surjectivity inference from a one-sided estimate.

For an arbitrary z, (5) implies

    ||(T-z)v_n|| -> |lambda_tau-z|.

If z is a resolvent point, applying its inverse to these vectors yields

    1<=||(T-z)^(-1)|| |lambda_tau-z|.

Choose tau=Im z/c. The distance becomes |Re z-(cb-1)|, proving(6). The tau=0 sequence and its real finite constraint matrix give the zero-resolvent lower bound directly on the real realization as well.

If T is a C0 semigroup generator, every v_n lies in its domain and the variation identity is

    S(t)v_n-exp(lambda_tau t)v_n
       =int_0^t exp(lambda_tau s) S(t-s)
                                  (T-lambda_tau)v_n ds.

For fixed t, strong continuity gives a finite bound on ||S(s)|| for 0<=s<=t, so the right side tends to zero. Hence ||S(t)||>=exp(Re lambda_tau t), proving(7). Comparing this with M exp(-omega t) and letting t tend to infinity gives the required rate restriction.

#### 5. Consequences for S1

The source exponent c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248 gives gamma=1/c. At the critical choice b=gamma, the line passes through zero and recovers part P64. As b approaches gamma from below, the necessary inverse bound 1/(1-cb) diverges. At b=1/5 it is the exact rational number

    5/(5-c)=11258999068426240/7182522608187059.

This is a necessary lower bound in the explicitly defined X_(1/5,m) norm and its finite augmentations. It is not a replacement for the sufficient constant 40 in the different N_(s,R) theorem. A comparison between those completed spaces, domains and norms would be required for such a statement.

The argument also distinguishes a failed decay estimate from failed invertibility. If b>gamma, the spectral line has positive real part and a decaying forward semigroup is impossible. The theorem alone does not exclude an inverse at zero in that regime. It excludes an inverse there only at the actual critical value b=gamma.

## P66. Gaussian finite differences and sharper frozen Hoelder constants

### P66.1. Gaussian finite differences in the frozen Hoelder estimate

Status: the analytical estimates below are complete. A new numerical constant is not asserted until two independent evaluations pass.

#### 1. Setting and theorem

Let lambda>1, a>0, sigma=a/(lambda-1), and 0<alpha<min(1,sigma). On the real Fourier-annular Schwartz S1 core and its little homogeneous Hoelder completion, use the same generator realization as part P53:

    L0=lambda x partial_x+y partial_y-1+a R1^2,
    H(h)=sup_(t>0)t^((sigma-alpha)/2)
                         ||exp(t Delta)Lambda^sigma h||_infinity.

Its inverse obeys H(L0^-1 f)<=(1-alpha)^-1 H(f). We keep this realization and the whole coupled frozen operator. Write b=sigma-alpha and G=Gamma(sigma/2). For 0<theta<1 and z>0 set

    A=(1-theta)^(-b/2),  k=1/(4 sqrt(theta)),
    s=(1-alpha)/2,
    B_(theta,z)=4 k^alpha/(alpha G)
       [ z^(-alpha)(1-A erf(z))
                             + A gamma_lower(s,z^2)/sqrt(pi) ].  (1)

Here gamma_lower(s,x)=int_0^x u^(s-1)exp(-u)du. Then

    [h]_alpha<=B_(theta,z) H(h).                         (2)

Every choice of theta,z is valid. No optimal parameter choice is required. Replacing the gradient bound in part P55 by the exact Gaussian translation norm gives (1).

For a forward estimate define m(r)=r^sigma exp(-r^2) and

    I_j=int_0^infinity r m(r) (-Delta_rad)^j m(r)dr,
                 0<=j<sigma+1.                        (3)

Only integer j are used. These integrals are strictly positive and

    int_(R2) |X|^(2j)|k_sigma(X)|^2 dX=I_j/(2pi),
    k_sigma=F^-1(m).

Let P be a polynomial of degree d with nonnegative real coefficients p_j, p_0>0, p_d>0, alpha+1<d<sigma+1. Then

    H(h)<=A_P [h]_alpha,
    A_P^2=(int_0^infinity r^(2alpha+1)/P(r^2)dr)
                                      sum_(j=0)^d p_j I_j.       (4)

In particular the following explicit choices are available, where a1=alpha+1:

    P(t)=(1+mu t)^d:
    A_P^2=mu^(-a1) Gamma(a1)Gamma(d-a1)/(2Gamma(d))
                         sum_(j=0)^d binom(d,j)mu^j I_j;         (5)

    P(t)=1+mu t^d:
    A_P^2=pi/(2d sin(pi a1/d)) mu^(-a1/d)(I_0+mu I_d).          (6)

For (6), the positive choice mu=a1 I_0/((d-a1)I_d) minimizes its expression over mu>0. Finite selection of rational mu in (5), or theta,z in (1), is sufficient for a certified bound.

Combining the two directions with the already proved heat inverse gives

    [L0^-1 f]_alpha<=A_P B_(theta,z)/(1-alpha) [f]_alpha.        (7)

The forward bound of part P55 can also be used with (1). Equations(1)-(7) estimate the ordinary seminorm of h itself, not a derivative. They do not control the strain trace or the full variable-coefficient normalized operator.

#### 2. Exact Gaussian finite differences

For the heat kernel in two dimensions, separation into the direction of a vector e and its perpendicular gives

    ||G_u(.+e)-G_u||_1=2 erf(|e|/(4sqrt(u))).             (8)

To verify the constant, the perpendicular one-dimensional Gaussian integrates to 1. In the remaining coordinate the two Gaussian densities cross at the midpoint of their centers. Integrating their signed difference on either side gives twice the Gaussian mass of the interval between -|e|/2 and|e|/2, namely 2 erf(|e|/(4sqrt(u))).

Put g=Lambda^sigma h. Split a heat time t into theta t and (1-theta)t. Equation(8) and the definition of H give, for d0=|X-Y|,

    |H_t g(X)-H_t g(Y)|
       <=2 A erf(k d0/sqrt(t)) H(h)t^(-b/2).           (9)

The separate bound by twice the supremum is

    |H_t g(X)-H_t g(Y)|<=2 H(h)t^(-b/2).              (10)

Use (10) on 0<t<(k/z)^2 d0^2 and (9) on larger t. The heat representation

    h=G^-1 int_0^infinity t^(sigma/2-1)H_t g dt

holds on the core. Its differences converge because 0<alpha<1. Dividing the resulting difference estimate by d0^alpha gives

    G^-1 [ (4/alpha)(k/z)^alpha
                    +4 A k^alpha int_0^z u^(-alpha-1)erf(u)du ].

Integration by parts, with the zero boundary limit at u=0 since alpha<1, yields

    int_0^z u^(-alpha-1)erf(u)du
       =-z^(-alpha)erf(z)/alpha
                          +gamma_lower(s,z^2)/(alpha sqrt(pi)).

This proves (1),(2). The bracket in (1) may contain a negative first summand for some choices of z, but their full sum is positive by the preceding integral representation. No term is discarded based on its sign. The first derivative with respect to z vanishes exactly when A erf(z)=1; we do not rely on finding that zero.

The same argument allows different values of theta on different heat-time intervals. In this result a single theta and a single explicit split suffice. The estimates extend by continuity to the little completion, preserving the same inverse domain, injectivity and surjectivity already established in part P53.

#### 3. Spatial moments of the kernel

For integer j<sigma+1, m has square-integrable weak derivatives through order j: near zero the worst derivative has size O(r^(sigma-j)), which is L2 when sigma-j>-1; at infinity it decays exponentially. Plancherel therefore gives the moment identity in (3). To identify its radial integral directly, integrate by parts j times on the frequency annulus epsilon<r<R. Every boundary term at epsilon is O(epsilon^(2sigma-2j+2)); it vanishes because j<sigma+1. The outer terms vanish by Gaussian decay. Equivalently, summing the Cartesian derivative squares yields the integral against (-Delta)^j. It is positive because the nonzero multiplier m cannot have all derivatives of order j zero; I_0 is positive directly.

Cauchy-Schwarz with weight P(|X|^2) gives

    int |X|^alpha |k_sigma(X)|dX
       <=[int |X|^(2alpha)/P(|X|^2)dX]^(1/2)
                          [int P(|X|^2)|k_sigma(X)|^2dX]^(1/2).

The first integral is finite because d>alpha+1 and p_0>0. The second is finite by (3). Polar integration and the moment identity cancel the factors 2pi and prove(4). The same argument with alpha=0 gives k_sigma in L1. Its integral is m(0)=0, so kernel cancellation and scaling give H(h)<=A_P[h]_alpha exactly as in part P55.

For (5), substitute v=mu r^2 and use the beta integral. For (6), substitute v=mu r^(2d) and use int_0^infinity v^(q-1)/(1+v)dv=pi/sin(pi q),0<q<1. These integral identities follow respectively from the beta function definition and its reflection identity. Their parameters lie in the convergence ranges stated in section 1. Differentiation of mu^(-a1/d)(I_0+mu I_d) shows its derivative changes sign only at the positive value given after (6), proving the claimed minimum.

#### 4. Exact moment evaluation and verification plan

For a Laurent polynomial Q(r)=sum_l q_l r^(2l), the radial Laplacian of r^sigma exp(-r^2)Q(r) changes each q_l by

    l-1: (sigma+2l)^2 q_l,
    l:   -4(sigma+2l+1)q_l,
    l+1: 4q_l.

Starting with q_0=1 and applying this j times gives Delta_rad^j m=m sum_l q_l r^(2l). Therefore

    I_j=(-1)^j sum_l q_l
                   Gamma(sigma+l+1)/(2*2^(sigma+l+1)).           (11)

The smallest gamma argument is sigma-j+1>0. The formula is finite, even when the individual summands have large cancellation. Directed high-precision arithmetic, not ordinary floating cancellation, must certify its sign and all numerical bounds.

The independent evaluator will form the radial derivatives by a different polynomial differentiation rule, verify(11), and evaluate erf and gamma_lower by explicitly bounded alternating series at the selected 0<z<1. ## P67. Fractional Gaussian kernels and the frozen Hoelder constant 87

### P67.1. Fractional Gaussian kernels from integer kernels

Status: analytical argument complete before computation. Numerical sufficient constants will be stated only after independent directed verification.

#### 1. Statement

Use the Fourier transform and frozen little Hoelder generator realization of parts P53 and P66. Fix 0<alpha<1, an integer n>=1 and 0<epsilon<1. Put

    sigma=2n+2epsilon, q=n-alpha/2>0,
    G_t(X)=(4pi t)^-1 exp(-|X|^2/(4t)),
    K_j=(-Delta)^j G_1,
    A_j=int_(R2)|X|^alpha |K_j(X)|dX.

Let k_sigma be the inverse Fourier transform of |xi|^sigma exp(-|xi|^2). For any T>0 define

    x=T/(1+T), v=(1+T)^(-q),
    J0=B_x(1-epsilon,q+epsilon),
    Jtot=Gamma(1-epsilon)Gamma(q+epsilon)/Gamma(q+1),

and

    C_(n,epsilon,alpha,T)
      = { (A_(n+1)/q)[-T^(-epsilon)(1-v)+q J0]
            +A_n[T^(-epsilon)(1+v)-q(Jtot-J0)] }
                                                   /Gamma(1-epsilon). (1)

Both bracketed quantities in (1) are positive. Then

    int |X|^alpha |k_sigma(X)|dX<=C_(n,epsilon,alpha,T). (2)

Consequently the frozen heat norm obeys

    H(h)<=C_(n,epsilon,alpha,T)[h]_alpha.

If B is any rigorously established reverse constant [h]_alpha<=B H(h), the complete coupled frozen generator obeys

    [L0^-1 f]_alpha <= B C_(n,epsilon,alpha,T)/(1-alpha)
                                                        [f]_alpha. (3)

Here lambda>1, a>0, sigma=a/(lambda-1), and L0=lambda x partial_x+y partial_y-1+a R1^2. The same little-space generator domain, inverse and parity convention as part P53 are used. No center trace, normalized rank column or variable coefficient is added to this statement.

#### 2. Fractional heat representation with an integrable majorant

For lambda0>=0, integration by parts gives

    lambda0^epsilon
       =epsilon/Gamma(1-epsilon)
           int_0^infinity(1-exp(-t lambda0))t^(-1-epsilon)dt.

At lambda0=0 both sides are zero. For positive lambda0, the boundary terms vanish since 0<epsilon<1; substitution then gives the gamma integral. Apply the identity to the Fourier multiplier of K_n. Formally it yields

    k_sigma=epsilon/Gamma(1-epsilon)
           int_0^infinity (K_n-exp(t Delta)K_n)t^(-1-epsilon)dt. (4)

We now justify this as a Bochner integral and bound its weighted L1 norm. Scaling of derivatives of G_t gives

    int |X|^alpha |(-Delta)^j G_(1+t)(X)|dX
                            =(1+t)^(alpha/2-j) A_j.

The triangle inequality gives

    ||K_n-exp(t Delta)K_n||_(L1(|X|^alpha dX))
                            <=A_n[1+(1+t)^(-q)].       (5)

The heat derivative identity gives instead

    K_n-exp(t Delta)K_n
                =int_0^t(-Delta)^(n+1)G_(1+u)du,

and hence

    ||K_n-exp(t Delta)K_n||_(L1(|X|^alpha dX))
                <=(A_(n+1)/q)[1-(1+t)^(-q)].          (6)

Use (6) for t<T and (5) for t>=T. Near zero the first bound is O(t); at infinity the second is bounded. Multiplication by t^(-1-epsilon) is integrable at both ends. The same reasoning with alpha=0 proves convergence in unweighted L1. Thus (4) is a well-defined L1 Bochner integral. Taking its Fourier transform is justified by that integrability, and the scalar identity identifies it with k_sigma. Its weighted absolute integral is bounded by the integral of (5),(6).

The two remaining integrals are

    I1=int_0^T t^(-1-epsilon)[1-(1+t)^(-q)]dt,
    I2=int_T^infinity t^(-1-epsilon)[1+(1+t)^(-q)]dt.

Both are positive. Integration by parts yields

    epsilon I1=-T^(-epsilon)(1-v)+q J0,
    epsilon I2= T^(-epsilon)(1+v)-q(Jtot-J0).

Indeed the derivative integrals are int t^(-epsilon)(1+t)^(-q-1)dt; substituting z=t/(1+t) gives the incomplete beta parameters 1-epsilon and q+epsilon, both positive. The full integral is Jtot. These identities prove(1),(2), including positivity of each bracket. No cancellation is dropped or estimated by an unsigned subtraction.

The canonical kernel has integral 0, since its continuous Fourier multiplier vanishes at zero. Kernel cancellation and scaling now give the forward heat bound. Combining it with the already proved heat inverse and reverse conversion gives (3). The extension to the completed little Hoelder space is by continuity on the same Fourier-annular core.

#### 3. Exact integer kernel moments

Put u=|X|^2/4 and define polynomials P_0(u)=1 and

    P_(j+1)=(1-u)P_j+(2u-1)P'_j-u P''_j.              (7)

The identity Delta_rad=q partial_q^2+partial_q in the variable q=|X|^2/4 proves by induction

    K_j(X)=(4pi)^-1 exp(-u) P_j(u).

In particular,

    P_3(u)=6-18u+9u^2-u^3,
    P_4(u)=24-96u+72u^2-16u^3+u^4.

Polar integration gives

    A_j=2^alpha int_0^infinity u^(alpha/2)exp(-u)|P_j(u)|du. (8)

For j=3 the intervals(0,1),(2,3),(6,7) each contain a root by exact opposite endpoint signs. For j=4 the intervals(0,1),(1,2),(4,5),(9,10) have the same property. The intervals are disjoint and the number of roots already equals the degree, so these are all roots, each simple and positive. Each polynomial is positive at zero and changes sign at each successive root.

Write P_j(u)=sum_l p_l u^l, with increasing positive roots r_1,...,r_j, and put

    F_j(z)=sum_l p_l gamma_lower(1+alpha/2+l,z),
    F_j(infinity)=sum_l p_l Gamma(1+alpha/2+l).

Splitting(8) at every root gives the exact expression

    A_j=2^alpha[(-1)^j F_j(infinity)
                       +2 sum_(k=1)^j(-1)^(k-1)F_j(r_k)].       (9)

A certified interval for every root inserted in (9) gives a directed enclosure of A_j. The root enclosure and all polynomial signs use exact rational arithmetic. The gamma functions and the alternating signs must be retained with directed arithmetic.

For the actual frozen S1 parameters, use n=3, alpha=1/2 and epsilon=(sigma-6)/2. Its membership in (0,1) is an exact source check. Formula (1) can be evaluated for a finite list of rational T; every entry is a valid upper constant, and selection among them needs no global optimization claim.
