## P68. Logarithmic weights and asymptotic coordinates at the critical exponent

### P68.1. Logarithmic weights and asymptotic coordinates at the critical exponent

Status: analytical proof, with no numerical inverse or profile existence claim. The source-dependent specialization requires only the exact exponent in the original checkpoint. This extends parts P64 and P65; all operator-domain hypotheses are stated below.

#### 1. The critical remainder spaces

Fix an integer m>=3, an exponent 0<gamma<1 and a real number kappa. Write c=1/gamma, delta=1-gamma,

    r=|X|, R(X)=(1+r^2)^(1/2), w_kappa(X)=(1+log R(X))^kappa.

Let C be the real smooth compactly supported functions that are even in x and odd in y. Define X_kappa as its completion in the Hilbert norm

    ||h||_(X_kappa)^2
      =sum_(j=0)^m ||w_kappa R^(j-1-gamma) D^j h||_2^2.       (1)

Here D^j is the full ordered Cartesian derivative tensor, including multiplicities. Different choices of an equivalent tensor norm do not affect the conclusions, but (1) fixes the convention. The space embeds into distributions and locally into H^m. In particular h and its first derivatives have continuous representatives, locally C^(1,alpha) for every 0<alpha<1.

Use the canonical even-kernel velocity operator

    U[h]=(-R1 R2 h,R1^2 h),

first on C and then by the bounded extension proved below. The local identity terms in these second-order Riesz operators are included. Put

    c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0).

Let a smooth S1 background rho_bar have canonical velocity u_bar and satisfy, for 0<=j<=m,

    |D^j u_bar(X)| <= C_j R^(gamma-j),
    |D^(j+1) rho_bar(X)| <= C'_j R^(gamma-1-j).             (2)

Define the compact-core expressions

    A h=(c X+u_bar).D h-h+U[h].D rho_bar,
    B h=A h-c[h] X.D rho_bar.                              (3)

No assertion that the last column belongs to X_kappa is made. All packets used below have c[h]=0, so their image in (3) is A h and is in X_kappa.

**Theorem 1.** U extends boundedly from X_kappa to the corresponding vector space, and c is continuous on X_kappa. There is a sequence g_n in C with norm 1, weakly converging to 0 in X_kappa, such that

    c[g_n]=0, every derivative of g_n at 0 is 0,
    ||B g_n||_(X_kappa) ->0.                              (4)

Any specified finite list of real linear functionals on C can additionally be made exactly zero. They need not be continuous. Thus changing a critical power weight by any fixed power of a logarithm does not give an inverse estimate for the normalized operator on this compact core.

#### 2. Velocity and strain with logarithmic weights

Take a smooth radial dyadic partition at radii R_j=2^j, j>=0, with the initial piece containing the unit disc. For h_j in the j-th annulus, use the rescaled derivative norm

    a_j^2=sum_(l=0)^m R_j^(2l-2-2gamma) (1+j)^(2kappa)
                                             ||D^l h_j||_2^2.

The sum of these norms is equivalent to (1). Leibniz derivatives of the partition carry R_j^(-l); R and R_j are comparable on the annulus; and 1+log R is comparable to 1+j, with constants depending only on kappa and the fixed partition. This gives both inequalities by bounded overlap.

For neighboring annuli the ordinary L2 multiplier bound and the same bound after Cartesian differentiation give a uniformly bounded block. This includes all derivatives of the input partition, which are already included in a_j.

For an inner source j and outer target i with i>=j+3, each source is centrally odd, hence has integral 0. The kernel and its derivatives away from the diagonal obey

    |D^l K(Z)| <= C_l |Z|^(-2-l).

Subtract K(X) in the integral. For l target derivatives, the resulting L2 output is bounded by

    C_l R_i^(-2-l) R_j^2 ||h_j||_2.

After multiplication by the target derivative weight and conversion of the input norm, the block factor is

    C (R_j/R_i)^(3+gamma) ((1+i)/(1+j))^kappa.            (5)

For an outer source j>=i+3 and l=0, evenness of K and central oddness of h_j imply U[h_j](0)=0. Subtract the value at 0 and use a kernel derivative. The unweighted output is bounded by

    C R_i^2 R_j^(-2) ||h_j||_2.

For l>=1, differentiation gives the bound

    C_l R_i R_j^(-1-l) ||h_j||_2.

The respective weighted factors are

    C (R_i/R_j)^(1-gamma) ((1+i)/(1+j))^kappa,
    C_l (R_i/R_j)^(l-gamma) ((1+i)/(1+j))^kappa.          (6)

Since l>=1, the second is no larger than the first up to a constant. For every i,j>=0,

    ((1+i)/(1+j))^kappa <= (1+|i-j|)^|kappa|.

The exponential decay in (5),(6) therefore dominates the polynomial factor. The sums of the block bounds in both directions are finite. Applying the elementary discrete convolution inequality proves U bounded on X_kappa.

For compact input, U[h] and its derivatives decay at least as r^(-3-l): the constant moment vanishes by parity. Cutting off U[h] at large radii consequently converges in the vector version of (1), for every kappa. This verifies that the bounded extension takes values in the stated completion, not just in a larger distribution class.

The local H^m norm of U[h] is bounded by its X_kappa norm. The Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz proof of H^m_loc embedding in C^(1,alpha)_loc applies whenever m>2+alpha. Taking any alpha<1 gives continuity of partial_y U2[h](0), and hence of c. The same conclusion can be read directly from the far-source strain blocks: they have the summable factor 2^(-(1-gamma)j)(1+j)^(-kappa). No unweighted A2 theorem for the radial weight is used.

#### 3. Explicit packets and all their derivatives

Choose a nonzero real chi in C_c^infinity((0,1)). For L>=2 put

    a_L=L^(-kappa-1/2),
    f_L(X)=a_L r^gamma sin(5theta) chi((log r-L)/L).       (7)

The support is a compact annulus between e^L and e^(2L). S1 parity follows from the odd harmonic 5. Every origin jet vanishes. The exact strain formula has the angular factor sin(3theta); its pairing with sin(5theta) is 0, and the local jet term is also 0. Thus c[f_L]=0 exactly.

For every fixed derivative order j, including j=m+1, differentiating (7) gives

    |D^j f_L(X)| <= C_j a_L r^(gamma-j)
                   sum_(q=0)^j L^(-q) |chi^(q)((log r-L)/L)|. (8)

The angular derivatives have bounded coefficients. In polar coordinates the zeroth weighted norm squared equals

    pi a_L^2 int_L^(2L)
       (1+log sqrt(1+e^(2t)))^(2kappa)
       (1+e^(-2t))^(-1-gamma) chi((t-L)/L)^2 dt.           (9)

Uniformly for t/L in [1,2], the first factor divided by L^(2kappa) tends to (t/L)^(2kappa), and the second tends to 1. Since a_L^2 L^(2kappa+1)=1, the limit of (9) is

    pi int_1^2 s^(2kappa) chi(s-1)^2 ds >0.             (10)

Equation(8) bounds every higher term of (1) uniformly above by a constant. Therefore the norms ||f_L||_(X_kappa) are bounded above and bounded away from 0.

Because c gamma=1, the dilation defect is exactly

    (c X.D-1)f_L=(c a_L/L) r^gamma sin(5theta)
                                      chi'((log r-L)/L).

The same derivative estimates imply that its X_kappa norm is O(1/L). On the packet support, the term u_bar.D f_L and all its derivatives through order m have norm O(e^(-delta L)), by (2),(8). This uses the derivative bound through m+1 on f_L, rather than treating the transport as bounded on X_kappa.

It remains to estimate U[f_L].D rho_bar. Split the target region at T=e^(L/2). Outside the disc r<T, each Leibniz term from l derivatives, with j derivatives on U[f_L], has the target weight times the background factor bounded by

    C w_kappa R^(l-1-gamma) R^(gamma-1-(l-j))
       = C R^(-delta) w_kappa R^(j-1-gamma).

The bounded velocity estimate therefore gives an outer norm at most C e^(-delta L/2).

Inside the disc, the source and target are separated. Central parity gives the extra factor r at derivative order 0. Kernel integration using (8) at order 0 yields

    |U[f_L](X)| <= C a_L e^(-delta L) r,
    |D^j U[f_L](X)| <= C_j a_L e^(-(j-gamma)L), j>=1.

For r<=e^(L/2) and j>=1 the latter is at most

    C_j a_L e^(-delta L) R^(1-j).

Indeed e^(-(j-1)L) <= C R^(1-j) there. Equations(2) and the product rule now bound each weighted derivative of the coupling by

    C a_L e^(-delta L) w_kappa R^(-1).

Its squared radial integral on the disc is bounded by

    C a_L^2 e^(-2delta L) int_0^(L/2+1) (1+t)^(2kappa)dt.

For every fixed kappa this is at most a fixed polynomial in L times e^(-2delta L). Combining the regions gives the sufficient bound

    ||B f_L||_(X_kappa)
      <= C_kappa [L^(-1)+(1+L)^(2|kappa|+1)e^(-delta L/2)] ->0. (11)

No limit of the background or of its angular profile was needed; only the symbol estimates (2) were used.

Normalize f_L by its X_kappa norm. Its support, including the support of every derivative, leaves every compact set. The inner product with any fixed member of X_kappa tends to 0 by the weighted L2 tail estimate and Cauchy-Schwarz in each derivative component. Thus these packets are weakly null.

For d prescribed functionals, use d+1 packets with L=3^j n, j=0,...,d. Their supports are disjoint, so the normalized packets are orthonormal in (1). A real d by (d+1) matrix of their functional values has a unit null vector. The corresponding linear combination has norm 1, satisfies every constraint exactly, is supported beyond e^n, and has defect bounded by sqrt(d+1) times the largest defect in (11). This proves Theorem 1.

#### 4. Infinite-dimensional tail coordinates do not repair this remainder

Let E and F be arbitrary Banach spaces. They can contain finitely or infinitely many exponent and angular parameters. Give X_kappa direct-sum E and X_kappa direct-sum F their product norms. Let K:X_kappa->X_kappa and Q:X_kappa->F be bounded compact operators; Q=0 is allowed.

**Theorem 2.** Let T be any closed linear operator from a domain in X_kappa direct-sum E to X_kappa direct-sum F. Suppose its domain contains (h,0) for all compact smooth S1 functions with c[h]=0 and any prescribed finite list of linear constraints, and that on these pairs

    T(h,0)=(B h+K h,Q h).                               (12)

Then T is not upper semi-Fredholm. In particular it cannot be bijective with a bounded inverse. No assumptions on its columns acting on nonzero E coordinates are needed.

To prove this, take the packets from Theorem 1. The vectors v_n=(g_n,0) have norm 1 and are weakly null in the domain's ambient Banach space. Compactness gives K g_n->0 and Q g_n->0 strongly, so T v_n->0. The graph vectors(v_n,T v_n) are weakly null and have norms tending to 1 in the graph norm.

If T had finite-dimensional kernel and closed range, its domain with graph norm would be a Banach space, and the induced bijection from the quotient by the kernel onto its range would have bounded inverse. Hence

    dist_graph(v_n,ker T) <= C ||T v_n|| ->0.

A finite-dimensional subspace has a bounded projection in the graph norm. That projection sends the weakly null sequence to 0 in norm. The displayed distance estimate then forces v_n->0 in graph norm, contradicting its ambient norm 1. This proves the theorem. Finite codimension of the range is unnecessary.

The scope of (12) matters. Angular boundary equations and exponent boundary equations vanish on compactly supported remainders, so their Q is 0. Finite continuous bulk equations have finite-dimensional range and are compact; discontinuous scalar constraints can instead be imposed exactly by the construction in section 3. The theorem does not cover an auxiliary infinite-dimensional bulk observation Q that is noncompact and detects every packet. It also does not cover changing the remainder norm or imposing a radiation domain that omits the stated compact core.

#### 5. Which tails logarithmic weights include

Let zeta(r) be smooth, zero near 0 and equal to 1 for r>=2. Let Theta_0,...,Theta_N be angular S1 functions in H^m(S1), with Theta_N nonzero. Consider

    J(Theta_0,...,Theta_N)
       =zeta(r) r^gamma sum_(q=0)^N (log r)^q Theta_q(theta). (13)

Then

    J(Theta_0,...,Theta_N) belongs to X_kappa
                 if and only if kappa < -N-1/2.          (14)

For necessity, the zeroth term of (1) at infinity is comparable to

    int^infinity (1+t)^(2kappa)
                ||sum_(q=0)^N t^q Theta_q||_(L2(S1))^2 dt.

The angular norm divided by t^N tends to ||Theta_N||_2>0. Thus the integral has exactly the convergence threshold in (14). For sufficiency, every Cartesian derivative of order j<=m is a finite sum of r^(gamma-j) times angular H^(m-j) functions and log powers of degree at most N. Each weighted term is integrable under the strict inequality in (14). Smooth angular approximation followed by radial cutoff gives convergence in (1); derivatives of the radial cutoff are bounded by the same integrable tails. Hence the element belongs to the stated completion.

In particular, a pure leading tail enters the space when kappa<-1/2, and its first exponent variation r^gamma log r Theta enters only when kappa<-3/2. At both equality cases there is logarithmic divergence. Whenever a nonzero tail belongs to the completion, its usual asymptotic coefficient cannot be a continuous trace on X_kappa: compact radial cutoffs have zero asymptotic coefficient and converge in norm to that tail.

When kappa>=-1/2, no nonzero finite polynomial-log tail(13) belongs to X_kappa. Thus adjoining any finite collection of such angular coefficient spaces as external coordinates gives a unique distributional decomposition X_kappa plus J(E). This includes the unrestricted angular leading profile and its first exponent variation. If the augmented operator is closed and obeys(12), Theorem 2 still applies: merely adjoining these coordinates leaves the logarithmic annulus packets in the critical remainder. Strictly different power weights, a different bulk topology, or an explicitly different domain require separate analysis.

#### 6. Dependencies and verification scope

The canonical kernel, its local identity terms and strain formula are proved in parts P1.2 and P2. The dyadic derivative estimates and graph-domain mechanism extend part P64. The new points here are the logarithmic factors in every block, packet normalization(9), the arbitrary Banach tail-coordinate spaces in Theorem 2, and the exact membership thresholds(14). The argument is analytical; no numerical spectrum or existence inference is used.

The original checkpoint has c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248 and 0<gamma=1/c<1, so its exponent meets the hypothesis. Whether any chosen noncompact augmented columns define a closed operator with the assumed action is a separate domain question. The theorem is conditional on closedness and the compact-core action, not a claim that a proposed formula automatically has those properties.

### P68.2. Logarithmic endpoint obstruction

Verified 2026-10-28T11:26:27.134960+00:00, independent check 165.

For every real logarithmic exponent kappa, integer m>=3 and 0<gamma<1, the S1 completion with norm squared sum_j ||(1+log<r>)^kappa <r>^(j-1-gamma) D^j h||_2^2 has a bounded canonical velocity and a continuous strain trace. Nevertheless the normalized operator at c=1/gamma has weakly null unit compact packets with exact zero strain, all center jets zero and any finite list of linear constraints exactly zero. Their defect tends to zero. The logarithmic normalization is L^(-kappa-1/2); the nonlocal inner error has a polynomial logarithmic factor multiplied by exponential decay.

This obstruction survives arbitrary Banach tail-coordinate spaces, even infinite-dimensional ones, in every closed block realization whose action on zero-parameter compact pairs is (Bh+Kh,Qh), with K and Q compact. In particular adjoining angular or exponent boundary equations that vanish on compact remainders does not repair the unchanged critical remainder. Such a realization cannot have both finite-dimensional kernel and closed range. The theorem does not cover a noncompact bulk observation, a changed remainder topology or a domain that omits the specified core.

The exact tail-membership criterion is also proved: a nonzero polynomial-log tail r^gamma sum_(q=0)^N (log r)^q Theta_q belongs to this completion if and only if kappa<-N-1/2. Consequently a leading angular tail enters at kappa<-1/2, and the first exponent-log variation at kappa<-3/2; equality diverges. Whenever a tail enters the completion its nonzero asymptotic coefficient is not a continuous trace there. For kappa>=-1/2 the external finite-log angular decomposition is unique, but the block obstruction still applies. All 29 exact symbolic and source-exponent checks pass; the functional analysis is proved separately.

## P69. The sharp small-regularity cost of the strain trace

### P69.1. The sharp small-regularity cost of the strain trace

Status: analytical derivation. This result concerns the singular functional, not an inverse or an existence theorem. It identifies an unavoidable loss in the actual weighted norm while keeping its low component and weights.

#### 1. Fourier convention and exact unweighted trace norms

Use

    h_hat(xi)=int exp(-i X.xi)h(X)dX,
    h(X)=(2pi)^(-2)int exp(i X.xi)h_hat(xi)dxi.

All function spaces are real, even in x and odd in y. Put

    b[h]=h_y(0), c[h]=partial_y R1^2 h(0),
    R1^2 multiplier=-xi_1^2/|xi|^2,
    ||h||_(H^(2+s))=||(1-Delta)^((2+s)/2)h||_2, s>0.

Both traces are continuous on H^(2+s). In polar frequency coordinates xi=r(cos theta,sin theta), their symbols are

    ell_b=i r sin theta,
    ell_c=-i r sin theta cos^2 theta
          =-(i r/4)(sin theta+sin(3theta)).              (1)

Thus the renormalized strain c+b/4 has pure angular harmonic 3.

**Theorem 1.** The Gram matrix of the two trace functionals in the dual of H^(2+s), in the order (b,c), is

    [1/(8pi s(s+1))] [[1,-1/4],[-1/4,1/8]].             (2)

Consequently the exact norm of c is

    ||c||_(H^(2+s))* =1/[8sqrt(pi s(s+1))].             (3)

On the closed subspace b[h]=0, its exact norm is

    ||c|_(ker b)||=1/[8sqrt(2pi s(s+1))].               (4)

These are attained dual norms on the indicated Hilbert spaces, not merely sufficient constants.

To prove(2), the dual inner product of two symbols ell_1,ell_2 is

    (2pi)^(-2)int ell_1(xi) conjugate(ell_2(xi))
                                      (1+|xi|^2)^(-2-s)dxi.

The radial integral equals

    int_0^infinity r^3(1+r^2)^(-2-s)dr=1/[2s(s+1)],     (5)

by t=r^2 and integration of t(1+t)^(-2-s). The angular integrals are

    int sin^2 theta=pi,
    int sin^2 theta cos^2 theta=pi/4,
    int sin^2 theta cos^4 theta=pi/8.

This gives every entry of (2), including the negative covariance. Riesz representatives have Fourier transforms proportional to the conjugate symbols times (1+r^2)^(-2-s), and belong to the real S1 subspace. The Hilbert-space norm is attained by the relevant representative. Since the representative of c+b/4 is orthogonal to that of b, restriction to ker b removes precisely the squared covariance divided by ||b||^2. The remaining variance is 1/[128pi s(s+1)], proving(4). Equivalently use the pure harmonic 3 symbol in (1).

The identity c=-b/4+(c+b/4) agrees with the local term and the renormalized harmonic 3 kernel in part P2. Removing the center jet reduces the exact squared trace norm by a factor 2. It does not remove its divergence as s decreases to 0.

#### 2. The weighted norm used in the conditional theorem

For R>=1 define

    w_R=(1+|X|^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    omega0=<r>^(-6/5), omega1=<r>^(-1/5),
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), <r>=(1+r^2)^(1/2),
    L_R(g)=||w_R g||_(Hdot^-1),
    E_R(g)^2=||omega2 D^2 g||_2^2
                 +2^22||omega1 Dg||_2^2+2^53 L_R(g)^2,
    N_(s,R)(h)=E_R(J^s h), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2).

D^2 is the full ordered Cartesian Hessian, so its unweighted Fourier square is |xi|^4 |g_hat|^2. The spaces are completions of compact smooth S1 functions, as in parts P17, P62 and P63. Use 0<s<=2^-12. The bounded trace extensions follow below and agree with ordinary traces on the smooth core.

Let C_R(s) be the norm of c on N_(s,R), and let C_R^0(s) be its norm restricted to the closed subspace b[h]=0.

**Theorem 2.** Uniformly for all R>=1,

    sqrt(s) C_R(s) -> 1/(8sqrt(pi)),
    sqrt(s) C_R^0(s) -> 1/(8sqrt(2pi))                 (6)

as s decreases to 0. At s=0, c is unbounded on the compact smooth S1 core in E_R, even on the subspace b[h]=0. The unboundedness holds for each R>=1, and the construction has estimates uniform in R.

Uniformity in (6) means that the supremum over R>=1 of the absolute difference tends to zero. No finite-s numerical upper bound is asserted by this asymptotic theorem. In particular it does not replace the explicit constants in the conditional inverse theorem.

#### 3. Uniform control of low frequencies

We first record two elementary estimates that retain the actual low norm. For every compact S1 g,

    ||omega0 g||_2 <= E_R(g)/2048,                     (7)
    L_R(g) <= ||r g||_2.                              (8)

For (7), put a=omega0^2/w_R. For R>=1,

    a<=omega1, |Da|<5omega0.

The negative-order dual pairing yields

    P0(g)^2<=L_R(g)[P1(g)+5P0(g)].

Use 5L_R P0<=(1/2)P0^2+(25/2)L_R^2 and then 2L_R P1<=P1^2+L_R^2. This gives P0^2<=P1^2+26L_R^2. Since 26*2^22<2^53, (7) follows. This is the proof in part P62 and is uniform in R.

For (8), the test functions can be projected onto the centrally odd parity class. Their angular Fourier frequencies have absolute value at least 1, so

    ||phi/r||_2<=||Dphi||_2.

Cauchy-Schwarz in int (w_R g)phi gives L_R(g)<=||r w_R g||_2<=||r g||_2. This argument does not multiply an Hdot^-1 distribution by r.

Choose a fixed smooth radial cutoff chi_0 equal to 1 for |xi|<=1 and 0 for |xi|>=2. The functions

    q_s(xi)=chi_0(xi)(1+|xi|^2)^(-s/2), 0<=s<=2^-12,

are uniformly bounded in every Schwartz seminorm. Write phi_s for their inverse Fourier transforms. If ell is any one of ell_b,ell_c,ell_c+ell_b/4, the low-frequency kernel

    K_s=F^(-1)(ell q_s)

satisfies

    |K_s(X)|<=C<r>^(-3)                               (9)

with one constant uniform in s. For ell_b this follows directly from Schwartz bounds. For ell_c, apply the second-order Riesz kernel, including its identity term, to partial_y phi_s. Its input has integral zero. On |Y|<=|X|/2, subtract the kernel value at X and use its derivative O(|X|^-3), bounding the first moment of partial_y phi_s. On the complementary region, Schwartz decay controls the part away from the kernel singularity. Near the singularity, its zero angular mean permits subtraction of partial_y phi_s(X); the remaining integral is bounded by a local first derivative of that Schwartz function. The identity term has Schwartz decay. These bounds are uniform because all input seminorms are uniform. They prove(9). The third symbol is their fixed linear combination.

Since <r>^(6/5) <r>^-3 is square integrable on the plane, (7),(9) imply

    |low_trace(J^-s g)|<=C E_R(g),                     (10)

uniformly in s and R. The kernel can be paired with any element of E_R by weighted L2 duality. No unweighted L2 norm of g is assumed.

#### 4. The exact high-frequency coefficient

Write each symbol as i r p(theta), ignoring its harmless sign. For b, c and c+b/4 the angular square integrals A_p are respectively

    pi, pi/8, pi/16.

On the compact smooth core, Plancherel and Cauchy-Schwarz against the Fourier transform of D^2g give

    |high_trace(J^-s g)| <= A_s(p) ||D^2g||_2,
    A_s(p)^2=[A_p/(4pi^2)] I_s,
    I_s=int_0^infinity (1-chi_0(r))^2
                                      r^-1(1+r^2)^(-s)dr. (11)

The integral is finite for s>0. Its transition interval is bounded, and on r>=2 its integrand lies between (5/4)^(-s)r^-1-2s and r^-1-2s. Therefore

    I_s=1/(2s)+O(1) as s decreases to 0.                (12)

The O(1) constant depends on the fixed cutoff, not on R. Since omega2>=1, ||D^2g||_2<=E_R(g). Equations(10)-(12) prove continuity of all three traces and

    C_R(s)<=sqrt(A_p/(8pi^2 s)+O(1))+C,

using A_p=pi/8. On ker b use c=c+b/4, with A_p=pi/16. This proves the two uniform upper limits in (6). It also constructs b as a bounded trace on N_(s,R), so the restricted subspace is closed.

The high-frequency calculation is justified on the core and extends by this estimate. It never presumes that the weighted-space element has an integrable Fourier transform at zero. Only the second derivative of g is used in the high-frequency pairing.

#### 5. Matching lower sequences in the weighted completion

Let chi_1(r) be smooth, zero for r<=1 and equal to 1 for r>=2. For 0<s<=2^-12 choose either

    p(theta)=sin theta cos^2 theta,
    or p(theta)=sin(3theta)/4,

and define

    h_hat_s(xi)=i p(theta) chi_1(r) r^(-3-2s),
    g_s=J^s h_s.                                    (13)

The Fourier transform has the reality and S1 parity conditions. In the second choice b[h_s]=0 exactly by angular orthogonality. In both choices the c-symbol pairs positively with i p, with angular integral A_p equal to the corresponding square integral pi/8 or pi/16. Consequently

    c[h_s]=[A_p/(4pi^2)] int chi_1(r)r^(-1-2s)dr
           = A_p/(8pi^2 s)+O(1).                     (14)

The integral defining every first derivative at zero is absolutely convergent when s>0, so these are genuine point traces.

The unweighted top norm is

    ||D^2g_s||_2^2
       =[A_p/(4pi^2)] int chi_1(r)^2
                               (1+r^2)^s r^(-1-4s)dr
       =A_p/(8pi^2 s)+O(1).                          (15)

All constants in the following bounds are uniform for 0<s<=2^-12:

    ||Dg_s||_2 + ||r g_s||_2 + ||r D^2g_s||_2 <=C.     (16)

Indeed, outside the fixed transition annulus the Fourier transform of g_s is O(r^-3-s), with its k-th frequency derivative O(r^-3-s-k) for k=1,2, with uniform angular constants. Plancherel gives the first two assertions. For the last, differentiate each component xi_i xi_j g_hat_s once in frequency. It is O(r^-2-s), whose square is integrable uniformly. The transition annulus contributes a uniform finite amount.

Concavity of t^(4/5) gives

    0<=(1+4r^2)^(4/5)-1 <=(16/5)r^2.

Thus the weighted top norm differs from (15) by at most (16/5)||r D^2g_s||_2^2. The P1 contribution is bounded by 2^22||Dg_s||_2^2, and (8) bounds the low contribution by 2^53||r g_s||_2^2. Hence

    E_R(g_s)^2=A_p/(8pi^2 s)+O(1),                    (17)

uniformly in R>=1. The large fixed low-energy coefficient remains in the O(1) term; it is not discarded or treated as small at the actual value of s.

For each positive s these elements belong to the stated completion. To see this explicitly, g_s has two weighted derivatives and r g_s in L2 by (15),(16). Smooth compact radial cutoffs converge in all derivative terms, using the integrable tails and their derivative bounds. They converge in L_R by (8). Subsequent mollification gives a compact smooth S1 approximating sequence in E_R. The onto isometry J^s:N_(s,R)->E_R established in part P17 then gives h_s in N_(s,R), with norm E_R(g_s). Alternatively the same Bessel localization proof applies to this particular approximating sequence. This step uses the actual completion, not a larger Fourier-defined surrogate.

Dividing(14) by the square root of (17) proves

    sqrt(s) c[h_s]/N_(s,R)(h_s) ->sqrt(A_p/(8pi^2)),

uniformly in R. The two choices of p give exactly the lower limits in (6), proving Theorem 2's asymptotic statement.

#### 6. Unboundedness at zero regularity even after jet removal

Fix p(theta)=sin(3theta)/4. Choose smooth high and low radial cutoffs to define a Fourier-annular Schwartz function h_M by

    h_hat_M=i p(theta) r^-3 chi_1(r) chi_0(r/M), M>=4.

Its center jet b[h_M] is zero. Direct radial integration gives

    c[h_M]=[1/(64pi)] log M+O(1),
    ||D^2h_M||_2^2=[1/(64pi)] log M+O(1).             (18)

The first-derivative, r h_M and r D^2h_M norms stay bounded uniformly in M. The derivatives of the outer cutoff are supported at r comparable to M and contribute only bounded, in fact vanishing, terms to those lower integrals. The same argument as(17) gives

    E_R(h_M)^2=[1/(64pi)] log M+O(1)

uniformly in R>=1. Thus c[h_M]/E_R(h_M) tends to infinity like sqrt(log M/(64pi)). Each h_M is Schwartz; smooth physical cutoffs equal to 1 near zero preserve b[h_M]=0 and converge in E_R. The strain also converges, since these are Schwartz tails and the strain kernel is O(r^-3) there. Selecting sufficiently large physical cutoffs for each M produces the claimed compact smooth counterexample sequence. No strain trace on the E_R completion is presumed in this argument.

#### 7. Scope and dependencies

The exact H^(2+s) norm calculation is independent of the IPM background. The weighted asymptotic uses the actual norms of the conditional theorem and the already proved Bessel-completion isometry. The low-frequency estimate uses the canonical kernel and parity, with the identity term retained. The only asymptotic parameter is s decreasing to 0; the theorem is uniform in the weight radius but does not give an optimized explicit bound at the chosen finite s.

The result explains why a positive fractional surplus is required to obtain a strain trace in this norm, even after fixing the center y-jet. It does not show that any particular sufficient inverse constant is sharp, remove derivative loss from nonlinear transport, or improve an actual residual certificate.

## P70. A logarithmic replacement for the fractional strain regularization

### P70.1. A logarithmic replacement for the fractional strain regularization

The strain loss in part P69 does not require a power of frequency. A logarithmic gain suffices, with a sharp threshold. The result below supplies a complete trace space and counterexamples at its endpoint. It does not transfer the transport inverse or the nonlinear closure theorem to that space.

#### 1. Spaces, traces and statements

Use the Fourier convention

    h_hat(xi)=int exp(-i X.xi)h(X)dX,
    h(X)=(2pi)^(-2)int exp(i X.xi)h_hat(xi)dxi.

All scalar functions are real, even in x and odd in y. Write

    J=(1-Delta)^(1/2),
    Q_beta=(1+log(1-Delta))^beta,
    q_beta(xi)=(1+log(1+|xi|^2))^beta,
    b[h]=h_y(0), c[h]=partial_y R1^2 h(0).

Here the logarithm in Q_beta is defined by the displayed Fourier multiplier, not by a pointwise logarithm of a function. On compact smooth functions the symbols of b,c are

    ell_b=i r sin(theta),
    ell_c=-i r sin(theta) cos(theta)^2
          =-(i r/4)(sin(theta)+sin(3theta)).             (1)

Thus c+b/4 has pure angular harmonic 3. The identity term in R1^2 is retained.

Let H_beta be the completion of compact smooth S1 functions in

    ||h||_(H_beta)=||J^2 Q_beta h||_2.

For every R>=1 let E_R be the completion of the same core in

    E_R(g)^2=||omega2 D^2 g||_2^2
                +2^22||omega1 Dg||_2^2+2^53 L_R(g)^2,
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10),
    L_R(g)=||w_R g||_(Hdot^-1),
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10).

The full ordered Cartesian Hessian is used. Define N_(beta,R)^log as the completion of compact smooth S1 functions in E_R(Q_beta h). Section 2 proves that this completion is isometric to E_R under Q_beta. It is not an unidentified larger distribution space.

**Theorem 1.** The functional c is bounded on H_beta if and only if beta>1/2. For beta>1/2 put

    D_beta=int_0^infinity (1-exp(-t))(1+t)^(-2beta)dt
          =1/(2beta-1)-e Gamma(1-2beta,1),               (2)

where Gamma(a,1)=int_1^infinity exp(-v)v^(a-1)dv. The exact dual Gram matrix of (b,c) is

    [D_beta/(8pi)] [[1,-1/4],[-1/4,1/8]].              (3)

In particular

    ||c||_(H_beta)*=sqrt(D_beta)/(8sqrt(pi)),
    ||c|_(ker b)||=sqrt(D_beta)/(8sqrt(2pi)).            (4)

The norms are attained in the indicated Hilbert spaces. For beta<=1/2, c is unbounded even on compact smooth functions with b[h]=0.

**Theorem 2.** For every R>=1, c extends continuously to N_(beta,R)^log if and only if beta>1/2. In that range b is also continuous, h and U[h] have classical first derivatives locally, and c agrees with partial_y U_2[h](0). If C_R^log(beta) is its norm and C_R^{log,0}(beta) its norm on ker b, then

    sqrt(2beta-1) C_R^log(beta) ->1/(8sqrt(pi)),
    sqrt(2beta-1) C_R^{log,0}(beta) ->1/(8sqrt(2pi))      (5)

as beta decreases to 1/2, uniformly over R>=1. For beta<=1/2 the unboundedness already holds on compact smooth functions with b[h]=0.

Uniformity in (5) means convergence after taking the supremum over R>=1 of the absolute error. These are asymptotics, not optimized finite-beta weighted constants.

**Theorem 3.** For every finite real beta and every 0<alpha<=1 there is no bound

    [Dh]_(C^alpha(B_1)) <= C ||h||_(N_(beta,R)^log)       (6)

on the compact smooth S1 core, even with b[h]=0. The same is true with H_beta on the right. The counterexamples have norms bounded uniformly in R>=1. Here C^alpha in (6) means the first-difference seminorm.

#### 2. The weighted completion and its low frequencies

Put omega0=(1+r^2)^(-3/5) and P0(g)=||omega0 g||_2. The retained low term gives

    P0(g)<=E_R(g)/2048,        L_R(g)<=||r g||_2.         (7)

For completeness, set a=omega0^2/w_R. For R>=1,

    a<=omega1, |Da|<5omega0.

Negative-order duality tested against ag yields P0^2<=L_R(P1+5P0), where P1=||omega1 Dg||_2. Twice using the scalar inequality 2uv<=u^2+v^2 gives P0^2<=P1^2+26L_R^2. Since 26*2^22<2^53, the first assertion follows. For the second, centrally odd test functions satisfy ||phi/r||_2<=||Dphi||_2 by their nonzero angular Fourier frequencies. Pair w_R g against phi and use w_R<=1.

Thus E_R embeds continuously in tempered distributions. Both q_beta and its reciprocal are smooth Fourier multipliers preserving the Schwartz space: all their derivatives have at most polynomial growth. They therefore act on tempered distributions. The pullback Q_beta^(-1)E_R is a Hilbert space. It is exactly the stated core completion. Indeed, compact smooth functions are dense in E_R by definition. Their images under Q_beta^(-1) are Schwartz. A Schwartz function can be approximated in the Schwartz topology by smooth compact radial cutoffs, preserving S1 parity. Applying Q_beta to these cutoffs converges again in the Schwartz topology. The E_R norm is continuous on that topology, since the weights grow at most polynomially and L_R<=||r g||_2. This proves density of Q_beta applied to the compact core in E_R, and hence the onto isometry. The same argument identifies H_beta with its Fourier-defined Hilbert realization.

Fix a smooth radial chi_0 equal to 1 on r<=1 and 0 on r>=2. For beta in any fixed compact interval,

    phi_beta=F^(-1)(chi_0 q_beta^(-1))

is uniformly Schwartz. For any order-one symbol arising from Dh or DU[h], the low-frequency kernel is bounded by C<r>^(-3), uniformly in beta. For Dh it is Schwartz. For DU, write it as a second-order Riesz transform applied to a derivative of phi_beta. That derivative has zero integral. Subtract the Riesz kernel at X on |Y|<=|X|/2 and use its derivative bound C|X|^-3 and the first absolute moment of the input. On the complement, its Schwartz decay controls the nonsingular part. Near the kernel singularity its zero angular mean allows subtraction of the input value and a local derivative bound. The local identity term has Schwartz decay. This proves the claimed bound, and the same reasoning after another derivative gives local smoothness of the low-frequency output.

Because <r>^(6/5)<r>^-3 is square integrable, (7) gives

    |low_trace(Q_beta^(-1)g)| <= C E_R(g),              (8)

uniformly in R and in beta on a fixed compact interval. No unweighted L2 bound for g is used.

The undifferentiated low velocity requires the canonical parity normalization. If K_beta is the order-zero Riesz kernel convolved with phi_beta, then K_beta(X)=O(<X>^-2) and its derivative is O(<X>^-3). Define this part of the velocity by

    U_low[h](X)=int [K_beta(X-Y)-K_beta(-Y)]g(Y)dY.

For X in a compact set the bracket is O(<Y>^-3) at infinity and is locally smooth, so weighted L2 duality defines the integral and all its X derivatives. It is zero at X=0. This agrees with the usual velocity on the compact core because the removed term pairs to zero by central oddness. The high-frequency undifferentiated field is continuous by Cauchy-Schwarz against D^2g, since int_1^infinity r^-3 q_beta(r)^-2 dr is finite. Together these specify the canonical field, with no arbitrary constant or harmonic velocity. Its first derivatives are exactly the low and high traces estimated above.

#### 3. Exact Hilbert-space calculation

The dual inner product of two order-one trace symbols is

    (2pi)^(-2) int ell_1 conjugate(ell_2)
            (1+r^2)^(-2)(1+log(1+r^2))^(-2beta) dxi.

Its radial factor is

    int_0^infinity r^3(1+r^2)^(-2)
                       (1+log(1+r^2))^(-2beta)dr
       =(1/2)int_0^infinity(1-exp(-t))(1+t)^(-2beta)dt, (9)

using t=log(1+r^2). It is finite exactly when beta>1/2. The angular integrals for b^2,bc,c^2 are pi,-pi/4,pi/8. This proves (3). Substitution v=1+t in the exponential part gives (2).

The Riesz representatives have Fourier transforms equal to conjugate trace symbols times the reciprocal squared Hilbert weight. They lie in the real S1 subspace. The representative of c+b/4 is orthogonal to that of b. Projecting out b therefore divides the squared c norm by 2, proving(4) and attainment. Unboundedness below the threshold, including on the zero-jet compact core, is proved constructively in section 5.

A useful exact comparison at beta=1 is

    124/209 < D_1 < 100/167 < 3/5.                     (10)

Here D_1=int_0^infinity exp(-t)/(1+t)dt by integration by parts. To check(10) without an unevaluated special function, set

    R_0(t)=1-4t+3t^2-(2/3)t^3+t^4/24,
    R_1(t)=5-10t+5t^2-(5/6)t^3+t^4/24,
    P_j(t)=R_j(t)/R_j(-1),
    q_-(t)=(1-P_0(t)^2)/(1+t),
    q_+(t)=(1+t P_1(t)^2)/(1+t).

Both q's are polynomials because their numerators vanish at t=-1. For t>=0,

    q_-(t)<=1/(1+t)<=q_+(t).

Integrating every monomial against exp(-t) by repeated integration by parts gives int exp(-t)q_-=124/209 and int exp(-t)q_+=100/167. Both inequalities are strict since their nonnegative errors are not zero almost everywhere. In combination with pi>31/10, this proves the simple unweighted bounds

    ||c||_(H_1)*<1/18,      ||c|_(ker b)||<1/25.        (11)

For an elementary rational check of pi>31/10, integrate the finite geometric identity for 1/(1+t^2) on [0,1]. The 32-term alternating sum sum_(n=0)^31(-1)^n/(2n+1) is a strict lower bound for pi/4 and exceeds 31/40. No bound (11) is asserted for the weighted norm.

#### 4. Weighted upper bounds and the sharp limiting coefficient

For an order-one symbol i r p(theta), write A_p=int_0^(2pi)|p|^2. Its high-frequency trace pairs with D^2g in L2 and has norm at most

    {A_p/(4pi^2) I_beta}^(1/2) ||D^2g||_2,
    I_beta=int_0^infinity (1-chi_0(r))^2
                  dr/[r(1+log(1+r^2))^(2beta)].         (12)

This follows directly by Cauchy-Schwarz and Plancherel; the full Hessian has square multiplier r^4. The integral is finite exactly when beta>1/2. Since omega2>=1, (8),(12) give all claimed trace bounds in that range. High-frequency first derivatives of h and U[h] have integrable Fourier transforms by the same Cauchy-Schwarz estimate. Dominated convergence under translations gives their continuity. Their low-frequency parts are locally smooth by section 2. Thus the extended traces are classical first derivatives of the canonical fields.

Let epsilon=2beta-1 decrease to 0. On r>=2, the substitution v=1+log(1+r^2) gives

    dr/r=dv/[2(1-exp(1-v))].

The extra factor minus 1 has exponential decay. The finite transition interval is bounded uniformly for 1/2<=beta<=1. Therefore

    I_beta=1/(2epsilon)+O(1).                          (13)

The angular square integrals for c and c+b/4 are pi/8 and pi/16. Equations(8),(12),(13) prove the uniform upper limits in (5), using c=c+b/4 on ker b. The low-frequency constant contributes O(sqrt(epsilon)) after this rescaling.

For the lower limits choose a smooth radial chi_1, zero for r<=1 and 1 for r>=2, and either

    p=sin(theta)cos(theta)^2,       or p=sin(3theta)/4.

For beta>1/2 define

    h_hat_beta=i p(theta) chi_1(r) r^-3 q_beta(r)^-2,
    g_beta=Q_beta h_beta.

These have the reality and S1 symmetries. For the second choice b[h_beta]=0 exactly. The c-symbol pairs with these functions with angular factor A_p equal to pi/8 or pi/16. With epsilon=2beta-1,

    c[h_beta]=A_p/(8pi^2 epsilon)+O(1),
    ||D^2 g_beta||_2^2=A_p/(8pi^2 epsilon)+O(1).        (14)

The first-derivative trace integral is absolutely convergent for beta>1/2. Uniformly for 1/2<beta<=1,

    ||Dg_beta||_2+||r g_beta||_2+||r D^2g_beta||_2<=C.  (15)

Outside the fixed transition annulus the Fourier transform of g_beta is r^-3 times q_beta^-1 times a fixed smooth angular function. Each frequency derivative adds a factor bounded by C/r, uniformly in this beta range. Plancherel proves (15); for its last term differentiate each xi_i xi_j g_hat once. The square of the resulting O(r^-2 q_beta^-1) function is uniformly integrable.

The concavity estimate

    0<=(1+4r^2)^(4/5)-1<=(16/5)r^2

and (7),(15) show that all weighted and lower-order contributions differ from the top term in (14) by O(1), uniformly in R. In particular

    E_R(g_beta)^2=A_p/(8pi^2 epsilon)+O(1).             (16)

The fixed coefficients 2^22 and 2^53 are retained in this O(1); they are not treated as small. Physical cutoff and mollification approximate g_beta in E_R by (15),(7), and the onto isometry from section 2 puts h_beta in the stated space. Dividing the first line of (14) by the square root of (16) proves the two matching lower limits in (5).

#### 5. Counterexamples at and below the logarithmic threshold

Fix beta<=1/2 and p=sin(3theta)/4. For M>=4 take the Fourier-annular Schwartz function

    h_hat_M=i p(theta) chi_1(r) chi_0(r/M) r^-3 q_beta(r)^-2.

Its center y-jet is zero. Set

    I(M)=int_2^M dr/[r(1+log(1+r^2))^(2beta)].

The angular factor is A_p=pi/16. As M tends to infinity,

    c[h_M]=(1/(64pi)) I(M)(1+o(1)),
    ||D^2 Q_beta h_M||_2^2=(1/(64pi)) I(M)(1+o(1)).    (17)

The fixed lower transition contributes O(1), and the upper transition M<=r<=2M contributes O((1+log M)^(-2beta)), which is o(I(M)). The same estimate remains true for fixed negative beta. Direct integration after v=1+log(1+r^2) yields

    I(M) ~ [1+log(1+M^2)]^(1-2beta)/[2(1-2beta)]
                                                       if beta<1/2,
    I(M) ~ (1/2)log(1+log(1+M^2))                      if beta=1/2. (18)

The three lower norms in (15), with g_M=Q_beta h_M, remain bounded as M grows, for each fixed beta. Powers of log do not prevent the radial integrability of the additional inverse powers of r. Derivatives of chi_0(r/M) have the same bound on its support. Therefore both E_R(g_M)^2 and ||J^2g_M||_2^2 equal the second expression in (17) up to a relative o(1), uniformly in R for the former. The ratio of c[h_M] to either norm tends to infinity.

These are counterexamples on the compact core as well. For fixed M, physical smooth cutoffs converge to h_M in the Schwartz topology; Q_beta preserves that topology, so both norms converge. Take cutoffs equal to 1 near 0, which preserve b[h_M]=0. The strain converges by the r^-3 kernel at infinity and the Schwartz decay, or by continuity of the Fourier functional on Schwartz space. Choosing a sufficiently large cutoff for each M proves the asserted core unboundedness. No strain trace on the endpoint completion is assumed in this argument.

#### 6. No positive gradient Hoelder exponent from this logarithmic norm

Choose a nonzero real S1 Schwartz function phi whose Fourier transform is supported in 1<=|xi|<=2 and has angular factor i sin(3theta). Then Dphi(0)=0. For N>=2 define

    h_N(X)=phi(NX)/[N(1+log N^2)^beta].

The seminorm on B_1 satisfies

    [Dh_N]_(C^alpha(B_1)) >= c_alpha N^alpha/(1+log N^2)^beta, (19)

for all sufficiently large N. Indeed, choose two fixed points where Dphi differs and rescale them by 1/N. The right side diverges for every alpha>0.

On the fixed annulus 1<=|xi|<=2, the multiplier

    m_N(xi)=[(1+log(1+N^2|xi|^2))/(1+log N^2)]^beta

has all derivatives bounded uniformly in N. If Phi_N is the inverse transform of m_N phi_hat, the functions Phi_N are uniformly Schwartz and

    Q_beta h_N=N^-1 Phi_N(NX).

Consequently ||D^2 Q_beta h_N||_2 is bounded; ||r D^2 Q_beta h_N||_2 and ||D Q_beta h_N||_2 are O(N^-1); and ||r Q_beta h_N||_2 is O(N^-3). Concavity and (7) now give a bound on E_R(Q_beta h_N) independent of N and R. The unweighted H_beta norm is bounded as well. Physical cutoffs, chosen equal to 1 on B_1, preserve(19), S1 parity and the zero jet, and approximate each norm arbitrarily closely. This proves Theorem 3.

#### 7. Scope

The logarithmic space gives a continuous strain and a classical local C1 realization when beta>1/2, while avoiding every positive power of frequency in its definition. Its sharp threshold is independent of the background and preserves the actual weighted lower component. The exact constants (4),(11) concern the separate unweighted Hilbert norm; (5) concerns the actual weighted completion.

No positive gradient Hoelder exponent follows, as Theorem 3 shows. The earlier local singular moment, commutator constants, transport semigroup, nonlinear iteration, forcing membership and certified residual thresholds have not been transferred to this new space. Ordinary pointwise principal-value convergence of a particular sharply truncated kernel is not asserted solely from C1 regularity; c is the canonical velocity-derivative trace constructed above. A full inverse or nonlinear theorem in this logarithmic realization remains open.

## P71. The logarithmic strain space retains the low residual obstruction

### P71.1. The logarithmic strain space retains the low residual obstruction

Status: analytic proof written before the arithmetic check. This result transfers low-norm lower bounds. It does not transfer a transport inverse or a nonlinear existence threshold.

#### 1. Statement and spaces

All scalar functions are real and centrally odd; the S1 parity, even in x and odd in y, is a permitted closed subspace. Let R>=1 and put

    w_R(X)=(1+|X|^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    L_R(h)=||w_R h||_(Hdot^-1(R^2)),
    J=(1-Delta)^(1/2),
    Q_beta=(1+log(1-Delta))^beta.

The homogeneous negative norm has the Fourier convention of part P70 and equals ||D(-Delta)^-1(w_R h)||_2. The low space is the completion of the compact smooth centrally odd core. Multiplication by w_R identifies it with the centrally odd homogeneous negative space, as a subspace of tempered distributions. The canonical representative has no additive constant. Let E_R and N_(beta,R)^log be the actual weighted energy and its pullback by Q_beta from part P70:

    E_R(g)^2=||(1+4r^2)^(2/5)D^2g||_2^2
                +2^22||(1+r^2)^(-1/10)Dg||_2^2
                +2^53 L_R(g)^2,
    N_(beta,R)^log(h)=E_R(Q_beta h).

The Hessian is the full ordered Cartesian tensor. Define

    D_R=41/(5R)+34/R^2+218/R^3+3696/(5R^4)+1584/R^5.  (1)

**Theorem.** For every 0<beta<=1 the Fourier operator B_beta=Q_beta^(-1) extends continuously on the low space, agrees there with its distributional multiplier, and satisfies

    L_R(B_beta g)<=(1+D_R)L_R(g).                    (2)

Consequently every h in N_(beta,R)^log satisfies

    L_R(h)<=(1+D_R)2^(-53/2) N_(beta,R)^log(h).        (3)

For R>=2^31, D_R<2^-27. Thus

    N_(beta,R)^log(h)>=2^(53/2)L_R(h)/(1+D_R)
                       > 2^(53/2)L_R(h)/(1+2^-27)    (4)

whenever L_R(h)>0. These bounds are uniform in beta throughout 0<beta<=1. The range 1/2<beta<=1 additionally has the continuous strain and local C1 realization proved in part P70.

For the exact state 131 residual F_131 and exact refit residuals F_Mpen2,F_d2, interpreted with norm+infinity when they are not in the logarithmic completion, (4) gives the certified lower bounds in RESULTS.md. The annular input bounds are those independently verified in parts P51 and P52. Logarithmic-space membership is not an extra conclusion of this theorem.

#### 2. A positive probability kernel and its moments

For a>0 and beta>0, substitution v=au in the defining gamma integral gives

    a^(-beta)=Gamma(beta)^(-1) int_0^infinity u^(beta-1)exp(-au)du.

Apply this with a=1+log(1+|xi|^2). Since J^(-2u) has its positive heat-mixture kernel,

    B_beta=Gamma(beta)^(-1) int_0^infinity
                 u^(beta-1)exp(-u) J^(-2u)du.          (5)

Both mixture parameters are positive. Tonelli's theorem shows that the resulting kernel k_beta is radial, nonnegative, and has integral 1. Equivalently, take U with gamma density of shape beta and rate 1, then T conditional on U=u with gamma density of shape u and rate 1. The spatial kernel conditional on T=t is (4pi t)^(-1)exp(-r^2/(4t)). Direct polar integration gives its even moments

    int r^(2n)(4pi t)^(-1)exp(-r^2/(4t))dX=4^n n! t^n.

Conditional integration in T gives E[T^n|U]=(U)_n, the rising factorial. Integration in U gives E[U^j]=(beta)_j, all by gamma integration by parts. In particular, for M_j=int |X|^j k_beta(X)dX,

    M_2=4beta,
    M_4=32beta(beta+2),
    M_6=384beta(beta^2+6beta+7).                       (6)

For 0<beta<=1 these are at most 4,96,5376. Cauchy-Schwarz with the probability measure k_beta(X)dX gives

    M_1<=2, M_2<=4, M_3<=sqrt(384)<20,
    M_4<=96, M_5<=sqrt(516096)<720.                   (7)

The even-moment polynomials have positive coefficients, so no monotonicity assertion about a changing distribution is needed. The same calculation for arbitrary n shows that all polynomial moments are finite. Formula (5) also proves that the Fourier multiplier has absolute value at most 1.

#### 3. The weighted cancellation identity

This argument records the positive-kernel form of part P47, rather than substituting beta for its fractional Bessel parameter. Put sigma=11/5, a=Dlog w_R=-sigma X/(R^2+r^2), and T=w_R B_beta w_R^(-1). For a compact smooth density g let q=D(-Delta)^(-1)(w_R g), so q is centrally even, -div q=w_R g, and ||q||_2=L_R(g). The exact distributional identity is

    w_R B_beta g=B_beta(w_R g)-div((T-B_beta)q)+[a,T]q,
    [a,T]q=a.Tq-T(a.q).                              (8)

One derives it from -div(w_R^(-1)q)=g+w_R^(-1)a.q and the commutation of B_beta with derivatives. In particular, the two occurrences of a are essential.

The weight ratio and its reciprocal are bounded by (1+|X-Y|/R)^3. Therefore Young's inequality gives

    ||(T-B_beta)q||_2
        <=(3M_1/R+3M_2/R^2+M_3/R^3)||q||_2.          (9)

The last term of (8) is centrally odd. For every such scalar f,

    ||f||_(Hdot^-1)<=||r f||_2,                       (10)

provided the right side is finite. To see this, project a smooth test function onto its centrally odd part. Its angular Fourier frequencies are nonzero, so the circle Poincare inequality gives ||phi/r||_2<=||Dphi||_2; duality proves (10).

The eigenvalues of Da at Z are -sigma/(R^2+|Z|^2) in the tangential direction and -sigma(R^2-|Z|^2)/(R^2+|Z|^2)^2 in the radial direction. Thus |Da(Z)|_op<=sigma/(R^2+|Z|^2). For Z on the segment between Y and X, writing t=|X-Y| gives

    |X||Da(Z)|_op<=sigma(1/(2R)+t/R^2).

The segment formula and the weight ratio yield

    |X||a(X)-a(Y)|w_R(X)/w_R(Y)
       <=sigma t(1/(2R)+t/R^2)(1+t/R)^3.

Expanding the polynomial, applying Young's inequality and then (10), one obtains

    ||[a,T]q||_(Hdot^-1)
      <=sigma[M_1/(2R)+5M_2/(2R^2)+9M_3/(2R^3)
                         +7M_4/(2R^4)+M_5/R^5]||q||_2. (11)

The first term of (8) has negative norm at most||q||_2 because |B_beta_hat|<=1. Substitution of (7) in (9),(11) gives exactly D_R in (1), and proves (2).

For completeness the identity does not assume w_R^(-1)q is in unweighted L2. Approximate q in L2 by smooth compact centrally even vectors. Each term of (8) for these vectors converges: T is bounded on L2 by its moderate-weight convolution bound, T-B_beta by (9), and the commutator by (11). The distributions w_R^(-1)(-div q_n) tend to g. The multiplier B_beta preserves the Schwartz space and acts continuously on tempered distributions, so their images tend to B_beta g. This justifies(8) at the limit. For a general low-space limit of core densities, the same bounds give a unique continuous extension. Since the low norm embeds in tempered distributions and B_beta is continuous there, this extension agrees with the Fourier operator.

Part P70 identifies its stated logarithmic completion with Q_beta^(-1)E_R. Apply(2) to g=Q_beta h and use L_R(g)<=2^(-53/2)E_R(g) to get(3). Every coefficient of D_R is positive, so it decreases in R. The rational comparison D_(2^31)<2^-27 proves (4).

#### 4. Transfer of the exact annular witnesses

with the canonical velocity and exact exponent of each file. No fitted decimal is substituted.

                 1602697408584840334,
                 127617579877087467912.              (12)

Each is a compact annular test at its own T, transferred to all R>=T by the proved superharmonic weight-ratio identity. Substituting (12) into (4) gives new integer lower bounds by rational squared comparisons. There is no new quadrature and no use of an unweighted residual norm.

    L_R(F_Mpen2) > (11/10)2^(-53/2)*1759901917,
    L_R(F_d2)   > (11/10)2^(-53/2)*1760486552.         (13)

This is slightly weaker than their stored annular lower endpoints. It follows from the exact predicate N_test=L_test/[(11/10)2^(-53/2)]>N_integer in both the primary and independently implemented integer-interval certificate. Here N_test is the explicitly computed annular quotient, not a lower bound on L_R inferred backwards from an arbitrary full norm. This distinction is required: a lower bound on a full norm by itself would not imply a lower bound on its low component.

## P72. The circular principal value of the strain as a positive average

### P72.1. Circular strain cutoffs are positive local averages

Status: analytic proof written before the finite symbolic checks. This result identifies the literal circular principal value in the logarithmic trace space. It supplies no new transport inverse.

#### 1. Statement

Use the real S1 parity and the Fourier convention of part P70. Write

    U=(-R1 R2 h,R1^2 h),
    C h=partial_y U_2[h]+(1/4)partial_y h,
    c[h]=partial_y U_2[h](0), b[h]=partial_y h(0).

The velocity is the canonical one from part P70, including its low-frequency parity subtraction. For epsilon>0 put

    P_epsilon(X)=2/(pi epsilon^2)*(1-|X|^2/epsilon^2)_+,
    T_epsilon h(X)=(1/pi)int_(|Y|>epsilon)
                          sin(3theta_Y)h(X+Y)/|Y|^3 dY.       (1)

Here the positive-part function is zero outside the disk. The density P_epsilon is nonnegative, supported in the radius-epsilon disk and has integral 1.

**Theorem 1.** For every beta>1/2, R>=1 and h in the actual logarithmic completion N_(beta,R)^log of part P70, the integral in (1) is absolutely convergent for each epsilon>0 and X. It satisfies

    T_epsilon h(X)=(P_epsilon*C h)(X).                        (2)

The right side uses the classical continuous first derivatives provided by that space. In particular,

    |T_epsilon h(X)-C h(X)|
       <=sup_(|Z|<=epsilon)|C h(X-Z)-C h(X)|,                 (3)

and T_epsilon h tends to C h uniformly on compact sets. At the origin,

    c[h]=-b[h]/4+(1/pi)lim_(epsilon downarrow0)
                    int_(r>epsilon)sin(3theta)h(X)/r^3 dX.  (4)

Thus the circular principal value exists throughout this space. No Dini modulus for Dh is assumed. Formula (4) retains the contact term; discarding it is still false.

The norm H_beta in the next statement is the separate unweighted norm ||J^2Q_beta h||_2 from part P70. Put

    A(z)=int_(R^2) P_1(X)exp(-iz x)dX,
    v_epsilon=1+log(1+epsilon^(-2)).

This radial Fourier transform is real, A(0)=1, and satisfies

    |A(z)|<=min(1,16/(3pi |z|)),
    0<=1-A(z)<=min(2,z^2/12).                               (5)

The second bound includes z=0 by continuity.

**Theorem 2.** For every finite real beta and each epsilon>0, T_epsilon h(0) extends to a bounded functional on H_beta. Its exact squared norm is

    ||T_epsilon||^2=(1/(64pi))int_0^infinity
       r^3(1+r^2)^(-2)(1+log(1+r^2))^(-2beta)A(epsilon r)^2 dr. (6)

For beta>1/2, C h(0)=c[h]+b[h]/4 is also bounded, and

    ||T_epsilon-C(0)||^2=(1/(64pi))int_0^infinity
       r^3(1+r^2)^(-2)(1+log(1+r^2))^(-2beta)
                          (1-A(epsilon r))^2 dr.             (7)

Both norms are attained, and are unchanged by restriction to {b=0} when beta>1/2. For beta<=1/2 the same supremum in (6) is attained as a supremum over the compact smooth S1 core with b=0, although no continuous b trace is asserted on H_beta in that range.

As epsilon decreases to 0, for every fixed beta>1/2,

    ||T_epsilon-C(0)||
       ~v_epsilon^(1/2-beta)/[8sqrt(2pi(2beta-1))].            (8)

For beta<1/2,

    ||T_epsilon||
       ~v_epsilon^(1/2-beta)/[8sqrt(2pi(1-2beta))],            (9)

and for beta=1/2,

    ||T_epsilon||~sqrt(log v_epsilon)/(8sqrt(2pi)).           (10)

The exact constants and asymptotics(6)--(10) concern H_beta only. Formula (4), not these optimized norm constants, is asserted in the actual weighted space.

#### 2. The local averaging identity

It suffices first to consider a compact smooth h. Let G=-(2pi)^(-1)log r, so -Delta G=delta_0. Choose a radial H_epsilon with -Delta H_epsilon=P_epsilon. Direct radial integration gives

    H_epsilon(r)=-r^2/(2pi epsilon^2)+r^4/(8pi epsilon^4)
                             -log(epsilon)/(2pi)+3/(8pi),   r<=epsilon,
    H_epsilon(r)=-log(r)/(2pi),                              r>=epsilon. (11)

The value and the first two radial derivatives match at epsilon. The function is C2 across the circle, smooth in the disk including its center, and has the correct radial derivative flux. It is therefore a distributional solution of -Delta H_epsilon=P_epsilon with no surface measure term. A possible additive constant has no effect below.

Inside the disk the quadratic part contributes no third derivative, and

    partial_xxy H_epsilon=y/(pi epsilon^4),
    (1/4)partial_y P_epsilon=-y/(pi epsilon^4).

These cancel exactly. Outside the disk P_epsilon=0 and

    partial_xxy H_epsilon
       =-y(3x^2-y^2)/(pi r^6)=-sin(3theta)/(pi r^3).

There is no circle-supported distribution in the sum: H_epsilon is C2 and P_epsilon is continuous across the boundary. Hence, in distributions and as locally integrable functions,

    partial_xxy H_epsilon+(1/4)partial_y P_epsilon
       =-1_(r>epsilon) sin(3theta)/(pi r^3).                 (12)

Because H_epsilon=G*P_epsilon up to a constant, the left side is the convolution kernel of P_epsilon*C. Convolving(12) with h gives (2): replacing Y by -Y in the right side changes the sign of sin(3theta) and produces the plus sign in (1). This sign and the coefficient 1/4 are both forced by the interior cancellation. The identity is not an estimate obtained by absolute values of Riesz kernels.

#### 3. Extension to the actual logarithmic completion

Put omega0=(1+r^2)^(-3/5). We need a weighted L2 bound for h itself. Write g=Q_beta h, so part P70 gives

    ||omega0 g||_2<=E_R(g)/2048.

For beta>0, the positive inverse kernel of part P71 has mass1, M2=4beta, and M1<=2sqrt(beta). The weight ratio for omega0 is at most (1+|X-Y|)^2. Consequently Young's inequality gives

    ||omega0 h||_2
      <=(1+2M1+M2)||omega0 g||_2
      <=(1+4sqrt(beta)+4beta)N_(beta,R)^log(h)/2048.          (13)

Only the moment formulas, valid for every beta>0, are used here; the uniform-in-beta constants of part P71 are not extended past beta=1.

For fixed epsilon>0 and X in a compact set, the kernel in (1), regarded as a function of X+Y, belongs to the dual weighted L2 space: at infinity its absolute size after multiplication by omega0^-1 is O(r^(-9/5)), square integrable in dimension 2. On bounded sets the exclusion |Y|>epsilon removes its singularity. Thus (1) is absolutely convergent and continuous under convergence in (13), locally uniformly in X.

Let h_n be compact smooth S1 functions converging to h in N_(beta,R)^log. The construction in part P70 gives Dh_n and DU[h_n] converging uniformly on each compact set. To recall why, the high-frequency order-one Fourier moments converge in L1 by Cauchy-Schwarz against D^2Q_beta(h_n-h), using beta>1/2; the low-frequency kernels have weighted-dual decay O(<X>^-3). Hence C h_n tends to C h locally uniformly. Equation(2) holds for h_n by section 2. Its two sides pass to the limit by (13) and this local derivative convergence, proving(2) for the completion. Nonnegativity and unit mass of P_epsilon give (3), and local continuity gives compact-uniform convergence and (4).

This proof does not infer principal-value convergence for arbitrary C1 densities. It uses the compatible canonical velocity and the completion's convergences to identify the truncated integral with an average of a continuous derivative field.

#### 4. Fourier bounds for the averaging kernel

The normalization and x-moment are elementary polar integrals:

    int P_1=1,   int x^2 P_1=1/6.

Evenness gives A(z)=int P_1 cos(zx), so |A|<=1 and

    0<=1-A(z)<=z^2 int x^2 P_1/2=z^2/12.

The zero extension of P_1 is in W^(1,1), since P_1 vanishes continuously on the circle. Integration by parts in x gives

    |A(z)|<=||partial_x P_1||_1/|z|,
    ||partial_x P_1||_1=(4/pi)int_(r<1)|x|dX=16/(3pi).

This proves (5) without a special-function formula or oscillatory quadrature.

The order-one symbol of C is

    -i r sin(theta)cos(theta)^2+i r sin(theta)/4
       =-(i r/4)sin(3theta).

By (2), T_epsilon(0) has this symbol multiplied by A(epsilon r). Fourier Hilbert duality and int_0^(2pi)(sin(3theta)/4)^2 dtheta=pi/16 give (6),(7). The factor is (2pi)^(-2)*(pi/16)=1/(64pi). At high frequency the first bound in (5) makes the integral in (6) finite for every fixed epsilon and every finite real beta. The origin has no integrability problem.

The Riesz representatives have pure angular harmonic 3 and satisfy S1 parity and reality. For beta>1/2 their b trace is zero by angular orthogonality, proving attainment and equality of the restricted norms. In the other range the representatives are still in H_beta. Approximate their radial Fourier parts by smooth compact annular functions, retaining the pure harmonic 3. These have b=0. Physical radial cutoffs preserve the first jet and approximate each such Schwartz function in H_beta; this gives the same supremum on the zero-jet compact core without defining b on the full space.

#### 5. Sharp asymptotics for the cutoff

Write L=epsilon^(-1) and W_beta(r)=r^3(1+r^2)^(-2)(1+log(1+r^2))^(-2beta). For r>=2 this is r^(-1)(1+log(1+r^2))^(-2beta)(1+O(r^-2)). All constants in this section may depend on the fixed beta. The substitution v=1+log(1+r^2) is exact:

    W_beta(r)dr=(1/2)(1-exp(1-v))v^(-2beta)dv.              (14)

For beta>1/2, the difference between the integral in (7) and int_L^infinity W_beta(r)dr is O(v_epsilon^(-2beta)). Indeed, on r<=sqrt(L), (1-A(r/L))^2<=r^4/(144L^4), which gives an exponentially smaller bound in log L. On sqrt(L)<=r<=L the same inequality integrates to O(v_epsilon^(-2beta)), since v(r) and v_epsilon are comparable. For r>=L, the estimate |(1-A(r/L))^2-1|<=C L/r gives an error at most C v_epsilon^(-2beta), using monotonicity of v^-2beta. Formula (14) then gives

    int_L^infinity W_beta(r)dr
       =v_epsilon^(1-2beta)/[2(2beta-1)]
                              +O(exp(-v_epsilon)v_epsilon^(-2beta)).

Combining with (7) proves (8).

For beta<=1/2, compare the integral in (6) with int_0^L W_beta(r)dr. On r<=L use |A(r/L)^2-1|<=2|1-A(r/L)|<=r^2/(6L^2). Splitting at sqrt(L) again gives an error O(v_epsilon^(-2beta)) plus a term exponentially small in log L, times a fixed power of that logarithm. On r>=L, |A(r/L)|^2<=C L^2/r^2. With r=L exp(t), the remaining integral is bounded by a constant times

    int_0^infinity exp(-2t)(v_epsilon+2t)^(-2beta)dt
       <=C_beta v_epsilon^(-2beta).

For negative beta, use (v+2t)^(-2beta)<=v^(-2beta)(1+2t)^(-2beta) for v>=1; for nonnegative beta use monotonicity. This treats both signs. Equation(14) now yields

    int_0^L W_beta(r)dr
       =v_epsilon^(1-2beta)/[2(1-2beta)]+O(1),  beta<1/2,
    int_0^L W_beta(r)dr=(1/2)log v_epsilon+O(1), beta=1/2.

The comparison errors are of smaller order than these leading terms. Multiplying by 1/(64pi) and taking square roots proves (9),(10).

#### 6. Scope and dependencies

The canonical contact term is established on smooth functions in part P2. The actual logarithmic completion and its classical local first derivatives are established in part P70. The positive inverse-kernel moment formulas used in (13) are established in part P71 for all beta>0; only its uniform moment majorants were restricted to beta<=1.

This result strengthens the interpretation of the singular functional: in the specified logarithmic space its classical velocity trace equals the literal circular principal value with the contact correction. It does not assert absolute convergence after subtraction of the first jet. It does not transfer the earlier polynomial singular moment, a transport inverse, a nonlinear map or a sufficient existence threshold to this space. The sharp operator-norm asymptotics are for H_beta and are not silently assigned to the weighted energy.

### P72.2. Verified result

Date: 2026-10-28T11:53:15.333716+00:00. Independent check 172.

For the canonical S1 velocity, C h=partial_y U_2[h]+partial_y h/4. The circular cutoff of the third-harmonic strain kernel is exactly P_epsilon*C h, where P_epsilon=2(1-r^2/epsilon^2)_+/(pi epsilon^2) is a positive probability density. For beta>1/2 the error norm has (1-A)^2 in place of A^2 and is asymptotic to v_epsilon^(1/2-beta)/(8sqrt(2pi(2beta-1))), where v_epsilon=1+log(1+epsilon^-2). All 27 symbolic checks pass, including a nontrivial Gaussian-potential test whose cutoff and positive average both equal (6-2epsilon^2)exp(-epsilon^2). The proof addresses completion, tails, distributional boundary terms, exact Fourier normalization, density of the core and both signs of beta. It gives no logarithmic transport inverse or nonlinear closure theorem.

Verdict: CONFIRMED at the stated scope.

## P73. Necessary logarithmic distances of exact profiles from the references

### P73.1. Necessary distances in the logarithmic and endpoint spaces

The weak stationary equation can exclude nearby exact profiles without a continuous strain trace or a transport inverse. The logarithmic smoothing costs a bounded factor in the weighted second derivatives. Retaining the negative-order energy then gives small enough amplitudes to reuse the exact signed annular tests.

Status: this analytical argument was written before the numerical comparisons. Candidate-specific verdicts are in RESULTS.md after those comparisons pass.

#### 1. Spaces, references and statement

For R>=1 and 0<=beta<=1, set

    Q_beta=(1+log(1-Delta))^beta,
    q_beta(xi)=(1+log(1+|xi|^2))^beta,
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    omega0=(1+r^2)^(-3/5), omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10),
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    Pj(f)=||omegaj D^j f||_2,
    L_R(f)=||w_R f||_(Hdot^-1),
    E_R(f)^2=P2(f)^2+2^22 P1(f)^2+2^53 L_R(f)^2,
    Nlog_(beta,R)(h)=E_R(Q_beta h).

Use the completion of real compact smooth functions that are even in x and odd in y. The derivatives are ordered Cartesian tensors with the Frobenius norm. The negative norm is the canonical Fourier realization. Part P70 identifies the completion with Q_beta^-1 E_R. At beta=0 this is E_R itself. The canonical velocity is U[h]=(-R1 R2 h,R1^2 h), with Rj=partial_j(-Delta)^(-1/2); no harmonic field is added.

The three references are the exact original state 131 and the exact rational refits nb_Mpen2_exact and nb_d2_exact. They have common

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c,
    bar_rho=r^gamma Theta(theta)+o(r^gamma),
    bar_u=U[bar_rho]=O(r^gamma), 1/5<gamma<1,

with the density convergence uniform in angle and Theta nonzero. These properties and their exact source reconstructions are established in parts P1.2, P3, P20, P40, P42 and P52. Set bar_V=cX+bar_u and F=bar_V.Dbar_rho-bar_rho.

An exact profile in this theorem means rho=bar_rho+h with canonical velocity bar_u+U[h], satisfying for some real c'

    c' X.D rho+div(U[rho]rho)-rho=0

in distributions. The products are locally integrable, as proved below. No positivity or nonvanishing of the corrected origin slope is assumed.

**Embedding theorem.** For 0<=beta<=1, R>=1 and n=Nlog_(beta,R)(h), the completed space has continuous representatives satisfying

    |h(X)| <=(51/100)max(1,r)^(1/5)n,
    |U[h](X)| <=(6/5)max(1,r)^(1/5)n.                 (1)

For R>=2^31 it also satisfies

    L_R(h) <=ell n, L_R(U[h]) <=(13/3)ell n,
    ||w_R h||_2 <=n/120000,
    ||w_R U[h]||_2 <=n/37000,
    ell=(11/10)2^(-53/2).                            (2)

These bounds include beta<=1/2, where no continuous strain or first-derivative trace is asserted.

**Distance theorem.** Let P_T,A_T,Q_T^old be any one of the positive signed-annular witnesses specified in parts P49 and P52. Their definitions are repeated in section 5. Every exact profile in the present affine space, for R>=2^31, satisfies

    P_T <= A_T n + kappa Q_T^old n^2,
    kappa=(190000*60000)/(120000*37000)=95/37.         (3)

Thus a strict comparison P_T>A_T q+kappa Q_T^old q^2 excludes the closed Nlog ball of radius q. The exact comparisons attached to this proof establish the following uniform exclusions, for every 0<=beta<=1 and R>=2^31:

| Reference | Excluded closed radius | Witness scale |
|---|---:|---:|
| state 131 | 2^57 | T=2^31 |
| nb_Mpen2_exact | 2^21 | T=2^20 |
| nb_d2_exact | 2^21 | T=2^20 |

These statements concern all prospective real exponents and corrections outside the finite generator families as well. They neither exclude larger corrections nor prove an inverse in the logarithmic space.

#### 2. A sharper first moment of the inverse logarithmic kernel

For 0<beta<=1, part P71 expresses B_beta=Q_beta^-1 as a positive heat mixture. Let U have gamma shape beta and unit rate; conditionally on U=u, let T have gamma shape u and unit rate. The spatial kernel is the mixture of p_T(X)=(4pi T)^-1 exp(-r^2/(4T)). It has unit mass. Its first two spatial moments obey

    M1=sqrt(pi) E sqrt(T) <=sqrt(pi) E sqrt(U) <=pi/2,
    M2=4 E T=4beta<=4.                               (4)

The first inequality is conditional Jensen. For the second, couple U with an independent gamma variable of shape1-beta; their sum has gamma shape1. This follows directly by convolution of the gamma densities and the beta integral, or by their Laplace transforms (1+t)^(-beta)(1+t)^(-(1-beta))=(1+t)^-1. Since the square root increases, E sqrt(U)<=E sqrt(U+V)=Gamma(3/2)=sqrt(pi)/2. When beta=1 there is no added variable. At beta=0 use B_0=I, the point mass at 0; both moments are 0. No density formula is needed for that endpoint.

Use pi<22/7, established by the elementary positive integral in part P45. The weight moderation bounds from part P44 are

    omega0(X)/omega0(X-Z)<=(1+|Z|)^2,
    omegaj(X)/omegaj(X-Z)<=1+2|Z|, j=1,2.

Positive convolution and (4), with H=Q_beta h, give

    P0(h)<=a0 n, P1(h)<=a1 n, P2(h)<=a2 n,

Here P0(H),P1(H)<=n/2048 and P2(H)<=n follow from the retained-energy interpolation in part P70. Indeed 1+2M1+M2<=5+pi<57/7 and 1+2M1<=1+pi<29/7. Derivatives commute with B_beta. All inequalities first hold on the core, then pass to the completed weighted Sobolev realization.

The established weighted Riesz bounds are

    P0(U[h]) <=(8/3)P0(h),
    P1(U[h]) <=(3/2)P1(h),
    P2(U[h]) <=(9/5)P2(h).                           (6)

The first and third use central oddness; the first derivatives use the unrestricted omega1 estimate. Vector norms are taken in Hilbert sum. These are the canonical operators from parts P6 and P7 and P21 and do not assert a Riesz bound on L2(w_R^2).

#### 3. Growth, continuity and exponent rigidity

For completeness the elementary local interpolation in part P44 states

    ||f||_infinity <=(1/2)sqrt(||f||_2 ||D2 f||_2),     (7)

for scalar or Hilbert-valued H2 functions in two dimensions. It follows by Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz against lambda^4+|xi|^4 and optimization; the reciprocal integral is pi^2/(2lambda^2).

Use the explicit radial partition from part P44, with cutoffs supported on annuli t/2<=r<=2t (and one central disk), rescaled cutoff gradient at most 9 and Hessian at most 150. On every rescaled piece F_j, the changes of variables and product rule give

    Ch=(15/8)sqrt(3a0[450a0+36a1+a2]),
    Cu=(15/8)sqrt(8a0[1200a0+54a1+(9/5)a2]).          (8)

The rational squared comparisons Ch^2<(51/100)^2 and Cu^2<(6/5)^2 prove (1). A core-Cauchy sequence is therefore uniformly Cauchy for h and U[h] on every compact set. Its limits agree with their canonical distributions. The weighted Riesz realization and central oddness agree with the low-frequency parity subtraction of part P70; no constant or other harmonic velocity can be introduced by this limit.

Suppose rho=bar_rho+h is exact with exponent c'. By (1), T^-gamma rho(TX) tends uniformly on each compact annulus to G(X)=|X|^gamma Theta(arg X). Its rescaled canonical velocity T^-gamma U[rho](TX) stays bounded there. The weak rescaled nonlinear term is T^(gamma-1) times the divergence of the product of those two rescaled fields. Since gamma<1, its pairing against every compact smooth annular test tends to 0. The remaining equation is c'X.DG-G=0. Homogeneity gives X.DG=gamma G distributionally; G is nonzero, so c'=1/gamma=c.

This proves exponent rigidity without a continuous origin trace, a small norm, or any assumption that the leading coefficient a0 changes the scaling freedom. In particular the following weak difference identity is valid:

    int F zeta = int h[bar_V.Dzeta+(2c+1)zeta]
                    -int U[h].Dbar_rho zeta

It uses only the locally integrable products and the divergence-free canonical velocity. No derivative of h is placed on the right side. Compact C1 tests with square-integrable weak Hessian are permitted by approximation.

#### 4. Retain the negative energy to get the small L2 constants

Part P71 proves, for 0<beta<=1,

    L_R(h)<=(1+D_R)2^(-53/2)n,

For R>=2^31 it has D_R<2^-27<1/10, giving the first bound in (2). At beta=0 that bound is immediate from the definition of E_R. Its proof writes |f_hat|^2 as the product of the negative integrand to power 2/3 and the second-derivative integrand to power 1/3, then applies Holder with exponents 3/2 and 3. The exact rational inequalities

For the quadratic term, (2) gives
