## P74. An explicit density with divergent strain at the logarithmic endpoint

### P74.1. A continuously differentiable density with divergent circular strain

The endpoint failure of the strain trace is visible in a single compactly supported density. Its first derivative tends to zero at the origin, but positive contributions from nested annuli accumulate in the strain integral. The construction belongs to the actual weighted logarithmic completion, not only to its unweighted counterpart.

#### 1. Statement and conventions

All functions are real on R^2. Write X=(x,y), r=|X| and let theta be its polar angle. The S1 symmetry means evenness in x and oddness in y. Use the Fourier convention

    f_hat(xi)=int exp(-i X.xi)f(X)dX,
    f(X)=(2pi)^(-2)int exp(i X.xi)f_hat(xi)dxi.

Set

    J=(1-Delta)^(1/2),
    Q_beta=(1+log(1-Delta))^beta,
    q_beta(xi)=(1+log(1+|xi|^2))^beta.

The Hilbert space H_beta is the completion of compact smooth S1 functions in ||J^2 Q_beta h||_2. For R>=1 define the actual weighted completion N_(beta,R)^log by the norm

    E_R(Q_beta h)^2
      =||omega2 D^2 Q_beta h||_2^2
         +2^22 ||omega1 D Q_beta h||_2^2
         +2^53 ||w_R Q_beta h||_(Hdot^-1)^2,
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10),
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10).

The Hessian has all ordered Cartesian entries. The homogeneous negative norm is defined by Fourier duality, equivalently by the supremum against compact smooth test functions whose gradient has L2 norm at most one. Completion is from compact smooth S1 functions. These are the conventions of part P70; the membership argument below proves convergence in the stated core norm directly.

For a compact continuous density define the circularly truncated integral

    T_epsilon h(0)
       =(1/pi)int_(r>epsilon) sin(3theta) h(X)/r^3 dX.   (1)

For every fixed epsilon>0 the integral is absolutely convergent. On compact smooth densities the canonical strain is

    c[h]=-h_y(0)/4+lim_(epsilon->0)T_epsilon h(0).

The contact term is essential in this identity. The density below has h_y(0)=0, so no contact term can remove its divergence.

**Theorem.** There is one compactly supported S1 function h in C^1(R^2), smooth away from the origin, with Dh(0)=0, such that:

1. For every finite real beta<=1/2 and every R>=1, h belongs to H_beta and N_(beta,R)^log. For each fixed beta its weighted norm is bounded uniformly over R>=1.
2. There are compact smooth S1 partial sums h^(N) with Dh^(N)(0)=0 which converge to h in H_beta and uniformly in the norms N_(beta,R)^log over R>=1, for every fixed beta<=1/2.
3. The nonnegative integrals T_epsilon h(0) tend to positive infinity as epsilon decreases to zero. They grow proportionally to log log log(1/epsilon), in the precise sense in section 5.

Thus continuously differentiable densities with zero origin jet can fail to have a finite circular strain principal value at and below the logarithmic endpoint. The result does not claim that c extends to these spaces, or that this density solves a profile equation.

#### 2. A positive logarithmic quadratic form

Let Q=Q_(1/2). For every Schwartz function f, Plancherel and the scalar identity

    log(1+lambda)=int_0^infinity exp(-t)(1-exp(-t lambda))dt/t

give

    ||Q f||_2^2
      =||f||_2^2+(1/2)int k(z)||f-tau_z f||_2^2 dz,
    k(z)=int_0^infinity exp(-t)p_t(z)dt/t,
    p_t(z)=(4pi t)^(-1)exp(-|z|^2/(4t)),                (2)

where tau_z f(X)=f(X-z). Both integrands are nonnegative. The scalar identity follows by differentiating in lambda, obtaining 1/(1+lambda), and using the value zero at lambda=0. The heat identity follows by expanding the square and using the symmetry and mass one of p_t. Tonelli's theorem therefore justifies (2), without requiring the kernel k to be integrable at zero.

Suppose finitely many smooth functions f_n have pairwise disjoint supports. At each X at most one f_n(X) and at most one f_n(X-z) is nonzero. There are consequently at most two nonzero terms in the sum of their differences. Pointwise Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    |sum_n(f_n(X)-f_n(X-z))|^2
       <=2 sum_n |f_n(X)-f_n(X-z)|^2.

The L2 squares of the f_n add exactly. Applying (2) proves

    ||Q sum_n f_n||_2^2 <=2 sum_n ||Q f_n||_2^2.        (3)

This estimate also holds for vectors and tensors with Euclidean norms, and for any finite tail of the sum.

For 0<epsilon<=1 and f(X)=A Phi(X/epsilon), a change of Fourier variable and

    log(1+|xi|^2/epsilon^2)
       <=2log(1/epsilon)+log(1+|xi|^2)

give the exact scaling estimate

    ||Q f||_2^2
      <=|A|^2 epsilon^2
          [||Q Phi||_2^2+2log(1/epsilon)||Phi||_2^2].   (4)

The constants in (3) and (4) are independent of the support size.

#### 3. The annular construction

Choose the fixed nonnegative smooth radial function

    chi(s)=exp(-1/((s-1)(3/2-s)))  if 1<s<3/2,
           0                     otherwise,

and set

    Phi(X)=r sin(3theta)chi(r)
          =y(3x^2-y^2)chi(r)/(x^2+y^2).

The expression is defined as zero near the origin. It is compact and smooth, has S1 symmetry, and is not zero. For n>=2 put

    epsilon_n=4^(-n),
    a_n=1/[n log(n+1)],
    h_n(X)=a_n epsilon_n Phi(X/epsilon_n),
    h^(N)=sum_(n=2)^N h_n,
    h(X)=sum_(n=2)^infinity h_n(X), h(0)=0.           (5)

The supports lie in epsilon_n<r<(3/2)epsilon_n and are disjoint. They have gaps because (3/2)epsilon_(n+1)<epsilon_n. Every partial sum is compact smooth, has S1 symmetry and vanishes near the origin. On an occupied annulus,

    |h(X)|/|X| <=a_n sup_(1<=r<=3/2)|Phi(X)|/r,
    |Dh(X)| <=a_n ||D Phi||_infinity.

Both right sides tend to zero as n tends to infinity. The same quantities vanish in the gaps. It follows that h is differentiable at zero with derivative zero, and Dh is continuous there. At all nonzero points the sum is locally finite; the flat endpoints of chi ensure smoothness across annulus boundaries. This proves the stated regularity and compact support.

The distributional derivatives through order two are the corresponding sums. One way to check this without a boundary assertion at zero is to note the uniform convergence of the functions and first derivatives, and the L2 convergence of the second derivatives established next. Integration by parts for the partial sums then passes to distributions.

#### 4. Membership in the weighted completion

For clarity, it is enough first to prove convergence for Q=Q_(1/2). Apply (3) and (4) to each finite tail. For the four sequences needed below, their amplitudes and the squared scaling factors |A_n|^2 epsilon_n^2 are

| Function | Fixed smooth tensor Phi replaced by | Squared scaling factor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| h_n | Phi | a_n^2 epsilon_n^4 |
| D^2 h_n | D^2 Phi | a_n^2 |
| X_j h_n | Y_j Phi(Y) | a_n^2 epsilon_n^6 |
| X_j D^2 h_n | Y_j D^2 Phi(Y) | a_n^2 epsilon_n^2 |

All the fixed tensors are compact smooth on the same annulus. Because log(1/epsilon_n)=n log4, their energies are bounded by fixed constants times the displayed factor times (1+n). The largest series is

    sum_(n>=2)(1+n)a_n^2
       =sum_(n>=2)(1+n)/[n^2 log(n+1)^2] < infinity.    (6)

Indeed its summands are at most 2/[n log(n)^2], whose integral from 2 to infinity converges. Thus Q applied to h^(N), D^2 h^(N), X_j h^(N) and X_j D^2 h^(N) gives Cauchy sequences in L2. The bounds are independent of R.

Fix now any finite beta<=1/2. Since q_beta<=q_(1/2),

    ||Q_beta f||_2<=||Q f||_2.                         (7)

The gradient of the multiplier is

    D_xi q_beta
       =2 beta xi(1+|xi|^2)^(-1)
           (1+log(1+|xi|^2))^(beta-1).

Since beta-1<=0 and 2|xi|/(1+|xi|^2)<=1, its Euclidean norm is at most |beta|. The Fourier commutator with multiplication by X therefore gives

    ||X Q_beta f||_2
       <=||Q_beta(X f)||_2+|beta| ||f||_2,             (8)

where the first term is the L2 norm of the vector with components Q_beta(X_j f). The formula applies componentwise to tensors, with the same constant |beta| after summing the squares. Equations (6)-(8) imply convergence of Q_beta h^(N), D^2 Q_beta h^(N), X Q_beta h^(N) and X D^2 Q_beta h^(N) in L2.

The weights satisfy omega1<=1 and

    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5)<=sqrt(1+4r^2)<=1+2r.

Hence

    ||omega2 D^2 Q_beta f||_2
       <=||D^2 Q_beta f||_2+2||X D^2 Q_beta f||_2.      (9)

Also 2|xi|^2<=1+|xi|^4 implies

    ||D Q_beta f||_2^2
       <=(1/2)(||Q_beta f||_2^2+||D^2 Q_beta f||_2^2). (10)

For the low term, a centrally odd compact smooth test function v has no zero angular Fourier mode. The angular Poincare inequality at each radius gives

    ||v/r||_2<=||Dv||_2.

Every centrally odd distribution pairs only with the centrally odd part of v, whose gradient norm does not increase under that projection. Since w_R<=1,

    ||w_R Q_beta f||_(Hdot^-1)<=||r Q_beta f||_2       (11)

for S1 functions with the latter norm finite, uniformly R>=1. This also proves that the negative norm is well defined in the present argument.

Apply (9)-(11) to any tail h^(M)-h^(N). All right sides tend to zero, uniformly R>=1. The partial sums are consequently Cauchy in the actual weighted core norms. Their distributional limit is h, since they converge in L2 and Q_beta is a smooth tempered Fourier multiplier with tempered inverse. This identifies the completed element with the displayed density. The same estimates, using

    ||J^2 g||_2^2=||g||_2^2+2||Dg||_2^2+||D^2g||_2^2,

prove convergence in H_beta. This establishes both membership claims, including every finite negative beta, and the uniformity over R.

#### 5. Divergence of the circular integral

On the support of h_n the expression in (5) is

    h_n(X)=a_n r sin(3theta)chi(r/epsilon_n).

Its integrand in (1) is nonnegative, and its full annular contribution is

    (a_n/pi)int_0^(2pi)sin(3theta)^2 dtheta
                int_(epsilon_n)^((3/2)epsilon_n)chi(r/epsilon_n)dr/r
       =a_n A_chi,
    A_chi=int_1^(3/2)chi(s)ds/s>0.                    (12)

The angular integral is pi. In particular

    T_(epsilon_N) h(0)=A_chi sum_(n=2)^N 1/[n log(n+1)]. (13)

The series diverges. More precisely,

    0<=1/[n log n]-1/[n log(n+1)]
       <=1/[n^2 (log n)^2].

The difference is summable, and integral comparison for the decreasing function 1/(t log t) gives

    sum_(n=2)^N 1/[n log(n+1)]=log log N+O(1).         (14)

Nonnegativity makes T_epsilon nondecreasing as epsilon decreases. If epsilon lies between two successive epsilon_n, its value lies between the corresponding two full sums. Since log(1/epsilon_n)=n log4, (13)-(14) yield

    T_epsilon h(0)=A_chi log log log(1/epsilon)+O(1)    (15)

as epsilon tends to zero, with natural logarithms and epsilon sufficiently small that they are defined. In particular the circular principal value is positive infinity, despite h being C1 and having zero origin jet.

#### Dependencies and scope

The proof uses the definitions and contact convention of part P70 and the circular truncation convention of part P72. The construction, core convergence, heat quadratic form and divergence argument are proved here independently. No inverse theorem, equation for h, pointwise velocity derivative, or numerical certificate for a profile is asserted. The finite symbolic audit checks the constants and identities used above; the convergence and regularity arguments are analytical proofs, not consequences of a finite test count.

## P75. A fixed-background inverse with a logarithmic gain

### P75.1. A conditional full linear inverse with logarithmic regularity

A small coefficient in front of the logarithmic multiplier makes its commutator with the background operator small. This changes the norm, while preserving the underlying logarithmic space. Differentiating the previously proved fractional commutator at order zero gives the required bound without a new singular-kernel estimate.

#### 1. Spaces and reference hypotheses

Let R=2^31, X=(x,y), r=|X| and J=(1-Delta)^(1/2). All scalar densities are real, even in x and odd in y. Define the weights and energy

    w=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    omega0=(1+r^2)^(-3/5), omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10),
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    L(h)=||wh||_(Hdot^-1), Pj(h)=||omegaj D^j h||_2,
    E(h)^2=P2(h)^2+2^22 P1(h)^2+2^53 L(h)^2.

The negative norm uses the full-plane Fourier inverse and the centrally odd homogeneous H^1 dual. Ordered Cartesian derivative tensors have Euclidean norms. E is the completion of compact smooth S1 densities. It embeds in tempered distributions and satisfies P0<=E/2048. No additive harmonic velocity is allowed. Define

    K=log(1-Delta),
    Q_tau=I+tau K, B_tau=Q_tau^(-1),
    N_tau(h)=E(Q_tau h), 0<tau<=2^-12.

The logarithm is the Fourier multiplier log(1+|xi|^2), with Fourier inversion factor (2pi)^(-2). N_tau is the completion of the same compact smooth core. Write N_log(h)=E((I+K)h), the beta=1 space of part P70. This notation distinguishes the coefficient tau from the power beta used there.

Let rho be a smooth sublinear S1 reference, with all its derivatives of at most polynomial growth, and with canonical sublinear velocity

    u=U[rho]=(-R1R2 rho,R1^2 rho),
    -Delta psi=rho_x, U=(-psi_y,psi_x).

Require also that every derivative of u has at most polynomial growth. Require 9/5<c<37/20, a0=rho_y(0)>=1, and c+c[rho]=1, where c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0). Put V=cX+u and

    A=[[rho_y,-rho_x/2],[-rho_x/2,0]],
    M=(2c+1)I+sym Du+A,
    Mj=(1+c+V.D log omegaj)I-j sym DV+A, j=1,2.

Assume the pointwise inequalities

    M >= [2/5+(11/5)c r^2/(R^2+r^2)]I on r<=R,
    M1>=I/2, M2>=I/2 throughout R^2.

With d=4/9 require the global decay bounds

    sup r^d(|D rho|+r|D^2 rho|)<=186,
    sup r^(-1+d)|u|<=22, sup r^d|Du|<=22,
    sup r^(1+d)|D^2u|<=56,

and the global derivative bounds

    |Du|<=14/5, |D rho|<=16,
    <r>|D^2u|<=3, <r>|D^3u|<=16,
    |D^2rho|<=3, <r>|D^2rho|<=8,
    <r>^2|D^3rho|<=32, <r>^2|D^4rho|<=512.

Every displayed bound holds everywhere, not merely on a grid. For the normalized-domain conclusion suppose also

    T^(-gamma)rho(TX)->G(X)=r^gamma Theta(theta),
    gamma=1/c, Theta continuous and not identically zero,                (1)

uniformly on compact annuli. The coefficient bounds already give |D rho(X)|=O(r^(-d)) at infinity.

The fixed-exponent and full normalized linearizations are

    A_fix h=(cX+u).Dh-h+U[h].D rho,
    B h=A_fix h-c[h]X.D rho.                                            (2)

The notation A_fix is distinct from the 2 by 2 matrix A above.

**Theorem.** Under these hypotheses:

1. For 0<tau<=2^-12, B_tau is bounded on E with norm at most 1+8tau. N_tau and N_log are the same space of distributions, with

       N_tau(h)<(29/7) N_log(h),
       N_log(h)<(2/tau+7)N_tau(h).                                      (3)

   Non-strict inequalities apply at h=0. The corresponding core completions and their canonical fields agree.

2. On E the logarithmic commutator extends boundedly and satisfies

       ||[K,A_fix]||_(E->E)<=9325421/600.

   The conjugated commutator obeys

       ||[Q_tau,A_fix]B_tau||_(E->E)
           <=(9325421/600)tau(1+8tau)<2^14 tau.                         (4)

3. Set tau=2^-20. The maximal distributional realization of A_fix on N_tau is a bijective closed generator and

       ||exp(t A_fix)||_(N_tau->N_tau)<=exp(-t/29),
       N_tau(A_fix^(-1)f)<=29 N_tau(f).                                 (5)

   On the original space N_log, the same maximal realization is bijective and

       N_log(A_fix^(-1)f)<=2^28 N_log(f).                               (6)

4. In either space, with (1), the maximal distributional domain of B is precisely D(A_fix) intersect ker c. Its range is exactly the hyperplane f_y(0)=0, and its inverse on that hyperplane satisfies the corresponding bound 29 or 2^28.

All derivative traces in the fourth conclusion are classical, by the beta=1 trace theorem and (3). This is a conditional linear theorem. It does not transfer the rough-velocity nonlinear iteration or a sufficient residual threshold to N_log.

#### 2. The logarithmic inverse kernel

The scalar Laplace identity gives

    B_tau=int_0^infinity exp(-u)J^(-2tau u)du.                           (7)

Thus B_tau has a radial positive probability kernel. A useful probabilistic notation is U with density exp(-u), T conditional on U with gamma density of shape a=tau U and rate 1, and X conditional on T with density (4pi T)^(-1)exp(-r^2/(4T)). All integrals below are integrations against these explicit densities; no probabilistic limit theorem is used.

Polar integration gives

    E[|X|^j|T]=2^j Gamma(1+j/2)T^(j/2).

For every a>0, the beta integral gives

    Gamma(a+1/2)/Gamma(a+1)
      =(1/sqrt(pi))int_0^1 t^(a-1/2)(1-t)^(-1/2)dt
      <=sqrt(pi).

Here the beta integral at a=0 equals pi by t=sin^2(theta). Consequently Gamma(a+1/2)/Gamma(a)<=sqrt(pi)a. The gamma recurrence and E[U^k]=k! yield, for Mj=int|X|^j B_tau(X)dX,

    M1<=pi tau,
    M2=4tau,
    M3<=6pi(2tau^2+tau/2),
    M4=32(2tau^2+tau),
    M5<=60pi(6tau^3+4tau^2+3tau/4).                                    (8)

For 0<tau<=2^-12, pi<22/7 gives the convenient bounds

    (M1,M2,M3,M4,M5)<=(4,4,10,33,160)tau.                               (9)

Both derivative weight ratios, in either direction, are at most 1+2|X-Y|, as proved in part P43. Positive convolution and Young's inequality give

    Pj(B_tau h)<=(1+2M1)Pj(h)<=(1+8tau)Pj(h), j=1,2.                    (10)

The general positive-kernel cancellation identity of part P71 applies to (7). Its proof uses only positivity, radiality, mass one, and the first five moments. In detail, with sigma=11/5 it gives

    L(B_tau h)<= [1+(3+sigma/2)M1/R
                    +(3+5sigma/2)M2/R^2
                    +(1+9sigma/2)M3/R^3
                    +(7sigma/2)M4/R^4+sigma M5/R^5] L(h).              (11)

This follows by writing q=D(-Delta)^(-1)(wh), conjugating the kernel by w, and retaining the commutator of Dlog w with that conjugate. The term outside a divergence has central oddness, so its negative norm is bounded by its r-weighted L2 norm. In particular (11) does not assume a weighted L2 Riesz bound in the low weight.

By (9), the excess in brackets is at most

    tau[82/(5R)+34/R^2+109/R^3+2541/(10R^4)+352/R^5]<tau               (12)

at R>=2^31. All coefficients are positive. Equations (10)-(12) prove the first assertion of part 1.

For comparison with N_log, let B_1=(I+K)^(-1). The first moment improvement in part P73 is M1(B_1)<=pi/2: conditional Jensen gives E|X|<=sqrt(pi)E sqrt(U)=pi/2. Thus its derivative-component norm is at most 1+pi. Its low-component norm is at most 1+D_R<1+2^-27, by part P71, so

    ||B_1||_(E->E)<=1+pi<29/7.                                           (13)

The exact identities

    Q_tau h=tau(I+K)h+(1-tau)h,
    (I+K)h=tau^(-1)[Q_tau h-(1-tau)h]

and (10)-(13) imply

    N_tau(h)<(29/7)N_log(h),
    N_log(h)<[1+(1-tau)(1+8tau)]N_tau(h)/tau
             <(2/tau+7)N_tau(h).

Initially these hold on the compact core. Each multiplier Q_tau and B_tau preserves Schwartz functions and acts continuously on tempered distributions. Images of Schwartz functions can be approximated by compact smooth radial cutoffs in the Schwartz topology, in which E is continuous because L(g)<=||rg||_2. Therefore Q_tau maps the stated completion onto E isometrically, just as in part P70. The inequalities extend to the completed spaces and identify them as the same subspace of tempered distributions. This proves (3).

#### 3. Differentiate the established fractional commutator

The bound already proved in part P43, under the present derivative hypotheses, is

    ||[J^s,A_fix]J^(-s)||_(E->E)<=C s,
    C=9325421/1200, 0<s<=2^-12.                                       (14)

It includes the low negative component and its weight commutators. No unweighted replacement is made here.

For a compact smooth S1 test density f, differentiation of the Fourier multipliers at s=0 gives, in tempered distributions,

    s^(-1)[J^s,A_fix]J^(-s)f->[log J,A_fix]f.                           (15)

To justify the differentiation when A_fix f is not Schwartz, test against a compact smooth function. J^(-s)f and its s derivatives converge in Schwartz seminorms. Canonical U applied to these functions and their derivatives converges locally and in polynomially weighted distribution bounds: its high-frequency part is a smooth multiplier, while the low-frequency part uses the parity subtraction of the kernel at the origin. Multiplication by u, X, D rho and their finite derivatives is continuous in the needed polynomially weighted bounds, by the displayed growth and derivative hypotheses. Moving the remaining J^s to the test function then differentiates a Schwartz-valued function. This proves the distributional product rule in (15). The same argument with Schwartz test functions proves convergence in tempered distributions. The polynomial growth assumption on every derivative permits multiplication on tempered distributions; the canonical U commutes with K on the core and by continuous distributional extension. In particular U[Kf] here means K U[f], not an unspecified inverse on arbitrary tempered inputs.

By (14), the left side is uniformly bounded in the Hilbert space E. Every sequence s decreasing to zero has a weakly convergent subsequence in E, and the continuous embedding E into tempered distributions identifies its weak limit with (15). Weak lower semicontinuity gives

    E([log J,A_fix]f)<=C E(f).

Density extends the commutator to a bounded operator on E. Since K=2log J, its bound is 2C. The commutator is still the distributional one: approximate any E input by compact smooth inputs and use the continuous distributional action of each term. Finally

    [Q_tau,A_fix]B_tau=tau[K,A_fix]B_tau.

Combining this identity with ||B_tau||_E<=1+8tau proves the first inequality in (4). The strict comparison 2C(1+8*2^-12)<2^14 proves its second inequality throughout the stated range.

#### 4. Generator, maximal domain and inverse

The complete reference contract in section 1 is the contract used in parts P24, P43 and P63. Their established base theorem supplies the maximal distributional E generator G=A_fix, with

    ||exp(tG)||_(E->E)<=exp(-t/20).                                    (16)

Its domain is {g in E:A_fix g in E}. This is an input about the realization, not an inference from a coercive quadratic form. Part P63 verifies it through the common P0 space and radial cutoff and local Friedrichs approximation.

On N_tau, conjugation by Q_tau yields

    Q_tau A_fix B_tau=G+C_tau,
    C_tau=[Q_tau,A_fix]B_tau.                                          (17)

The bounded perturbation is on the same E space as G. Its Duhamel series converges in operator norm on every bounded time interval. Applying (16) to that series, or its integral inequality, proves

    ||exp(t(G+C_tau))||<=exp[-t(1/20-||C_tau||)].                       (18)

The generator domain is D(G). The distributional identity (17) holds first on the core and then for all N_tau inputs as a distributional identity, using (4). Consequently

    A_fix h in N_tau
       iff A_fix(Q_tau h)+C_tau(Q_tau h) in E
       iff Q_tau h in D(G).

This identifies the conjugated domain as the maximal distributional domain. It also proves closedness and strong continuity after transporting the semigroup by the onto isometry Q_tau.

At tau=2^-20, (4) gives

    1/20-||C_tau|| >=1/20-(9325421/600)tau(1+8tau)>1/29.

Thus (5)'s semigroup bound holds. The integral

    A_fix^(-1)f=-int_0^infinity exp(t A_fix)f dt

converges in N_tau. The closed-generator integral identity proves that it maps onto the maximal domain and is a right inverse. If A_fix h=0, the semigroup fixes h, and strict decay forces h=0. This proves injectivity, surjectivity and the inverse bound 29.

Equivalent norms preserve the maximal domain, generator and inverse. Applying (3) on the input and output gives

    N_log(A_fix^(-1)f)
       <(29*29/7)(2/tau+7)N_log(f)<2^28 N_log(f)

at tau=2^-20. This proves (6). Its large constant is a sufficient conversion bound, not an optimal inverse norm. The N_log semigroup is also exponentially stable, with the finite prefactor(29/7)(2/tau+7) obtained from (3).

#### 5. Normalized domain and range

By (3) and part P70 at beta=1, h and U[h] have classical first derivatives locally and c[h] is continuous. Part P73 gives

    |h(X)|<= (51/100)max(1,r)^(1/5)N_log(h),
    |U[h](X)|<= (6/5)max(1,r)^(1/5)N_log(h).                            (19)

Every f in N_log has the same density growth. These bounds make the normalized-domain statement precise even when X.D rho is not in the forcing space.

Suppose h and B h=f belong to N_log. Test the equation on an annulus after X=TY and divide its distributional form by T^gamma. The terms involving cX.Dh-h tend to zero: integrate the derivative off h and use (19), since gamma>1/5. The term u.Dh tends to zero after integration by parts, since div u=0, u=O(T^(1-d)) and h=O(T^(1/5)); its size after rescaling is O(T^(1/5-d-gamma)). The term U[h].D rho is O(T^(1/5-d-gamma)) by the decay bound on D rho. The forcing f tends to zero for the same reason as h. Finally (1) gives

    T^(-gamma)(X.D rho)(TY)->Y.DG=gamma G

in distributions, by integrating the derivative off rho. The limit equation is -c[h]gamma G=0. Since gamma>0 and G is not zero, c[h]=0. Hence A_fix h=f belongs to N_log, proving

    D(B)=D(A_fix) intersect ker c.                                    (20)

The converse inclusion is immediate. Norm equivalence gives the same statement in N_tau. This argument does not suppose an arbitrary derivative asymptotic for rho or for h.

For h in D(A_fix), write f=A_fix h. Its derivative at the origin can be computed from first-order expansions, without a second derivative of h. Symmetry and reference normalization give

    DV(0)=diag(2c-1,1), D rho(0)=(0,a0),
    h(X)=b[h]y+o(r), Dh(X)=b[h]e_y+o(1),
    U[h](X)=DU[h](0)X+o(r).

The y derivative of V.Dh-h at zero is b[h]-b[h]=0. The remaining term gives

    f_y(0)=a0 c[h].                                                    (21)

If f_y(0)=0, the already proved inverse h=A_fix^(-1)f has c[h]=0 because a0>=1. Conversely every h in the domain (20) gives f_y(0)=0. Therefore the range is exactly the stated hyperplane, and the inverse bounds restrict to it.

The same growth comparison fixes the full leading angular function and excludes the scaling vector rho-X.D rho from the correction space. Exponent changes and their logarithmic tails are not freely accommodated here. No conclusion about nonlinear transport U[k].Dh on this logarithmic space follows from the smooth-reference commutator argument.

#### Dependencies and scope

Part P43 supplies the exact smooth fractional commutator (14), with all coefficient and low-weight terms included. parts P24 and P63 supply the base E generator and its maximal domain under the full section 1 contract. parts P70, P71 and P73 supply, respectively, the original logarithmic completion and classical traces, the general positive-kernel low cancellation identity, and the beta=1 moment and growth bounds. The new coefficient-dependent kernel estimates, the commutator derivative, norm equivalence, and normalized logarithmic inverse are proved here.

No new candidate has been certified to satisfy the reference hypotheses. In particular the known W3 failures of the refits remain failures, and none of the residual lower bounds is made small by this theorem. The rough transport energy estimate, nonlinear contraction and sufficient residual threshold remain open in the logarithmic realization.

## P76. The quadratic transport term is not continuous in the logarithmic space

### P76.1. Quadratic transport is not continuous into the logarithmic forcing space

The logarithmic linear inverse does not turn quadratic transport into a bounded forcing map. A compact velocity which is constant on a small region transports a rapidly oscillating density there. One extra derivative remains in the output. Both the center jet and the nonlocal strain can be exactly zero in this example.

#### 1. Statement

Use the S1 parity, canonical velocity and energy from part P70:

    U[h]=(-R1R2 h,R1^2 h),
    Q_beta=(1+log(1-Delta))^beta,
    N_(beta,R)^log(h)^2
       =||(1+4r^2)^(2/5)D^2 Q_beta h||_2^2
          +2^22||(1+r^2)^(-1/10)D Q_beta h||_2^2
          +2^53||w_R Q_beta h||_(Hdot^-1)^2,
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), R>=1.

All derivative tensors have ordered Cartesian entries. The Fourier transform has inversion factor (2pi)^(-2). The space is the completion of compact smooth S1 densities. For such densities put b[h]=h_y(0), c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0), and

    T(h)=U[h].Dh.

**Theorem.** For every fixed finite beta>=0 there is a sequence v_n of compact smooth S1 densities such that

    b[v_n]=c[v_n]=0,
    sup_(R>=1) N_(beta,R)^log(v_n)->0,
    inf_(R>=1) N_(beta,R)^log(T(v_n))->infinity.        (1)

All v_n and all their velocities have supports in one fixed compact set disjoint from the origin. In particular T has no continuous extension at zero from the logarithmic space into itself, even on the exactly normalized compact core. There is no bound N(T(h))<=C N(h)^2 on that core.

For beta=1 this applies to the linear inverse space of part P75 and, by its norm equivalence, to the small-coefficient logarithmic norm used there. The statement concerns treating T as a forcing map; it is not a counterexample to a characteristic or two-norm iteration.

#### 2. Modulated compact functions

Write

    L_n=1+log(1+n^2), n>=2.

For any fixed f in C_c^infinity(R^2), any nonnegative integer k and fixed beta>=0, Fourier translation and differentiation give

    ||Q_beta D^k(f exp(i n y))||_2
       +||X Q_beta D^k(f exp(i n y))||_2
          <=C_(f,k,beta) n^k L_n^beta.               (2)

The constant is independent of n and R. Indeed the shifted transform is f_hat(eta), and

    1+log(1+|eta+n e_y|^2)
       <=C L_n(1+|eta|^2).

Multiplication by X differentiates that transform. A derivative hitting Q_beta has at most polynomial growth in eta, uniformly after division by L_n^beta. A derivative hitting a polynomial frequency factor has degree at most k-1. All these factors are integrable against the rapidly decreasing f_hat and its derivatives. Plancherel proves (2). The same bounds hold for sine and cosine and for frequency 2n.

For a fixed Cartesian derivative of order k, there is also an L2 asymptotic: after division by n^k L_n^beta, Q_beta applied to the modulated derivative equals its leading y-derivative term divided by n^k, up to a term tending to zero in L2. To prove it, translate the Fourier variable and observe

    [1+log(1+|eta+n e_y|^2)]^beta/L_n^beta ->1

for each fixed eta. The polynomial frequency factor divided by n^k converges to its value at e_y. The polynomial majorants used in (2) justify dominated convergence. For real sine and cosine, apply this argument to both shifted packets. Finally

    ||f sin(ny)||_2^2, ||f cos(ny)||_2^2 ->||f||_2^2/2,                (3)

because repeated integration by parts in y makes int f(X)^2 exp(2iny)dX tend to zero. This argument includes beta=0.

The inequalities omega1<=1, omega2<=1+2r, and the centrally odd Hardy dual estimate give, for S1 f,

    N_(beta,R)^log(f)
       <=||D^2 Q_beta f||_2+2||X D^2 Q_beta f||_2
           +2^11||D Q_beta f||_2+2^(53/2)||X Q_beta f||_2.             (4)

Here ||w_R Q_beta f||_(Hdot^-1)<=||r Q_beta f||_2 uniformly R>=1. The estimate follows by projecting tests onto central oddness and using the nonzero angular Fourier frequencies, as in parts P70 and P74. Thus the weighted tails introduced by Q_beta are accounted for in (4); compact support of f alone is not used to discard them.

#### 3. A compact constant-velocity region

Choose an even smooth compact cutoff chi_x equal to 1 on |x|<=1. Choose a smooth compact function theta supported in (1/2,5/2) and equal to 1 on [1,2]. Define the S1 potential

    phi_0(x,y)=(x^2/2)chi_x(x)[theta(y)-theta(-y)],
    h_0=-Delta phi_0.

Let b be a nonzero real smooth function, even in x and odd in y, supported in

    {|x|<1/2, 5/4<y<7/4}
       union {|x|<1/2, -7/4<y<-5/4}.

For example b is the product of a nonzero even x bump with an upper y bump minus its reflection. Smooth cutoffs with these plateau and support properties can be made from exp(-1/t) for t>0, extended by zero; their precise values are immaterial to the proof.

For every compact smooth potential phi with S1 parity,

    h=-Delta phi,
    psi=partial_x phi,
    U[h]=(-partial_xy phi,partial_xx phi).             (5)

The displayed psi solves -Delta psi=h_x, and its compact support fixes the canonical full-plane inverse. Equivalently (5) follows from the Fourier symbols, including their zero-frequency continuous extension for this input. There is no added harmonic term.

On a neighborhood of the support of b, (5) gives

    U[h_0]=(0,s(y)), h_0=-s(y), Dh_0=0,               (6)

where s(y)=1 on the upper component and -1 on the lower one. Both h_0 and U[h_0] vanish near the origin, so b[h_0]=c[h_0]=0. In (6), s may be extended to a smooth function constant on neighborhoods of both components; its values elsewhere will not enter any product.

#### 4. The high-frequency density and the exact cross term

Set

    A_n=1/(n^4 L_n^beta),
    phi_n=A_n b(x,y)cos(ny),
    h_n=-Delta phi_n.

These are real compact smooth S1 functions. Formula (5) again gives compact velocities and b[h_n]=c[h_n]=0 exactly. All supports stay in the region (6). From (2) and (4),

    sup_(R>=1) N_(beta,R)^log(h_n)<=C_beta.            (7)

The leading term in its top derivative component has scale A_n n^4 L_n^beta=1. Lower derivative and coordinate terms are bounded by the same estimate.

The quadratic expansion is exact:

    T(h_0+h_n)=T(h_0)+g_n+T(h_n),
    g_n=U[h_0].Dh_n=s(y)partial_y h_n.               (8)

There is no term U[h_n].Dh_0, because Dh_0 is zero on the whole support of U[h_n]. Put b_tilde=s b. This is a smooth compact function, even in both coordinates, with ||b_tilde||_2=||b||_2. Since s is locally constant wherever b or any of its derivatives is supported,

    g_n=-A_n partial_y Delta(b_tilde cos(ny)).        (9)

This is S1 despite b_tilde being even in y, because the outside derivative is odd. Its leading contribution to the ordered Hessian is the yy entry. Applying the asymptotic in section 2 with five y derivatives yields

    ||D^2 Q_beta g_n||_2/n ->||b||_2/sqrt(2)>0.       (10)

Every other Hessian entry or derivative on the fixed envelope has one fewer high-frequency factor and tends to zero after the same division. Formula (3) gives the constant in (10).

For the self-interaction, (5) gives

    U1[h_n]=-A_n partial_xy(b cos(ny)),
    U2[h_n]= A_n partial_xx(b cos(ny)).

The first component has at most one high-frequency factor and the second has none. The x and y density derivatives have at most two and three factors respectively. Therefore T(h_n) is a finite sum of compact smooth fixed envelopes, multiplied by A_n^2 n^j for j<=3 and by sine or cosine at frequency 0 or 2n. The envelope functions do not depend on n. Equations (2) and (4) prove

    sup_(R>=1) N_(beta,R)^log(T(h_n))
       <=C_beta A_n^2 n^5 L_n^beta
        =C_beta n^(-3)L_n^(-beta)->0.                (11)

Any cancellation between leading self-interaction terms only improves this bound; none is assumed.

#### 5. Discontinuity at zero

The fixed compact smooth function T(h_0) has uniformly bounded logarithmic norm by (4). For any R>=1, the norm dominates the unweighted top component. Apply the triangle inequality to (8) in that component, and use (10)-(11). There are n_0 and c_beta>0 such that

    inf_(R>=1) N_(beta,R)^log(T(h_0+h_n))>=c_beta n,
    sup_(R>=1) N_(beta,R)^log(h_0+h_n)<=C_beta        (n>=n_0).         (12)

Now define

    v_n=n^(-1/4)(h_0+h_n).

The first inequality in (1) follows from the second bound of (12). Bilinearity of U[h].Dh gives

    inf_(R>=1)N_(beta,R)^log(T(v_n))

The support, symmetry and exact normalization assertions were proved above and are preserved by scaling. This completes the proof.

## P77. The logarithmic inverse at every power above the trace threshold

### P77.1. A conditional inverse at every logarithmic power above the trace threshold

The inverse of part P75 extends to every logarithmic power beta in (1/2,1]. A resolvent integral controls the fractional power of the logarithmic multiplier. A positive convolution factor and a convergent binomial series identify its norm with the original logarithmic norm.

#### 1. Statement and hypotheses

Set R=2^31, X=(x,y), r=|X|, J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), and K=log(1-Delta). Fourier inversion has factor (2pi)^(-2). All scalar densities are real, even in x and odd in y. The canonical velocity is U[h]=(-R1R2 h,R1^2 h), where Rj=partial_j(-Delta)^(-1/2); no harmonic velocity may be added. Define

    w=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), omega0=(1+r^2)^(-3/5),
    omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10), omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    L(h)=||wh||_(Hdot^-1), Pj(h)=||omegaj D^j h||_2,
    E(h)^2=P2(h)^2+2^22 P1(h)^2+2^53 L(h)^2.

Derivatives are ordered Cartesian tensors with their Euclidean norm. The negative norm is the canonical full-plane Fourier norm, equivalently the dual norm against centrally odd homogeneous H^1 functions. E denotes the completion of compact smooth S1 densities in this energy. In particular P0<=E/2048. For 0<beta<=1 and 0<tau<=2^-12 put

    N_(tau,beta)(h)=E(Q_(tau,beta)h),

These also mean completions of the same compact smooth core.

Let rho and u=U[rho] be smooth sublinear S1 reference fields. Require every derivative of rho and u to have at most polynomial growth. Suppose 9/5<c<37/20, a0=rho_y(0)>=1, c+c[rho]=1, and c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0) when that trace exists. Set V=cX+u and

    A=[[rho_y,-rho_x/2],[-rho_x/2,0]],
    M=(2c+1)I+sym Du+A,
    Mj=(1+c+V.D log omegaj)I-j sym DV+A, j=1,2.

Assume everywhere the pointwise inequalities

    M>=[2/5+(11/5)c r^2/(R^2+r^2)]I on r<=R,

With d=4/9 assume the global decay bounds

    sup r^d(|D rho|+r|D^2rho|)<=186,

and all the global derivative bounds

For the normalized conclusion assume additionally

    T^(-gamma)rho(TX)->G(X)=r^gamma Theta(theta), gamma=1/c,             (1)

uniformly on compact annuli, with Theta continuous and not identically zero. Write

    A_fix h=(cX+u).Dh-h+U[h].D rho,
    B h=A_fix h-c[h]X.D rho.                                           (2)

**Theorem.** Under these hypotheses:

(a) For every 0<beta<=1 and 0<tau<=2^-12, B_(tau,beta) is bounded on E with norm at most 1+8tau. The two logarithmic completions coincide as spaces of tempered distributions, and

    N_(tau,beta)(h)<(29/7)N_beta(h),
    N_beta(h)<(2 tau^(-beta)+16)N_(tau,beta)(h).                        (3)

Strict inequalities here and below are replaced by equality at the zero input where necessary.

(b) For tau=2^-20, the maximal distributional realization of A_fix on N_(tau,beta) is a bijective closed generator, with

It is the same maximal realization on N_beta. For 1/2<=beta<=1 its inverse obeys

(c) For 1/2<beta<=1, with (1), the maximal distributional domain of B on either space is D(A_fix) intersect ker c. Its range is precisely the hyperplane f_y(0)=0. The inverse has the bounds (4) and (5) in the corresponding norms.

#### 2. Positive inverse kernels and integer powers

The scalar Laplace formula is

    B_(tau,beta)=Gamma(beta)^(-1) int_0^infinity
                    exp(-u) u^(beta-1) J^(-2tau u)du.                 (6)

Each Bessel multiplier J^(-2a) is a positive radial probability kernel, obtained by integrating the heat kernel at time T against the gamma density of shape a and rate 1. Thus (6) is also a positive radial probability kernel.

First consider P=B_(tau,1). For its n-th power, n>=1, the outer variable U has gamma shape n, the Bessel shape is a=tau U, and the inner heat time has gamma shape a. Put v=n tau. Polar integration gives heat moments 2^j Gamma(1+j/2) T^(j/2). The beta integral implies Gamma(a+1/2)/Gamma(a)<=sqrt(pi)a. Consequently, for the spatial moments of P^n,

    M1<=pi v<=4v, M2=4v,
    M3<=6pi[v^2+(tau+1/2)v]<=20v^2+30v,
    M4=32[v^2+(tau+1)v]<=32v^2+64v,

          <=200v^3+1000v^2+1000v.                                    (7)

The last bounds use tau<=1 and pi<22/7<10/3. They retain polynomial, rather than exponential, dependence on n.

The general low-kernel identity of part P71, with sigma=11/5, states for a radial positive probability convolution T that

    L(Th)<= [1+(3+sigma/2)M1/R+(3+5sigma/2)M2/R^2
                 +(1+9sigma/2)M3/R^3+(7sigma/2)M4/R^4
                 +sigma M5/R^5]L(h).                                (8)

It follows by conjugating the kernel by w and writing wh as the divergence of its canonical Hdot^-1 potential gradient. Central oddness bounds the remaining zero-order commutator by its r-weighted L2 norm. It uses no weighted Riesz assertion for w. The derivative weight ratios satisfy omegaj(X)/omegaj(Y)<=1+2|X-Y|, so Pj(Th)<=(1+2M1)Pj(h).

Substitution of (7) in (8) bounds its excess by l1 v+l2 v^2+l3 v^3, where

    l1=82/(5R)+34/R^2+327/R^3+2464/(5R^4)+2200/R^5,
    l2=218/R^3+1232/(5R^4)+2200/R^5,

Each li is less than 1 at R=2^31. Taking the larger component bound gives

    ||P^n||_(E->E)<=1+8n tau+(n tau)^2+(n tau)^3.                      (9)

For a gamma outer shape beta<=1, couple U_beta and an independent U_(1-beta), whose sum has shape1. Conditional gamma heat times can also be added. The radial heat moments are increasing functions of that time. Every spatial moment of B_(tau,beta) is therefore no larger than the corresponding moment of P. Part P75's sharper n=1 bounds then give

This also follows directly by replacing every rising factorial of beta in the moment formula by its value at 1.

#### 3. Equivalence with the original logarithmic norm

Let S=Q_(tau,beta) B_(1,beta). For a scalar z>=0 its symbol is

    s(z)=[(1+tau z)/(1+z)]^beta
        =exp[-int_0^infinity(1-exp(-tz)) nu(t)dt],

The integrable nonnegative density nu has mass beta log(1/tau). Expanding the exponential shows that S is a positive convolution probability: an atom at time 0 and a compound-Poisson mixture of the positive kernels exp(-tK)=J^(-2t). This is an explicit series of finite positive measures and requires no unproved functional calculus on E.

The identity B_(1,beta)=B_(tau,beta)S, together with Jensen's inequality conditional on a centered radial summand, shows Mj(S)<=Mj(B_(1,beta)) for j>=1. The gamma coupling above further bounds those moments by B_(1,1). Its first moment is at most pi/2, and its low excess in (8) is D_R<2^-27, by parts P71 and P73. Thus

    ||S||_(E->E)<=1+pi<29/7.                                         (12)

For the reverse factor put q=1-tau and P=B_(tau,1). The scalar identity is

    S^(-1)=tau^(-beta)(I-qP)^beta
          =tau^(-beta)[I-sum_(n>=1) a_n q^n P^n],

For beta=1 only a1=1 is nonzero. For 0<beta<1 the series is norm convergent on E by (9) and q<1. It agrees with the Fourier symbol on Schwartz functions, hence supplies the inverse on E. To bound it let S_k=sum a_n q^n n^k. Differentiating 1-(1-q)^beta gives

    S0=1-tau^beta,
    S1=beta q tau^(beta-1),
    S2=beta q tau^(beta-1)+beta(1-beta)q^2 tau^(beta-2),

In particular tau S1<=beta tau^beta, tau^2 S2<=2beta tau^beta and tau^3 S3<=6beta tau^beta. Equation (9) in (13) therefore gives

Equations (12) and (14) prove the core inequalities (3). All multipliers used here preserve Schwartz functions and act continuously on tempered distributions. Radial cutoffs approximate a Schwartz function in its Schwartz topology, and E is continuous in that topology, since L(g)<=||rg||_2 for centrally odd g. Given a compact smooth E input g, B_(tau,beta)g is Schwartz and is thus approximable by compact smooth densities in N_(tau,beta). This proves that Q_(tau,beta) is an onto isometry from its completion to E. The same argument applies to Q_(1,beta). Part P75 proves, with exactly the reference hypotheses above,

## P78. A sharp half-logarithmic product estimate

### P78.1. The critical logarithmic multiplier estimate in two dimensions

A half logarithmic derivative is enough to multiply an H^1 function into L2. This is the endpoint product needed in one part of the low nonlinear estimate, but transferring it to the weighted IPM spaces requires a separate localization argument.

#### 1. Exact statement

Use Fourier inversion f(X)=(2pi)^(-2)int exp(iX.xi)fhat(xi)dxi on R^2. Let

    Q_beta=(1+log(1-Delta))^beta,
    H_beta={g in tempered distributions:Q_beta g in L2},
    ||g||_(H_beta)=||Q_beta g||_2,
    ||phi||_(H^1)=||(1-Delta)^(1/2)phi||_2.

Real or complex scalar functions are allowed. These are inhomogeneous norms. No parity condition is imposed.

**Theorem.** Multiplication extends continuously from Schwartz inputs to H_beta times H^1 with values in L2 if and only if beta>=1/2. At the endpoint,

    ||g phi||_2 <= (8/sqrt(pi)) ||Q_(1/2)g||_2 ||phi||_(H^1)
                 <5 ||Q_(1/2)g||_2 ||phi||_(H^1)                      (1)

for nonzero inputs. The same bound applies for beta>=1/2 after replacing Q_(1/2) by Q_beta. For every beta<1/2 there are smooth compactly supported g_n with bounded H_beta norm and compactly supported phi_n in H^1 with bounded H^1 norm such that ||g_n phi_n||_2 tends to infinity. Smooth compact approximations of phi_n may also be used.

This is an unweighted multiplication theorem. It does not assert a weighted IPM bilinear bound, a rough-transport energy estimate or a nonlinear inverse.

#### 2. Orthogonal frequency decomposition

Let P0 be Fourier projection to |xi|<1, and for j>=1 let Pj project to 2^(j-1)<=|xi|<2^j. Put g_j=Pj g, phi_j=Pj phi,

    a_j=||g_j||_2, b_j=2^j||phi_j||_2.

The projections are orthogonal on L2; values on boundary circles do not affect any norm. Cauchy-Schwarz in Fourier space gives, for a function with Fourier support in |xi|<=2^j,

    ||f||_infinity <= 2^j/(2sqrt(pi)) ||f||_2.                         (2)

The factor is (2pi)^(-1) times the square root of the disk area, using Plancherel with the stated normalization. Also

    sum b_j^2 <=4||phi||_(H^1)^2,
    sum (j+1)a_j^2 <=2||Q_(1/2)g||_2^2.                               (3)

For the second inequality, j=0 is immediate. For j>=1 the Fourier weight is at least 1+log(1+2^(2j-2)); since log2>1/2 this weight is at least (j+1)/2. For the first inequality, 2^(2j)<=4|xi|^2 on the j-th annulus and the j=0 term is controlled by the inhomogeneous L2 part.

For finite frequency sums, decompose the product into the three sets of index pairs j>=k+3, k>=j+3, and |j-k|<=2. The estimates below are uniform in the number of bands.

#### 3. High g and low phi

Set T_j=g_j sum_(0<=k<=j-3) phi_k, j>=3. Its Fourier support is contained in

    3*2^(j-3)<=|xi|<=9*2^(j-3).

These annuli have overlap at most 2: an annulus and the one two indices later are disjoint. Hence Plancherel and pointwise Cauchy-Schwarz imply ||sum T_j||_2^2<=2 sum||T_j||_2^2. By (2), (3) and Cauchy-Schwarz in k,

    ||sum_(k<=j-3)phi_k||_infinity
       <=(1/(2sqrt(pi))) sum_(k<=j-3)b_k
       <=sqrt(j-2)/sqrt(pi) ||phi||_(H^1).

It follows that

    ||sum T_j||_2 <=(2/sqrt(pi)) ||Q_(1/2)g||_2 ||phi||_(H^1).          (4)

#### 4. High phi and low g

Set U_k=phi_k sum_(0<=j<=k-3)g_j. The same overlap 2 assertion holds. Equation (2) gives

    ||U_k||_2 <= b_k/(2sqrt(pi)) sum_(j<=k-3)2^(j-k)a_j
              <= b_k/(2sqrt(48pi)) ||g||_2,

since sum_(m>=3)2^(-2m)=1/48. Summing with overlap 2 and using (3) yields

    ||sum U_k||_2 <=1/sqrt(24pi) ||g||_2 ||phi||_(H^1).                (5)

#### 5. Neighboring bands and passage to the completed spaces

For |j-k|<=2, (2) directly gives

    ||g_j phi_k||_2 <=a_j b_k/(2sqrt(pi)).

For each of the five offsets k-j, Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the sum of a_j b_k by ||a||_(ell2)||b||_(ell2), with missing negative indices set to zero. The triangle inequality therefore gives

    ||sum_(|j-k|<=2)g_j phi_k||_2
       <=5/sqrt(pi) ||g||_2 ||phi||_(H^1).                            (6)

No false annular support claim is made for these products, which may have low frequencies. Combining (4)-(6), and using ||g||_2<=||Q_(1/2)g||_2, gives the stronger factor (7+1/sqrt(24))/sqrt(pi), hence (1). The comparison 8/sqrt(pi)<5 follows from pi>3 and 64<75.

Finite frequency sums converge in H_(1/2) and H^1 respectively. The uniform bilinear bound makes their products Cauchy in L2. They also converge to the pointwise product in local L1 by Cauchy-Schwarz and local L2 convergence, so the L2 limit is that product. This proves the continuous extension and its uniqueness. Since Q_beta dominates Q_(1/2) in Fourier modulus for beta>=1/2, the same bound holds in that range.

#### 6. Sharpness below one half

Fix a nonzero smooth chi supported in |X|<1/2. For L>=1 let epsilon=exp(-L), and set

    phi_L(r)=sqrt(L)                         if 0<=r<=epsilon,
             log(1/r)/sqrt(L)               ifepsilon<r<1,
             0                              ifr>=1.

This continuous piecewise radial function belongs to H^1. Direct polar integration gives

    ||D phi_L||_2^2=2pi,
    ||phi_L||_2^2=pi L exp(-2L)
                    +(2pi/L)int_0^L t^2 exp(-2t)dt
                <=pi L exp(-2L)+pi/(2L).

In particular ||phi_L||_(H^1)^2<3pi, uniformly for L>=1. Here L exp(-2L)<=exp(-2)<1/4, since it decreases for L>=1 and exp(1)>2.

For 0<=beta<1/2 define

    g_L(X)=epsilon^(-1) L^(-beta) chi(X/epsilon).

Fourier scaling and

    1+log(1+epsilon^(-2)|zeta|^2)
       <=(1+2L)(1+log(1+|zeta|^2))

give ||Q_beta g_L||_2<=3^beta ||Q_beta chi||_2. On the support of g_L, phi_L=sqrt(L), so

    ||g_L phi_L||_2=L^(1/2-beta)||chi||_2 -> infinity.                 (7)

Thus no finite multiplication constant exists below beta=1/2. If beta<0, use the beta=0 construction: its H_beta norm is at most its bounded L2 norm. Finally, for each fixed L, approximate phi_L by compact smooth functions in H^1. Because g_L is bounded for that fixed L, the products converge in L2. ## P79. Commutators of the logarithmic multiplier with moderate weights

### P79.1. Logarithmic commutators with moderate weights

The half logarithmic multiplication theorem extends to the two derivative weights used in the IPM energy. The proof uses a positive integral of Bessel kernels, so it controls the commutator in the actual weighted norm. This result alone does not replace a homogeneous test norm by an inhomogeneous one on the full plane.

#### 1. Statement and domains

Use Fourier inversion with factor (2pi)^(-2) on R^2. Let K=log(1-Delta), Q_beta=(I+K)^beta, and B_beta=Q_beta^(-1). The multipliers act on tempered distributions. Functions may take values in a finite-dimensional real or complex Hilbert space H, with all L2 norms using its Euclidean norm. Let omega be a smooth positive weight such that omega, its reciprocal and all their derivatives have at most polynomial growth. Assume, for some a>=0,

    |omega(X)/omega(Y)-1| <= a|X-Y| for all X,Y.                      (1)

The weighted space L2_omega consists of measurable f with omega f in L2(H). It embeds into tempered distributions: applying (1) in both directions bounds omega and its reciprocal by constants times 1+|X|. Multiplication by omega is therefore defined on these distributions.

**Commutator theorem.** For 0<beta<=1, the distributional commutator extends from Schwartz functions to a bounded map on the weighted space, and

    ||[Q_beta,omega]f||_2 <= a pi beta ||omega f||_2.                  (2)

Here the expression means Q_beta(omega f)-omega Q_beta f as a distribution; (2) states that this difference is in L2, even when its two summands separately are not. At beta=0 the commutator is zero. If 1/2<=beta<=1 and omega Q_beta f is in L2, then

    ||Q_(1/2)(omega f)||_2
        <= (1+a pi/2)^2 ||omega Q_beta f||_2.                        (3)

In particular this statement includes membership of omega f in the domain of Q_(1/2) on L2. It is an implication from the stated distributional weighted domain, not an assumption that arbitrary multiplication preserves that domain.

For the IPM weights

    omega1=(1+|X|^2)^(-1/10), omega2=(1+4|X|^2)^(2/5),

(1) holds with a=2. Let R>=1 and let Nlog_(beta,R)(h)=E_R(Q_beta h) be the completion in part P70, explicitly

    E_R(H)^2=||omega2 D^2H||_2^2
        +2^22||omega1 DH||_2^2
        +2^53||w_R H||_(Hdot^-1)^2,
    w_R=(1+|X|^2/R^2)^(-11/10).

Here h is real, even in x and odd in y; D^2h is the full ordered Cartesian tensor. For 1/2<=beta<=1 and any scalar phi in H1(R^2),

    ||omega2 D^2h phi||_2
        <= 5(1+pi)^2 Nlog_(beta,R)(h)||phi||_(H1).                    (4)

If phi is centrally odd in homogeneous H1, then

    ||omega2 D^2h phi/<r>||_2
        <= 5 sqrt(5)(1+pi)^2 Nlog_(beta,R)(h)||Dphi||_2.              (5)

The homogeneous space in (5) is the gradient-norm completion of centrally odd compact smooth functions. Its angular Hardy representative is used. No positive strain trace is asserted at beta=1/2.

#### 2. Positive-power integral and the first Bessel moment

For 0<beta<1 and k>=0, differentiating in k and using the gamma integral gives

    (1+k)^beta-1
       = [beta/Gamma(1-beta)] int_0^infinity
                     exp(-t)(1-exp(-tk))t^(-1-beta)dt.               (6)

Both sides vanish at k=0, so differentiation determines the constant and sign. By Fourier transformation,

    Q_beta=I+[beta/Gamma(1-beta)] int_0^infinity
                       exp(-t)(I-J^(-2t))t^(-1-beta)dt,
    J=(1-Delta)^(1/2).                                              (7)

On a Schwartz input the integral holds in tempered distributions. To check convergence directly, each Schwartz seminorm of (I-J^(-2t))f is O(t) at zero, with constants depending on f and its seminorm; at infinity it has at most polynomial growth in t. The factor exp(-t) handles the latter range.

The kernel of J^(-2t) is a positive probability measure, represented by first taking a gamma variable S of shape t and unit rate, and then a heat kernel of time S. The first moment of that heat kernel in two dimensions is sqrt(pi S), so

    M1(t)=sqrt(pi) Gamma(t+1/2)/Gamma(t) <= pi t.                     (8)

For the last inequality, divide by t and use the beta integral:

    Gamma(t+1/2)/Gamma(t+1)
       =(1/sqrt(pi)) int_0^1 u^(t-1/2)(1-u)^(-1/2)du
       <= (1/sqrt(pi)) int_0^1 u^(-1/2)(1-u)^(-1/2)du
       =sqrt(pi).

This proves (8) for every t>0, without a numerical gamma estimate.

The kernel of [J^(-2t),omega]f at X is

    int k_t(X-Y)(omega(Y)-omega(X))f(Y)dY.

Its Hilbert norm is bounded by convolution of a|Z|k_t(Z) with |omega f|. Young's inequality, which is also valid for this vector-valued convolution, gives norm at most a M1(t)||omega f||_2. Integrating this bound in (7) gives exactly a pi beta, since the remaining scalar integral is Gamma(1-beta). The integral of the commutator is absolutely convergent in L2 at both endpoints. It agrees with the distributional commutator on Schwartz inputs by (7).

For beta=1 use instead

    K=int_0^infinity exp(-v)(I-exp(vDelta))dv/v.

This is the scalar identity log(1+lambda)=int exp(-v)(1-exp(-v lambda))dv/v, checked by differentiation and the value at zero. The heat kernel has first moment sqrt(pi v). Thus the commutator norm is at most a sqrt(pi)Gamma(1/2)=a pi, proving (2) at this endpoint as well.

Schwartz functions are dense in L2_omega: truncate and mollify compactly supported weighted L2 inputs, where omega is bounded above and below. The bound just proved gives an L2 limit of the commutators. Weighted convergence gives convergence in tempered distributions; Q_beta and multiplication by omega are continuous there under the stated polynomial derivative assumptions. Consequently the limit is exactly the distributional commutator. This proves (2) on its full stated domain.

#### 3. Inverse moments and weighted domain transfer

For 0<delta<=1 the gamma integral expresses B_delta as the positive probability convolution

    B_delta=Gamma(delta)^(-1) int_0^infinity
                       u^(delta-1)exp(-u)J^(-2u)du.                 (9)

If U has gamma shape delta and S conditional on U has gamma shape U, its first spatial moment is sqrt(pi) E sqrt(S). Conditional Jensen and gamma convolution give

    M1(B_delta) <=sqrt(pi) E sqrt(U) <=pi/2.                         (10)

Indeed add an independent gamma variable of shape 1-delta to U. Their sum has gamma shape 1, its square-root mean is Gamma(3/2)=sqrt(pi)/2, and addition increases the square root. At delta=1 no additional variable is needed. At delta=0 use B_0=I and moment zero.

Equation (1), positivity and Young's inequality imply, on L2_omega,

    ||omega B_delta g||_2 <= (1+a pi/2)||omega g||_2,
                       0<=delta<=1.                               (11)

As with the commutator, the extension agrees with the Fourier multiplier in distributions by weighted density. If g=Q_beta f is in L2_omega, then f=B_beta g and Q_(1/2)f=B_(beta-1/2)g. Using (2) with power 1/2 and then (11),

    ||Q_(1/2)(omega f)||_2
       <=||omega Q_(1/2)f||_2+(a pi/2)||omega f||_2
       <=(1+a pi/2)^2||omega g||_2.

Every equality holds first in distributions and the resulting right side proves L2 membership. This is (3).

#### 4. The actual derivative weights

The Euclidean triangle inequality in the augmented vector (1,bX) gives

    sqrt(1+b^2|X|^2)/sqrt(1+b^2|Y|^2) <=1+b|X-Y|.

For omega2 take b=2 and raise this bound to power 4/5; for omega1 take b=1, exchange X,Y, and raise to power 1/5. Concavity gives (1+t)^nu<=1+nu t<=1+t for 0<=nu<=1. Thus both the ratio and the reciprocal ratio of either weight are at most 1+2|X-Y|. If a positive ratio z and its reciprocal are bounded by 1+2d, then

    |z-1| <=2d,

because its lower bound is 1/(1+2d). This proves (1) with a=2. All derivatives of these two weights and their reciprocals have polynomial growth, as required.

#### 5. Hilbert-valued multiplication and the homogeneous test

Part P78 proves ||g phi||_2<=5||Q_(1/2)g||_2||phi||_(H1) for scalar g. Its complete proof also gives the same constant for Hilbert-valued g. To verify this extension, apply the same orthogonal Fourier disks and annuli componentwise. Hilbert-valued Plancherel and Cauchy-Schwarz give the identical disk bound ||g_j||_infinity<=2^j||g_j||_2/(2sqrt(pi)). High-g, low-phi products have the same annular supports and overlap two, and the squared Hilbert norms sum by Plancherel. In the reverse pairs use the disk bound for the Hilbert norm of low g and scalar L2 norm of high phi. For neighboring bands use scalar ||phi_k||_infinity and Hilbert ||g_j||_2, then the same five Cauchy-Schwarz sums. These give respectively 2/sqrt(pi), 1/sqrt(24pi) and 5/sqrt(pi). Their sum is less than 5. Finite band approximations converge in the same Hilbert norms and in local L1, identifying the product exactly as in part P78. No dimension factor is introduced.

Apply (3) with omega=omega2 and f=D^2h. Derivatives commute with Q_beta in distributions, and the definition of Nlog bounds ||omega2 Q_beta D^2h||_2 by Nlog. The Hilbert multiplication theorem now proves (4), including the tensor contraction convention.

For a centrally odd compact test phi, its nonzero angular Fourier modes give

    ||phi/r||_2 <=||Dphi||_2.

Set psi=phi/<r>. Then ||psi||_2<=||Dphi||_2 and, by the product rule and r^2/<r>^3<=1,

    ||Dpsi||_2 <=||Dphi||_2+||phi r/<r>^3||_2
                  <=2||Dphi||_2.

Thus ||psi||_(H1)<=sqrt(5)||Dphi||_2. Applying (4) proves (5); completion in the gradient norm proves it for every stated homogeneous test.

#### Scope and dependencies

The multiplier estimate is independent of the numerical reference. Its proof uses the scalar gamma and beta integrals, positive heat kernels, Young's inequality and the fully reproduced vector extension of part P78. The weighted energy completion is the one identified in part P70. The bound does not yet estimate ||D^2h phi||_2 for a homogeneous H1 test: omega2 grows only like r^(4/5), so dividing phi by omega2 does not have an automatically bounded H1 norm by the angular Hardy inequality. A separate localization is needed for the actual low nonlinear IPM estimate. Rough high-energy transport, a nonlinear inverse and numerical residual smallness are not conclusions of this theorem.

## P81. A Lipschitz commutator bound for the logarithmic multiplier

### P81.1. Logarithmic transport commutators need only a Lipschitz velocity

The unweighted logarithmic commutator follows from the distortion of the Dirichlet form under a volume-preserving flow. The order-preserving integral for the operator logarithm converts that distortion into a bounded operator difference. A relative weight difference then gives an absolutely integrable error. No second derivative of the velocity is needed in these estimates.

#### 1. Statement and conventions

Work on R^2 with Fourier inverse factor (2pi)^(-2), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), K=log(1-Delta), and Q_(tau,beta)=(I+tau K)^beta. Let W be a real smooth divergence-free vector field with

    d=||DW||_(Linf,op)<infinity.

Assume all derivatives of W have at most polynomial growth; in particular |W(X)|<=|W(0)|+d|X|. This assumption makes every displayed commutator on Schwartz inputs a tempered distribution with its usual meaning. Write D_W=W.grad. Let omega be a positive smooth weight whose derivatives and reciprocal derivatives have polynomial growth. Put L2_omega={f:omega f in L2}. Scalars may be real or complex, or finite-dimensional Hilbert-valued; the same constants apply.

**Theorem 1.** The commutator [K,D_W], initially on smooth compact inputs, extends to a bounded operator on ordinary L2, with

    ||[K,D_W]||_(L2->L2) <=2d.                                      (1)

The constant 2 is sharp uniformly over these divergence-free fields.

Suppose, more generally, that nonnegative numbers a_1,...,a_m obey

    |omega(X)/omega(Y)-1|
          <=sum_(j=1)^m a_j |X-Y|^j.                               (2)

Then the commutator extends to L2_omega and

    ||omega[K,D_W]f||_2
       <=[2+sum_(j=1)^m a_j C_j]d||omega f||_2,
    C_j=2^(j+1)Gamma((j+4)/2)Gamma(j/2).                            (3)

In particular C_1=3pi, C_2=16, C_3=15pi and C_4=192. For the actual derivative weights omega1=<r>^(-1/5), omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), the bound is (2+6pi)d<21d. For omega0=<r>^(-6/5), the bound is (18+6pi)d<37d. For w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), R>=1, it is

    [2+9pi/R+48/R^2+15pi/R^3]d.                                    (4)

These are bounds for the commutator on each individual weighted L2 space. They are not a bound on the full energy containing two derivatives and a negative-order component.

**Theorem 2.** Suppose (2) has only the linear term a_1=a. For tau>0 and 0<beta<=1, the conjugated commutator extends on L2_omega and satisfies

    ||[Q_(tau,beta),D_W]Q_(tau,beta)^(-1)||_(L2_omega->L2_omega)
       <= beta tau (2+3pi a)d (1+a pi tau)^3.                       (5)

For ordinary L2 set a=0: the bound is 2beta tau d. For either actual derivative weight set a=2. The operators on the left are interpreted first on the natural multiplier core and then by the bounded extension proved below. The bounds are Lipschitz in W through DW. Consequently they extend by operator-norm limits to any uniformly Lipschitz C1 divergence-free field approximated by such smooth fields with uniformly convergent gradients; an additive constant in W has zero commutator.

#### 2. Dirichlet-form distortion under the flow

The vector field is globally Lipschitz, so its ordinary differential equation has a complete flow Phi_t. The elementary differential inequality for differences gives

    ||D Phi_t||_op, ||D Phi_t^(-1)||_op <=exp(d|t|).

For completeness, differentiate D Phi_t along a trajectory and apply Gronwall to its action on each vector. The Jacobian determinant solves its derivative equal to div W times itself, and thus equals one. Therefore T_t f=f composed with Phi_t is unitary on L2. It maps H1 onto H1, with quadratic-form bounds

    exp(-2d|t|)J^2 <= T_t^* J^2 T_t <= exp(2d|t|)J^2.               (6)

This includes the L2 part of the J^2 form: its norm is unchanged, and exp(-2d|t|)<=1<=exp(2d|t|). No bound on D^2W is used.

We need the order implication for the logarithm, so record its proof. If positive self-adjoint operators A and B, both bounded below by a positive scalar, satisfy A<=B in form order, their resolvents satisfy

    (B+lambda)^(-1) <=(A+lambda)^(-1), lambda>=0.

Indeed the variational identity

    <f,(A+lambda)^(-1)f>
       =sup_u [2Re<f,u>-<u,(A+lambda)u>]

proves the implication directly, using the form domains and their inclusion. The scalar integral

    log z=int_0^infinity[(1+lambda)^(-1)-(z+lambda)^(-1)]dlambda

follows by elementary integration. To make the domain passage explicit, choose c>0 below both spectral lower bounds. For either operator S=A,B the bounded positive operators

    int_0^L[(c+lambda)^(-1)I-(S+lambda)^(-1)]dlambda

increase as L tends to infinity. Their quadratic forms increase to the form of log(S/c), by the scalar spectral theorem and monotone convergence. The resolvent order bounds the truncated A form by the truncated B form. Hence finiteness of the B logarithmic form implies finiteness of the A logarithmic form, and the limiting inequality holds with exactly this domain inclusion. In (6) the outer two operators have logarithmic form domain Dom(K^(1/2)); applying these inclusions twice shows that the middle operator has the same domain. Thus no common-domain hypothesis is assumed in the passage. Using unitary conjugation and log(aJ^2)=log(a)I+K gives

    -2d|t|I <= T_t^* K T_t-K <=2d|t|I.                              (7)

The difference is bounded even though its two terms are unbounded. Its quadratic-form inequality, initially on the common logarithmic form domain, defines this bounded self-adjoint difference by polarization.

Differentiate <T_t f,K T_t f> at t=0 for compact smooth f. The derivative is <f,[K,D_W]f>, since D_W is skew-symmetric and K is self-adjoint. Differentiation is justified in H1: W and DW are bounded on the transported compact support, so the flow difference quotient converges in H1 to W.grad f, and K maps H1 continuously to L2. Divide (7) by |t| and pass to zero to obtain

    |<f,[K,D_W]f>|<=2d||f||_2^2.

The commutator is symmetric on this core. Polarization and the bounded self-adjoint quadratic form give (1) and its unique bounded extension. The same proof with the Hilbert sum applies to vector inputs.

#### 3. Sharpness of the constant

Take W=(dx,-dy), d>0. A direct Fourier calculation gives

    [K,D_W]fhat(xi)
       =2d(xi1^2-xi2^2)/(1+|xi|^2) fhat(xi).                       (8)

This real multiplier has essential supremum 2d in absolute value. Smooth Fourier packets at arbitrarily large |xi| in an arbitrarily narrow cone about the xi1-axis approach that supremum. They are Schwartz inputs; compact smooth approximation in the graph expressions, or the bounded multiplier extension itself, gives the same norm on the stated core closure. Thus a universal constant smaller than 2 cannot hold.

#### 4. The weight error is absolutely integrable

Let p_t(Z)=(4pi t)^(-1)exp(-|Z|^2/(4t)). The logarithm has the heat representation

    K=int_0^infinity exp(-t)(I-exp(tDelta))dt/t.                    (9)

Since div W=0, integration by parts gives

    [exp(tDelta),D_W]f(X)
       =int Dp_t(X-Y).(W(Y)-W(X))f(Y)dY.                           (10)

Initially use compact smooth inputs. Conjugating (10) by omega changes its kernel by the factor omega(X)/omega(Y). Subtract the unweighted kernel. Equations (2), |W(X)-W(Y)|<=d|X-Y| and Young's inequality bound the weighted-error operator by

    d sum_j a_j int_0^infinity exp(-t)dt/t
                         int |Z|^(j+1)|Dp_t(Z)|dZ.

Because |Dp_t|=|Z|p_t/(2t), the spatial moment is the heat moment of order j+2 divided by 2t. Polar integration gives

    int |Z|^m p_t(Z)dZ=2^m Gamma(1+m/2)t^(m/2).

The remaining time integral is therefore exactly C_j in (3). For j>=1 it converges at zero and infinity. The difference of the weighted and unweighted commutators consequently converges absolutely in bounded-operator norm. Combined with (1), this proves (3). It also identifies the weighted extension with the distributional commutator by compact smooth density in L2_omega.

For the two derivative weights, part P79 proves (2) with a_1=2. For omega0 both the ratio and its reciprocal are at most (1+|X-Y|)^(6/5)<=(1+|X-Y|)^2, so their distance from 1 is at most 2|X-Y|+|X-Y|^2. For w_R both ratios are at most (1+|X-Y|/R)^(11/5)<=(1+|X-Y|/R)^3. Expansion gives a_1=3/R, a_2=3/R^2 and a_3=1/R^3. The fact that reciprocal ratios have the same upper bound supplies the lower-ratio case as well. Substitution proves (4) and the other stated constants.

#### 5. Resolvent formula for a logarithmic power

Suppose now that (2) is linear. For eta>0 let B_(eta,b)=(I+eta K)^(-b), b>0. Its gamma/Bessel probability representation is

    B_(eta,b)=Gamma(b)^(-1) int_0^infinity
                        u^(b-1)exp(-u)J^(-2eta u)du.

The Bessel first moment bound M1(t)<=pi t from part P79 gives M1(B_(eta,b))<=pi eta b. Hence positive convolution and the ratio bound give

    ||B_(eta,b)||_(L2_omega->L2_omega) <=1+a pi eta b.                (11)

Let A=I+tau K. For lambda>=0,

    ||(lambda+A)^(-1)|| <= (1+lambda)^(-1)
                       [1+a pi tau/(1+lambda)]
                       <=(1+a pi tau)/(1+lambda).                  (12)

For 0<beta<1, differentiating the scalar resolvent representation, or subtracting its two operator products, yields

    [A^beta,D_W]
       =[sin(pi beta)/pi] int_0^infinity
             lambda^beta (lambda+A)^(-1)[A,D_W]
                                    (lambda+A)^(-1)dlambda.         (13)

To justify the identity, first truncate the scalar integral representation for A^beta, use the exact resolvent commutator identity, and pass to distributions on smooth core inputs. The norm majorant below is integrable at both endpoints, so the commutator side has a bounded extension. The resolvents map the Schwartz space to itself, and the polynomial-growth assumptions make all distributional products valid there.

By (3), ||[A,D_W]||<=tau(2+3pi a)d. Use (11) with eta=tau,b=beta for A^-beta, (12) twice, and

    [sin(pi beta)/pi] int_0^infinity
                    lambda^beta/(1+lambda)^2 dlambda=beta.

The last identity is the beta integral followed by Gamma(beta+1)Gamma(1-beta)=pi beta/sin(pi beta). It follows as well by integration by parts from the elementary Stieltjes representation of z^beta. This proves the sharper bound

    beta tau(2+3pi a)d (1+a pi tau)^2(1+a pi tau beta),

and hence (5). At beta=1 simply use [A,D_W]A^-1 and (11); the same stated upper bound applies.

The estimates are linear in d and invariant under addition of a constant velocity. Applying them to W_m-W_n proves the stated operator-norm extension to uniform-gradient limits. The limiting commutator on compact smooth inputs agrees with the distributional limit there. This conclusion does not require bounds for higher velocity derivatives along the approximating sequence.

#### Scope and dependencies

This is a transport commutator estimate at derivative order zero. The full high energy has additional commutators with DW and D^2W after differentiation, and its weighted negative-order part has its own factorization. Neither is removed by (5). The result supplies one missing input for a rough logarithmic transport theory; it is not that theory. The elementary order and flow arguments have been included rather than imported as an unverified operator-monotonicity assertion. The only outside dependency is the explicitly proved relative weight and Bessel first-moment facts in part P79, whose proofs are also repeated where used.
