## P82. A derivative product estimate in the logarithmic space

### P82.1. Logarithmic multiplication by a profile derivative

A profile derivative need not be in unweighted L2. Its Fourier transform is nevertheless integrable above the logarithmic trace threshold, and its next derivative has the required logarithmic L2 bound. A frequency difference gains one power at small coefficient frequency. This gives a multiplier estimate using exactly these two quantities.

#### 1. Spaces and statement

On R2 use Fourier inversion (2pi)^(-2), J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), K=log(1-Delta), and

    Q=Q_(tau,beta)=(1+tau K)^beta, 0<tau<=1, 1/2<=beta<=1.

Let a take values in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, with a represented by an integrable Fourier transform. Put

    A(a)=(2pi)^(-2) int |ahat(xi)| dxi,
    D(a)=||D Q a||_2.

Assume A(a) and D(a) are finite. Let f be Hilbert-valued with Qf in L2. Products below may mean any fixed bilinear contraction whose operator norm is at most one. No component-count factor is needed.

**Multiplier theorem.** The distributional product has Q(af) in L2 and

    ||Q(af)||_2 <= [A(a)+8 tau^(-1/2)D(a)]||Qf||_2.                 (1)

Let omega be a positive smooth weight with polynomially growing derivatives and reciprocal derivatives, and

    |omega(X)/omega(Y)-1|<=2|X-Y|.

Then, on the completion of smooth inputs in ||omega Qf||_2,

    ||omega Q(af)||_2
        <=[100 A(a)+400 tau^(-1/2)D(a)]||omega Qf||_2.               (2)

The constants hold for both actual weights omega1=<r>^(-1/5) and omega2=(1+4r2)^(2/5).

For the actual S1 density space define, for R>=1,

    w_R=(1+r2/R2)^(-11/10), L_R(h)=||w_R h||_(Hdot^-1),
    E_R(H)^2=||omega2 D2H||_2^2+2^22||omega1 DH||_2^2
                                         +2^53 L_R(H)^2,
    N_(tau,beta,R)(g)=E_R(Qg).

Take the compact smooth S1-core completion, with canonical U[g]=(-R1R2g,R1^2g) and no harmonic addition. If beta>1/2, epsilon=2beta-1, and a is Dg or DU[g], then

    A(a)<=4 tau^(-beta) N_(tau,beta,R)(g)/sqrt(epsilon),
    D(a)<=N_(tau,beta,R)(g).                                      (3)

Consequently for either derivative weight and any f in its weighted Q space,

    ||omega Q(af)||_2
       <=800 tau^(-beta) N_(tau,beta,R)(g)/sqrt(epsilon)
                                      *||omega Qf||_2.             (4)

The result controls differentiated products. It does not prove the full energy estimate for rough transport, its low negative-order commutator, or a nonlinear inverse.

#### 2. A frequency-difference bound

Write l_tau(xi)=1+tau log(1+|xi|2), q=l_tau^beta. Since

    1+|xi+eta|2 <=2(1+|xi|2)(1+|eta|2),

and tau log2<1, we have l_tau(xi+eta)<=l_tau(xi)+l_tau(eta). Concavity gives

    q(xi+eta)<=q(xi)+q(eta).

Apply this twice, with opposite xi, to obtain |q(xi+eta)-q(eta)|<=q(xi). Also

    |Dq(z)|=2tau beta |z|/(1+|z|2) l_tau(z)^(beta-1)<=tau beta<=1.

The mean-value theorem supplies the small-xi gain. Together,

    |q(xi+eta)-q(eta)|<=m(xi)q(xi),
    m(xi)=min(1,|xi|).                                            (5)

This bound is uniform in eta. It is the reason that an L2 norm of a itself is unnecessary.

#### 3. The critical product and the unweighted multiplier

Part P78 proves

    ||uv||_2<=5||Q_(1,1/2)u||_2||v||_(H1).                         (6)

The same bound holds for two finite-dimensional Hilbert-valued factors and a bilinear contraction of norm one. To verify this extension, use the orthogonal Fourier bands in that proof. In the low-high region the band sum of the H1 factor is bounded in Hilbert-valued Linfinity by its Fourier L1 norm and Cauchy-Schwarz. In the high-low region reverse the two factors. In the comparable-band region use the same Hilbert-valued Bernstein inequality and the triangle inequality, then scalar Cauchy-Schwarz on the band norms. The pointwise contraction is bounded by the product of the two Hilbert norms in all three regions. Orthogonality and all numerical constants are unchanged. These arguments also apply to the scalar nonnegative Fourier majorants below.

Initially take smooth Fourier inputs with compact support. In the Fourier formula for Q(af), separate a Qf from the difference (5). The first part has L2 norm at most A(a)||Qf||_2. For the difference, let a_* and f_* be the inverse Fourier transforms of m q |ahat| and |fhat|. Plancherel and the nonnegative convolution majorant give

    ||[Q,a]f||_2<=||a_* f_*||_2.

The normalization is exact: each product has Fourier convolution factor (2pi)^(-2). By (6),

    ||a_* f_*||_2<=5||a_*||_(H1)||Q_(1,1/2)f_*||_2.

Now J(xi)m(xi)<=sqrt(2)|xi|, hence ||a_*||_(H1)<=sqrt(2)D(a). Moreover

    (1+tau log(1+r2))^beta
        >=(1+tau log(1+r2))^(1/2)
        >=sqrt(tau)(1+log(1+r2))^(1/2).

Thus ||Q_(1,1/2)f_*||_2<=tau^(-1/2)||Qf||_2. Since 5sqrt(2)<8, this proves (1). Cutoffs and smooth approximation in Fourier space give simultaneous convergence in A and D, and in the Qf norm. In particular a converges uniformly, so the bounded extension agrees with the distributional product. The coefficient a can fail to lie in L2.

#### 4. Relative-weight transfer

The positive-kernel power formula of part P79, at the scale tau, gives

    ||[Q,omega]f||_2<=2pi tau beta ||omega f||_2.                    (7)

Indeed for beta<1 the first moment of its positive difference kernel is bounded by

    beta/Gamma(1-beta) int_0^infinity
         e^(-u)u^(-1-beta) M1(J^(-2tau u)) du <=pi tau beta,

using M1(J^(-2v))<=pi v. At beta=1 the heat representation of tau K gives the same limit directly. The inverse B=Q^-1 is a positive gamma/Bessel probability convolution with first moment at most pi tau beta. Hence

    ||omega B H||_2 <=(1+2pi tau beta)||omega H||_2.                 (8)

Put v=2pi tau beta<=2pi. Equations (7),(8) imply

    ||Q(omega f)||_2 <=(1+v+v2)||omega Qf||_2.

Apply (1) to a and omega f, then commute the output weight once by (7). Since ||a||infinity<=A(a), the resulting coefficient is

    (1+2v+2v2)A(a)+8(1+v+v2)tau^(-1/2)D(a).

The inequalities pi<22/7 and v<=2pi show that the first factor is below 100 and the second below 400. This proves (2). The same estimates show that omega f lies in the unweighted Q space exactly as used here. Distributional continuity follows from polynomial moderation and local L2 convergence; completion and the uniform operator estimates preserve the product definition. No weighted Fourier-Plancherel identity was used.

#### 5. Application to the actual profile space

Write H=Qg and n=E_R(H). The explicit physical partition and constants in part P80 give compactly supported rescaled H2 pieces F_j, at t_j=2^j, j>=0, with

    ||F_j||_(H2)<=K0 t_j^(1/5)n, K0=2595/2048,
    sum_(j>=0)2^(-4j/5)(1+2j log2)<31/4.

For q_tau=q_(tau,beta),

    q_tau(xi)^(-1)<=tau^(-beta)q_(1,beta)(xi)^(-1).

Consequently the Fourier derivative integral estimate of part P80 applies to each piece, with just the extra factor tau^(-beta). Its absolute Fourier convergence and the exact comparison K0^2(31/4)^2<64pi give

    (2pi)^(-2)int |xi||ghat(xi)|dxi
                  <=4 tau^(-beta)n/sqrt(2beta-1).                  (9)

Here ghat is understood through the absolutely convergent derivative series of that proof. Weighted distributional convergence identifies it with Dg and leaves no extra polynomial or zero-frequency contribution. The canonical velocity symbol has Euclidean norm at most one, so the same calculation controls the full ordered tensor DU[g]. These are the first bounds of (3), including bounded continuous representatives.

For the second bounds, Q commutes with Cartesian derivatives and with U. Since omega2>=1, ||D2Qg||_2<=n. The Euclidean norm of the U multiplier is at most one, so ||D2U[Qg]||_2<=n as well. This proves D(a)<=n for both choices.

Substitute (3) into (2). Since tau^(-1/2)<=tau^(-beta) and epsilon<=1, the coefficient is at most

    [400 tau^(-beta)/sqrt(epsilon)+400 tau^(-1/2)]n
                      <=800 tau^(-beta)n/sqrt(epsilon).

This proves (4). High-core approximation converges in both quantities in (3), hence in the multiplier operator norm. The result therefore holds on the actual completed density space and for arbitrary inputs in the indicated weighted Q completion.

#### Dependencies and scope

Part P78 supplies the sharp logarithmic product, whose Hilbert-valued extension was checked explicitly above. Part P79 supplies the relative-weight and Bessel first-moment facts; their scale dependence is derived here. Part P80 supplies the physical partition and absolute Fourier convergence, with its constants stated explicitly. The new frequency-difference estimate is (5). This result supplies the two products Q(DW D2g) and Q(D2W Dg) in a rough high-energy calculation, with appropriate canonical velocity weight bounds in the latter. It makes no claim about the negative-order part of that calculation or the closed realization of its generator.

## P83. The native logarithmic norm and its equivalence with the earlier norms

### P83.1. A logarithmic energy with the native low norm

The low norm can be left on the density while the logarithmic multiplier is applied to its first and second derivatives. This gives the same completed space. An interpolation estimate compares the lower derivative of the logarithmically transformed density with the native low norm. The resulting energy avoids a logarithmic commutator in its negative-order component.

#### 2. Native interpolation

The inverse B=Q^-1 is a positive gamma/Bessel probability convolution. If its random heat time is T, its outer gamma shape is beta and its inner shape is tau U. Thus

## P85. A conditional nonlinear theorem in the logarithmic space

### P85.1. A conditional nonlinear theorem with logarithmic surplus

The rough velocity can be handled after the negative-order energy is left on the density itself. The derivative commutator needs only a Lipschitz velocity, and the two remaining differentiated products are controlled by the logarithmic coefficient estimate. A contraction in the native negative norm then gives existence, conditional on explicit reference inequalities and a small residual. This theorem does not establish those conditions for a new reference.

#### 1. Reference, spaces and exact conclusion

Use Fourier inversion factor (2pi)^(-2) on R2, and the canonical velocity U=(-R1R2,R1^2) with no harmonic addition. All densities are real, even in x and odd in y. All derivatives are ordered Cartesian tensors with Euclidean norms. Fix

    R=2^31, tau=2^-24, 1/2<beta<=1, epsilon=2beta-1,

    omega0=<r>^(-6/5), omega1=<r>^(-1/5),
    omega2=(1+4r2)^(2/5), w=(1+r2/R2)^(-11/10),
    Pj(g)=||omegaj D^jg||_2, L(g)=||wg||_(Hdot^-1),
    M(g)^2=P2(Qg)^2+2^22P1(Qg)^2+2^53L(g)^2.                       (1)

The high and low spaces are completions of the compact smooth S1 density core. The high completion is the canonical tempered-distribution space identified in P83; the low completion uses the Fourier homogeneous negative norm, equivalently the dual of centrally odd homogeneous H1 tests. The strain c[h]=partial_y U_2[h](0) and b[h]=partial_y h(0) are the continuous functionals identified by parts P70, P72, P77 and P83. In particular c has the literal circular principal-value formula with contact term -b[h]/4.

Let rho and u=U[rho] be smooth sublinear S1 reference fields, with every derivative of polynomial growth. Suppose

    V=cX+u, A=[[rho_y,-rho_x/2],[-rho_x/2,0]],
    M_low=(2c+1)I+sym Du+A,
    Mj=(1+c+V.D log omegaj)I-j sym DV+A, j=1,2,
    M_low >= [2/5+(11/5)c r2/(R2+r2)]I for r<=R,

With d=4/9 require the four global decay bounds

    sup r^d(|D rho|+r|D2rho|)<=186,
    sup r^(-1+d)|u|<=22, sup r^d|Du|<=22,
    sup r^(1+d)|D2u|<=56,

and all eight global derivative bounds

    |Du|<=14/5, |D rho|<=16, <r>|D2u|<=3, <r>|D3u|<=16,

    <r>2|D3rho|<=32, <r>2|D4rho|<=512.                              (3)

These are everywhere inequalities, not values on a mesh. Require also the nonzero leading angular function:

uniformly on compact annuli, with Theta continuous and not identically zero. For k in the high space set

    A_kh=(cX+u+U[k]).Dh-h+U[h].D rho,
    B_kh=A_kh-c[h]X.D rho,

**Theorem.** Under (1)-(4):

(a) For every M(k)<=r0, the maximal distributional operator

    D(A_k)={h in M:A_kh in M}

is a closed strongly continuous semigroup generator, is bijective onto M, and satisfies

    ||exp(t A_k)||_(M->M)<=exp(-t/32),

Its high evolution agrees in the common lower topology P0 with a native low evolution having inverse bound 6 on common forcing. If h is high and A_kh is in L intersect P0, h belongs to the actual native low generator domain.

(b) The maximal distributional domain of B_k is exactly D(A_k) intersect ker c. If c[k]=0, its range is exactly

This is a conditional a posteriori theorem. It does not assert that quadratic transport maps an open high ball continuously into the high forcing space, does not allow free changes of leading tail or exponent, and does not prove a positive Holder exponent for the first derivative.

The last product is defined by homogeneous duality when q is only low; for high q it is the ordinary product. The coefficient multiplier says, for omega1 or omega2 and a=Dg or DU[g],

    ||omega Q(af)||2<=800C M(g)||omega Qf||2.                       (11)

It is valid for norm-one contractions of the full ordered tensors. Also

    ||omega2 Q D2U[k]||2<=(9/5)P2(Qk),                            (12)

by commutation and the centrally odd weighted velocity bound of 07/20. The fields D2k are centrally odd, so its parity hypothesis is satisfied.

For a smooth divergence-free W with d_W=||DW||_(infinity,op), part P81 gives

    ||[Q,W.D]Q^-1||_(L2_omegaj -> L2_omegaj)
        <=21 beta tau d_W(1+2pi tau)^3<=42tau d_W, j=1,2.          (13)

Only the velocity gradient is present in this bound. Finally the native low transport perturbation has energy cost at most 12d_W. Its proof uses the weighted homogeneous dual representation and angular Hardy, as in 18/63, and requires W(0)=0, central oddness and div W=0. The canonical W=U[k] has all these properties. This low estimate is applied directly to g; there is no low logarithmic commutator.

The smooth-reference part has the M energy lower bound

    -Re<g,A_0g>_M >=(1/25-2^16tau)M(g)^2,                         (14)

with the full contract (2),(3), from P83. Its realization and graph-core proof were established before this estimate was invoked.

#### 3. All differentiated rough terms

Initially let k be compact smooth S1 and take a Schwartz density g. Put W=U[k], H=Qg and mu=C M(k). Then d_W<=4mu by (10). The exact ordered derivative identities are

    D Q(W.Dg)=W.D(DH)+[Q,W.D]Dg+Q(DW.Dg),
    D2 Q(W.Dg)=W.D(D2H)+[Q,W.D]D2g
                 +Q(DW.D2g)+Q((DW.D2g) with the two indices exchanged)
                 +Q(D2W.Dg).                                    (15)

The two middle coefficient terms in the second line are estimated separately; their combined factor is 2. No third derivative of W appears.

Since W(0)=0, |W(X)|<=d_W r. Integration by parts and div W=0 give the principal derivative energy costs

    |W.D log omega1|<=(1/5)d_W,
    |W.D log omega2|<=(4/5)d_W.                                   (16)

The logarithmic commutator (13) contributes at most 168tau mu to each derivative-component diagonal. By (11), the DW product costs 800mu in the first derivative and 1600mu in the second. For the remaining top term use (11) with coefficient a=Dg and input f=D2W, then (12):

    ||omega2 Q(D2W.Dg)||2
       <=800C M(g)(9/5)P2(Qk)<=1440mu M(g).                        (17)

The pointwise contraction of Dg with D2W has norm one. Pairing (17) against the top energy component costs at most 1440mu M(g)^2.

Using tau<=1 to round the small commutator coefficient, the top diagonal is at most

    1600+168+16/5<1772,

the first diagonal is at most 800+168+4/5<970, and the native low diagonal is at most 48. The combined diagonal energy therefore costs at most 1772mu M(g)^2. Adding (17),

    |Re<g,W.Dg>_M| <=(1772+1440)mu M(g)^2
                       <2^12 C M(k)M(g)^2.                       (18)

This is an energy-form estimate on its domain, not a boundedness assertion for W.D on M. Equations (14),(18) yield the rate

    lambda(k)=1/25-2^16tau-2^12 C M(k).                            (19)

#### 4. A genuine high generator for rough k

For fixed compact smooth k, W=U[k] is smooth, of at most linear growth, with the finite weighted derivative bounds needed for the transported E space. Its derivatives have polynomial growth and, outside a compact set, the canonical multipole decay. Here E(H)^2=P2(H)^2+2^22P1(H)^2+2^53L(H)^2.

The complete characteristic flow of cX+u+W gives a strongly continuous transport group on E for finite time. Differentiating this flow twice and using the weight ratios gives the finite weighted derivative bounds; the native low transport is its consistent dual action. The smooth-reference coupling U[h].D rho is bounded on E by (3) and the established weighted velocity bounds. Its convergent finite-time Duhamel series constructs the E generator. Compact smooth parity functions are a graph core: approximate the transport resolvent integral by finite sums of transported compact smooth functions and then use the bounded coupling perturbation.

The smooth logarithmic commutator with this operator is bounded on E. To see that no extra uniform assumption is hidden here, apply the component kernel calculation 43/75 to u+W in the transport terms and rho in the coupling terms. For this fixed smooth W all coefficients, including its weighted third derivative, are finite. The positive-kernel low estimate and the resolvent integral 77 therefore give a finite bounded commutator. Its size may depend on k and is not used for the uniform rate. Conjugation by Q constructs the N_tau generator, and the equivalence 83 constructs the same semigroup on M. The conjugated graph core is Q^-1(C_c^infinity), a Schwartz class. Equations (15)-(18) hold there and pass to the graph closure. Consequently its M norm has exactly the uniform rate (19).

For general k in M choose compact smooth k_m->k in M. Equation (10) gives uniform convergence DU[k_m]->DU[k]. By parity W_m(0)=W(0)=0, hence

    |W_m(X)-W_n(X)|<=d_mn r,
    d_mn=||DW_m-DW_n||infinity ->0.                               (20)

The fixed field cX+u+W is globally Lipschitz and has at most linear growth. Its characteristics define a unique transport group on P0. The coupling U[h].D rho is bounded there by 16*(8/3). The finite-time Duhamel series thus constructs a unique P0 evolution for A_k.

For high solutions with the same initial datum the difference source is (W_m-W_n).Dh_n. Since r omega0<=omega1, (9) gives

    P0((W_m-W_n).Dh_n)<=d_mn P1(h_n)
                         <=d_mn(1+7tau)M(h_n)/2048.               (21)

The smooth high rates and hence all finite-time high bounds are uniform for large m. The P0 variation formula and Gronwall therefore give convergence in C([0,T];P0) to the unique lower evolution. At each time weak Hilbert compactness in M identifies the weak high limit with this lower limit. Lower semicontinuity passes (19), with M(k_m)->M(k). At time zero the unique weak high limit is the initial datum and the upper norm bound tends to its norm. Weak convergence plus the upper norm bound implies strong convergence in the Hilbert norm. This proves strong continuity. Lower uniqueness proves the semigroup law. The construction uses no uniform bounds for higher derivatives of k_m.

#### 5. Maximal domain and both inverse directions

The P0 realization of Lipschitz transport has the maximal distributional domain. Explicitly, if h and (cX+u+W).Dh are in P0, multiply h by radial cutoffs at radius T. The new transport term tends to zero in P0, because its coefficient is uniformly bounded and its support escapes to infinity. On each fixed compact set mollify. The Friedrichs commutator identity subtracts the Lipschitz difference of the transport field in the differentiated convolution. Its local L2 operator norm is uniformly bounded; it tends to zero first for smooth inputs, then for all local L2 inputs by density. These two approximations give the graph closure. Adding the bounded coupling and -1 leaves this description valid.

Passing the characteristic integral identity through these approximations gives

    S(t)h-h=int_0^t S(v)A_kh dv                                   (22)

in P0 for its maximal domain. If h,A_kh belong to M, the right side is also a high Bochner integral, and the two integrals agree under the continuous embedding into P0. Dividing by t proves membership in the high generator domain. Conversely, a high generator difference quotient converges as a distribution, so its value is A_kh. This proves the exact maximal high-domain description.

If lambda(k)>0, the integral

    -int_0^infinity S(t)f dt

converges in M. On finite intervals the generator identity sends it to f-S(T)f. Closedness and exponential decay prove surjectivity and the reciprocal-rate inverse bound. A kernel vector has a constant orbit and hence must vanish by strict decay. Thus injectivity has also been proved.

At the parameters (1),(5), C M(k)<=2^-20. Therefore

    lambda(k)>=1/25-1/256-1/256=1/25-1/128>1/32.                  (23)

This proves (a)'s high inverse, including its domain and both inverse directions.

#### 6. Low consistency and the nonlinear difference domain

The native low energy has rate at least

    1/5-12||DU[k]||infinity>=1/5-48*2^-20>1/6.                    (24)

There is a consistent low evolution with this rate. For smooth velocities it is obtained from the same characteristics and coupling series as the P0 evolution. To compare their completions, use inner and outer radial cutoffs, then mollification. The cutoffs are uniformly bounded in the parity-restricted homogeneous negative norm: their dual gradient term is bounded by C/r and angular Hardy. Density gives strong convergence. Compactly supported P0 inputs are locally L2, and smoothing converges in both spaces. Uniform convergence of the velocity gradients in (20) gives local C1 convergence of their flows, so the consistency passes to rough k. Equivalently the low construction follows by dual transport on centrally odd homogeneous H1 tests; the same energy estimate gives its extension. This selects the actual consistent low operator, with no arbitrary negative-distribution realization.

In particular the convergent low and high inverse integrals agree on common forcing when both rates are positive. If h is high and A_kh belongs to L intersect P0, the P0 identity (22) and consistency make its right side a low Bochner integral. The low difference quotient therefore converges to A_kh. This proves membership in the actual low generator domain and permits the inverse bound 6.

For the nonlinear difference the extra source is U[k1-k2].Dh. Its P0 norm is finite by (20),(21), with k1-k2 in place of k_m-k_n. Its low norm is finite by (10). Thus the low inverse is applied on its actual domain in the contraction argument below.

#### 7. Normalization and exact range

For every high h and k, the first derivatives of h,U[h],k,U[k] are continuous. Parity gives zero values for the densities and velocities at the origin. The reference normalization yields DV(0)=diag(2c-1,1). Expanding to first order,

    b[A_kh]=c[k]b[h]+a0 c[h].                                    (25)

No second derivative of h is assumed in this identity: the transport field vanishes at zero, and Dh(X)=Dh(0)+o(1). The coupling uses U[h](X)=DU[h](0)X+o(r). If c[k]=0, the high inverse therefore maps M_0 exactly to D(A_k) intersect ker c, since a0>=1.

To identify the maximal normalized domain, use the spatial growth proved in P70 and P73 and the norm equivalences P77 and P83: for each fixed beta,tau, every high h and U[h] is O(max(1,r)^(1/5)). If h and B_kh are high, rescale the distributional equation by T^-gamma on a fixed annulus. The forcing, identity and dilation terms tend to zero because gamma>1/5. For u.Dh integrate by parts; the remaining factor has size O(T^(1/5-d-gamma)), which tends to zero. For U[h].D rho use the derivative decay or integrate by parts, obtaining a vanishing factor. The rough transport has product size O(T^(2/5-1-gamma)) after integration by parts, and also tends to zero. In contrast (4) gives

    T^-gamma (X.D rho)(TX) -> gamma G

in distributions. Hence c[h]gamma G=0, so c[h]=0. The converse follows immediately if h is in D(A_k) and c[h]=0. This proves the exact domain and then (7). The rescaling argument controls the whole leading angular function, rather than only a finite list of its moments.

#### 8. Contraction in a complete native low metric

The reference residual satisfies b[F]=a0(c+c[rho]-1)=0. Let

    B={k in M:M(k)<=r0, c[k]=0}, T(k)=-A_k^-1 F.

By (6),(7) and 32eta=r0, T maps B into B. For k1,k2 in B its difference solves

    A_(k1)(T(k1)-T(k2))=-U[k1-k2].D T(k2).

Section 6 verifies the actual low-domain condition. The low inverse and (10) imply

    L(T(k1)-T(k2))
       <=6*2^15 C r0 L(k1-k2)=3/16 L(k1-k2).                     (26)

The high ball B is complete in this low metric. A low Cauchy sequence has a low limit; its uniformly bounded high norms give a weak high subsequence. Both limits agree as distributions. Weak lower semicontinuity retains the high bound, and the continuous high functional c retains zero. This also proves that the low metric separates points of B. The contraction theorem therefore supplies a unique fixed point.

At the fixed point, A_hh=-F is exactly (8). Conversely every normalized solution in B satisfies this high-domain equation, so high inverse uniqueness makes it a fixed point. The slope change satisfies

    |b[h]|<=4C r0=2^-18<a0.                                      (27)

For any solution in the entire high ball at the fixed c, the first-order identity for its nonlinear equation is (a0+b[h])c[h]=0. Equation (27) forces c[h]=0, proving the stated uniqueness without an additional normalization assumption on a competing solution.

Finally h=O(r^(1/5)) preserves (4). A freely changed exponent would not be subleading: rescaling an exact equation with any exponent c' gives (c'gamma-1)G=0, and hence c'=c. A spatial dilation changes the leading function by its nontrivial amplitude factor, so the fixed affine tail class excludes a different scale. Exponent-logarithmic variations and nonzero leading angular variations also lie outside this correction class. These are restrictions of the theorem, not estimates for those missing directions.

#### Dependencies and application status

The smooth-reference energy and native norm realization are 83. The rough logarithmic commutator is 81; the two coefficient products and native low product are 82/84. The weighted velocity and low transport facts are 07,18,20,24, with the common lower-domain argument audited in 63. The trace and literal principal value are 70,72,77. All hypotheses required from these results are included above.

The proof avoids the same-space quadratic forcing obstruction 76 by solving a family of transport equations and contracting only in the native low norm. ## P87. Four compatible outputs of the logarithmic inverse

### P87.1. Four compatible outputs from the native logarithmic inverse

The singular strain only sees the third angular harmonic away from its contact term. Projecting onto that harmonic before taking an absolute value gives a nonnegative singular moment which removes the neutral y-jet exactly. An elementary Fourier estimate controls this moment by the logarithmic norm. The same norm also controls an adapted Holder norm of the density itself.

#### 1. Spaces and statement

Use the real S1 completion and canonical velocity of parts P83 and P84. Fix R=2^31, 0<tau<=2^-20 and 1/2<beta<=1, and set

    epsilon=2beta-1, C=tau^(-beta)/sqrt(epsilon),
    Q=(1+tau log(1-Delta))^beta,
    omega0=<r>^(-6/5), omega1=<r>^(-1/5),
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), w=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    Pj(g)=||omegaj D^jg||_2, L(g)=||wg||_(Hdot^-1),
    M(h)^2=P2(Qh)^2+2^22P1(Qh)^2+2^53L(h)^2.

Fourier inversion uses (2pi)^(-2). Ordered derivatives have Euclidean tensor norms. The canonical continuous representative of h is even-x, odd-y and satisfies h(0)=0; its first derivatives are continuous by P84. Write b[h]=h_y(0).

For A_j={2^j<=r<=2^(j+1)}, j>=0, define the adapted density norm

    H(h)=||h||_(C^(1/2)(B2))
       +sup_(j>=0) 2^(-j/4)
             [||h||_(Linf(A_j))+2^(j/2)[h]_(C^(1/2)(A_j))].       (1)

Here the local C^(1/2) norm is the sum of its supremum and its ordinary Euclidean Holder seminorm. For r>0 define

    a3(r)=(1/pi)int_0^(2pi)sin(3theta)h(r cos theta,r sin theta)dtheta,
    P3 h(r,theta)=a3(r)sin(3theta),
    M3(h)=int_0^1 |a3(r)| dr/r^2
         =(1/4)int_(r<1) r^-3 |P3(h-b[h]y)| dX.                  (2)

The second equality includes the exact cancellation P3(y)=0. This is a weighted L1 moment of an angular projection of the remainder. It does not mean the absolute moment of the entire remainder.

**Theorem.** Every h in the completed M space satisfies

    H(h)<=64 M(h),
    M3(h)<=6 C M(h),
    |c[h]|<=|b[h]|/4+M3(h)+P0(h),
    |c[h]|<=4 C M(h).                                           (3)

The strain has the contact-corrected canonical formula

    c[h]=-b[h]/4+int_0^1 a3(r)dr/r^2
          +(1/pi)int_(r>=1) sin(3theta)h(X)r^-3 dX.               (4)

Both integrals in (4) converge absolutely after the stated angular projection in the local integral. In fact the stronger absolute radial integral int_0^infinity |a3(r)|dr/r^2 is bounded by 6CM(h).

Consequently the four requested quantities are compatible in one space:

    L(h)+H(h)+M3(h)+|c[h]| <=128 C M(h).                          (5)

If the full reference hypotheses of P85 hold, tau=2^-24, M(k)<=2^-20/C and h is in the maximal domain of A_k, its inverse estimate yields

    L(h)+H(h)+M3(h)+|c[h]|
                  <=2^12 C M(A_kh).                            (6)

The same conclusion holds for the normalized B_k on its exact domain and range when c[k]=0, as specified in P85. It does not assert a same-order Holder inverse with only a Holder forcing norm. It is an augmented-space estimate, with the density rather than a Holder derivative as output.

#### 2. A density Holder bound from the weighted second derivatives

Let m=M(h), H0=Qh. By 83 and positivity of Q^-1,

    P0(h)<=(1+11tau)P0(H0)<=2m/2048,
    P1(h)<=(1+7tau)P1(H0)<=2m/2048,
    P2(h)<=(1+7tau)P2(H0)<=2m.                                   (7)

The deliberately weaker bound P0(H0)<=m/2048 is sufficient here. These estimates hold at every beta in the stated interval.

Use the C3 radial partition of P80: P(v)=35v^4-84v^5+70v^6-20v^7 on [0,1], continued by 0 and 1; chi0(X)=1-P(|X|-1), chil(X)=chi0(2^-l X)-chi0(2^(-l+1)X) for l>=1. Put t_l=2^l, with t_0=1. These cutoffs sum to one and have rescaled gradient and Hessian bounds 9 and 150. The product rule gives, for F_l(Z)=chi_l(t_l Z)h(t_l Z),

    ||F_l||_(H2)<=t_l^(1/5)[507P0(h)+40P1(h)+P2(h)]
               <=2(2595/2048)t_l^(1/5)m <3t_l^(1/5)m.             (8)

Here the H2 norm has Fourier symbol(1+|xi|^2), and is bounded by ||F||2+2||DF||2+||D2F||2. Thus every coefficient in (8) includes the cutoff derivatives. The central piece has the same estimates.

For an unweighted planar H2 function F, Fourier Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    ||F||infinity <=1/(2sqrt(pi))||F||H2 <(1/2)||F||H2,
    [F]_(C^(1/2)) <=(1/2)||F||H2.                                (9)

For the first inequality int(1+|xi|^2)^-2 dxi=pi. For the second use |exp(i xi.Z)-1|^2<=2|xi||Z| and

    int_0^infinity r^2/(1+r^2)^2 dr=pi/4.

The squared Fourier dual bound is then |Z|/4. Approximation extends(9) to all H2 inputs. It controls ordinary Holder seminorms without choosing Littlewood-Paley conventions.

On A_j only pieces with max(0,j-1)<=l<=j+2 can contribute; this slightly enlarged index range has at most four members. They have 1/2<=t_l/t_j<=4. Rescaling(9),(8), each contributes at most

    (3/2)[1+(t_j/t_l)^(1/2)]t_l^(1/5)m
                  <8 t_j^(1/5)m

to ||h||infinity+t_j^(1/2)[h]_(C^(1/2)) on A_j. For example sqrt(2)<3/2 and 4^(1/5)<4/3 make the displayed constant less than 5, so 8 is conservative. Summing gives 32t_j^(1/5)m. Multiplication by t_j^-1/4 makes this at most 32m.

## P88. A consolidated dependency and domain audit of the logarithmic theorem

### P88.1. Audit of the logarithmic conditional theorem and its dependencies

This is a complete dependency and domain audit of part P85. Its conclusion is conditional. No accepted numerical reference or refit has been shown to meet its residual hypothesis. We retain the native negative norm throughout the nonlinear argument.

#### 1. Exact spaces, reference hypotheses and conclusion

On R2 use Fourier inversion with factor (2pi)^(-2) and the canonical velocity U=(-R1R2,R1^2). Densities are real, even in x and odd in y; the velocity is centrally odd, divergence free and has no harmonic addition. Derivatives are full ordered Cartesian tensors with Euclidean norm. Let

The high space M and low space L are the completions of the compact smooth S1 core in the indicated norms. These completions are identified as tempered distributions as proved below. Set b[h]=h_y(0) and c[h]=partial_y U2[h](0), continuous high-space functionals.

Let rho and u=U[rho] be smooth sublinear reference fields with the stated parities and every derivative of polynomial growth. Let

    9/5<c<37/20, a0=rho_y(0)>=1, c+c[rho]=1,

Require the following everywhere inequalities, with the first restricted to r<=R:

With d=4/9 require

    sup r^(1+d)|D2u|<=56,                                      (4)

and

    |Du|<=14/5, |D rho|<=16, <r>|D2u|<=3, <r>|D3u|<=16,
    |D2rho|<=3, <r>|D2rho|<=8,
    <r>2|D3rho|<=32, <r>2|D4rho|<=512.                           (5)

Here <r>=(1+r2)^(1/2). Impose the nonzero leading profile

uniformly on compact annuli, with Theta continuous and not identically zero. Part P85 additionally states the polynomial growth of all higher reference derivatives used by its distributional multiplier construction. This is a regularity hypothesis; it is not certified merely by the finite list (5). For smooth finite algebraic reference formulas it follows directly from those formulas. No claim of equivalence with fewer regularity hypotheses is needed here.

Put

    Akh=(cX+u+U[k]).Dh-h+U[h].D rho,
    Bkh=Akh-c[h]X.D rho,
    r0=2^-20/C, eta=r0/32.                                     (7)

**Audited theorem.** For M(k)<=r0, the maximal distributional Ak has domain {h in M:Akh in M}, generates a strongly continuous semigroup with norm at most exp(-t/32), is injective and onto M, and has inverse norm at most 32. Its evolution is consistent in P0 with the native low evolution. On common forcing, the latter inverse has norm at most 6. If h is high and Akh belongs to L intersect P0, h belongs to the actual native low generator domain.

The maximal distributional Bk has domain D(Ak) intersect ker c. If c[k]=0, its range is exactly M0={f in M:b[f]=0} and its inverse on that range has norm at most 32. Bk is not asserted to generate a semigroup on all of M.

If the actual residual F=(cX+u).D rho-rho belongs to M and M(F)<=eta, there is a unique exact correction in the entire closed high ball M(h)<=r0 at fixed c. #### 4. Existence of the operator before the energy argument

For smooth core k the full velocity is smooth, globally Lipschitz and of at most linear growth. Its complete characteristics construct a transport group on the base E space. The reference coupling U[h].D rho is bounded there by the weighted coefficient and velocity bounds. Its convergent finite-time Duhamel series gives a generator. Compact smooth parity functions are a graph core: approximate the transport resolvent integral by finite sums of transported compact functions, and then apply the bounded coupling perturbation.

For this fixed smooth k, the smooth logarithmic commutator is bounded on E by the kernel estimates 75/77. Its construction constants may involve higher derivatives of k. They are finite for each k and are used only to construct the generator. Conjugation by Q, then the norm equivalence (10), constructs the same generator on M. Its graph core is Q^-1(Cc-infinity), not automatically the untransformed compact class. These functions are Schwartz. The direct rough form bound (12), which uses only M(k), holds on this core and passes to its graph closure. Therefore its semigroup has the uniform high rate just derived.

For arbitrary high k choose smooth compact km->k in M. The gradients DU[km] converge uniformly by the estimate 4CM. Because every velocity vanishes at 0, |U[km](X)-U[kn](X)|<=dmn r with dmn->0. In P0 the limiting Lipschitz characteristics and the coupling, bounded by 16*(8/3), construct a unique evolution. Differences of high solutions have P0 forcing at most dmn P1(hn), bounded by (1+7tau)dmn M(hn)/2048. The P0 Duhamel identity and Gronwall give convergence in C([0,T];P0). Uniform high bounds give weak Hilbert limits; injective distributional realization identifies them with that same P0 limit. Lower semicontinuity gives the high rate. At 0, weak convergence and the limiting upper bound on the norm give strong convergence in M. P0 uniqueness gives the semigroup law. Thus a strongly continuous high semigroup has actually been constructed; the energy inequality is not used as a substitute for surjectivity.

#### 5. Maximal domains, inverse directions, and the low forcing space

The P0 realization of globally Lipschitz transport has maximal distributional domain. Radial cutoffs give vanishing graph-norm errors because the velocity has at most linear growth; local mollification uses the Friedrichs commutator identity and the Lipschitz bound. Adding the bounded reference coupling preserves this domain. Consequently if h and Akh are high, the P0 identity

    S(t)h-h=int_0^t S(v)Akh dv

has a high Bochner integral on its right. The high difference quotient converges to Akh, proving inclusion in the generator domain. The reverse inclusion follows by testing strong high difference quotients against compact smooth functions. This proves the asserted maximal domain equality.

Strict decay proves injectivity: a kernel vector has a constant orbit and must vanish. For any f in M the integral -int_0^infinity S(t)f dt converges in M. The finite-time generator identity gives Ak(-int_0^T S(t)f dt)=f-S(T)f; closedness and strict decay prove surjectivity and inverse norm 32.

The native low evolution is constructed by the dual transport action on centrally odd homogeneous H1 tests and the same reference coupling. Inner and outer radial cutoffs, bounded uniformly by angular Hardy, followed by smoothing give a simultaneous dense core for L and P0. For smooth velocities the characteristic and coupling constructions agree there. The convergence of velocity gradients passes the agreement to the rough limit. The low and high inverse integrals consequently agree on common forcing.

A nonlinear difference may belong to L without belonging to M. For h high and Akh in L intersect P0, the preceding P0 identity and consistency show that its right side is also a low Bochner integral. Its low difference quotient converges to Akh. This proves membership in the actual low generator domain and justifies the bound 6 on that forcing. Specifically U[k1-k2].Dh is in P0 because its velocity is bounded by a constant times r and r omega0<=omega1. It is in L by the dual product 2^15 C M(h)L(k1-k2). This is the precise forcing-space compatibility needed for the iteration. No arbitrary maximal-domain assertion on negative-order distributions is substituted for it.

#### 6. Normalization and the nonlinear fixed point

All high fields and their velocities are C1; both vanish at 0 by parity. Since the transport field also vanishes at 0, a first-order expansion uses only Dh(X)=Dh(0)+o(1), giving

    b[Akh]=c[k]b[h]+a0 c[h], b[F]=0.                           (13)

It needs no continuous Hessian. For c[k]=0 the inverse takes the hyperplane b[f]=0 exactly to D(Ak) intersect ker c.

Every high density and velocity grows at most r^(1/5). If h and Bkh are high, rescale the distributional equation on a compact annulus by T^-gamma. The dilation, identity and forcing terms vanish. Integrating background transport by parts gives decay T^(1/5-d-gamma); the rough transport gives T^(2/5-1-gamma); the reference coupling also vanishes. But T^-gamma(X.D rho)(TX) tends distributionally to gamma G, nonzero by (6). Thus c[h]=0. The converse domain inclusion is immediate, proving the exact normalized domain. This is why the rank-one-looking term is not treated as a bounded high-space perturbation.

On the normalized closed ball define T(k)=-Ak^-1F. The high inverse 32 and 32eta=r0 show that it preserves the ball. Its difference equation and the actual low inverse give

    L(T(k1)-T(k2))<=6*2^15 C r0 L(k1-k2)=3L(k1-k2)/16.

The ball is complete in L: a low Cauchy sequence has a low limit, a weak high subsequence remains in the closed high ball, and the distributional embeddings identify both limits. Weak continuity of the bounded linear functional c retains its zero value. Therefore the contraction theorem applies on a complete metric space and gives a unique fixed point.

Any exact correction in the entire high ball has (a0+b[h])c[h]=0 by (13) for the full nonlinear equation. Since |b[h]|<=4CM(h)<=2^-18<a0, it is normalized and hence is that fixed point. The leading profile is unchanged because 1/5<gamma. Rescaling an equation with a putative different exponent c' gives (c'gamma-1)G=0 and forces c'=c. Leading angular and logarithmic variations are excluded by the same growth restriction. This is a fixed affine tail theorem, not a free tail-coordinate theorem.

#### 7. Meaning of the four outputs and limitations

Let Aj={2^j<=r<=2^(j+1)} and define

    H(h)=||h||_(C^(1/2)(B2))
       +sup_(j>=0)2^(-j/4)(||h||infinity(Aj)+2^(j/2)[h]_(C^(1/2)(Aj))),
    a3(r)=(1/pi)int_0^(2pi) sin(3theta)h(r,theta)dtheta,

    c[h]=-b[h]/4+int_0^1 a3(r)dr/r2+int_1^infinity a3(r)dr/r2.

Projection in theta is performed before taking the absolute value in M3. The first three angular moments of the plane wave cancel; the resulting radial Fourier bound is controlled by the finite absolute Fourier gradient integral 4CM. This proves M3 and the literal circular principal value without claiming absolute integrability of the full jet remainder. Together these estimates give (8).

The theorem neither asserts a positive Holder exponent for Dh nor estimates a prescribed full-jet singular Lp moment. It does not prove a bounded nonlinear forcing map on an open M ball;76 disproves the corresponding assertion even on a compact normalized core. It makes no claim that a Holder-only forcing norm suffices. The original and final two refits have native residual floors far above eta and excluded correction balls by P86. ## P91. Exact global derivative caps for finite potentials

### P91.1. Exact global derivative caps from finite potential coefficients

Every finite potential in the recovered algebraic family has explicit finite bounds for the three derivatives left adjustable in P89. The bounds below are intentionally coarse. They require a short exact coefficient calculation instead of a spatial mesh, and distinguish finiteness of these three quantities from the remaining reference hypotheses.

#### 1. Statement

Let 0<gamma<1, delta=1-gamma, and let a finite potential be

    chi(X)=sum_(j,m,k) a_(j,m,k) P_(m,k)(X)(1+r^2)^(p_j-k),
    P_(m,k)=(x^2+y^2)^(k-m) Re(x+iy)^(2m),
    p_j=(3+gamma-j delta)/2, j>=0, k>=m>=0,                    (1)

with real coefficients. Define rho=-partial_y Delta chi and u=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy). These expressions represent the canonical IPM velocity for the references considered here, as verified in their source audit; the derivative bounds below are statements about these explicit expressions and require no Fourier argument.

For a real q, write (q)_l=q(q-1)...(q-l+1), with (q)_0=1. Define

    R_d(q)=sum_(z=0)^floor (d/2)
             [d! 2^(d-2z)/((d-2z)! z!)] |(q)_(d-z)|,
    S_d(j,m,k)=2^d 2^(k+m)
                sum_(l=0)^min(d,2k) binom(d,l)(2k)_l R_(d-l)(p_j-k),
    C_d=sum_(j,m,k) b_(j,m,k) S_d(j,m,k),                       (2)

where b_(j,m,k) is any nonnegative upper bound for |a_(j,m,k)|. For rational coefficients the ceiling of the absolute coefficient is an admissible integer choice. Terms with zero coefficient can be omitted.

**Theorem.** With ordered Cartesian tensor norms, the following global inequalities hold:

    |D^d chi(X)| <= C_d <r>^(3+gamma-d) for every integer d>=0,
    <r>|D^3u(X)| <= 2 C_6,
    <r>^2|D^3rho(X)| <= 2 C_6,
    <r>^2|D^4rho(X)| <= 2 C_7.                                (3)

The bounds apply at the origin as well as at infinity. If all data in (1) are rational, C_d is rational and can be checked using integer arithmetic. Thus finite upper caps U3=B3=2C_6 and B4=2C_7, or any larger rational or dyadic values, satisfy exactly the three adjustable derivative inequalities of P89.

This does not certify the other five fixed derivative bounds, any matrix inequality, a small residual, or existence of a profile. In particular, increasing the three caps does not evade the exclusions of P90.

#### 2. Polynomial and radial estimates

The sum of the absolute coefficients of (x^2+y^2)^(k-m) is 2^(k-m). For m>=1 the corresponding sum for Re(x+iy)^(2m) is

    sum_(b=0)^m binom(2m,2b)=2^(2m-1)<=2^(2m),

and for m=0 it equals 1. Submultiplicativity of the coefficient sum therefore gives

    coefficient_sum(P_(m,k))<=2^(k+m).                         (4)

Each monomial has homogeneous degree n=2k. An ordered l-fold partial derivative of a degree-n monomial has coefficient factor at most (n)_l, and its absolute value on |X|=r is at most that coefficient times r^(n-l). Consequently, for any particular ordered derivative of P,

    |partial_I P(X)| <= (2k)_l 2^(k+m) r^(2k-l), l<=2k.        (5)

It is zero for l>2k. At r=0 the usual convention for the constant term applies.

To differentiate (1+r^2)^q d times, partition the d ordered differentiations among first and second derivatives of 1+r^2. No block can have size greater than 2. If there are z pairs and s=d-2z singletons, the number of partitions is d!/(s! z! 2^z). A singleton contributes a factor bounded by 2r; a pair by 2. The outer derivative is (q)_(d-z)(1+r^2)^(q-d+z). Since r^s<= <r>^s,

    |partial_I (1+r^2)^q| <= R_d(q) <r>^(2q-d).               (6)

The identity 2q-2d+2z+s=2q-d gives the exponent. Absolute values of falling factorials handle all signs of q; no positivity assumption on q is used.

#### 3. Product, tensor and field bounds

For a specified ordered d-fold derivative of one generator, Leibniz' rule has binom(d,l) terms in which l derivatives hit P. Combining(5),(6) and r^(2k-l)<= <r>^(2k-l), each term has common radial exponent

    2k-l+2(p_j-k)-(d-l)=3+gamma-j delta-d.

There are 2^d ordered Cartesian tensor components. Their Euclidean norm is at most 2^(d/2) times the maximum component, bounded in turn by 2^d times that maximum. This proves

    |D^d[P_(m,k)(1+r^2)^(p_j-k)]|
        <= S_d(j,m,k)<r>^(3+gamma-j delta-d).                  (7)

Since j delta>=0 and <r>>=1, summing with |a|<=b proves the first inequality of (3).

For an ordered q-fold derivative of rho, the defining expression is a sum of two selected (q+3)-fold potential derivatives. Squaring and summing gives

    |D^q rho|<=sqrt(2)|D^(q+3)chi|<=2|D^(q+3)chi|.

The selected derivatives of the two velocity components form a subset of the full ordered tensor, so the same constant 2 is also valid for u. With d=6, multiplication by <r> for D^3u yields exponent gamma-2<0, and multiplication by <r>^2 for D^3rho yields gamma-1<0. With d=7, multiplication by <r>^2 yields gamma-2<0. Dropping these nonpositive powers proves the other three inequalities of (3).

All functions in (1) are smooth because 1+r^2 never vanishes. Formula (7) for arbitrary fixed d also proves that every derivative has polynomial growth. This supplies the additional smoothness and growth condition used in the logarithmic generator construction, separately from its quantitative energy hypotheses.

#### 4. Exact input recovery and reproducible certificate

The original is recovered directly from the read-only state 131 checkpoint, using exact binary64 hex values, its center-strain constraint and the integer shifted-Legendre expansion. Its reconstructed canonical serialization must equal the original checkpoint's recorded hash and our independent source audit. The two refits are recovered directly from their exact producer JSON and compared with the independently reconstructed canonical arrays and hashes in 19 and 52. The calculation does not import producer evaluation code.

For each finite canonical array, the verification chooses b=ceil(|a|), computes the rational quantities in (2) at d=6,7, and rounds 2C_6,2C_7 upward to powers of 2. ## P92. An independent global matrix certificate for the checkpoint

### P92.1. Independent recomputation of the original state's global matrix margin

This certificate uses compactified polynomial bounds, independently of the numerical polar Taylor boxes. Its purpose is to check the global matrix number from the original exact state, including the origin, the axes and infinity.

#### 1. Exact claim and reference

Let chi be the exact state 131 potential recovered from the read-only checkpoint in part P1.1 and independently reconstructed coefficient by coefficient in P91. Set

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248,
    rho=-partial_y Delta chi, u=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy),
    A=[[rho_y,-rho_x/2],[-rho_x/2,0]],
    M=(2c+1)I+sym Du+A.

The claim checked here is the global rational inequality

    M(X) >= (38103/10000)I = 3.8103 I, for every X in R^2.       (1)

The certificate is valid only if every leaf of the finite partition described below passes the directed lower bound in (6), all leaves cover the compactified rectangle, and the exact input and polynomial identities match. A partial search would give no global conclusion. Verification files record whether these conditions hold.

#### 2. Exact matrix and compactification

Direct differentiation cancels the mixed fourth derivative chi_xyyy in the off-diagonal entry:

    M=(2c+1)I + [[-2chi_xxyy-chi_yyyy, chi_xxxy],
                 [chi_xxxy, chi_xxyy]].                       (2)

Work first in the closed first quadrant, with

    t=r^2/(1+r^2), z=(x^2-y^2)/r^2=cos(2theta),
    gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma, w=(1-t)^(delta/2).

Each fourth derivative of a canonical generator r^(2k)cos(2m theta)(1+r^2)^(p_j-k) is a finite polynomial in t and cos(2theta), times w^(j+1); the sine fourth derivative also carries sin(2theta). Exact polar differentiation gives polynomials P22_j,P04_j,P31_j with

    chi_xxyy=sum_(j=0)^3 w^(j+1)P22_j(t,z),
    chi_yyyy=sum_(j=0)^3 w^(j+1)P04_j(t,z),
    chi_xxxy=sqrt(1-z^2) sum_(j=0)^3 w^(j+1)P31_j(t,z).        (3)

The rational polynomials, of degrees at most 28 in t and 11 in z, are stored in JSON. They are reconstructed from the exact coefficients, not interpolated from values. The recurrence differentiates each factor by the product rule, then uses the exact Chebyshev identities for cos(2m theta) and sin(2m theta)/sin(2theta). Polynomial equality is checked coefficient by coefficient against the earlier independent compactification.

The formulas extend to t=0 by continuity: chi_xxyy=1-c, chi_xxxy=0, and -chi_xxyy-chi_yyyy=rho_y(0). Their apparent angle dependence cancels exactly. At t=1, delta>0 makes all three sums zero. Thus the entire compact rectangle [0,1] times [-1,1] can be used, and includes the limit at infinity. The other quadrants change only the off-diagonal sign in (2), leaving eigenvalues unchanged.

#### 3. Directed polynomial enclosures

On a dyadic rectangle Q=[t0,t1] times [z0,z1], express each P in tensor Bernstein form. The Bernstein basis is nonnegative and sums to 1, so each polynomial value lies between its smallest and largest Bernstein coefficient.

To retain the four-branch cancellations, first combine the branch coefficients with the degree 4 Bernstein representation in the independent variable w on

    [(1-t1)^(delta/2),(1-t0)^(delta/2)].

The resulting three-variable tensor basis is again nonnegative and sums to 1. Therefore it rigorously bounds the quantities

    a=-2chi_xxyy-chi_yyyy, b=chi_xxyy,
    q=sum_j w^(j+1)P31_j(t,z)

by intervals [a-,a+], [b-,b+], [q-,q+]. Although w is a function of t, using its full independent interval only enlarges the range.

Let

    s_Q=1 if 0 belongs to [z0,z1],
        sqrt(1-min(|z0|,|z1|)^2) otherwise,
    C_Q=s_Q max(|q-|,|q+|).                                   (4)

The off-diagonal magnitude is at most C_Q. Lowering each diagonal in (2) and choosing the worst off-diagonal magnitude gives the eigenvalue lower bound

    ell_Q=(2c+1)+(a-+b--sqrt((a--b-)^2+4C_Q^2))/2.             (5)

The alternative lower bound (2c+1)+min(a-,b-)-C_Q is also valid; taking the maximum is allowed. All rational coefficient transformations are enclosed by directed Arb arithmetic, as are all powers and square roots. A leaf is accepted only when Arb proves

    max(ell_Q, (2c+1)+min(a-,b-)-C_Q) >=38103/10000.            (6)

No binary64 comparison is used to accept a leaf.

#### 4. Coverage and implication

Begin with the full rectangle. Every unsuccessful rectangle is divided exactly at the midpoint of one coordinate. Each accepted leaf stores its path and rational endpoints. A separate independent check reconstructs the binary tree, checks that every internal node has both children of the same split type, checks all endpoints and excludes ancestor/descendant duplicates. Thus the leaves cover the rectangle with disjoint interiors. It also reevaluates each leaf's Bernstein bound by direct restriction from the original global polynomials, rather than replaying the adaptive split transforms.

If all finite checks succeed, every point lies in an accepted leaf and satisfies (1) by (2)-(6). This is a proof over the whole plane. It is stronger than a bound at sampled points and does not require the numerical Taylor remainder code. The value at the origin is exactly c+2=3.810319210199998..., so this rational lower bound is consistent with the known upper bound on the global infimum.

#### 5. Scope

The certificate concerns only the unweighted matrix M for original state 131. It does not certify the logarithmic theorem's other hypotheses for the refits, prove residual smallness, or establish existence of an exact profile. Input reconstruction 91 and the polar identities of 02 are dependencies. No source file is modified, and no formal build is run.

## P94. The sharp global matrix margin of the checkpoint

### P94.1. Sharp global negative-order matrix margin for original state 131

#### Statement and hypotheses

Use the exact original state 131, the canonical coefficients, and the matrix M of part P92. Let

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248,
    t=r^2/(1+r^2), z=cos(2theta), delta=1-1/c, t0=1/40001.

Subject to the finite directed checks specified below, the sharp global lower bound is

    M(X) >= (c+2)I for every X in R^2.

The smaller eigenvalue equals c+2 only at X=0. Thus the infimum is attained, and its exact value is c+2. This statement concerns the original state only. It is neither a residual estimate nor an existence theorem.

#### Dependencies and notation

Part P92 proves the exact matrix and compactification identities. Write

    M=(2c+1)I+[[a,sqrt(1-z^2) q],[sqrt(1-z^2) q,b]],
    f(t,z)=sum_(j=0)^3 (1-t)^((j+1)delta/2) P_f,j(t,z),

for f=a,b,q, with P_a,j=-2P22_j-P04_j, P_b,j=P22_j and P_q,j=P31_j. Every polynomial is rational and recovered from the original coefficients. Their origin identities are

    b(0,z)=1-c, q(0,z)=0,
    a(0,z)=c-1+a0, a0=rho_y(0).

Part P93 proves M>=lambda_cells I on r>=1/200, where lambda_cells is the exact binary64 value 1072512771322849/281474976710656. An exact rational comparison shows lambda_cells>c+2. Since r=1/200 corresponds to t=t0, only 0<=t<=t0 remains.

#### Origin neighborhood argument

For alpha_j=(j+1)delta/2 define the rational polynomial

    D_f,j=(1-t) partial_t P_f,j-alpha_j P_f,j.

Ordinary differentiation gives the exact identity

    partial_t f=(1-t)^(-1) sum_j (1-t)^alpha_j D_f,j.

Use the tensor Bernstein enclosure of part P92 on [0,t0] times [-1,1], with w=(1-t)^(delta/2). The directed certificate is asked to verify the convenient rational bounds

    c-1+a >= 10,
    partial_t b >= 1/4,
    |partial_t q| <= 20.                                      (1)

The factor (1-t)^(-1) lies in [1,40001/40000]. Exact differentiation and the Bernstein convex-hull property justify these bounds once the recorded directed comparisons pass. A failure of any comparison would leave this theorem unproved, and is not evidence for its negation.

For fixed z the fundamental theorem of calculus and the origin identities give

    b(t,z)-(1-c)>=t/4, |q(t,z)|<=20t.

Therefore the diagonal entries of M-(c+2)I are at least 10 and t/4, while its off-diagonal magnitude is at most 20t. Its determinant is at least

    (10t/4)-400t^2 >= t(5/2-400/40001)>0

for 0<t<=t0. Both diagonal entries are positive there. The elementary two-by-two positive-definiteness criterion gives strict M>(c+2)I away from the origin in this neighborhood. At the origin the matrix is diag(3c+a0,c+2); the exact coefficients verify 3c+a0>c+2. The exterior estimate supplies strict positivity elsewhere. Reflection changes only an off-diagonal sign and preserves the eigenvalues, completing the full-plane proof.

#### Verification requirements and scope

The primary program checks polynomial origin identities as exact rational equalities, computes the Bernstein enclosures using directed Arb arithmetic, checks every inequality in (1), and binds the exact input and part P93 certificate hashes. A separate program uses direct rational power-to-Bernstein conversion at a different precision and independently forms the derivative polynomials. It must reproduce all three bounds. Neither a spatial sample nor floating-point eigenvalue computation is used to establish this theorem.

## P95. Global hypotheses of the exact refits: the matrix, derivative and decay bounds for the reference d2

### P95.1. Global reference hypotheses for exact algebraic refits

#### 1. Exact objects and certificate scope

The references considered here are the exact potentials nb_d2_exact and nb_Mpen2_exact delivered by the numerical work and independently reconstructed in parts P20 and P91. They have the original rational exponent c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248. Every coefficient is rational. The coefficient arrays, original generator arrays and hashes are part of the certificate inputs. The density, canonical velocity and transport are

    rho=-partial_y Delta chi, u=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy), V=cX+u.

The potential has the finite form

    chi=sum a_jmk r^(2k) cos(2m theta) (1+r^2)^(p_j-k),
    p_j=(3+gamma-j delta)/2, gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma.

Each result below is conditional on a COMPLETE directed certificate for the specified reference and target. An incomplete subdivision is not a global bound. There is no claim here that the a posteriori residual threshold is met. parts P86 and P90 prove that it is not met.

The target matrix inequalities are

    M=(2c+1)I+sym Du+A >=19I/5,
    M1=(1+c+V.D log omega1)I-sym DV+A >=I/2,
    M2=(1+c+V.D log omega2)I-2sym DV+A >=I/2,
    A=[[rho_y,-rho_x/2],[-rho_x/2,0]],
    omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10), omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5).

The additional target coefficient bounds are |Du|<=14/5 and |D rho|<=16, with the Euclidean norm of the ordered Cartesian tensor. Only targets whose complete certificate and independent recheck pass may be reported as proved. The remaining higher-derivative and decay hypotheses are separate.

#### 2. Exact compactified fields

Set t=r^2/(1+r^2), z=cos(2theta), w=(1-t)^(delta/2). For q in {chi22,chi04,chi31,chi13} there are rational polynomials P_q,j(t,z) such that

    chi22=sum_j w^(j+1) P_22,j,
    chi04=sum_j w^(j+1) P_04,j,
    chi31=sqrt(1-z^2) sum_j w^(j+1) P_31,j,
    chi13=sqrt(1-z^2) sum_j w^(j+1) P_13,j.       (1)

Here chiab denotes partial_x^a partial_y^b chi. To obtain these polynomials, differentiate each term in polar coordinates by

    partial_x=cos(theta) partial_r-sin(theta) partial_theta/r,
    partial_y=sin(theta) partial_r+cos(theta) partial_theta/r.

At total derivative order d write a term as r^(-d)(1+r^2)^p t^k cos(n theta), or its sine version. Its radial Euler derivative is

    [2k-d+2(p-k)t] r^(-d)(1+r^2)^p t^k.

The angle products split into frequencies n+1 and n-1. At d=4 the radial prefactor becomes w^(j+1)t^(k-2). Smoothness cancels all negative powers of t exactly. Replace cos(2m theta) by the Chebyshev polynomial T_m(z) and sin(2m theta) by sqrt(1-z^2) U_(m-1)(z). This proves (1) by finite exact algebra, without interpolation.

The radial velocity quotient e=u.X/r^2 is also regular at t=0 as an angle-dependent function. Since psi=chi_xy and u=grad-perp psi,

    e=-partial_theta chi_xy/r^2.

The same recurrence stopped at d=2 followed by the angle derivative and division by r^2 yields

    e=sum_j w^(j+1) P_e,j(t,z).                 (2)

There are no negative t powers: chi_xy has no constant or linear Taylor term and is O(r^2). The possible angle dependence at r=0 is harmless because e always occurs multiplied by t below.

#### 3. Matrices and norms

Direct substitution gives the exact formulas

    M=(2c+1)I+[[-2chi22-chi04,chi31],[chi31,chi22]],
    M1=[1-t(c+e)/5]I+[[-chi04,chi13],[chi13,-chi22]],
    M2=[1-c+(16/5)t(c+e)/(1+3t)]I
       +[[chi22-chi04,(-chi31+3chi13)/2],
          [(-chi31+3chi13)/2,-2chi22]].          (3)

The first-derivative norms satisfy

    |Du|^2=2chi22^2+chi13^2+chi31^2,
    |D rho|^2=(chi31+chi13)^2+(chi22+chi04)^2.  (4)

In (4), combinations can be formed before interval evaluation to preserve cancellation. The square and sum operations are then directed. Reflection changes the signs of chi31 and chi13 together and preserves all targets.

#### 4. Complete interval proof

The compactified first quadrant is [0,1] times [-1,1]. On every rational rectangular cell express the polynomials in tensor Bernstein form. For the branch variable use its exact containing interval [(1-t_hi)^(delta/2),(1-t_lo)^(delta/2)] and the degree-six Bernstein representation of the sum of its six powers. Nonnegativity and partition of unity of all Bernstein bases enclose every field in (1)-(2). The factor sqrt(1-z^2) has its exact interval enclosure. At t=1 all fields vanish since delta>0; the formulas have their continuous limits there.

For a symmetric matrix with diagonal lower bounds a,b and off-diagonal absolute bound C, a lower eigenvalue bound is

    (a+b-sqrt((a-b)^2+4C^2))/2.

The alternative min(a,b)-C is also valid. The larger of these two directed bounds can be used. A cell is accepted for a target only if the entire directed bound meets that target. Binary64 may guide subdivision but cannot accept a cell.

Every rejected cell is bisected exactly along one coordinate. A successful certificate consists of finitely many accepted leaves covering the initial rectangle with disjoint interiors. The independent checker reconstructs the binary tree, checks the rational endpoints and reevaluates each leaf directly from the original power coefficients at a different precision. This proves the corresponding inequality for every point of the full plane. A finite point comparison checks implementation conventions but does not replace the complete partition.

#### 5. What this would imply

Together with the independent remaining decay and derivative hypotheses, these matrix and first-derivative bounds can supply part of the reference contract in parts P85, P88 and P89. Adjustable higher-derivative caps in P91 do not replace the remaining five fixed derivative bounds or the four decay bounds. Even a complete reference contract for a refit would leave the certified residual exclusions unchanged. No existence claim follows from this certificate alone.

For M2 one may first multiply M2-(I/2) by the strictly positive denominator1+3t. This gives a polynomial numerator plus the same six w powers. For M1 and M the denominator is 1. The scalar parts and the t e term may be combined with each matrix entry before computing its Bernstein enclosure. This retains algebraic correlation and proves exactly the same matrix inequalities.

#### Remaining fixed derivative and decay hypotheses

The same exact polar recurrence computes the third derivatives chi_xyy, chi_xxy and fifth derivatives chi_xxxxy, chi_xxxyy, chi_xxyyy, chi_xyyyy, chi_yyyyy. After cancellation of the zero coefficients at lower radial powers, third derivatives have the form r times sum_j w^(j+1) P_j(t,z), and fifth derivatives have the form sqrt(t(1-t)) times sum_j w^(j+1) P_j(t,z). Each P_j includes either cos(theta) or sin(theta); removing this factor leaves a rational polynomial in t,z, by the odd Chebyshev identities. These identities hold by continuity at r=0.

With full ordered Cartesian tensor norms,

    |Du|^2 = 2 chi22^2 + chi13^2 + chi31^2,
    |D rho|^2 = (chi31+chi13)^2 + (chi22+chi04)^2,
    |D2u|^2 = chi41^2 + 3 chi32^2 + 3 chi23^2 + chi14^2,
    |D2rho|^2 = (chi41+chi23)^2 + 2(chi32+chi14)^2 + (chi23+chi05)^2.

Thus the fixed bounds |Du|<=14/5, |D rho|<=16, <r>|D2u|<=3, |D2rho|<=3 and <r>|D2rho|<=8 are finite interval inequalities on the same compactified rectangle. The first two use fourth-derivative fields as above. The last three use the fifth-derivative polynomials, with the factors sqrt(t) or sqrt(t(1-t)) required by the displayed identities. Correlated sums such as chi41+chi23 must be formed before interval evaluation.

For d=4/9 set F_d(t)=t^(d/2)(1-t)^((delta-d)/2). The reference exponent has delta>d, so 0<=F_d<=1. Write S_m for the derivative-m field with its common w factor removed, keeping its angular factors. Then the decay quantities are

    r^(d-1)|u| = F_d |S_3|,
    r^d|Du| = F_d |S_4,u|,
    r^(d+1)|D2u| = F_d t |S_5,u|,
    r^d(|D rho|+r|D2rho|) = F_d (|S_4,rho|+t|S_5,rho|).

For each sum the remaining branches are 1,w,...,w^5. These identities reduce the four decay bounds to interval inequalities as well. Dropping F_d gives a valid upper bound, although direct interval evaluation may be sharper. A completed directed cover and independent recheck are required separately for every asserted cap. These formulas alone are not numerical certificates.

The weaker matrix target M>=5I/2 is also sufficient for the low hypothesis in P85 and P89. Indeed, on r<=R the required lower bound is at most 2/5+(11/10)c; using c<=37/20, this is at most 487/200<5/2. A certificate of this weaker target must be labeled with its actual target and does not assert M>=19I/5.

#### Optional correlated radial enclosure

A second valid enclosure retains the relation between t and the branch powers. On a cell [a,b] with b<1, put s=(t-a)/(b-a). For q>=0 let T_N(s) be the degree-N Taylor polynomial of (1-t)^q about t=a. For N>=q, its uniform remainder is bounded by

    R_q = |q(q-1)...(q-N)| (b-a)^(N+1)
          (1-b)^(q-N-1)/(N+1)!.

For integral q<=N the remainder is zero. The coefficient of s^l is (-1)^l binom(q,l)(b-a)^l(1-a)^(q-l). This is the ordinary Taylor theorem with the maximum absolute (N+1)st derivative on the cell. All powers and coefficients may be enclosed by directed arithmetic.

If a branch polynomial has degree-n Bernstein coefficients p_i(z) in s, and T_N has degree-N Bernstein coefficients v_l, then the product has coefficients

    sum_(i+l=k) [binom(n,i)binom(N,l)/binom(n+N,k)] p_i(z)v_l.

This follows by multiplying the Bernstein basis functions exactly. Sum these product coefficients over branches before taking their convex hull. The error is at most sum_j R_(q_j) sup_cell |P_j|, with the latter supremum bounded by the original Bernstein coefficients. Use one such error for each matrix entry or scalar field. On cells touching t=1, the previous independent branch-variable enclosure remains available. Each is an enclosure of the same exact field, so their intersection or the better resulting lower bound is valid. This refinement changes no target or acceptance rule.

## P97. The full absolute jet moment needs more than three halves of a logarithm

### P97.1. The absolute jet moment needs three halves of a logarithm

#### 1. Statement and spaces

Use the Fourier convention of part P70, with inversion factor (2pi)^(-2). All functions are real, even in x and odd in y. Set J=(1-Delta)^(1/2), Q_beta=(1+log(1-Delta))^beta and

    ||h||_H_beta=||J^2 Q_beta h||_2.

For beta>1/2 the continuous jet is b[h]=partial_y h(0). Define the full absolute near-origin moment

    I(h)=int_(|X|<1) |h(X)-b[h]y|/|X|^3 dX.             (1)

The actual weighted spaces N_(beta,R)^log are the core completions of part P70:

    N_(beta,R)(h)^2=||omega2 D^2 Q_beta h||_2^2
       +2^22||omega1 D Q_beta h||_2^2
       +2^53||w_R Q_beta h||_(Hdot^-1)^2,
    omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5), omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10),
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), R>=1.

Theorem.

(a) On H_beta, for beta>3/2, I(h)<=C_beta||h||_H_beta, where the finite explicit constant is

    C_beta^2=2pi int_0^infinity B(s)^2 s
                 /[(1+s^2)^2(1+log(1+s^2))^(2beta)] ds,
    B(s)=s^2/2                       for 0<=s<=1,
         s(1/2+3log s)               for s>=1.          (2)

(b) There is one compactly supported C1 S1 density h, smooth away from 0, such that b[h]=c[h]=0, h belongs to H_beta and N_(beta,R)^log for every finite beta<=3/2 and every R>=1, uniformly in R for each beta, but I(h)=infinity. Compact smooth approximants h_N with b[h_N]=c[h_N]=0 converge in all these stated spaces and in C1. Each h_N and h has zero third angular harmonic, so its projected singular moment of part P87 is zero.

Thus the boundedness threshold for the full absolute moment in the H_beta scale is beta>3/2. In particular no bound for that full moment holds on the native logarithmic spaces used in P85, whose exponents satisfy1/2<beta<=1. Projection onto the third angular harmonic before taking the absolute value cannot be silently omitted from P87. No claim of failure is made for that projected moment or the canonical strain, both of which vanish for this example.

#### 2. Upper bound

First take a compact smooth S1 function. It has h(0)=0 and Dh(0)=(0,b[h]). Fourier inversion gives the remainder by multiplying h_hat by exp(iX.xi)-1-iX.xi. The elementary inequalities

    |exp(iu)-1-iu|<=u^2/2,
    |exp(iu)-1-iu|<=2+|u|<=3|u| when |u|>=1

imply the uniform bound min(s^2 r^2/2,3sr) for |X|=r and |xi|=s. In the second inequality one may use |exp(iu)-1|<=min(2,|u|): this gives |exp(iu)-1-iu|<=2|u| for all u, hence the weaker3|u| holds without an assumption on direction. Integrating in r yields

    int_0^1 |exp(iX.xi)-1-iX.xi| dr/r^2 <= B(s).

For s<=1 use the quadratic bound throughout. For s>=1 split at r=1/s, use the quadratic bound below it and 3sr above it. Integrate over theta, apply Tonelli and then Cauchy-Schwarz in xi. Plancherel gives exactly (2), including its 2pi factor. At infinity its radial integrand is comparable to s^(-1)(log s)^(2-2beta), so it is integrable precisely for beta>3/2. At zero it is O(s^5). Approximation in H_beta and its continuous C1 embedding from 70 identify the pointwise jet remainder and extend the inequality by Fatou.

#### 3. A nested smooth construction

Choose a fixed C-infinity radial nonincreasing chi with 0<=chi<=1, chi=1 on [0,1], and chi=0 on [2,infinity). For example obtain it from the normalized integral of exp(-1/((s-1)(2-s))) on 1<s<2, integrating from s to 2. Set

    Phi(X)=y chi(r), epsilon_n=4^(-n),
    g_n(X)=epsilon_n Phi(X/epsilon_n)=y chi(r/epsilon_n),
    a_n=1/[n^2 log(n+1)], n>=2,
    h_N=sum_(n=2)^N a_n(g_n-Phi),
    h=sum_(n=2)^infinity a_n(g_n-Phi).                (3)

Every term is smooth and compactly supported in the disk r<=2. The series of C1 norms is summable because the C1 norm of g_n is bounded uniformly in n and sum a_n<infinity. Hence h_N converges in C1, h is C1, and Dh(0)=0 because each summand has zero first jet. At every X!=0 only finitely many g_n are nonzero; the remaining terms combine into a constant multiple of the fixed smooth Phi. Consequently h is smooth away from 0.

Each term is y times a radial function and therefore has only the first angular harmonic. Its third angular harmonic vanishes identically. Its circular strain integral is zero at every cutoff. Since the jet is zero, the contact-corrected formula gives c[h_N]=0. Membership in H_(3/2), proved below, gives continuity of the canonical strain and hence c[h]=0 as well. Alternatively the zero circular integral and b[h]=0 give the same value directly.

#### 4. Logarithmic almost orthogonality

We prove convergence at beta=3/2; smaller exponents follow afterwards. Write F=D^2 Phi as its full ordered Hessian. Its components have mean and first moments zero, by integration by parts. They are compact smooth. Their Fourier transforms therefore obey

    |F_hat(eta)|<=C min(|eta|^2,|eta|^(-4)).          (4)

For |eta|<=1, subtract the constant and linear Taylor terms of exp(-iX.eta) and use the finite second absolute moment of F. For |eta|>=1 integrate by parts four times in a coordinate with |eta_j|>=|eta|/sqrt2. This proves (4) with one finite constant C.

The Hessians F_n=D^2 g_n satisfy F_n(X)=epsilon_n^(-1)F(X/epsilon_n), so F_n_hat(xi)=epsilon_n F_hat(epsilon_n xi). On the disjoint frequency annuli4^k<=|xi|<4^(k+1), k>=0, (4) and their area give

    ||1_annulus F_n_hat||_2<=C0 4^(-3|k-n|).          (5)

Changing C0 covers the bounded factor 4 at endpoints. On the low disk|xi|<1 the bound is C0 4^(-3n). On the kth annulus the multiplier (1+log(1+|xi|^2))^(3/2) is at most C1(1+k)^(3/2).

Put A_n=(1+n)^(3/2)|a_n|, extend it by zero to all integer n, and put K_l=(1+|l|)^(3/2)4^(-3|l|). The inequality 1+k<=(1+n)(1+|k-n|) shows that the weighted block norm of any finite Hessian sum is bounded by C2(K*A)_k. Since sum_l K_l<infinity, the elementary discrete convolution inequality ||K*A||_(ell2)<=||K||_(ell1)||A||_(ell2) gives

    ||Q_(3/2) sum a_n D^2g_n||_2^2
             <=C3 sum (1+n)^3 a_n^2.                (6)

The low block is controlled by the same right side by Cauchy-Schwarz. The right side has convergent tails because

    (1+n)^3 a_n^2 <=4/[n log(n)^2] for n>=2.          (7)

Here (1+1/n)^3<=27/8<4 and log(n+1)>=log n. Integral comparison proves convergence. This establishes that the Hessian series is Cauchy in the required logarithmic L2 norm.

For any fixed compact smooth f and 0<epsilon<=1, a Fourier change of variables gives

    ||Q_(3/2)[A f(X/epsilon)]||_2
         <=C_f |A| epsilon(1+log(1/epsilon))^(3/2).   (8)

Indeed1+log(1+|eta|^2/epsilon^2) is at most (1+2log(1/epsilon))(1+log(1+|eta|^2)). Apply(8) and the triangle inequality to g_n, X_j g_n and X_jD^2g_n. Their respective factors |A|epsilon are epsilon_n^2, epsilon_n^3 and epsilon_n. After multiplication by a_n their series all converge. The fixed Phi term in (3) converges because sum a_n does.

For each fixed finite beta, the multiplier gradient

    D_xi q_beta=2beta xi(1+|xi|^2)^(-1)
                         (1+log(1+|xi|^2))^(beta-1)

is bounded: it is continuous and tends to 0 at infinity. Consequently

    ||X Q_beta f||_2<=||Q_beta(Xf)||_2+C_beta' ||f||_2. (9)

For beta<=3/2 also q_beta<=q_(3/2). Equations(6)-(9) prove that Q_beta h_N, D^2Q_beta h_N, XQ_beta h_N and XD^2Q_beta h_N converge in L2. The inequality 2s^2<=1+s^4 then controls the first derivatives. This proves convergence in H_beta.

#### 5. The actual weighted completions

The same four convergences imply convergence in N_(beta,R), uniformly R>=1. Indeed omega1<=1, omega2<=1+2r, and the centrally odd angular Hardy inequality gives

    ||w_R Q_beta f||_(Hdot^-1)<=||r Q_beta f||_2,

because w_R<=1 and every centrally odd homogeneous H1 test satisfies ||test/r||_2<=||D test||_2. This is precisely the weighted argument of 74, reproduced here for the nested construction. Thus the compact smooth h_N converge in the stated weighted core norm. Their distributional limit is the same C1 function h. No assertion about completion is inferred merely from finiteness of a formal expression.

The native norms M in P83 and Mstar in P89 at any fixed admissible parameters are equivalent to these N norms by parts P77, P83 and P89. Thus h also belongs to those native spaces when 1/2<beta<=1. The equivalence is used only for membership and continuity, with no claim of a uniform constant in the parameters.

#### 6. Divergence of the full absolute moment

For m>=3, consider the gap 2epsilon_m<r<epsilon_(m-1)=4epsilon_m. Then chi(r)=1, every g_n with n<=m-1 equals y, and every g_n with n>=m vanishes. Therefore

    h(r,theta)=-r sin(theta) sum_(n>=m) a_n.

Its contribution to (1) is exactly

    4log2 sum_(n>=m) a_n.

The gaps are disjoint and lie inside r<1. Tonelli gives

    I(h)>=4log2 sum_(m>=3)sum_(n>=m)a_n
          =4log2 sum_(n>=3)(n-2)/[n^2 log(n+1)]
          =infinity.                              (10)

The divergence follows by comparison with 1/(n log n). The identical finite-gap calculation for h_N proves I(h_N) tends to infinity while all the stated norms remain bounded. Hence no constant can bound I on the smooth zero-jet, zero-strain core for any beta<=3/2. For beta<=1/2 this last statement is interpreted on that core and the constructed C1 zero-jet function, without asserting a bounded jet functional on the whole space.

The proof depends on 70 for the canonical continuous strain at beta=3/2 and on 77,83,89 only for the optional native-space conversion. The Fourier almost-orthogonality, weighted membership and divergent moment are proved here. No numerical profile claim or inverse theorem is needed.

### P97.2. Verified result

Date: 2026-10-28T14:01:08.715488+00:00. Independent check 206.

For beta>3/2 the explicit integral constant in P97 bounds I(h)=int_(r<1)|h-b[h]y|/r^3. One compact C1 density, smooth away from 0, belongs to H_beta and actual N_beta,R uniformly R>=1 for every finite beta<=3/2, has b=c=0 and no third angular harmonic, but I(h)=infinity. Its smooth zero-jet zero-strain partial sums have bounded norms and unbounded I. Thus the angular projection before absolute value in P87 is essential.
