## P98. Exact origin remainder bounds for the checkpoint through radius one tenth

### P98.1. Independent origin remainder bounds for the exact original state

#### Statement and inputs

Use the exact accepted state 131 reconstructed from the original, with potential chi, rho=-partial_y Delta chi, u=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy), c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248 and a0=rho_y(0). For each radius and target recorded in a complete certificate, the conclusion is an everywhere bound on the closed disk of that exact rational radius. The fields are rho_y-a0, rho_x, the four entries of Du-Du(0), and the two entries of u-Du(0)X. Divide the first six by r^2 and the last two by r^3, with their bounded angular limits at zero.

This is an independent recomputation from the original coefficients. It is not a claim that the numerical  floating sample inflation or decimal displays are directed bounds. An incomplete tree proves no disk bound. The final results table and audit identify the completed statements.

#### Exact compactified representation

Put t=r^2/(1+r^2), z=cos(2theta), delta=1-1/c and q_j=(j+1)delta/2 for j=0,1,2,3. All four q_j lie strictly between zero and one. Each fourth derivative of chi is a sum

    f(t,z)=s(z) sum_j (1-t)^(q_j) P_j(t,z),

where P_j is a rational polynomial. For even-even derivatives s=1; for odd-odd derivatives s=sqrt(1-z^2) on the first quadrant. The third derivatives have the form r s(z) times the same type of sum, with s=sqrt((1+z)/2) for u1 and s=sqrt((1-z)/2) for u2. Their exact derivative recurrence is obtained by applying partial_x=cos(theta)partial_r-sin(theta)partial_theta/r and partial_y=sin(theta)partial_r+cos(theta)partial_theta/r to each potential generator. Negative sine frequencies change sign. The sine or cosine factors are removed using the exact Chebyshev polynomial identities. All remaining powers of t are nonnegative.

For each field the sum_j P_j(0,z) is exactly its constant origin coefficient after its angular factor has been removed. For fourth derivatives this is rho_y(0)=a0, rho_x(0)=0, and the corresponding entries of Du(0)=diag(c-1,1-c). For third derivatives it is c-1 or 1-c. Denote this constant by b.

#### A uniformly controlled Taylor division

For 0<q<1, write

    (1-t)^q = 1-sum_(n>=1) a_n(q)t^n,
    a_n(q)>0, a_(n+1)/a_n=(n-q)/(n+1)<1.

Let W_N be its Taylor polynomial through degree N. For 0<=t<=t0<1,

    |(1-t)^q-W_N(t)| <= a_(N+1)(q)t^(N+1)/(1-t).

This follows term by term from the ratio bound. Define the exact rational polynomial

    H(t,z)=(1-t)[sum_j W_(N,j)(t)P_j(t,z)-b]/t.

The numerator's constant t coefficient vanishes identically in z, so this is polynomial division, not a numerical subtraction near zero. For the normalized remainder,

    |(1-t)[sum_j (1-t)^(q_j)P_j(t,z)-b]/t-H(t,z)|
       <= t0^N sum_j a_(N+1)(q_j) sup |P_j|
       <= t0^N sum_j a_(N+1)(q_j) sum_(i,k)|p_(j,i,k)|t0^i = E.

The last estimate uses |z|<=1. It is rational and holds on the entire rectangle, including the limiting value at t=0. Multiplication by the angular factor s gives the required remainder divided by r^2, or by r^3 in the velocity cases. In all cases |s|<=1.

#### Directed covering proof

On each rational t,z rectangle, the tensor Bernstein convex hull gives an interval for H. Multiply its absolute upper bound plus E by an upper bound for |s(z)|. If the resulting Arb ball is strictly below the exact target, the field inequality holds on that cell. Complete binary trees cover [0,t0] times [-1,1], where t0=r0^2/(1+r0^2). Reflection preserves the absolute inequalities. A separate direct power-polynomial restriction checks every accepted leaf and the exact tree at a different precision. A second construction of the polynomial identities checks the source derivative and Taylor-division algebra.

#### Analytic radius and scope

For a fixed real unit vector omega, every original generator evaluated at X=r omega is r^(2k)(1+r^2)^(p_j-k) times a fixed angular coefficient. Its binomial series, with every fixed number of derivatives, converges absolutely for |r|<1. The finite sum has the same guaranteed disk of convergence. A Cauchy estimate on a chosen complex polydisc of radius 1/5 can be very loose at real radius 1/10; that does not reduce the true guaranteed radial Taylor convergence radius to about 1/4. No statement here asserts that every individual nonzero field has a singularity on every angular ray at |r|=1.

#### Completed statements

All 32 original numerical targets, interpreted as exact binary64 rationals and listed in certificate file certificates.original32.json, pass for the exact rational radii 1/100,1/50,1/20 and 1/10. In addition, the seven rounded decimal displays of the numerical work pass independently, although they did not follow by outward rounding from the originally cited endpoints.

A simpler improved statement on the disk r<=1/10 is

    |rho_y-a0| <= 3.04 r^2,       |rho_x| <= 1.24 r^2,
    |Du11-(c-1)| = |Du22-(1-c)| <= 0.65 r^2,
    |Du12| <= 0.59 r^2,          |Du21| <= 0.66 r^2,
    |u1-(c-1)x| <= 0.285 r^3,    |u2-(1-c)y| <= 0.293 r^3.

Every terminating decimal in this statement denotes its exact rational value. The improved radius 1/10 estimates require no Cauchy polydisc bound. All numerical claims depend on the complete primary and independent records, plus the exact algebra audit. They do not establish residual smallness or an exact nonlinear profile.

## P101. A directed exterior residual bound for the checkpoint

### P101.1. Directed exterior residual bound for the original state

#### Exact object and scope

Let chi be the exact original state 131 potential reconstructed from the read-only case4 checkpoint. Put c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma, rho=-partial_y Delta chi, u=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy), and F=(cX+u).D rho-rho. All tensor and vector norms in this proof are Euclidean norms in Cartesian coordinates. The desired numerical statement is |F(X)| <= B r^(2gamma-1) for r>=R, with R=300 and an explicitly certified rational B. This document is a certificate scheme; a numerical value is proved only after a complete directed cover and an independent recheck have passed.

#### Finite expansion and remainder

Truncate the convergent binomial expansion of each potential generator at radial descendant q=Q. Write the resulting potential as chi_Q and its density and velocity as rho_Q,u_Q. The exact residual F_Q=(cX+u_Q).D rho_Q-rho_Q is a finite sum

    F_Q=sum_(h,q) r^(gamma-h delta-2q) E_(h,q)(theta).

Here E_(h,q) is a rational sine polynomial, h ranges from 0 to 7, and q ranges from 0 to 2Q. The (0,0) term vanishes exactly. Every nonzero term has a=(h-1)delta+2q>=0, with equality only for (1,0). The arrays are computed by exact differentiation and multiplication, rather than numerical interpolation. The exact recurrence and an independent algebraic audit are in part P3.

For each j let A_j be the sum of the absolute values of the original canonical potential coefficients in branch j. The generator parameters satisfy |p_j-k|<26 and the angular frequencies are at most 18. After d Cartesian derivatives, a descendant of index q has coefficient sum at most

    binom(q+25,q)(2q+32)^d sum_j A_j r^(-j delta)

relative to r^(gamma+3-d-2q). This follows from |binom(p_j-k,q)|<=binom(q+25,q) and from the polar differentiation recurrence: at derivative step l the sum of the two absolute frequency coefficients is at most |2p_j-2q-l|+18+l <=2q+32 for d<=4. The inequality uses the exact range 0<2p_j<4 and l<=3.

Set q0=Q+1 and

    ratio_d=((q0+26)/(q0+1))*((2q0+34)/(2q0+32))^d/R^2,
    T_d=binom(q0+25,q0)(2q0+32)^d R^(-2q0)
        (sum_j A_j R^(-j delta))/(1-ratio_d).

If ratio_d<1, this is a geometric majorant for every component of D^d(chi-chi_Q), normalized by r^(gamma+3-d), for r>=R. The normalized component majorants decrease with r. The same construction with all q<=Q and their exact derivative coefficient sums gives finite constants M_d for each component of D^d chi_Q.

The density is the sum of two third potential derivatives, the velocity has two components, and the density gradient has two components, each a sum of two fourth derivatives. Consequently

    |rho-rho_Q| <=2T_3 r^gamma,
    |D(rho-rho_Q)| <=2 sqrt(2) T_4 r^(gamma-1),
    |u-u_Q| <=sqrt(2) T_3 r^gamma,
    |u_Q| <=sqrt(2) M_3 r^gamma,
    |D rho_Q| <=2 sqrt(2) M_4 r^(gamma-1).

For the linear part, the extra scaling factor r^delta is absorbed into the descendant decay: every omitted exponent has 2q+j delta-delta>0, so its maximum on r>=R is at R. Therefore

    |F-F_Q|/r^(2gamma-1) <= epsilon_R,
    epsilon_R=R^delta(2 sqrt(2)c T_4+2T_3)
              +4(T_3 M_4+M_3 T_4+T_3 T_4).                 (1)

No float serialization of a tail bound is an input to (1).

#### Directed compactified cover

Put t=R/r in [0,1] and z=cos(2theta) in [-1,1]. Because every sine frequency n is odd,

    sin(n theta)=sin(theta) P_n(z),
    P_n(z)=U_(n-1)(sqrt((1+z)/2)),

where the displayed Chebyshev expression is a rational polynomial in z: n-1 is even. On the first quadrant sin(theta)=sqrt((1-z)/2). The parity of the exact residual reduces its absolute supremum on the full circle to this quadrant. Thus

    F_Q/r^(2gamma-1)=sqrt((1-z)/2)
       sum_(h,q) R^(-a_(h,q)) t^a_(h,q) P_(h,q)(z),
    a_(h,q)=(h-1)delta+2q.

On a rectangle [t0,t1] times [z0,z1], every nonnegative power t^a is enclosed by its endpoint values. Convert each exact angular polynomial to Bernstein coefficients on [z0,z1], multiply by these directed radial intervals and sum sectors coefficient by coefficient before taking a convex hull. Multiplication by the exact interval for sqrt((1-z)/2) then encloses the residual throughout the rectangle. At t=0, positive powers are zero and the zero power is one. This handles infinity without a limiting grid argument.

A leaf is accepted only when the resulting absolute bound plus the directed error (1) is at most the specified rational target B. Every subdivision is an exact rational bisection. A complete binary leaf tree covers the compactified rectangle. An independent checker reconstructs the exact endpoints and recomputes the angular Bernstein restriction directly from power coefficients at a different precision. The complete cover and passing recheck prove the exterior bound for all r>=R. Floating arithmetic may choose which rectangle to split but never accepts a leaf.

#### Limitations

A finite sample, an unfinished tree, or an error bound based on unverified floating trigonometric evaluation does not prove this statement. This estimate concerns the residual of the numerical reference, not an exact stationary solution or a smallness condition for an existence theorem.

## P102. The divergent absolute jet moment lies outside the fractional weighted spaces

### P102.1. Scope of the divergent absolute jet moment

#### Statement

Let 0<alpha<=1, and let h be a real C^(1,alpha) function on the closed unit disk in R^2, even in x and odd in y. Write b=h_y(0) and H=[Dh]_(C^alpha(B1)), using the Euclidean norm for the gradient. Then

    integral_(|X|<1) |h(X)-b y| |X|^-3 dX
       <= 2 pi H/[alpha(1+alpha)].                         (1)

In particular, for every 0<s<=2^-12 and every R>=1, every element h of the fractional weighted space N_(s,R)^w of part P17 has finite full absolute jet moment. Using its established gradient estimate gives

    integral_(|X|<1) |h(X)-b y| |X|^-3 dX
       <= 2^14 pi s^(-3/2)/(1+s/2) N_(s,R)^w(h).            (2)

Consequently the compact C1 function with divergent absolute jet moment in part P97 does not belong to any of these positive-fractional-gain spaces. Part P97 proves its membership in the weighted logarithmic spaces N_(beta,R)^log and the equivalent native logarithmic spaces, not the fractional spaces of the earlier weighted theorem.

#### Proof

Parity gives h(0)=0 and Dh(0)=(0,b). The fundamental theorem of calculus on the segment from 0 to X gives

    h(X)-b y = integral_0^1 [Dh(tX)-Dh(0)].X dt.

Its absolute value is at most H |X|^(1+alpha) integral_0^1 t^alpha dt = H |X|^(1+alpha)/(1+alpha). In polar coordinates the integral in (1) is therefore at most

    [2 pi H/(1+alpha)] integral_0^1 r^(alpha-1) dr,

which is exactly (1). Part P17 proves for the actual fractional core completion that h has a C^(1,s/2) representative and [Dh]_(C^(s/2)) <=2^12 s^(-1/2) N_(s,R)^w(h), uniformly in R>=1. Substitute alpha=s/2 into (1) to obtain (2). If the part P97 function belonged to such a space, (2) would contradict its proved infinite moment. This proves nonmembership.

#### Report correction and dependencies

An earlier version of the report said the part P97 example belongs to "the weighted spaces of the weighted theorem". Read as the positive-fractional-gain spaces of Theorem D_w, this assertion is false by (2); the report now refers to "the weighted logarithmic spaces N_(beta,R)^log". The standalone P97 proof and its native logarithmic conclusion remain valid. This correction does not affect any existence theorem or its stated hypotheses.

The only external proof dependency is the already verified part P17 fractional gradient estimate and its completion interpretation. Formula (1) is proved here without numerical computation. No formal sources or Lean build were used.

The phrase "in the weighted spaces of the weighted theorem" of an earlier version of the report is false if read as Theorem D_w; the report now refers to "in the weighted logarithmic spaces N_(beta,R)^log". ## P103. Polynomial growth passes from the density to the canonical velocity

### P103.1. Polynomial growth passes from the density to its canonical velocity

#### Statement and scope

Let rho and u=(u1,u2) be smooth real fields on the full plane satisfying

    Delta u1 = partial_x partial_y rho,
    Delta u2 = -partial_x^2 rho.                                      (1)

Suppose u has polynomial growth and every derivative of rho has polynomial growth. Then every derivative of u has polynomial growth. More precisely, fix a nonnegative integer m. If |u(X)| <= C(1+|X|)^B and |D^j rho(X)| <= C_j(1+|X|)^(N_j) for 0<=j<=m+2, with nonnegative B,N_j, then

    sup_X (1+|X|)^(-N) |D^m u(X)| < infinity,
    N=max(B,N_0,...,N_(m+2)).                                        (2)

All norms on derivatives are the full ordered Euclidean tensor norms. The constants in (2) may depend on m, the displayed growth constants and the fixed cutoff below. This is a qualitative growth result, not an evaluated numerical derivative cap.

For the canonical IPM velocity U=(-R1R2,R1^2), (1) holds in distributions and hence classically whenever the fields are smooth. Thus the reference assumptions in part P85 that all derivatives of both rho and u have polynomial growth follow already from polynomial growth of every density derivative and the stated sublinear velocity bound. In particular the report's abbreviated growth assumption does not omit a necessary independent hypothesis.

#### Proof of the local estimate

Fix a smooth cutoff eta on the plane, equal to 1 on the disk of radius 3/4 and zero outside the disk of radius 1. Its derivatives of every fixed finite order are bounded. For a point X0 and one component v of u put f=Delta v, let eta_0(Y)=eta(Y-X0), and set

    w(X) = integral_R2 Gamma(X-Y) eta_0(Y) f(Y) dY,
    Gamma(Z) = (1/(2 pi)) log|Z|.

The identity Delta Gamma=delta_0 follows by integration by parts on the complement of the radius-epsilon disk: the radial flux of D Gamma through its boundary is 1, and the logarithmic boundary contribution vanishes as epsilon tends to 0. Consequently Delta w=eta_0 f. The logarithm is locally integrable and the source is compact smooth. Moving derivatives onto the source in the distributional convolution gives, for every multi-index alpha,

    partial^alpha w = Gamma * partial^alpha(eta_0 f).                (3)

This is a smooth function. For X in the disk of radius 3/4 about X0, the convolution uses only |X-Y|<2. The integral of |Gamma| on that fixed disk is finite. Leibniz's rule in (3) therefore gives

    sup_(B_(3/4)(X0)) |D^m w|
      <= C_m max_(0<=j<=m) sup_(B1(X0)) |D^j f|,                    (4)

where C_m is finite and independent of X0. The same assertion for m=0 bounds w itself.

The difference h=v-w is harmonic on B_(3/4)(X0). Choose a fixed smooth radial function zeta supported in the radius 1/4 disk with integral 1. The mean-value identity on circles and radial integration show h=zeta*h on the radius 1/2 disk about X0. Differentiate this convolution at X0 to obtain

    |D^m h(X0)| <= ||D^m zeta||_1 sup_(B_(1/4)(X0)) |h|.             (5)

For completeness, the circular mean-value identity follows from the divergence theorem: the derivative of the circular average at radius r is (2 pi r)^(-1) times the integral of Delta h over the radius-r disk, which is zero. Its value at radius 0 is h at the center. Thus (5) needs no global representation of a harmonic function.

Combining (4), (5), the m=0 bound for w, and v=h+w gives the local estimate

    |D^m v(X0)| <= C'_m [sup_(B1(X0)) |v|
                       +max_(0<=j<=m) sup_(B1(X0)) |D^j f|].       (6)

Every constant here is finite, depends only on m and the fixed kernels, and is independent of the translated center. Taking the two components and using (1) proves the same bound with derivatives of rho through order m+2 on the right.

#### Polynomial growth and the IPM identities

For |Y-X0|<=1 one has 1+|Y|<=2(1+|X0|). Substitute the assumed bounds into (6), absorb the finitely many factors 2^B and 2^(N_j), and take N to be their maximum. This proves (2) for every m.

With the convention R_j has Fourier multiplier i xi_j/|xi|, the multipliers of -R1R2 and R1^2 are respectively xi_1 xi_2/|xi|^2 and -xi_1^2/|xi|^2. Multiplication by the Laplacian multiplier -|xi|^2 gives respectively -xi_1 xi_2 and xi_1^2, exactly the multipliers of partial_xy and -partial_xx. This proves (1). Equivalently, for rho=-partial_y Delta chi and u=(-chi_xyy,chi_xxy), commute the displayed derivatives to obtain (1) directly.

The reference bound |u|<=22 r^(5/9) in P85 supplies polynomial growth of u. Smoothness supplies harmless bounded values near 0. Therefore the report's assumption on all density derivatives implies the full polynomial-growth hypothesis used by P85. The result says nothing about whether any particular numerical derivative cap or residual threshold is met.

### P103.2. Result

Independent check 218, 2026-10-28T15:05:26Z. Verdict: CONFIRMED by complete manual proof.

For smooth canonical IPM fields, polynomial growth of u and every density derivative implies polynomial growth of every velocity derivative. A localized logarithmic Poisson potential and the harmonic mean-value identity give a center-uniform interior estimate, with density derivatives through order m+2 controlling D^m u. Consequently the report may abbreviate the growth assumption to density derivatives: its separate velocity decay bound supplies the remaining input. This is a qualitative implication, not a certified numerical derivative cap.

### P104.1. Direct full-plane decay bounds for the original state

#### Exact reference and targets

Use the exact original state 131 potential chi, reconstructed from the read-only case4 checkpoint as in parts P1.2, P4 and P96. Put

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248, gamma=1/c, delta=1-gamma,

The proposed numerical targets are

    sup_R2 r^d |Du| <=1.85619,
    sup_R2 r^(d-1) |u| <=0.97743.                                 (1)

All decimals in (1) denote exact rationals. All vector and derivative norms are Euclidean, with the full ordered derivative tensor. The value of r^(d-1)|u| at 0 is its continuous limiting value 0. A target in (1) becomes a theorem only after its complete directed cover and independent recheck pass. This document specifies the proof scheme; it does not declare an unrun computation successful.

#### Exact compactified formulas

Set t=r^2/(1+r^2), z=cos(2theta), w=(1-t)^(delta/2). On the first quadrant define the polynomials from P96 and the third-potential-derivative recurrence from P95 by

    chi22=w sum_(j=0)^3 w^j P22,j,
    chi04=w sum_(j=0)^3 w^j P04,j,
    chi13=w sqrt(1-z^2) sum_(j=0)^3 w^j P13,j,
    chi31=w sqrt(1-z^2) sum_(j=0)^3 w^j P31,j,
    u1=r w cos(theta) sum_(j=0)^3 w^j Pu1,j,
    u2=r w sin(theta) sum_(j=0)^3 w^j Pu2,j.

Each P is a rational polynomial in t,z recovered by exact differentiation of the original canonical coefficients. The derivative recurrence is the polar identity partial_x=cos(theta)partial_r-sin(theta)partial_theta/r and its y analogue. Smoothness cancels every negative power of t. Odd angular cosine and sine modes factor respectively cos(theta) and sin(theta), leaving polynomials in z. The third-derivative signs are fixed by u1=-chi_xyy and u2=chi_xxy.

Write Sj for a corresponding sum of branch polynomials after removing the common w. Then

    |Du|^2 = w^2 [2 S22^2+(1-z^2)(S13^2+S31^2)],
    |D rho|^2 = w^2 [(S22+S04)^2+(1-z^2)(S31+S13)^2],
    |u|^2 = r^2 w^2 [((1+z)/2) Su1^2+((1-z)/2) Su2^2].           (2)

The sums used in D rho are formed before interval evaluation. All three squared weighted quantities in (1) are the respective brackets in (2) times the same factor

    f(t)=t^d(1-t)^(delta-d).                                      (3)

Here 0<d<delta, so f extends continuously with value 0 at both endpoints. On (0,1) its logarithmic derivative is d/t-(delta-d)/(1-t). It is increasing until t=d/delta and decreasing afterwards. Therefore its maximum on any exact cell [a,b] is f(d/delta) if a<=d/delta<=b, and otherwise the larger of its endpoint values. This is an exact rational critical point, evaluated using directed real powers.

#### Directed enclosure and independent verification

On every rational rectangle in [0,1] times [-1,1], enclose each branch sum by the tensor Bernstein convex-hull property, using the exact containing interval for w. The correlated Taylor enclosure of P95 is also valid: expand (1-t)^(j delta/2) to degree 4 at the left endpoint, use its fifth-derivative maximum for the uniform remainder, and multiply its Bernstein coefficients with those of P. Cells touching t=1 retain the independent branch-variable enclosure. Take the smaller of two valid upper bounds. The branch powers have j<=3 and satisfy j delta/2<4, as required by the remainder formula.

Multiply the squared field bounds from (2) by the directed maximum of (3), and accept a leaf only if the result is no greater than the square of its exact target. A complete exact bisection tree covers the compactified quadrant. The independent checker reconstructs the tree and every rational endpoint and recomputes polynomial restrictions directly from power coefficients at a different precision. It does not reuse the producer's subdivided coefficient arrays.

Reflection preserves the three norms. Thus a complete passing certificate proves its corresponding inequality on the full plane, including the limiting value at 0. Infinity is handled by the continuous compactification, not a radial sample or extrapolation. The third-derivative polynomials must additionally pass an independent per-generator angular expansion check; fourth derivatives already have the exact source audit in P96. All source and certificate hashes must match before registering a result.

#### Scope

These bounds check three reported numerical constants. They do not cover the second-density-derivative part of the first decay hypothesis, or the second-velocity-derivative decay hypothesis. They do not imply residual smallness or existence. An incomplete cover remains an open numerical target even if every sampled value lies below it. No values serialized by a floating trigonometric supremum routine are used in this proof.

## P106. The actual residuals lie in the logarithmic forcing spaces

### P106.1. The actual residuals belong to the logarithmic forcing spaces

#### 1. Statement

All functions and distributions are on R^2. Let f be smooth, even in x and odd in y. Suppose that for some q<1/5 and finite constants C_m,

    |D^m f(X)| <= C_m <X>^(q-m), 0<=m<=4,                 (1)

where <X>=(1+|X|^2)^(1/2) and every derivative norm is the full ordered Euclidean tensor norm. Fix any finite R>=1, A>0, tau>0 and 0<=beta<=1. Set

    omega1=<X>^(-1/5), omega2=(1+4|X|^2)^(2/5),
    w=(1+|X|^2/R^2)^(-11/10), K=log(1-Delta),
    Q=(1+tau K)^beta,
    L(f)=||wf||_(Hdot^-1),
    M_A(f)^2=||omega2 D^2Qf||_2^2
                +A^2||omega1 DQf||_2^2+A^2 2^31 L(f)^2.    (2)

The homogeneous negative norm is the canonical Fourier norm on centrally odd distributions, equivalently the dual norm against centrally odd homogeneous H1 functions. The space in (2) is the completion of the compact smooth S1 core in this norm, realized as distributions.

**Theorem.** Under (1), f belongs to this completed space, with finite M_A norm. No numerical upper bound on that norm is asserted.

Consequently the exact residuals of state 131, nb_Mpen2_exact and nb_d2_exact all belong to every forcing space (2), including the native logarithmic spaces used in P85 and P89. Their large certified lower bounds are finite-norm obstructions, not merely extended-norm alternatives.

#### 2. Weighted heat and Bessel bounds

For either omega=omega1 or omega2 there is a finite constant C such that

    omega(X)/omega(Y) <= C(1+|X-Y|)^p,                       (3)

with p=1/5 or p=4/5 respectively. For example, the elementary inequality <X><=sqrt(2)<Y><X-Y> and its scaled version prove (3); for a negative exponent interchange X and Y. In particular 0<p<1.

Let H_t=exp(t Delta). Its positive Gaussian kernel has mass1 and radial moment

    integral |Z|^p (4pi t)^(-1) exp(-|Z|^2/(4t)) dZ
       =(4t)^(p/2) Gamma(1+p/2).

Multiplying a convolution by omega, using (3), and applying the ordinary L2 convolution inequality gives

    ||omega H_t g||_2 <= C'(1+t^(p/2))||omega g||_2.          (4)

Thus H_t acts boundedly on this weighted L2 space. It is strongly continuous at 0, first on compact smooth functions by the Gaussian approximate identity and then by density and the uniform bound for 0<t<=1.

For a>0 the Bessel multiplier J^(-2a)=(1-Delta)^(-a) has the positive kernel representation

    J^(-2a) = Gamma(a)^(-1) integral_0^infinity
                         s^(a-1)e^(-s) H_s ds.

Using (4) and concavity of s^(p/2), its weighted L2 norm is at most

    C'[1+Gamma(a+p/2)/Gamma(a)] <= C'(1+a^(p/2)).             (5)

The second inequality is Jensen's inequality for a gamma random variable of mean a. At a=0 use the identity operator. All integrals are Bochner integrals in the stated weighted L2 space; the displayed integrable majorants justify them.

#### 3. One logarithmic derivative costs two ordinary derivatives

For compact smooth g, the scalar identity log(1+lambda)=integral_0^infinity e^(-t)(1-e^(-t lambda))dt/t gives

    Kg=integral_0^infinity e^(-t)(g-H_tg) dt/t.               (6)

For 0<t<=1, g-H_tg=-integral_0^t H_s Delta g ds, so (4) bounds its weighted L2 norm by 2C't||omega Delta g||_2. For t>=1, (4) bounds it by [1+C'(1+t^(p/2))]||omega g||_2. Both resulting integrals in (6) converge. Hence

    ||omega Kg||_2 <= C_omega (||omega g||_2
                                  +||omega Delta g||_2),   (7)

with a finite constant independent of g. The identity and bound extend by completion whenever both terms on the right are finite and are approximated by compact smooth functions. The extension agrees with the Fourier multiplier as a tempered distribution, because the heat representation agrees there on the dense core and the same bounds give local distributional convergence.

For 0<b<=1, the positive inverse B_b=(1+tau K)^(-b) has the representation

    B_b=Gamma(b)^(-1) integral_0^infinity
                         t^(b-1)e^(-t) J^(-2tau t) dt.

Equation (5) gives the finite weighted L2 bound

    ||B_b|| <= C'[1+tau^(p/2) Gamma(b+p/2)/Gamma(b)].          (8)

At b=0 again use the identity. For 0<beta<=1 the exact Fourier identity

    Q=B_(1-beta)(I+tau K)

therefore proves

    ||omega Qg||_2 <= C_(omega,tau,beta)
                        (||omega g||_2+||omega Delta g||_2).
                                                                    (9)

For beta=0 this conclusion is immediate. Derivatives commute with every multiplier here. Apply (9) with omega1 and g=Df, and with omega2 and g=D^2f. The required right sides involve only Df,D^3f,D^2f,D^4f.

#### 4. Integrability and membership in the actual completion

At infinity, each principal weighted derivative in (9) is O(r^(q-6/5)); the two extra derivatives decay two powers faster. The radial L2 integral is dominated by a constant times

    integral_1^infinity r^(2q-7/5) dr,

which is finite exactly when q<1/5. Smoothness handles the origin. Thus the high components in (2) are finite.

For the low component, a centrally odd smooth test phi has zero circular mean and satisfies the angular Hardy inequality

    ||phi/r||_2 <= ||Dphi||_2.

Indeed its angular Fourier series contains no zero mode, so the circular Poincare inequality has constant 1; integrate it with measure dr/r. Consequently

    |integral wf phi| <= ||r wf||_2 ||phi/r||_2,
    L(f)<=||r wf||_2.                                      (10)

Since R is finite, r wf=O(r^(q-6/5)) at infinity and is O(r) near 0. The same q<1/5 condition makes (10) finite.

It remains to show membership in the core completion, rather than only finiteness of formal components. Choose a smooth radial cutoff chi_T, equal to 1 on r<=T and zero on r>=2T, with |D^j chi_T|<=C_j T^(-j). Set f_T=chi_T f. These are compact smooth S1 functions. By Leibniz's rule and (1),

    ||omega_j D^j(f-f_T)||_2 ->0,
    ||omega_j Delta D^j(f-f_T)||_2 ->0, j=1,2.

For terms where a derivative hits the cutoff, its factor T^(-l) on the annulus T<=r<=2T combines with D^(m-l)f to give the same bound O(r^(q-m)); the preceding integrable tail dominates each term. Equation (9) then proves convergence of both high components of f_T to those of f. Equation (10), applied to f-f_T, proves convergence of the low component. Thus f_T is Cauchy in M_A and its distributional limit is f. This proves the theorem for the actual compact-core completion.

#### 5. Application to the exact case4 residuals

For the exact original state 131, let gamma=1/c and delta=1-gamma with

    c=4076476460239181/2251799813685248.

The exact asymptotic algebra of P3 and the differentiated remainder proof P21.2 give (1), in fact at every finite derivative order, for its actual residual with

    q_original=2gamma-1=427123167131315/4076476460239181 <1/5.

The leading linear density term cancels because c gamma=1. The remaining first residual power is q_original. The convergent binomial expansion of every finite regularized-power generator, with its differentiated remainder, gives a uniform symbol bound for r>=2; smoothness supplies the bounded interior constants.

For the exact refits nb_Mpen2_exact and nb_d2_exact, the source audits19,42 and 52 certify cancellation of every residual sector above

    q_refit=gamma-6delta=-8696260065638350/4076476460239181 < -2.

The same differentiated finite-generator expansion gives (1) with this smaller q. The additional d2 descendant cancellation does not weaken the conclusion. Hence the theorem applies to all three actual residuals.

This result supplies finiteness and compact-core membership, but no favorable size estimate. In the parameterized d2 space A=2^189,tau=2^-210, the prior lower bound remains M_A(F)>2^178*1936535207, and the ratio to the sufficient threshold remains greater than 2^243. The original and other refit exclusions remain unchanged.

#### Dependencies and scope

Sections 1 to 4 are self-contained apart from the elementary Fourier/heat definition of the displayed multipliers. The exact source and differentiated asymptotic facts for the three applications were independently audited in parts P3, P21, P20, P42 and P52. Verification checks the rational exponents, these source bindings, the displayed radial powers, and the Gamma/Jensen parameter ranges. No quadrature, spatial mesh, remote computation or formal build is needed. The result does not permit varying the leading profile or exponent in the correction space.

## P108. The power one fifth is the sharp forcing-tail threshold of the logarithmic spaces

### P108.1. Sharp power and logarithmic thresholds for the forcing tail

#### Statement, notation and spaces

Let R>=1, A>0, tau>0 and 0<=beta<=1 be finite. On R^2 put

    omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10), omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    w=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10), Q=(1+tau log(1-Delta))^beta,
    M_A(f)^2=||omega2 D^2 Qf||_2^2
             +A^2||omega1 DQf||_2^2+A^2 2^31||wf||_(Hdot^-1)^2.

The space is the compact smooth S1 core completion in this norm, realized as tempered distributions. S1 means real, even in x and odd in y. Let Theta be a nonzero smooth real function on the circle with the corresponding S1 symmetries. Fix real q,a. Let f be any smooth S1 function which agrees, for r>=e^2, with

    f(r,theta)=r^q (log r)^(-a) Theta(theta).                 (1)

**Theorem.** The following are exact membership criteria:

* If q<1/5, then f belongs to M_A for every a.
* If q>1/5, then f does not belong to M_A for any a.
* If q=1/5, then f belongs to M_A if and only if a>1/2.

These criteria hold for every displayed beta and every finite choice of R,A,tau. The logarithmic Fourier surplus does not change this spatial tail threshold. The result concerns the explicit eventual tail (1); it does not classify arbitrary oscillating tails.

#### 1. A necessary first-derivative condition

The positive Bessel-mixture argument of P106 gives a bounded map

    Q^-1:L2(omega1^2 dX) -> L2(omega1^2 dX)                 (2)

for beta>0, and it is the identity for beta=0. In particular there is a finite constant C such that

    ||omega1 Dg||_2 <= C ||omega1 DQg||_2                   (3)

on the compact smooth core. Derivatives commute with Q and its inverse. If a core sequence converges in M_A, (3) makes its gradients Cauchy in the weighted L2 space. That limit is its distributional gradient, because the high completion is realized as distributions and weighted L2 convergence implies local distributional convergence. Thus every f in the completed space has finite ||omega1 Df||_2. This argument uses the actual completion, not an assumption that formal norm components already define it.

For (1), direct polar differentiation gives

    integral_0^(2pi) |Df(r,theta)|^2 dtheta
      =r^(2q-2)(log r)^(-2a)
        [ (q-a/log r)^2 ||Theta||_2^2 + ||Theta'||_2^2 ].     (4)

S1 parity excludes a nonzero constant Theta, so ||Theta'||_2>0. The bracket in (4) is therefore bounded below by a positive constant for all r>=e^2 and bounded above by a finite constant for sufficiently large r. Also omega1^2 is comparable to r^(-2/5) there. Hence the first-derivative energy on the exterior is finite exactly when

    integral_(e^2)^infinity r^(2q-7/5)(log r)^(-2a) dr       (5)

is finite. If q>1/5 it diverges, regardless of a. At q=1/5 the substitution s=log r makes (5) equal to the integral of s^(-2a) on [2,infinity), which is finite exactly when a>1/2. Equations (3)-(5) prove every nonmembership assertion.

#### 2. Sufficiency below the power threshold

If q<1/5, choose q' strictly between q and 1/5. For every fixed derivative order m, ordinary differentiation of (1) gives

    |D^m f(X)| <= C_m r^(q-m)(log r)^(-a), r>=e^2,

after increasing C_m to bound the finitely many inverse logarithmic factors. A power r^(q'-q) dominates any fixed logarithmic power. Therefore the hypothesis of P106 holds with q' through order 4. That theorem proves membership in the actual compact-core completion.

#### 3. Sufficiency at the critical power

Suppose q=1/5 and a>1/2. The same derivative calculation through order 4 gives the displayed bound with q=1/5. Both principal weighted derivative terms omega1 Df and omega2 D^2f have magnitude at most

    C r^(-1)(log r)^(-a).

Their radial squared integrals are bounded by a constant times (5), which is now finite. The extra two derivatives used in the estimate

    ||omega Qg||_2 <= C_(omega,tau,beta)
                         (||omega g||_2+||omega Delta g||_2)

from P106 decay two additional powers and are also integrable. The native low component satisfies ||wf||_(Hdot^-1)<=||r wf||_2 by centrally odd angular Hardy. Since R is finite, r wf has the same critical upper bound C r^(-1)(log r)^(-a). Thus all required bounds are finite.

To prove completion membership, set f_T=chi(r/T)f for a fixed smooth radial cutoff chi equal to 1 on [0,1] and 0 on [2,infinity). When a derivative hits chi(r/T), its factor T^(-l), on T<=r<=2T, combines with D^(m-l)f to give exactly the same r^(q-m)(log r)^(-a) bound. The tails of the integrable majorants tend to zero. The weighted logarithmic estimate and angular Hardy therefore show M_A(f-f_T)->0. Every f_T is in the compact smooth S1 core. This proves sufficiency in the actual completion.

#### Dependencies and consequences

The only analytic input is the weighted positive-mixture and logarithmic-multiplier proof P106, including its cutoff argument and angular Hardy estimate. Formula (4) and the integral test are exact. No numerical quadrature or remote computation is used.

The original state 131 residual has q=427123167131315/4076476460239181<1/5 and hence lies on the admissible side of this threshold. The profile itself has exponent gamma=2251799813685248/4076476460239181>1/5, so a nonzero pure leading profile direction with that exponent is outside the correction space. The same holds for its logarithmic exponent-variation direction. This agrees with, and does not enlarge, the fixed leading-profile scope of P89. A rigorous implication for a function only asymptotic to (1) requires the corresponding derivative asymptotics; the theorem above avoids that extra unstated assumption.

## P111. Direct exclusion radii in the native logarithmic norm

### P111.1. Direct exclusion radii in the native logarithmic norm

The signed annular tests already proved for the unregularized energy give stronger native-norm distances than the conversion through a logarithmic low component. This is a direct corollary of the positive inverse kernel and part P73. It requires no transport inverse, origin trace, or reference derivative contract.

#### 1. Exact statement

Write r=|X| on R^2. Fix R>=2^31, A>=2048, 0<tau<=2^-20 and 0<=beta<=1. Define

    omega1=(1+r^2)^(-1/10), omega2=(1+4r^2)^(2/5),
    w_R=(1+r^2/R^2)^(-11/10),
    Pj(f)=||omega_j D^j f||_2, j=1,2,
    L_R(f)=||w_R f||_(Hdot^-1),
    Q=(1+tau log(1-Delta))^beta,
    E_R(f)^2=P2(f)^2+2^22 P1(f)^2+2^53 L_R(f)^2,
    Mstar(f)^2=P2(Qf)^2+A^2 P1(Qf)^2+A^2 2^31 L_R(f)^2.

The derivatives are full ordered Cartesian tensors with the Euclidean norm. Both spaces are the completions of real compact smooth functions even in x and odd in y, with their canonical tempered-distribution realizations. The homogeneous negative norm is the Fourier norm, equivalently duality against centrally odd homogeneous H^1 tests. The velocity is U=(-R1 R2,R1^2), with Rj=partial_j(-Delta)^(-1/2); no harmonic field is added.

**Theorem.** The identity on the common compact core extends to a continuous injective map from the Mstar completion into the E_R completion, and

    E_R(h)<=(1+2 pi tau beta)Mstar(h)<=(1+7tau)Mstar(h).       (1)

Let bar_rho be any of the exact references state 131, nb_Mpen2_exact, or nb_d2_exact defined and source-bound in part P73. An exact profile means a density rho=bar_rho+h with the canonical velocity bar_u+U[h], which solves

    c' X.D rho+div(U[rho]rho)-rho=0

in distributions for some real c'. There is no assumption on the corrected origin slope. No such profile has

    Mstar(h)<=2^57/(1+7tau)    for state 131,                  (2)
    Mstar(h)<=2^21/(1+7tau)    for either refit.              (3)

The uniform rational radii 2^77/(2^20+7) and 2^41/(2^20+7), respectively, are therefore excluded as closed balls. The simpler radii 2^56 and 2^20 are also excluded. These conclusions apply to arbitrary corrections in the completed infinite-dimensional space, including corrections outside all finite generator families.

For the parameterized theorem P89, which additionally requires 1/2<beta<=1 and has r0=2^-20 tau^beta sqrt(2beta-1), the simpler excluded radii are strictly larger than 2^86 r0 for the original reference and 2^50 r0 for either refit. This comparison is conditional only on using that theorem's parameters; the distance theorem itself is independent of its coefficient hypotheses.

#### 2. Positive inverse kernel and weighted estimate

For beta>0 let S have gamma distribution of shape beta and unit rate. Conditionally on S=s, let T have gamma distribution of shape tau s and unit rate. Mix the two-dimensional heat kernels

    p_t(Z)=(4 pi t)^(-1) exp(-|Z|^2/(4t))

over T. Its Fourier transform is

    E exp(-T|xi|^2)
      =E(1+|xi|^2)^(-tau S)
      =(1+tau log(1+|xi|^2))^(-beta).

Thus this nonnegative probability kernel is B=Q^-1. It is rotation invariant and preserves the required parities. Its first spatial moment is

    int |Z|B(Z)dZ=sqrt(pi) E sqrt(T).

For every a>0, the beta integral gives

    B(a,1/2)=int_0^1 t^(a-1)(1-t)^(-1/2)dt>=1/a,
    Gamma(a+1/2)/Gamma(a)<=sqrt(pi) a.

Consequently E(sqrt(T)|S=s)<=sqrt(pi) tau s, and

    int |Z|B(Z)dZ<=pi tau E S=pi tau beta.                    (4)

The kernel also has moments of every finite order: the gamma moments of T are bounded by polynomials in tau S for integer orders, and the remaining moments follow by interpolation. This justifies the convolution on all the polynomially weighted spaces used here. For beta=0, B is the point mass at zero and (4) holds with both sides zero.

The triangle inequality for brackets gives, with Z=X-Y,

    <Y>/<X><=1+|Z|,
    <2X>/<2Y><=1+2|Z|.

Taking powers 1/5 and 4/5, respectively, yields

    omega_j(X)/omega_j(Y)<=1+2|X-Y|, j=1,2.                  (5)

If H=Qh, then D^j h=B*(D^j H). Minkowski's integral inequality, followed by translation invariance of unweighted L^2 and (4),(5), implies

    Pj(h)<=int B(Z)(1+2|Z|)dZ Pj(H)
           <=(1+2 pi tau beta)Pj(Qh).                       (6)

This proof works for tensor-valued derivatives without a component factor. It is a physical-space weighted convolution estimate, not a deduction from the pointwise Fourier multiplier size. Since beta<=1 and 2pi<7, (6) is bounded by 1+7tau.

#### 3. The unchanged low component and completion

Put kappa=1+2pi tau beta>=1. The native low quantity is the same L_R(h) on both sides. Since A^2>=2^22 and A^2 2^31>=2^53, (6) gives

    E_R(h)^2
      <=kappa^2[P2(Qh)^2+2^22P1(Qh)^2]+2^53L_R(h)^2
      <=kappa^2 Mstar(h)^2.

There is no low-weight commutator in this argument, and no factor growing with R or tau^-beta. The inequality first holds on the common compact core and extends by completion. The canonical distributions agree because both realizations are continuous extensions of the same compact densities (parts P70 and P83, and the norm equivalence for arbitrary finite A in P89). The E_R realization is faithful. Hence this extension is injective and identifies the same density h and canonical velocity U[h]. The E_R growth and local continuity statements of 73 apply to the resulting functions.

#### 4. Signed tests and exclusion

Part P73 proves, including its beta=0 case E_R, that no exact profile in the above affine spaces has E_R(h)<=2^57 for state 131 or E_R(h)<=2^21 for either exact refit. Its proof first obtains h,U[h]=O(max(1,r)^(1/5)), which fixes any prospective exponent c' to the common reference exponent c by the nonzero leading r^(1/c) tail. It then applies source-bound signed annular tests to the weak difference equation. All its hypotheses hold after the embedding in section 3. In particular products are locally integrable and the velocity has the same canonical normalization. The strict signed-test comparisons exclude closed balls, so (1) proves (2),(3), including equality at their boundaries.

Because tau<=2^-20, 1+7tau<2 and

    2^57/(1+7tau)>=2^77/(2^20+7)>2^56,
    2^21/(1+7tau)>=2^41/(2^20+7)>2^20.

For 1/2<beta<=1 and 0<tau<=2^-20, tau^beta<tau^(1/2)<=2^-10 and sqrt(2beta-1)<=1. Thus r0<2^-30. The two simpler radii exceed 2^86 r0 and 2^50 r0 as stated.

#### 5. Dependencies and scope

The reference identities, canonical leading tails, and strict signed-test comparisons are those of P73, whose primary directed and independent rational audits remain the numerical inputs. The positive inverse representation is also proved in P83 and P84. The present proof gives its first-moment estimate explicitly and uses only the beta=0 exclusion from 73. Part P89 supplies the formula for r0 solely for the final ratio comparison.

The result strengthens the distance estimates in P90 without changing any residual floor or sufficient smallness threshold. It is not global nonexistence, a residual upper bound, a new inverse, or a proof of existence. In particular the much larger numerical radii are radii in the specified strongly weighted norm, not in an unweighted pointwise metric.
